title: From Obligation to Specification: A Survey on Validating EU AI Act Requirements in RE
summary: With the EU AI Act entering into force, organizations developing or operating AI systems face new obligations on transparency, risk management, and traceability. For Requirements Engineering (RE), these obligations must be translated into testable, auditable requirements and verifiable evidence. However, many organizations currently lack systematic processes to achieve this. We hypothesize that LLM-based agentic validation tools can support this translation, thereby helping to close this gap. We present a mixed-method exploratory study with expert interviews (N=10) and an online survey (N=15) to assess organizational preparedness for EU AI Act-oriented RE and perceptions of LLM-based, agentic closed-loop validation tools, with participants spanning RE, data science, development, and compliance roles. Our results show that, although the EU AI Act is viewed as highly relevant, structured mechanisms to capture regulatory obligations, propagate updates into projects, and maintain lifecycle-wide traceability and evidence are often missing. Participants see LLM-based tools as promising for mapping obligations to requirements, assessing coverage, and organizing evidence, but express strong concerns about full automation and stress the need for safeguards. Based on these findings, we outline minimum requirements for an EU AI Act-ready closed-loop approach.

AI.tldr: This exploratory mixed-method study investigates organizational readiness for EU AI Act compliance in Requirements Engineering (RE) and examines perceptions of LLM-based agentic validation tools. Through expert interviews (N=10) and a survey (N=15), findings reveal significant gaps in structured regulatory translation, traceability, and evidence management, alongside cautious optimism for LLM-based tool support with necessary human safeguards.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act imposes new transparency, risk management, and traceability obligations on AI system developers and operators. These must be translated into testable, auditable RE requirements and verifiable evidence, yet many organizations lack systematic processes to do so. The authors hypothesize that LLM-based agentic validation tools can help bridge this gap.
AI.method: A mixed-method exploratory study combining semi-structured expert interviews (N=10) and an online survey (N=15). Participants span roles in requirements engineering, data science, development, and compliance, providing cross-functional perspectives on organizational preparedness and perceptions of LLM-based agentic closed-loop validation tools.
AI.result: The EU AI Act is perceived as highly relevant, but structured mechanisms for capturing regulatory obligations, propagating updates into projects, and maintaining lifecycle-wide traceability and evidence are largely absent. Participants view LLM-based tools as promising for obligation-to-requirement mapping, coverage assessment, and evidence organization, yet express strong concerns about full automation and emphasize the necessity of safeguards.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear gap between regulatory demands and current RE practices. Based on empirical findings, the authors outline minimum requirements for an EU AI Act-ready closed-loop approach that leverages LLM-based tooling while preserving human oversight and accountability.

title: Tool-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Repair for Securing LLM-Generated C Code
summary:
Large language models can generate C code from natural-language descriptions, but resulting programs often contain security vulnerabilities and compilation errors, posing risks for embedded and resource-constrained systems. This work investigates how feedback and retrieval improve reliability of LLM-generated C code. We present an analysis-and-repair workflow that combines compilation diagnostics, CodeQL static analysis, and KLEE symbolic execution with retrieval of prior repair patterns for iterative refinement.
  Evaluated on 5,000 C programming tasks exercising embedded relevant vulnerabilities, baseline models show substantial reliability gaps, with compilation failure rates up to 46% and security defect rates up to 49%. Our approach improves both metrics. For CodeLlama 7B, security defect rates decrease from 49% to 19% and total CodeQL errors drop from 15,088 to 2,463 (83.7%). For DeepSeek Coder 1.3B, compilation failures are reduced from 42% to 22% and security defects from 35% to 15%. These results show that integrating lightweight analysis tools can improve the safety of LLM-generated code for embedded development.

AI.tldr: LLMs generate buggy, vulnerable C code; an iterative analysis-and-repair workflow combining compilation diagnostics, CodeQL static analysis, and KLEE symbolic execution with retrieval of prior repair patterns substantially reduces compilation failures (up to 46%→22%) and security defects (up to 49%→19%) across multiple models.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated C code for embedded/resource-constrained systems suffers from high rates of security vulnerabilities and compilation errors. Existing code generation approaches lack systematic feedback mechanisms to detect and repair these defects, motivating a workflow that integrates lightweight program analysis to improve reliability.
AI.method: An analysis-and-repair workflow that iteratively refines LLM-generated C code through three complementary feedback channels: (1) compiler diagnostics to catch compilation errors, (2) CodeQL static analysis to identify security vulnerabilities, and (3) KLEE symbolic execution for deeper semantic bug detection. The system retrieves prior repair patterns to guide iterative code refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5,000 C programming tasks. For CodeLlama 7B: security defects dropped from 49% to 19%, total CodeQL errors from 15,088 to 2,463 (83.7% reduction). For DeepSeek Coder 1.3B: compilation failures reduced from 42% to 22%, security defects from 35% to 15%. Baseline compilation failure rates reached 46% and security defect rates up to 49% across models.
AI.conclusion: Integrating lightweight, off-the-shelf analysis tools (compilers, static analyzers, symbolic executors) with retrieval-augmented repair patterns significantly improves the safety and correctness of LLM-generated C code, making it more viable for security-sensitive embedded development contexts.

title: Vibe Coding in Software Development: A Multivocal Literature Review
summary: Vibe coding is a software development practice in which developers state intent in natural language and large language models generate code. It is often framed as one-shot prompting, but the evidence describes an intent-driven, iterative workflow whose outcomes depend on how generated code is evaluated and governed. Knowledge of how vibe coding is defined, practiced, and governed is scattered across academic and practitioner sources, and, to our knowledge, existing reviews have not yet integrated both evidence streams. We conducted a multivocal literature review of peer-reviewed and grey literature following established guidelines. Searches spanned 2022 to October 2025. After screening, credibility assessment, and snowballing, 47 sources were retained (28 peer-reviewed and 19 grey) and analyzed through descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis across eight research questions. Vibe coding is consistently described as an iterative generation-evaluation-revision loop rather than a one-shot activity, and developer work shifts from writing code towards specification, supervision, and validation. Short-term productivity and time-to-prototype gains are reported in 21 of 47 sources (45%), while evidence on maintainability, long-term quality, and safeguard effectiveness remains limited. Evidence is strongest for prototyping and user-interface work and weakest for production, data-intensive, and safety-critical use, and tool visibility does not imply effectiveness. This is one of the first reviews to integrate peer-reviewed and grey literature on vibe coding under a single documented protocol. Future work should evaluate safeguard effectiveness, study session-level dynamics and long-term maintainability, and test vibe coding in production, data-intensive, and safety-critical settings.

AI.tldr: Vibe coding is an iterative, intent-driven software development practice where developers use natural language to guide LLMs in generating code. This multivocal literature review (47 sources: 28 peer-reviewed, 19 grey) synthesizes definitions, practices, and governance. Findings show it shifts developer work from writing code to specification and validation, with short-term productivity gains reported in 45% of sources but limited evidence on long-term maintainability and safety. Evidence is strongest for prototyping/UI, weakest for production and safety-critical settings.
AI.motivation: Knowledge of how vibe coding is defined, practiced, and governed is scattered across peer-reviewed and grey literature, with no existing review integrating both evidence streams under a single protocol. A systematic synthesis is needed to clarify its nature, benefits, risks, and evidence gaps.
AI.method: The authors conducted a multivocal literature review (MLR) following established guidelines, covering 2022–October 2025. After screening, credibility assessment, and snowballing, 47 sources (28 peer-reviewed, 19 grey) were retained and analyzed through descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis across eight research questions.
AI.result: Vibe coding is consistently characterized as an iterative generation–evaluation–revision loop, not one-shot prompting. Developer roles shift toward specification, supervision, and validation. Short-term productivity and time-to-prototype gains appear in 21/47 sources (45%), but evidence on maintainability, long-term quality, and safeguard effectiveness is limited. Evidence is strongest for prototyping and UI work and weakest for production, data-intensive, and safety-critical contexts. Tool visibility does not imply effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: This is among the first reviews to integrate peer-reviewed and grey literature on vibe coding under a documented protocol. Future work should evaluate safeguard effectiveness, study session-level dynamics and long-term maintainability, and test vibe coding in production, data-intensive, and safety-critical settings.

title: Cross-Model LLM Code Review: Should you use Claude to review Codex or vice versa?
comment: This paper had been accepted by Agentic SE @ KDD'26
summary: Developers increasingly use two coding agents together: one writes a draft, and the other reviews it. However, it is not clear whether the pairing is worth its cost and time, or whether the order of the pairing matters. We run a controlled experiment on 116 recent hard and medium lcb tasks with Claude and Codex across six conditions to approximate a software practitioner's workflow: both solo baselines, both cross-model orderings, and both same-model orderings. The reviewer sees the problem and the writer's draft but cannot execute tests, which approximates a code review step. Claude review raises Codex drafts from 71.6% to 89.7% ($p_{BH}=.001$); Codex self review raises them to 84.5% ($p_{BH}=.022$). The reverse direction does not pay off: Codex reviewing Claude drafts drops the pass rate from 91.4% to 82.8% ($p_{BH}=.046$), and Claude self review leaves the 91.4% baseline unchanged. Our evaluation indicates that the useful pairing is asymmetric: use Claude to review Codex, not the other way around.

AI.tldr: An experiment on 116 coding tasks finds that pairing coding agents as writer-reviewer is only beneficial asymmetrically: Claude reviewing Codex significantly improves pass rates (71.6% → 89.7%), but Codex reviewing Claude is harmful (91.4% → 82.8%). Self-review shows mixed results.
AI.motivation: Developers increasingly pair two coding agents (writer + reviewer), but it is unclear whether this dual-agent workflow is worth the additional cost and time, and whether the ordering of agents matters.
AI.method: Controlled experiment with 116 recent hard and medium LiveCodeBench (LCB) tasks, using Claude and Codex across six conditions: both solo baselines, both cross-model orderings, and both same-model orderings. The reviewer sees the problem and the writer's draft but cannot execute tests, approximating a real-world code review step. Statistical significance assessed with Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-values.
AI.result: Claude reviewing Codex: 71.6% → 89.7% (p_BH = .001). Codex self-review: 71.6% → 84.5% (p_BH = .022). Codex reviewing Claude: 91.4% → 82.8% (p_BH = .046). Claude self-review: 91.4% baseline unchanged. The beneficial pairing is strictly asymmetric.
AI.conclusion: The useful pairing is asymmetric: use Claude to review Codex drafts, not the reverse. Cross-model review can yield substantial gains, but the wrong direction actively harms performance, suggesting practitioners should carefully choose the reviewer role.

title: SIREN (Luring LLMs onto the Rocks): PAIR-Driven Preference Manipulation in Web-RAG Recommenders
summary: This paper investigates the adversarial manipulation of the ranked recommendations produced by web-augmented large language models (LLMs). When an LLM answers a recommendation query by retrieving and reading live webpages, it acts as a recommender, and each retrieved page becomes a potential attack surface. Prior work has examined fabricated products, retrieval poisoning, and rank promotion. However, these studies do not compare how different edits to an already retrieved page change the model's final ranking while the surrounding source set remains unchanged. To address this gap, we propose SIREN, an automated attacker--judge method that adapts the PAIR jailbreaking loop to competitive rank manipulation, with the goal of moving a chosen entity to rank~1 in an LLM-generated recommendation. SIREN retrieves and captures webpages using Anthropic's web tools, then iteratively edits a retrieved source using an interpretable taxonomy of 23 content-poisoning techniques. The custom-RAG replay platform keeps the same sources in the same order, so changes in the model's ranking can be linked to changes in the supplied content rather than to differences in retrieval. Across two production Claude models, SIREN reaches rank~1 in 62 of 124 technique trials nested within eight query--model contexts. The payloads that reached rank~1 were then tested in fresh sessions, where they reproduced the result with a mean success rate of 0.805. Across the evaluated settings, declarative ranking claims and seeded lists were generally more effective than directive-form injections, although the strength of this difference depended on the target model. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first controlled studies of competitive rank manipulation in production LLMs where the supplied source context is kept fixed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SIREN, an automated method for manipulating LLM-generated ranked recommendations by poisoning retrieved web content. Using 23 interpretable content-poisoning techniques, SIREN achieved rank-1 placement in 62 of 124 trials across two Claude models, with an 80.5% reproduction rate. Declarative ranking claims and seeded lists proved more effective than directive-form injections.
AI.motivation: Prior work on adversarial manipulation of LLM recommendations has examined fabricated products, retrieval poisoning, and rank promotion, but no study has systematically compared how different edits to an already-retrieved page affect the model's final ranking while holding the surrounding source set constant. This gap prevents isolating content-level effects from retrieval-level effects.
AI.method: The authors propose SIREN, which adapts the PAIR jailbreaking loop for competitive rank manipulation. It retrieves and captures webpages using Anthropic's web tools, then iteratively edits a retrieved source using a taxonomy of 23 content-poisoning techniques. A custom-RAG replay platform ensures identical sources in identical order across trials, attributing ranking changes solely to content edits. The method is tested across two production Claude models in eight query-model contexts.
AI.result: SIREN achieved rank-1 placement in 62 of 124 technique trials. Rank-1 payloads reproduced in fresh sessions with a mean success rate of 0.805. Declarative ranking claims and seeded lists were generally more effective than directive-form injections, though the effect magnitude varied by target model.
AI.conclusion: This is among the first controlled studies of competitive rank manipulation in production LLMs with fixed source context. The findings demonstrate that content-level poisoning alone can reliably manipulate LLM recommendation rankings, with declarative and list-based techniques being particularly potent attack vectors.

title: Reliability-Contagion Feasibility in LLM Multi-Agent Networks
summary: Communication allows large language model agents to pool evidence, but it also creates paths along which an erroneous claim can spread. We formulate a correction-aware network model that tracks susceptible, exposed, infectious, and corrected agents and derive its early-invasion condition for heterogeneous communication networks. We then couple this propagation model to an analytic majority-vote benchmark in which a clean-task reliability target imposes a minimum connectivity requirement. Under fixed exposure per communication edge, reliability and error control impose opposing graph constraints. We characterize when their intersection is empty and when it contains an intermediate connectivity range, and identify regular graphs that attain the smallest invasion factor within the reliable graph class when such graphs exist. Under a fixed sender budget, the homogeneous first-order threshold is independent of network density, showing that the communication-budget convention determines whether added edges increase early propagation risk. Finite-network simulations on 21,000 trajectories illustrate these directional predictions. A controlled grok-4.3 experiment then evaluates three six-node topologies on 36 new closed-world tasks, with a balanced 12-task subset continued to full cascades. Mean first-generation offspring increased from 0.667 to 1.333 and 1.667 as degree increased from 2 to 4 and 5, while the adoption fraction among exposed neighbours remained 0.333. Mean non-seed erroneous adoption in the full-cascade subset was 0.200, 0.333, and 0.333. Together, these results provide a tractable basis for selecting connectivity under explicit reliability and propagation constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a mathematical framework coupling epidemic-style correction-aware propagation models with majority-vote reliability requirements to analyze how communication network structure creates trade-offs between task accuracy and error spread in LLM agent systems. Theoretical analysis identifies conditions under which reliability and error control constraints can be simultaneously satisfied, while simulations and a controlled grok-4.3 experiment confirm that higher-degree networks increase error propagation.
AI.motivation: LLM agents improve via communication but risk propagating erroneous claims through the same channels. The paper aims to formally characterize the tension between connectivity (needed for reliable collective decision-making) and error amplification, providing principled guidance for network design under explicit reliability and propagation constraints.
AI.method: The authors (1) formulate a correction-aware SEIC (Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Corrected) compartmental model on heterogeneous networks and derive its early-invasion threshold; (2) couple this to an analytic majority-vote benchmark where reliability targets impose minimum connectivity; (3) analyze the intersection of reliability and error-control constraints mathematically; (4) run 21,000 finite-network simulations; and (5) conduct a controlled experiment using grok-4.3 on 36 closed-world tasks across three six-node topologies of varying degree (d=2,4,5).
AI.result: Under fixed exposure per edge, reliability and error control impose opposing graph constraints whose intersection may be empty or contain an intermediate connectivity range. Regular graphs minimize the invasion factor when solutions exist. Under fixed sender budget, the homogeneous first-order threshold is density-independent. Simulations confirm directional predictions. The grok-4.3 experiment shows mean first-generation offspring rises from 0.667→1.333→1.667 as degree increases (2→4→5), while adoption fraction remains constant at 0.333. Non-seed erroneous adoption in full cascades: 0.200, 0.333, 0.333.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a tractable basis for selecting network connectivity under simultaneous reliability and propagation constraints. Intermediate connectivity ranges can satisfy both objectives, and regular graphs are optimal within the reliable class. The fixed-sender-budget regime yields density-independent thresholds, meaning the communication-budget convention critically determines whether adding edges increases early propagation risk.

title: Control panels to clarify user intent with Large Language Models
summary: Typical user interfaces for Large Language Models present a blank prompt window that invites a natural language query by users, but offers little guidance. This paper proposes a visual control panel interface that would provide more cues to the semantics of prompt formation, enabling users to more easily express their intent. By emphasizing recognition over recall, control panels help users formulate more effective prompts that match their intent.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes replacing blank LLM prompt interfaces with visual control panels that guide users in constructing effective prompts through recognition-based interaction rather than recall.
AI.motivation: Current LLM user interfaces offer a blank prompt window with minimal guidance, forcing users to rely on recall to formulate effective natural language queries. This creates a barrier for users who struggle to express their intent precisely, leading to suboptimal prompt construction and interaction outcomes.
AI.method: The authors propose a visual control panel interface for LLMs that provides structured visual cues, widgets, and affordances (e.g., sliders, toggles, dropdowns) that map to semantic dimensions of prompt formation. This shifts the interaction paradigm from pure recall (typing prompts from memory) to recognition (identifying and selecting desired options from presented visual elements), thereby scaffolding the prompt construction process.
AI.result: The paper argues that control panel interfaces enable users to more easily and accurately express their intent when interacting with LLMs, resulting in more effective prompts that better align with user goals.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from blank prompt interfaces to recognition-based visual control panels can significantly improve the usability of LLM systems by making prompt formation more guided and accessible, ultimately helping users bridge the gap between their intent and the prompts they construct.

title: CARE: Pre-Execution Command Verification for Shell-Executing LLM Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for coding and terminal automation, making shell-command dispatch a high-stakes runtime control point. We study command-level pre-execution mediation for individual shell commands produced by LLM agents under bounded path context. Existing safeguards remain limited: generic guardrails do not model shell structure in sufficient detail, always-on LLM judges are relatively costly and variable, and shell parsers do not directly prevent harmful execution. We present CARE (Canonicalization, Attribution, and Resolution Engine), a shell-specific, static-first verifier for individual shell commands before execution. CARE canonicalizes generated commands into stable verification targets, derives deterministic evidence over syntax, command semantics, path context, and provenance-backed risk patterns, and escalates only underdetermined cases to an LLM judge. This design keeps the common case fast, reproducible, and auditable while reserving neural adjudication for borderline commands. On the balanced main split, CARE reaches 85.64% F1 with a 0.91% false-positive rate at 2.32 ms mean latency. When deployed in its static enforcement profile, CARE retains 84.99% F1 at 0.34 ms and reduces realised harm on RedCode-gen to 37.33%. Across external-generalization tests and controlled Docker-sandbox execution, these profiles expose a practical trade-off between benign recovery, false-positive burden, latency, and harm reduction. Overall, command-level shell mediation can reduce dispatch-boundary risk for LLM agents while preserving most benign workflows.

AI.tldr: CARE is a shell-specific, static-first verifier that mediates LLM-generated shell commands before execution, using canonicalization and deterministic evidence with escalation to an LLM judge only for ambiguous cases, achieving 85.64% F1 at 2.32ms latency with low false-positive rates.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for coding and terminal automation, making shell-command dispatch a critical security control point. Existing safeguards are inadequate: generic guardrails lack shell-specific structure, always-on LLM judges are costly and variable, and shell parsers don't actively prevent harmful execution. A fast, reliable, shell-aware mediation layer is needed.
AI.method: CARE employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) Canonicalization — normalizes generated shell commands into stable verification targets; (2) Attribution — derives deterministic evidence from syntax, command semantics, path context, and provenance-backed risk patterns; (3) Resolution Engine — statically classifies commands and escalates only underdetermined borderline cases to an LLM judge, keeping the common case fast and auditable.
AI.result: On the balanced main split, CARE achieves 85.64% F1 with 0.91% false-positive rate at 2.32ms mean latency. In static-only enforcement, it retains 84.99% F1 at 0.34ms and reduces realized harm on RedCode-gen to 37.33%. External generalization and Docker-sandbox tests confirm a practical trade-off between benign recovery, false-positive burden, latency, and harm reduction.
AI.conclusion: Command-level pre-execution shell mediation is a viable strategy for reducing dispatch-boundary risk in LLM agents. CARE's static-first design balances speed, reproducibility, and safety, preserving most benign workflows while effectively mitigating harmful command execution.

title: Adversarial Style Optimization: Enhancing VLM Jailbreaks by GRPO-based Stylistic Triggers Optimization
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance, but their safety alignment remains vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing content-based jailbreaks are often inconsistent and show unsatisfying performance against the rapidly evolving MLLMs, failing to exploit non-content-based vulnerabilities. Unlike previous research, we empirically find that MLLMs exhibit a Stylistic Inconsistency between their comprehension ability and safety ability: MLLMs can robustly understand content regardless of visual style, yet their defense mechanisms can be easily bypassed by specific stylistic triggers. Based on this finding, we propose Adversarial Style Optimization (ASO), a plug-and-play enhancement module to amplify existing visual jailbreaks. ASO fine-tunes an image-editing model to superimpose an optimized stylistic modification onto a given adversarial image, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) agent guided by a Structurally-Tiered Reward Function that combines a logit-based signal for detecting explicit refusals with a high-fidelity semantic evaluation from a powerful judge model. Extensive experiments show that ASO significantly enhances the ASR of SOTA attacks, demonstrating that stylistic biases are a scalable vector for red-teaming MLLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/ASO.

AI.tldr: MLLMs have a stylistic inconsistency where comprehension is robust across visual styles, but safety alignment can be bypassed by specific stylistic triggers. The authors propose ASO, a method that fine-tunes an image-editing model with GRPO to amplify jailbreaks via optimized stylistic modifications, significantly boosting attack success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing content-based jailbreak attacks against MLLMs are inconsistent and fail to exploit non-content vulnerabilities. The authors empirically discover a "Stylistic Inconsistency" — MLLMs understand content robustly regardless of visual style, yet their safety defenses are easily circumvented by specific stylistic triggers. This gap motivates a new attack vector.
AI.method: Adversarial Style Optimization (ASO): a plug-and-play module that fine-tunes an image-editing model to superimpose optimized stylistic modifications onto adversarial images. It uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) guided by a Structurally-Tiered Reward Function that combines (1) a logit-based signal for detecting explicit refusals and (2) high-fidelity semantic evaluation from a powerful judge model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that ASO significantly enhances the Attack Success Rate (ASR) of state-of-the-art visual jailbreak attacks, confirming that stylistic biases are a scalable vector for red-teaming MLLMs.
AI.conclusion: Stylistic inconsistency in MLLMs represents a critical and scalable vulnerability. ASO provides an effective, plug-and-play method to amplify existing jailbreak attacks via adversarial style optimization, highlighting the need for style-robust safety alignment in future MLLM development.

title: Cloud-Native Evaluation-as-a-Service: A Microservices Architecture for Scalable AI Monitoring with Conformal Guarantees
summary: We present EaaS, a cloud-native reference architecture that operationalizes AI evaluation methods as six stateless Kubernetes microservices: conformal prediction with finite-sample-corrected Adaptive Prediction Sets, calibration assessment, drift detection via RFF-approximated Maximum Mean Discrepancy, fairness monitoring with bootstrap confidence intervals, a DAG-based pipeline orchestrator, and a result storage API. We validate four key methodological concerns. First, empirical coverage is consistent with the marginal conformal guarantee across K=50 random calibration/test splits, with mean coverage within 1.4 percentage points of the nominal target. Second, all four MMLU answer tokens appear in the top-20 logprobs with 0% imputation needed, and simulated imputation at 10% produces less than 1.5% coverage impact. Third, RFF-MMD achieves 100% detection power for mild and severe drift at the median heuristic bandwidth, with Type I error between 5-8.5%. Fourth, fairness monitoring on the UCI Adult Income dataset reveals significant demographic parity disparities by race (DP gap=0.33) with stable alerts across sequential batches. Conformal prediction and calibration services achieve sub-2ms p99 latency at batch size 100; RFF-MMD requires ~500ms suited for periodic batch monitoring. A comparison with four open-source tools suggests that, to the best of our knowledge, no current platform combines conformal-prediction-as-a-service, microservice decomposition, and DAG-based orchestration.

AI.tldr: EaaS is a cloud-native microservice architecture that operationalizes AI evaluation (conformal prediction, calibration, drift detection, fairness monitoring) as six Kubernetes services with DAG orchestration. Empirical validation shows strong coverage guarantees, 100% drift detection power, and sub-2ms latency for core services, filling a gap in combined conformal-prediction-as-a-service platforms.
AI.motivation: Existing AI evaluation tools lack an integrated, cloud-native platform that combines conformal prediction, calibration assessment, drift detection, and fairness monitoring under a unified microservice architecture with DAG-based orchestration. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a production-ready reference architecture.
AI.method: EaaS is implemented as six stateless Kubernetes microservices: (1) conformal prediction using Adaptive Prediction Sets with finite-sample correction, (2) calibration assessment, (3) drift detection via RFF-approximated Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), (4) fairness monitoring with bootstrap confidence intervals, (5) a DAG-based pipeline orchestrator, and (6) a result storage API. Validation uses K=50 random calibration/test splits, simulated logprob imputation, and the UCI Adult Income dataset for fairness.
AI.result: (1) Mean empirical coverage within 1.4pp of nominal target across 50 splits. (2) All four MMLU answer tokens appear in top-20 logprobs (0% imputation needed); simulated 10% imputation impacts coverage by <1.5%. (3) RFF-MMD achieves 100% detection power for mild/severe drift with Type I error of 5–8.5%. (4) Fairness monitoring reveals significant race-based demographic parity disparity (DP gap=0.33) with stable batch alerts. Conformal prediction and calibration achieve sub-2ms p99 latency (batch size 100); RFF-MMD takes ~500ms, suitable for periodic batch monitoring.
AI.conclusion: EaaS demonstrates that conformal prediction, calibration, drift detection, and fairness monitoring can be effectively deployed as cloud-native microservices with strong empirical performance and low latency. A comparison with four open-source tools confirms no existing platform offers the same combination of conformal-prediction-as-a-service, microservice decomposition, and DAG-based orchestration.

title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills
summary: Large language model agents increasingly solve complex tasks by constructing inference-time workflows that combine reasoning, tool use, and code execution. While such workflows enable flexible problem solving, the useful procedures discovered during execution are often transient: they help solve the current task but are not retained in a form that can systematically benefit future tasks. We present FlowEvo, a training-free framework that compiles successful traces into reusable skill records. Each record pairs a callable artifact with auxiliary structured guidance, and admission applies interface, replay, and safety checks where feasible. These skill records persist in a skill bank at inference time. FlowEvo is organized around three coupled mechanisms: (1)~workflow-to-skill compilation, which extracts reusable executable artifacts from successful traces; (2)~skill-to-workflow feedback, which retrieves accumulated skills to support future problem solving through either direct execution or structured context injection; and (3)~skill curation, which monitors downstream utility and suppresses skills that cause negative transfer. Through this workflow--skill--workflow feedback loop, FlowEvo enables agents to accumulate and refine task-solving capability over time without updating model parameters. Experiments on benchmarks spanning interactive environments (ALFWorld) and code/math generation (HumanEval, GSM8K) show that FlowEvo achieves the best accuracy-cost tradeoff among the evaluated baselines under our implementation settings. On ALFWorld, FlowEvo achieves an 82.8\% success rate, 23.6 percentage points above the strongest baseline, while its average token usage per episode is less than half that of the most efficient baseline. Controlled ablations confirm that each mechanism contributes to the overall result. The code is public at https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/FlowEvo.

AI.tldr: FlowEvo is a training-free framework that enables LLM agents to compile successful task-solving traces into reusable, curated skills stored in a skill bank, creating a feedback loop that improves performance over time without parameter updates.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often construct useful inference-time workflows (reasoning, tool use, code execution), but the procedural knowledge discovered is transient—it helps only the current task and is lost afterward, preventing systematic benefit to future tasks.
AI.method: FlowEvo introduces three coupled mechanisms: (1) workflow-to-skill compilation, extracting executable artifacts from successful traces with interface/replay/safety checks; (2) skill-to-workflow feedback, retrieving skills for direct execution or context injection; and (3) skill curation, monitoring downstream utility and pruning skills causing negative transfer. Skills persist in a runtime skill bank.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, FlowEvo achieves 82.8% success rate (23.6pp above the strongest baseline) with less than half the token usage of the most efficient baseline. It achieves the best accuracy-cost tradeoff across ALFWorld, HumanEval, and GSM8K benchmarks. Ablations validate each mechanism's contribution.
AI.conclusion: FlowEvo demonstrates that a workflow–skill–workflow feedback loop enables agents to accumulate and refine capabilities over time without fine-tuning, offering a practical path to continual improvement of LLM agents at inference time.

title: Pixels for Programs? A Cross-Provider Case Study of Input-Token Accounting for Source Code as Text and Images
summary: Long source-code contexts consume many text tokens, motivating the proposal to render code as images for vision-language models. Recent work asks whether models can still solve code tasks after this transformation. We examine a different systems question: how commercial APIs count the resulting requests. We present a reproducible measurement case study of provider-reported input tokens for raw source text and a compact rendered-image representation. The benchmark pairs requests across five programming languages, nine source lengths from 20 to 2,000 lines, and 15 available model aliases exposed by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google Vertex AI. These aliases collapse to approximately five distinct accounting signatures and are not independent model replications. Across 675 complete text/image pairs, aggregate image-to-text ratios are 0.135, 0.194, and 0.242, corresponding to reported input-token reductions of 86.5\%, 80.6\%, and 75.8\%, respectively. These totals conceal materially different break-even behavior: Anthropic and OpenAI images receive lower counts at every tested size, while Gemini images require 6.95 times as many tokens at 20 lines and cross below text only at 200 lines in the aggregate. A targeted audit also reproduces non-monotonic Gemini image accounting across a page boundary. This study measures black-box request accounting for one compact rendering pipeline. It does not measure semantic fidelity, task accuracy, latency, monetary cost, or coding-agent efficiency. We release the scripts, revision-pinned corpus specification, raw usage records, validators, and deterministic analysis needed to reproduce and extend the study.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a measurement study of how commercial LLM APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Vertex AI) count input tokens when source code is rendered as images instead of raw text, finding image-based representations yield 75-86% token reductions for most providers, though Gemini exhibits anomalous accounting behavior at small file sizes.
AI.motivation: Long source-code contexts consume many text tokens, motivating interest in rendering code as images for vision-language models. Rather than evaluating task accuracy, the authors investigate a practical systems question: how do commercial API providers actually count and bill for image-based code inputs compared to raw text?
AI.method: A reproducible measurement case study using benchmark requests across five programming languages, nine source lengths (20–2,000 lines), and 15 model aliases from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google Vertex AI. The study pairs identical code as raw text and as compact rendered images, then records provider-reported input token counts to compute image-to-text ratios and identify distinct accounting signatures.
AI.result: Across 675 text/image pairs, aggregate image-to-text ratios were 0.135 (Anthropic), 0.194 (OpenAI), and 0.242 (Google), corresponding to token reductions of 86.5%, 80.6%, and 75.8%. However, Gemini showed anomalous behavior: at 20 lines, images used 6.95× more tokens than text, only breaking even at ~200 lines. A targeted audit also reproduced non-monotonic Gemini image accounting across a page boundary. The 15 model aliases collapsed to approximately five distinct accounting signatures.
AI.conclusion: Rendering code as images can substantially reduce reported input token counts for Anthropic and OpenAI across all tested sizes, but Gemini's accounting model penalizes small images. The study measures only black-box request accounting, not task accuracy, latency, cost, or agent efficiency. All scripts and data are released for reproducibility.

title: LAMAR: An Open Language-Aware Multilingual Alignment Reranker
summary: In multilingual retrieval augmented generation, a retriever can retrieve relevant documents written in multiple languages, which are subsequently reranked before answer generation. However, it remains unclear whether existing multilingual rerankers consider document language when ordering semantically relevant candidates. Our analysis shows that these rerankers do not consistently prioritize documents written in the same language as the query when semantically equivalent documents are available across languages, even though document language can affect answer generation. We release LAMAR, a language aware multilingual cross encoder trained to account for both semantic relevance and language coherence. LAMAR first uses English anchored relevance distillation to establish consistent relevance scoring across multilingual inputs and then applies preference alignment for language coherence to encourage documents written in the same language as the query to receive higher rankings while retaining semantic relevance. In a controlled experiment designed to assess language coherence, LAMAR achieves the best performance overall and across all languages examined individually. LAMAR also remains competitive on established multilingual reranking benchmarks. In practical retrieval settings, LAMAR achieves the best results across all reported metrics when reranking candidates retrieved in the first stage. These results demonstrate that LAMAR accounts for language coherence while achieving strong performance on general multilingual reranking benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Existing multilingual rerankers fail to prioritize documents in the same language as the query, even when semantically equivalent. LAMAR addresses this via English-anchored relevance distillation and preference alignment for language coherence, achieving strong performance on both language coherence and standard multilingual reranking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In multilingual RAG systems, rerankers order retrieved documents before generation, but it is unclear whether they consider document language. Document language matters because it can affect downstream answer generation quality, yet current multilingual rerankers do not consistently prefer same-language documents when semantically equivalent cross-lingual options exist.
AI.method: LAMAR (Language Aware Multilingual cross encoder) uses two training stages: (1) English anchored relevance distillation — uses English as a pivot to establish consistent relevance scoring across multilingual inputs; (2) preference alignment for language coherence — encourages ranking same-language documents higher while preserving semantic relevance through preference-based optimization.
AI.result: In controlled language coherence experiments, LAMAR achieves the best overall and per-language performance. It remains competitive on established multilingual reranking benchmarks. In practical first-stage retrieval reranking, LAMAR achieves the best results across all reported metrics.
AI.conclusion: LAMAR successfully accounts for language coherence in multilingual reranking while maintaining strong semantic relevance performance, demonstrating that both objectives can be jointly optimized in a cross-encoder architecture.

title: When Language Models Meet NeuroGraphs: Exploring Enhanced Agentic LLM Framework Towards Brain Network Analysis
summary: Brain network analysis is crucial for understanding cognition and neurological disorders, yet existing deep learning methods mainly treat connectome analysis as a graph-to-logit classification problem, offering limited explanatory reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) provide a promising interface for knowledge-intensive scientific analysis, but directly applying general-purpose LLMs to brain networks remains challenging due to the structure-language gap, limited neuroscience grounding, and overconfident positive predictions. In this paper, we propose \textbf{BrainAgent}, an agentic LLM framework for knowledge-enhanced brain network analysis. BrainAgent reformulates connectome classification as an iterative process of topology-aware understanding, external retrieval, reasoning, and reflection. Specifically, it first converts raw brain networks into compact multi-level structural descriptions through brain-specific analysis tools, then retrieves relevant neuroscience knowledge and task-specific cases to ground the reasoning process, and finally generates structured predictions with reflective verification. Experiments on four public rs-fMRI datasets show that BrainAgent consistently improves different closed-source and open-source LLM backbones over direct prompting and standard reasoning baselines. Further ablation and interpretability analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of each component and show that BrainAgent produces more comprehensive, multi-level, and verifiable explanations.These results indicate that agentic LLMs provide a practical route toward interpretable and knowledge-grounded brain network analysis.

AI.tldr: BrainAgent is an agentic LLM framework that reformulates brain network classification as an iterative process of topology-aware understanding, external retrieval, reasoning, and reflection, achieving consistent improvements over direct prompting baselines on four rs-fMRI datasets while producing interpretable, knowledge-grounded explanations.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods for brain network analysis treat connectome analysis as a black-box graph-to-logit classification problem with limited explanatory reasoning. General-purpose LLMs cannot be directly applied due to the structure-language gap, limited neuroscience grounding, and overconfident positive predictions.
AI.method: BrainAgent converts raw brain networks into compact multi-level structural descriptions using brain-specific analysis tools, retrieves relevant neuroscience knowledge and task-specific cases for reasoning grounding, and generates structured predictions with reflective verification in an iterative agentic workflow.
AI.result: Experiments on four public rs-fMRI datasets show that BrainAgent consistently improves both closed-source and open-source LLM backbones over direct prompting and standard reasoning baselines. Ablation studies validate each component's contribution, and interpretability analyses demonstrate more comprehensive, multi-level, and verifiable explanations.
AI.conclusion: Agentic LLMs offer a practical route toward interpretable and knowledge-grounded brain network analysis, bridging the gap between complex connectome data and meaningful scientific reasoning.

title: Analyzing Middle School Students' Dialogue and Behaviors during Collaborative AI Chatbot Development Using Ordered Network Analysis
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) education has become a key component of K-12 curricula, activities such as designing and developing conversational agents are increasingly used as instructional practice. Prior work has primarily examined these activities by focusing on students' learning outcomes or the quality of final AI artifacts, offering limited insight into the collaborative processes through which learning unfolds during AI system development. Although the AIED community has a long history of studying collaborative learning in STEM and Computing education, the emergence of AI learning environments in which students build AI systems presents new opportunities to understand how collaboration unfolds in AI education contexts. Grounded in these foundational works, the current study examines collaborative interaction among middle school students engaged in the design and development of an AI chatbot. Using Ordered Network Analysis of students' dialogue and development actions, we characterize how collaboration is organized over time and how interaction patterns relate to chatbot quality and AI knowledge outcomes. Results reveal that higher-quality chatbots are associated with more integrated sequences linking explanation, testing, and refinement. Interaction patterns involving articulated reasoning and repeated testing and revision in response to chatbot output were also associated with stronger AI knowledge outcomes. These findings provide a process-oriented account of collaborative AI chatbot development and extend AIED research on collaborative learning processes to AI education contexts.

AI.tldr: This study uses Ordered Network Analysis to examine how middle school students collaborate when designing AI chatbots, finding that higher-quality chatbots and better AI knowledge outcomes are linked to integrated sequences of explanation, testing, and refinement during collaboration.
AI.motivation: Prior research on K-12 AI education has focused on learning outcomes or final artifact quality, neglecting the collaborative processes through which learning occurs during AI system development. The AIED community's rich history of studying collaborative learning in STEM/Computing education has yet to be extended to contexts where students actually build AI systems.
AI.method: Ordered Network Analysis (ONA) was applied to middle school students' dialogue and development actions during collaborative AI chatbot design and development. This method captures the temporal ordering and co-occurrence of collaborative processes, linking interaction patterns to two outcomes: chatbot quality and AI knowledge gains.
AI.result: Higher-quality chatbots were associated with more integrated sequences linking explanation, testing, and refinement. Stronger AI knowledge outcomes were associated with interaction patterns featuring articulated reasoning and repeated cycles of testing and revision in response to chatbot output.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer a process-oriented account of collaborative AI chatbot development, extending AIED research on collaborative learning processes into AI education contexts. The study demonstrates that integrated, iterative cycles of explanation, testing, and refinement are key collaborative mechanisms driving both product quality and learning.

title: StajChain: A Hyperledger Fabric-Based Multi-Party Internship Agreement System
summary: Many administrative processes, such as internship agreement processes, often rely on manual approval workflows and centralized record-keeping. This makes the process susceptible to delays and unauthorized modification while introducing limited traceability. This study presents StajChain, a permissioned blockchain-based multi-party internship management system developed using Hyperledger Fabric. The proposed system implements the complete internship agreement lifecycle through smart contracts and enforces role-based authorization using Hyperledger Fabric CA. The architecture consists of a React frontend, a Node.js backend, an off-chain SQLite database, and the on-chain Fabric ledger. Users such as students, companies, faculty internship committee members, and the central internship unit can perform specified operations according to their role and identity. The agreement lifecycle follows predefined sequential steps, and at each step, the ledger status is updated and recorded securely. Furthermore, the system was evaluated using functional and performance tests, indicating acceptable throughput and latency for verifiable administrative workflows. This implementation demonstrates how permissioned blockchain technology can improve transparency, integrity, and accountability while preserving controlled access to institutional data and providing a working prototype that can be used in various future systems.

AI.tldr: StajChain is a Hyperledger Fabric-based permissioned blockchain system that digitizes and secures the internship agreement lifecycle, replacing manual, centralized workflows with transparent, tamper-resistant, role-based smart contract execution.
AI.motivation: Manual approval workflows and centralized record-keeping in administrative processes (e.g., internship agreements) suffer from delays, vulnerability to unauthorized modification, and limited traceability.
AI.method: The authors built StajChain using Hyperledger Fabric with a React frontend, Node.js backend, off-chain SQLite database, and on-chain ledger. Smart contracts encode the full internship agreement lifecycle with sequential state transitions. Hyperledger Fabric CA enforces role-based access control for students, companies, faculty committee members, and central internship units.
AI.result: Functional and performance tests demonstrated acceptable throughput and latency for verifiable administrative workflows, confirming the system's practical viability.
AI.conclusion: Permissioned blockchain can improve transparency, integrity, and accountability in institutional workflows while preserving controlled data access. The StajChain prototype is reusable for future systems.

title: A Consensus-Based Framework for Relative Preference Evaluation of Large Language Models
summary:
Traditional benchmarks for LLMs primarily rely on static datasets and objective scoring metrics, which often fail to capture differences in response quality when multiple answers are acceptable. In such settings, correctness alone is insufficient to distinguish between responses that vary in clarity, completeness, and usefulness.
  This paper introduces a consensus-based evaluation framework that measures relative preference among model-generated responses rather than absolute correctness. Instead of evaluating outputs against a fixed ground truth, we assess how a panel of diverse LLMs ranks anonymized candidate responses to the same prompt. This approach treats aggregate inter-model agreement as a proxy for perceived response quality under blind conditions.
  We conduct a controlled study using five state-of-the-art LLMs across multiple domains, including programming, general knowledge, safety, logical reasoning, and mathematics. Each model generates responses and independently ranks peer outputs through a structured voting process. Scores are aggregated into a Relative Intelligence Index (RII), representing how frequently a model's responses are preferred by other models.
  Our findings reveal consistent preference patterns across domains, with certain models more frequently ranked highly by their peers. However, we emphasize that these results reflect inter-model preference alignment rather than objective correctness or human judgment. This framework provides a scalable, model-driven method for comparative evaluation, offering an alternative perspective on response quality in scenarios where multiple valid answers exist. While not directly aligned with human evaluation, prior work suggests that aggregated model preferences can partially correlate with human judgments, motivating this as a proxy signal.

AI.tldr: Proposes a consensus-based evaluation framework where multiple LLMs rank each other's responses, aggregating preferences into a Relative Intelligence Index (RII) as an alternative to static benchmark scoring.
AI.motivation: Traditional LLM benchmarks using static datasets and objective scoring fail to differentiate response quality when multiple valid answers exist — correctness alone cannot capture distinctions in clarity, completeness, and usefulness.
AI.method: A panel of five diverse state-of-the-art LLMs generates responses to identical prompts across programming, general knowledge, safety, logical reasoning, and mathematics domains. Each model then anonymizes and ranks peer outputs via structured voting. Aggregate inter-model agreement is computed into a Relative Intelligence Index (RII), reflecting how frequently a model's responses are preferred by other models.
AI.result: Consistent preference patterns emerged across domains, with certain models ranked more highly by peers. The authors caution that these patterns reflect inter-model preference alignment rather than objective correctness or human judgment.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, model-driven comparative evaluation method for scenarios with multiple valid answers. While not directly aligned with human evaluation, prior work suggests aggregated model preferences can partially correlate with human judgments, making RII a viable proxy signal.

title: On the Depth Scalability of Logic Gate Networks
comment: 7 pages of main text, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary:
Logic Gate Networks (LGNs) implement computation through compositions of Boolean operations, yet unlike classical Boolean circuits, existing LGNs do not reliably benefit from increased depth. We identify two distinct causes: optimization collapse in deep relaxed LGNs and a topology-induced limitation that persists even when skip-biased initialization and straight-through estimation stabilize training. Thus, trainability alone is insufficient; deeper layers must also receive information that supports useful computation.
  We introduce Input-Anchored Logic Gate Networks (IALGNs), in which each gate combines an evolving hidden feature with a direct input anchor. This topology preserves a computational spine while conditioning every layer on the original input. We show that a depth-D path can depend on up to D+1 input bits and establish a strict path-wise depth hierarchy. Random-k anchor relaxation further improves anchor selection without relaxing the spine.
  Across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, IALGNs achieve consistent fixed-width depth--accuracy improvements beyond 100 layers, whereas alternative LGN topologies saturate or degrade. Layer-wise probes, topology ablations, and effective-depth analysis show that input anchoring produces progressively more informative representations and preserves longer computational paths. These results demonstrate that scalable depth in LGNs requires both stable optimization and an information-access pattern that supports input-conditioned refinement.

AI.tldr: Logic Gate Networks (LGNs) traditionally fail to benefit from increased depth due to optimization collapse and topology-induced limitations. The authors propose Input-Anchored LGNs (IALGNs), which anchor each gate to original input features, establishing a provable depth hierarchy. This enables consistent accuracy gains beyond 100 layers on image classification benchmarks, where competing topologies saturate or degrade.
AI.motivation: Existing LGNs do not reliably improve with increased depth, unlike classical Boolean circuits. The authors identify two failure modes: (1) optimization collapse in deep relaxed LGNs, and (2) a topology-induced limitation where deeper layers receive insufficient information for useful computation, even when training is stabilized via skip-biased initialization and straight-through estimation. The core insight is that trainability alone is insufficient — deeper layers must have access to input-conditioned information.
AI.method: IALGNs introduce a topology where each logic gate combines an evolving hidden feature with a direct anchor to the original input. This creates a "computational spine" that conditions every layer on the input. The authors prove that a depth-D path can depend on up to D+1 input bits, establishing a strict path-wise depth hierarchy. They also introduce random-k anchor relaxation, which improves anchor selection without relaxing the spine. Evaluation uses layer-wise probes, topology ablations, and effective-depth analysis across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100.
AI.result: IALGNs achieve consistent fixed-width depth–accuracy improvements beyond 100 layers on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Alternative LGN topologies saturate or degrade with depth. Layer-wise probes confirm that input anchoring yields progressively more informative representations. Effective-depth analysis demonstrates preserved longer computational paths compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Scalable depth in Logic Gate Networks requires both stable optimization and an information-access pattern that supports input-conditioned refinement. Input anchoring satisfies both requirements, enabling LGNs to reliably exploit depth similarly to classical Boolean circuits. The results establish that topology design — specifically maintaining a direct input pathway — is critical for scaling LGN depth.

title: Risk Is Not the Target: A Monotonic Framework for Evaluating Wildfire Operational Risk Signals
comment: Accepted in 2026 IEEE 50th Annual Computers, Software, and Applications Conference (COMPSAC)
summary: Evaluating wildfire risk systems using standard machine-learning metrics such as F1-score or IoU is fundamentally flawed: these metrics assess event prediction accuracy, not the operational coherence of a continuous risk signal. This work proposes a novel monotonic evaluation framework that measures whether increases in a predicted risk score consistently correspond to increases in observed operational load, such as number of fires, intervention time, and deployed resources. Moreover, we compare three structurally different approaches on the French Alpes-Maritimes department: the expert-based DFE index, GRU- based predictive models, and FARS, a hybrid multi-agent system combining predictive AI with LLM-based reasoning. Experimental results reveal that the DFE, despite poor classification metrics, exhibits the most balanced monotonic behavior across the full risk scale. GRU models achieve strong local monotonicity but fail to produce well-distributed risk levels. FARS inherits and reveals the structural limitations of upstream signals rather than correcting them. The central finding is a paradigm shift: a good risk model does not predict fires accurately, but one whose ordinal scale meaningfully explains operational dynamics, as proved in this paper. Code of the monotonic framework is available on github.

AI.tldr: Standard classification metrics (F1, IoU) are inadequate for evaluating wildfire risk systems. The authors propose a monotonic evaluation framework that assesses whether risk scores consistently correspond to operational load, and compare DFE (expert), GRU (deep learning), and FARS (hybrid AI+LLM) on French wildfire data. DFE shows the best monotonic behavior despite poor classification metrics, revealing that a good risk model is one whose ordinal scale meaningfully explains operational dynamics, not one that predicts fires accurately.
AI.motivation: Standard machine-learning metrics like F1-score and IoU evaluate event prediction accuracy but fail to assess the operational coherence of continuous wildfire risk signals. There is a need for evaluation that measures whether risk scores meaningfully align with real operational demands (fire count, intervention time, resource deployment).
AI.method: The authors propose a monotonic evaluation framework that tests whether increases in predicted risk scores correspond monotonically to increases in operational load metrics. Three approaches are compared on data from the Alpes-Maritimes department in France: (1) DFE, an expert-based index; (2) GRU-based predictive models; and (3) FARS, a hybrid multi-agent system combining predictive AI with LLM-based reasoning.
AI.result: DFE exhibits the most balanced monotonic behavior across the full risk scale despite poor classification metrics. GRU models achieve strong local monotonicity but fail to distribute risk levels well. FARS inherits and reveals structural limitations of upstream signals rather than correcting them.
AI.conclusion: The paper calls for a paradigm shift: a good wildfire risk model is not one that predicts fires accurately, but one whose ordinal risk scale meaningfully explains operational dynamics. The monotonic evaluation framework (open-sourced on GitHub) provides a more operationally relevant alternative to standard classification metrics.

title: Output Format x Model Identity: Interaction Effects in Single-Round Coding Agent Performance
summary: Output format is not a neutral implementation detail -- it can reorder model rankings, amplify or suppress individual model differences, and determine whether a coding agent succeeds or fails. We conducted a controlled single-round experiment with 3 models (DeepSeek V4, Doubao 2.0 Pro, Qwen 3.7 Max) x 3 output formats (full file, JSON Patch, unified diff) x 6 tasks x 20 repetitions, totaling 4,013 runs across 4 open-source projects. Only one project (tqdm) yielded non-zero success rates: dotenv, requests, and jsoup yielded zero successes in 2,551 runs. Our central finding is a format x model interaction with no universally optimal format. Doubao achieves 94% success with JSON Patch (Cohen's h = 1.57, p < 0.001), DeepSeek excels at unified diff (66%, h = 0.63), and Qwen shows a small but significant full-file preference (50%, h = 0.29, p < 0.05). Beyond these headline results, we identify a distinct failure mechanism -- format misuse -- where agents correctly diagnose a problem but execute it with excessive scope, most vividly when a one-line fix is applied as a full-file replacement. We propose a model-specific output strategy, a tool-design principle that constrains format semantics to the agent's own localization step, and release all data and templates for reproducibility. All experimental data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21505157.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates that output format significantly impacts coding agent performance, with no universally optimal format across models. Through 4,013 controlled runs, the authors reveal strong format × model interactions: Doubao excels with JSON Patch (94%), DeepSeek with unified diff (66%), and Qwen shows a mild full-file preference (50%). They identify "format misuse" as a key failure mode and recommend model-specific output strategies.
AI.motivation: Output format is often treated as an implementation detail in coding agents, yet it may systematically affect model performance, success rates, and ranking. The authors aim to rigorously quantify whether and how output format shapes coding agent outcomes across different models.
AI.method: A controlled single-round factorial experiment: 3 models (DeepSeek V4, Doubao 2.0 Pro, Qwen 3.7 Max) × 3 output formats (full file, JSON Patch, unified diff) × 6 tasks × 20 repetitions, yielding 4,013 total runs across 4 open-source projects (tqdm, dotenv, requests, jsoup). Success rates and effect sizes (Cohen's h) were computed, with significance testing.
AI.result: Only the tqdm project yielded non-zero success rates; dotenv, requests, and jsoup produced zero successes across 2,551 runs. A significant format × model interaction emerged: Doubao achieved 94% success with JSON Patch (h=1.57, p<0.001), DeepSeek performed best with unified diff (66%, h=0.63), and Qwen showed a small full-file preference (50%, h=0.29, p<0.05). A novel failure mechanism — format misuse — was identified, where agents apply correct fixes with excessive scope (e.g., full-file replacement for a one-line fix).
AI.conclusion: There is no universally optimal output format; performance depends on the model-format pairing. The authors recommend model-specific output strategies and propose constraining format semantics to the agent's own localization step. All data and templates are publicly released for reproducibility.

title: Bringing GRACE to Recommendation: Fine-Tuning for Sustainable and Accurate Personalization
summary: Growing concern about environmental sustainability (e.g., reducing carbon emissions and resource use) and public health has motivated ``green'' recommender systems that steer users toward more eco-friendly and healthier choices. However, many existing green recommendation approaches require training new models from scratch, incurring substantial computational and energy costs. Reranking-based methods, meanwhile, introduce an additional sorting stage at inference, increasing latency and computational cost. In this work, we propose GRACE (Green Recommendation via Adaptive Conflict-rEsolution), a fine-tuning framework that integrates item-level sustainability signals (e.g., eco-scores or health indices) into pretrained recommendation models. Since these green values are usually discrete and non-differentiable, existing methods often rely on pairwise comparisons to promote greener items. GRACE instead introduces a differentiable approximation that enables direct optimization of the green criterion. To balance sustainability and personalization quality, GRACE further employs a gradient projection mechanism to mitigate conflicts between the green objective and the accuracy objective during fine-tuning. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GRACE improves sustainability-oriented recommendation outcomes while generally preserving recommendation accuracy through a controllable preference-anchored update mechanism.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a fine-tuning framework that integrates discrete, non-differentiable sustainability signals into pretrained recommendation models via a differentiable approximation and uses gradient projection to resolve conflicts between green objectives and recommendation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing green recommender systems either require training models from scratch (high computational/energy cost) or use reranking-based methods (increased inference latency). There is a need for a cost-efficient approach that retrofits pretrained models with sustainability awareness without sacrificing personalization quality.
AI.method: GRACE introduces: (1) a differentiable approximation of discrete sustainability scores (e.g., eco-scores, health indices) to enable direct optimization via gradient-based fine-tuning; (2) a gradient projection mechanism that resolves conflicts between the green objective and the accuracy objective during fine-tuning; and (3) a controllable preference-anchored update mechanism to preserve recommendation quality.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets show that GRACE improves sustainability-oriented recommendation outcomes while generally preserving recommendation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: GRACE offers a practical, computationally efficient pathway to greening existing recommendation systems by fine-tuning pretrained models with sustainability signals, balancing environmental goals with personalization through conflict-resolving gradient updates.

title: Draining the Energy Commons: Self-Defeating Over-Appropriation as a Coordination Failure in Agentic LLM Collectives
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that plan, use tools, and act over time. When they share persistent resources, such as compute pools or energy reserves, decisions by one agent affect the conditions faced by later agents. We study this coordination failure in a renewable energy commons. Four same-family GPT, Gemini, or Grok agents act in homogeneous self-play as electricity prosumers, instructed to maximize operational continuity. Holding aggregate residual demand and the decision protocol fixed, we vary the regeneration rate of a shared energy reserve from abundance to scarcity. All three families preserve the reserve when demand does not exceed peak renewable replacement, but over-appropriate it beyond that threshold (all nine exact scarcity contrasts survive Holm correction; largest adjusted p = 4.87e-5). The pattern is self-defeating: the same populations protect current service while undermining future service. At higher scarcity (rho = 1.2), early aggregate request pressure exceeds peak renewable replacement in every family and averages 1.21 times that level. Mean trajectories fall below the reserve level of maximum replenishment by rounds 5-7. Two offline benchmarks compare a social planner maximizing group-wide operational-service value with open access, where each prosumer maximizes its own value. At a discount factor of gamma = 0.95, both benchmarks sustain the reserve under the same dynamics. Realized depletion instead resembles outcomes under a more impatient open-access benchmark. The populations therefore behave like impatient optimizers at the level of the public trajectory. This system-level alignment failure would be missed by isolated-response evaluation.

AI.tldr: LLM agents managing a shared renewable energy reserve exhibit a "tragedy of the commons": they preserve the resource under abundance but over-appropriate it under scarcity, undermining future service. This coordination failure, resembling impatient open-access benchmarks, highlights a system-level alignment problem missed by isolated-response evaluation.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed as persistent agents sharing resources (e.g., compute, energy), coordination failures can emerge where individually rational decisions collectively degrade the shared resource. Traditional single-agent evaluations fail to capture these system-level dynamics. The authors aim to empirically demonstrate and characterize such failures in a controlled, reproducible setting.
AI.method: Four agents from the same LLM family (GPT, Gemini, or Grok) play as electricity prosumers in homogeneous self-play, instructed to maximize operational continuity. They face a shared renewable energy reserve with varying regeneration rates (from abundance to scarcity). Aggregate residual demand and the decision protocol are held fixed. Two offline benchmarks are used: a social planner maximizing group-wide value and an open-access benchmark where each agent maximizes its own value, both with a discount factor γ=0.95.
AI.result: All three LLM families preserved the reserve when demand ≤ peak renewable replacement, but over-appropriated beyond that threshold (all nine scarcity contrasts significant after Holm correction; max adjusted p=4.87e-5). At higher scarcity (ρ=1.2), early aggregate request pressure exceeded peak replacement in every family, averaging 1.21× that level. Mean trajectories fell below the reserve level of maximum replenishment by rounds 5–7. Both offline benchmarks sustained the reserve, but realized depletion matched outcomes under a more impatient open-access benchmark.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents collectively behave like impatient optimizers in resource-constrained environments, producing self-defeating depletion trajectories. This system-level alignment failure—a machine "tragedy of the commons"—would go undetected by isolated-response evaluation, underscoring the need for multi-agent, dynamic evaluation frameworks for deployed LLM systems.

title: Natural Language Processing in Health Professions Education: A Scoping Review
comment: This manuscript has been accepted at the 14th IEEE International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI 2026)
summary: Natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly transforming health professions education, yet no scoping review has systematically mapped their applications across the full spectrum of health education contexts, including public health. Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, this review synthesized evidence from 64 studies published between 2015 and 2026, identified through searches of PubMed, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Seven thematic domains were identified: automated assessment, large language models (LLMs) as student-facing learning support, virtual patients and clinical simulation, curriculum analysis and program evaluation, personalized and adaptive learning, public health and health promotion education, and educator and institutional integration. Findings reveal significant technical promise, particularly in automated assessment, clinical simulation, and curriculum analysis, alongside persistent challenges including hallucination and accuracy concerns, algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital divide, overreliance, and absence of standardized outcome measures. Only four studies explicitly addressed public health education, representing a major evidence gap. This review provides a foundation for evidence-informed integration of NLP and AI across health professions education and highlights public health education as a priority area for future research and investment.

AI.tldr: A scoping review of 64 studies (2015–2026) identifies seven thematic domains where NLP and AI are applied in health professions education, revealing significant promise in automated assessment, clinical simulation, and curriculum analysis, while highlighting persistent challenges like hallucination, bias, and a major evidence gap in public health education.
AI.motivation: Despite the rapid transformation of health professions education by NLP and AI, no scoping review had systematically mapped their applications across the full spectrum of health education contexts, including the notably underrepresented domain of public health.
AI.method: The review followed the Arksey and O'Malley scoping review framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. It synthesized evidence from 64 studies published between 2015 and 2026, identified through systematic searches across PubMed, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar.
AI.result: Seven thematic domains emerged: (1) automated assessment, (2) LLMs as student-facing learning support, (3) virtual patients and clinical simulation, (4) curriculum analysis and program evaluation, (5) personalized and adaptive learning, (6) public health and health promotion education, and (7) educator and institutional integration. Significant technical promise was evident in automated assessment, clinical simulation, and curriculum analysis. Persistent challenges included hallucination/accuracy concerns, algorithmic bias, data privacy, the digital divide, overreliance, and a lack of standardized outcome measures. Only four studies addressed public health education.
AI.conclusion: The review provides a foundational evidence base for integrating NLP and AI into health professions education and identifies public health education as a critically under-researched priority area requiring future investigation and investment.

title: A method of Risk Analysis and threat management using analytic hierarchy process
summary: Efficient risk analysis and threat management are essential requirements of modern air defense (AD) systems. The paper is halfway between the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) and practical reasoning to model and analyze the risks and threats associated with military AD applications. The models are applied for decision-making tasks of AD command and control (C2) for assessing and prioritizing the threat from hostile targets for efficient risk management.
