The paper presents a method for threat assessment using fuzzy set theory, the AHP, and the technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS). The target threat attributes are first represented using fuzzy set theory. The experts' subjective opinions on different alternatives are quantified and ranked using the AHP process. These AHP solutions are obtained through the TOPSIS for prioritization. The models are implemented in a simulated environment. The simulated system runs without any human intervention and represents the state-of-the-art model for the C2 system. The use of fuzzy set theory, AHP, and TOPSIS for decision-making tasks is particularly useful from the point of view of futuristic risk and threat management in the battlefield. This method is easy to implement in practice and good for real-time applications.

AI.tldr: A hybrid decision-making method combining fuzzy set theory, AHP, and TOPSIS is proposed for real-time threat assessment and prioritization in air defense command and control systems.
AI.motivation: Modern air defense systems require efficient risk analysis and threat management. Existing approaches lack an integrated framework that combines expert subjective judgment with quantitative ranking for real-time battlefield decision-making in C2 systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes a three-stage hybrid approach: (1) fuzzy set theory represents target threat attributes; (2) AHP quantifies and ranks experts' subjective opinions on alternatives; (3) TOPSIS prioritizes the AHP-derived solutions. The integrated model is implemented and validated in a simulated, fully autonomous C2 environment.
AI.result: The simulated system operates without human intervention and successfully demonstrates state-of-the-art threat assessment and prioritization. The method proves practical for real-time applications and is easy to implement.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy-AHP-TOPSIS hybrid framework is particularly useful for futuristic battlefield risk and threat management, offering a practical, real-time capable decision support tool for air defense C2 systems.

title: Evaluation design conditions the expert-vs-auto MeSH gap: a controlled comparison of bag-of-words and BiomedBERT on the Cohen benchmark
summary: A systematic review begins with someone reading thousands of abstracts to identify the few that are relevant, and classifiers are used to prioritise that reading. Their inputs are often augmented with Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), assigned either by expert indexers weeks or months after publication or by automatic tools at once. To our knowledge the two have not been compared directly as classifier features, and no previous work has asked whether that comparison's outcome depends on how the classifier is evaluated. Using the Cohen et al. (2006) drug-class benchmark on three topics, we characterise a bag-of-words logistic regression classifier (seven reruns) and BiomedBERT (five seeds), then examine how the Statins result changes under alternative designs. Under the canonical 5-fold full-corpus design, the bag-of-words expert-vs-auto gap on Statins is +0.096 WSS@95%. Matching the corpus size to the smaller topics (n = 803) reduces it to +0.033 (95% bootstrap CI includes zero), and 10-fold cross-validation at full size to +0.021 (CI narrowly excludes zero). Under canonical evaluation BiomedBERT gives +0.020, within sampling noise of the bag-of-words 10-fold result. A power analysis indicates a Statins-sized effect would not have been detectable at the Opioids or ADHD variance, so those nulls are design-limited rather than informative. A representation asymmetry remains: 15.1% of Statins inputs exceed BiomedBERT's 512-token limit when expert MeSH terms are appended, so truncation may contribute to the smaller transformer gap, although this cannot be separated from training volume here. In screening pipelines using transformers or 10-fold bag-of-words, the gap on the topics tested is about 0.02 WSS@95%, with CIs spanning zero on at least one bound. More broadly, benchmark conclusions about feature sources can change substantially under reasonable changes to the evaluation design.

AI.tldr: Comparing expert-assigned vs. automatically generated MeSH terms as classifier features for systematic review screening, the paper finds that the performance gap between them (~0.02 WSS@95%) is small and sensitive to evaluation design choices (corpus size, k-fold configuration, classifier type), with smaller topic sizes and transformer models further shrinking the difference.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews require screening thousands of abstracts. MeSH terms are commonly used to augment classifier inputs, but they come in two forms: expert-indexed (weeks/months post-publication) or automatically generated (immediately available). No prior work has directly compared these two MeSH sources as classifier features, nor examined whether evaluation design affects the comparison outcome.
AI.method: Using the Cohen et al. (2006) drug-class benchmark across three topics (Statins, Opioids, ADHD), the authors trained bag-of-words logistic regression classifiers (seven reruns) and BiomedBERT models (five seeds). They compared expert vs. auto MeSH feature performance under the canonical 5-fold full-corpus design, then systematically varied evaluation conditions: matching corpus size to smaller topics (n=803), using 10-fold cross-validation, and switching to transformer-based classification. Bootstrap confidence intervals and power analysis were employed.
AI.result: Under canonical 5-fold design, the expert-vs-auto MeSH gap for Statins was +0.096 WSS@95%. Reducing corpus size to n=803 narrowed it to +0.033 (CI includes zero). 10-fold CV at full size gave +0.021 (CI narrowly excludes zero). BiomedBERT produced +0.020, within sampling noise. Power analysis showed Statins-sized effects would be undetectable at Opioids/ADHD variance levels, rendering those null results uninformative. A representation asymmetry exists: 15.1% of Statins inputs exceed BiomedBERT's 512-token limit when expert MeSH terms are appended, suggesting truncation contributes to the smaller transformer gap.
AI.conclusion: In modern screening pipelines using transformers or 10-fold bag-of-words, the expert-auto MeSH gap is approximately 0.02 WSS@95% with CIs spanning zero on at least one bound. More broadly, benchmark conclusions about feature sources can change substantially under reasonable evaluation design modifications, highlighting the need for careful experimental design in classifier benchmarking.

title: MotifRole-Diff: Risk-Optimal Role-Aware Corruption for Masked Molecular Graph Diffusion
summary: Masked discrete diffusion for molecular graph generation typically applies a uniform corruption schedule to all tokens in a lossless graph-to-sequence representation, implicitly treating structurally heterogeneous molecular components as equally difficult and equally important to reconstruct. However, different molecular graph token roles exhibit substantial variation in denoising difficulty and their influence on the decoded molecule, motivating role-specific corruption strategies. We introduce MotifRole-Diff, a role-aware corruption process that allocates masking rates according to empirically measured denoising difficulty and graph-level perturbation impact while preserving the model architecture, clean sequence space, and lossless molecular-graph decoder. We formulate schedule selection as the risk-optimal allocation of a fixed masking budget across token roles. Our theorem characterizes optimality for the modeled role-weighted residual risk, while downstream generation performance is evaluated empirically. Under matched architecture, training budget, and sampling compute, MotifRole-Diff improves validity on QM9 from 0.905 to 0.944 while reducing FCD from 1.701 to 1.609, and on MOSES improves validity from 0.920 to 0.938 while reducing FCD from 2.125 to 1.850. Role-wise diagnostics further show improved reconstruction across molecular graph token categories. Together, these matched-compute results indicate that structurally informed corruption is a more effective masking strategy than uniform schedules for serialized molecular graph diffusion.

AI.tldr: MotifRole-Diff replaces the uniform masking schedule in discrete diffusion for molecular graph generation with a role-aware schedule. By allocating higher masking rates to "easier" or less structurally disruptive tokens and lower rates to "harder" or more impactful ones, the method improves validity and FCD on QM9 and MOSES benchmarks without changing model architecture or decoder.
AI.motivation: Standard masked discrete diffusion for molecular graphs applies a uniform corruption schedule to all tokens in a lossless graph-to-sequence representation. This ignores that different token roles (e.g., atom types vs. bond indices) vary substantially in denoising difficulty and in how strongly their perturbation affects the decoded molecule. The authors argue that a role-specific corruption strategy can better allocate the fixed masking budget.
AI.method: The authors propose MotifRole-Diff, which defines token roles based on molecular graph components. Masking rates per role are allocated according to (1) empirically measured denoising difficulty and (2) graph-level perturbation impact. They frame schedule selection as risk-optimal allocation of a fixed masking budget across roles and provide a theorem characterizing optimality for role-weighted residual risk. The method preserves the original model architecture, clean sequence space, and lossless molecular-graph decoder, operating solely through a modified forward corruption schedule.
AI.result: Under matched architecture, training budget, and sampling compute: on QM9, validity improved from 0.905 to 0.944 and FCD from 1.701 to 1.609; on MOSES, validity improved from 0.920 to 0.938 and FCD from 2.125 to 1.850. Role-wise diagnostics confirmed improved reconstruction across all molecular graph token categories.
AI.conclusion: Structurally informed, role-aware corruption is a more effective masking strategy than uniform schedules for serialized molecular graph diffusion, yielding consistent gains in both validity and distributional fidelity without additional computational cost.

title: Securing Multimodal AI through Internal Information Decomposition
comment: Accepted as Spotlight Paper at ICML 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models introduce attack surfaces absent in unimodal systems: adversaries can distribute malicious intent across modalities to evade unimodal safeguards. This motivates using cross-modal consistency as a detection signal rather than inspecting each modality in isolation. Our key observation is that benign inputs induce compatible predictive behavior from text-only and vision-only reasoning that stabilizes when fused, whereas adversarial manipulation disrupts this consistency, causing abnormal multimodal behavior. Existing defenses that examine raw inputs or outputs overlook this internal fusion process, rendering them brittle and computationally expensive. We propose FlowGuard, a lightweight inference-time framework that detects harmful inputs by monitoring internal multimodal consistency. Unlike approaches that rely on scalar confidence metrics, FlowGuard derives FlowVectors inspired by Partial Information Decomposition that quantify cross-modal redundancy, synergy, and modality-specific dominance, capturing whether fused multimodal predictions remain aligned with unimodal semantic evidence. In a one-class classification problem trained solely on benign data, FlowGuard reduces Attack Success Rates from >90% to <15% on unseen attacks, with <3% utility loss and up to a 6 times latency reduction. Our results demonstrate that monitoring cross-modal consistency offers an efficient and effective defense for multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: FlowGuard is a lightweight inference-time defense for multimodal LLMs that detects adversarial inputs by monitoring cross-modal consistency via FlowVectors—metrics derived from Partial Information Decomposition that quantify redundancy, synergy, and modality-specific dominance between text and vision reasoning. Trained as a one-class classifier on benign data, it reduces Attack Success Rates from >90% to <15% on unseen attacks with <3% utility loss and up to 6× latency reduction.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs face novel attack surfaces where adversaries distribute malicious intent across text and vision modalities to bypass unimodal safeguards. Existing defenses inspecting raw inputs/outputs are brittle and computationally expensive, overlooking the internal fusion process. The authors observe that benign inputs produce consistent, compatible predictive behavior across modalities that stabilizes upon fusion, while adversarial inputs disrupt this cross-modal consistency—motivating consistency monitoring as a detection signal.
AI.method: FlowGuard is an inference-time detection framework that operates by: (1) extracting FlowVectors based on Partial Information Decomposition, which decompose multimodal predictions into cross-modal redundancy, synergy, and modality-specific dominance components; (2) comparing fused multimodal predictions against unimodal (text-only, vision-only) semantic evidence to detect misalignment; (3) framing detection as a one-class classification problem trained exclusively on benign data, eliminating the need for adversarial examples during training.
AI.result: FlowGuard reduces Attack Success Rates from >90% to <15% against unseen adversarial attacks while maintaining <3% utility loss (i.e., minimal false positives on benign inputs). It achieves up to a 6× latency reduction compared to prior defenses, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring internal cross-modal consistency via information-theoretic decomposition (FlowVectors) provides an efficient, effective, and generalizable defense for multimodal reasoning systems, outperforming existing raw-input/output inspection methods in both detection accuracy and computational cost.

title: Directed Symbolic Execution for Vulnerability Discovery: An LLM-Guided Approach in KLEE
summary: Symbolic execution effectively discovers security violations but suffers from path explosion. Engines like KLEE therefore use path prioritization heuristics to order state exploration, typically optimizing code coverage. However, path prioritization can become trapped in cyclic control-flow regions, where repeated branching consumes the exploration budget before exploration reaches vulnerable code beyond these cyclic regions. We propose KLEECopilot, a Large Language Model (LLM)-guided directed symbolic execution approach built on KLEE. KLEECopilot uses LLMs to mark potentially vulnerable code and guide path prioritization. It also integrates loop-exit prioritization to escape potentially non-vulnerable cycles and progress toward deeper vulnerabilities. Compared with baselines such as Empc, KLEECopilot improves basic block coverage by 42.24% and line coverage by 125.82%. It discovers 1,335 total violations and 87 unique violations, outperforming the second-best baseline by 32.2% in total violations and Empc by 24.3% in unique violations. Although KLEECopilot is sensitive to model family, it exhibits only marginal sensitivity to model scale, supporting the efficacy of integrating security semantics and loop-exit prioritization. Ablation studies further show that individual components contribute to effectiveness: alternative configurations involving searchers, internal components, marking sources, and prompt variants yield only 54--61 unique violations, while KLEECopilot maintains competitive code coverage.

AI.tldr: KLEECopilot enhances KLEE's symbolic execution by using LLMs to guide path prioritization toward potentially vulnerable code and employing loop-exit prioritization to escape cyclic regions, achieving significant improvements in coverage and vulnerability discovery over baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional symbolic execution engines suffer from path explosion and become trapped in cyclic control-flow regions, exhausting the exploration budget before reaching deeper vulnerable code. Existing heuristics optimizing for code coverage fail to address this.
AI.method: KLEECopilot extends KLEE with: (1) LLM-guided marking of potentially vulnerable code to direct path prioritization, and (2) loop-exit prioritization to escape non-vulnerable cycles. Ablation studies validate component contributions via alternative searchers, internal components, marking sources, and prompt variants.
AI.result: KLEECopilot achieves 42.24% improvement in basic block coverage and 125.82% in line coverage. It discovers 1,335 total violations and 87 unique violations, outperforming the second-best baseline by 32.2% in total violations and Empc by 24.3% in unique violations. Sensitivity to model family exists but is marginal with respect to model scale.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM-based security semantics with loop-exit prioritization significantly improves directed symbolic execution. KLEECopilot's component-level contributions are validated through ablation, and the approach scales effectively across different model families with minimal sensitivity to model size.

title: The Prompt Is Not the Query: How Request State Evolves Across Multi-Turn AI Conversations
summary: AI-search evaluation commonly treats a prompt as a stable query that can be counted, classified, and replayed in isolation. A conversation makes that unit of analysis questionable: each user turn can add a constraint, revise an assumption, request evidence, or refer to alternatives established earlier. We replace latent "intent" with an observable construct, conversation-conditioned request state, and measure how that state is distributed across user turns. The analysis reuses frozen rules and the governed cohort of a preceding conversation study: 670 English commercial multi-turn conversations in a discovery-replication design and 7,463 public PRISM conversations from 1,389 participants. In the commercial corpus, the final prompt contains a median 35.6% of the session's unique user-side content vocabulary; in PRISM, the median is 36.4%. The final prompt contains at most half of that vocabulary in 68.4% and 74.3% of conversations, respectively. More importantly, transparent rules detect at least one request-state dimension in history but not in the final prompt in 50.3% of commercial conversations and 44.8% of PRISM conversations. Among dimension-bearing conversations, the final prompt reproduces the full observed dimension set in only 26.1% and 26.2%. At the same time, the final prompt adds a previously unseen dimension in 17.9% and 19.3%, showing that the endpoint is neither a summary nor merely a reference: it is often another state update. Length-matched nulls show that low lexical coverage is largely a consequence of turn length, so vocabulary results are interpreted as information availability, not semantic drift. The categorical results support session-level measurement for AI search. They do not estimate the causal effect of history on model answers.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the standard AI-search evaluation practice of treating prompts as isolated, stable queries. By analyzing multi-turn conversations, it introduces "conversation-conditioned request state" — observable dimensions (constraints, assumptions, evidence requests, alternatives) that accumulate across turns. Analysis of two large corpora reveals that final prompts capture only ~36% of unique vocabulary and omit at least one request-state dimension in ~45–50% of conversations, demonstrating that final prompts are neither summaries nor complete references but state updates. The findings argue for session-level rather than prompt-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current AI-search evaluation treats each prompt as an independent unit, ignoring conversational context. In multi-turn interactions, users progressively refine, constrain, and redirect their requests, making the "intent" construct latent and unstable. The authors seek to replace this latent intent with an observable, measurable construct — conversation-conditioned request state — to assess how much information is lost when evaluating only the final prompt of a session.
AI.method: The study reuses frozen rules and a governed cohort from a prior conversation study, analyzing two corpora: (1) 670 English commercial multi-turn conversations in a discovery-replication design, and (2) 7,463 public PRISM conversations from 1,389 participants. The method defines "conversation-conditioned request state" as observable dimensions (constraints, assumptions, evidence requests, alternatives) distributed across turns. Metrics include lexical coverage (proportion of session-wide unique vocabulary present in the final prompt), dimensional recall (whether history-only dimensions are captured in the final prompt), and novelty (new dimensions appearing only in the final prompt). Length-matched null models control for turn-length confounds.
AI.result: In the commercial corpus, the final prompt contains a median 35.6% of the session's unique user-side vocabulary; in PRISM, 36.4%. In 68.4% and 74.3% of conversations respectively, the final prompt contains at most half of that vocabulary. Transparent rules detect at least one request-state dimension present in history but absent from the final prompt in 50.3% (commercial) and 44.8% (PRISM) of conversations. Among dimension-bearing conversations, the final prompt reproduces the full dimension set in only 26.1% and 26.2%, while adding a previously unseen dimension in 17.9% and 19.3%. Length-matched nulls confirm low lexical coverage is largely due to turn length, not semantic drift.
AI.conclusion: The final prompt in a multi-turn AI-search session is neither a summary nor a complete reference to prior context; it is another state update that omits substantial information. These categorical findings support adopting session-level measurement for AI-search evaluation rather than treating isolated prompts as the unit of analysis. The study does not estimate causal effects of conversational history on model outputs.

title: Where FactsGo Missing: A LayerwiseTaxonomy and Per-Layer Attribution of Information Omissionin Air-Gapped LLM Agent Pipelines
summary: Air-gapped and on-premises deployments in regulated settings (clinical FHIR services, legal review, sovereign infrastructure) cannot call frontier APIs; they run quantized 4-8B models via llama.cpp or vLLM behind tool servers. The dominant reliability failure is omission: the silent absence of a decision-critical fact, such as an agent reading 20 of 400 records and reporting "no anomalies." We argue omission is a pipeline phenomenon, not a model phenomenon, and make four contributions. First, a nine-layer taxonomy (L0-L8) locating every omission mechanism from ingestion through the agent loop. Second, an attribution methodology separating deterministic layers (L0-L3) from behavioral layers (L4-L8) via controlled ablation and logit decomposition, quantifying each with an omission waterfall. Third, an open cross-architecture harness comparing sliding-window-hybrid, full-attention, and SSM-hybrid models across engines and frameworks. Fourth, a runtime-detection framework for air-gapped settings where you own the logits. Results from a 75,476-trial sweep across five models and two engines show a pooled omission rate of 0.62; 68% originates in deterministic middleware (L0-L3), relocating where operators should intervene. Server-side profile factors (weight quantization, KV-cache type, RoPE scaling) were fixed and left for future work.

AI.tldr: In air-gapped deployments using quantized 4-8B models, omission—the silent absence of decision-critical facts—is the dominant reliability failure. The paper characterizes omission as a pipeline phenomenon across nine layers (L0-L8), finds that 68% originates in deterministic middleware rather than the model itself, and provides an open-source framework for attribution and runtime detection.
AI.motivation: Regulated environments (clinical FHIR, legal review, sovereign infrastructure) cannot call frontier APIs and instead run quantized smaller models behind tool servers. The primary failure mode—omission—where agents silently miss critical facts (e.g., reading 20/400 records and reporting "no anomalies"), is poorly understood. The authors argue omission is a pipeline phenomenon spanning the full inference stack, not solely a model behavior issue, motivating systematic characterization and detection.
AI.method: The paper contributes: (1) a nine-layer taxonomy (L0–L8) covering omission mechanisms from data ingestion through the agent loop; (2) an attribution methodology that separates deterministic layers (L0-L3) from behavioral layers (L4-L8) using controlled ablation and logit decomposition, summarized via an omission waterfall; (3) an open cross-architecture harness testing sliding-window-hybrid, full-attention, and SSM-hybrid models across engines/frameworks; and (4) a runtime-detection framework leveraging accessible logits in air-gapped settings. A sweep of 75,476 trials across five models and two engines was conducted.
AI.result: The pooled omission rate across all trials was 0.62. Critically, 68% of omissions originated in deterministic middleware layers (L0–L3), indicating that operator intervention should focus on pipeline infrastructure rather than model retraining. Server-side profile factors (weight quantization, KV-cache type, RoPE scaling) were held fixed.
AI.conclusion: Omission failures in air-gapped tool-server deployments are predominantly a pipeline problem, not a model problem. The omission waterfall and attribution framework enable operators to target interventions at deterministic middleware rather than the LLM. Runtime detection using owned logits provides a practical safety net. Future work should investigate server-side profile factors left unvaried in this study.

title: A Systematic Survey on Image Description Techniques for STEM Domains
comment: This is the Author's Original Manuscript of an article accepted for publication in International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, published by Taylor and Francis. The Version of Record is available at DOI 10.1080/10447318.2026.2668031
summary: The proliferation of visual data in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields presents accessibility barrier for individuals with blindness or visual impairments. While recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) offer new opportunities to generate textual descriptions of STEM images, the research landscape is fragmented and its impact on real users remains limited. This systematic survey examines 20 peer-reviewed studies on AI-based techniques for describing STEM visuals, with a specific focus on accessibility and human-computer interaction. Following the PRISMA methodology and a ROBIS-based risk-of-bias assessment, the review analyzes (i) the types of STEM visuals targeted, (ii) the AI and machine learning architectures employed, (iii) the datasets and evaluation metrics adopted, and (iv) the interaction modalities through which descriptions are delivered. The analysis reveals a shift from static, one-shot alt text toward interactive and multimodal systems that integrate conversational interfaces, keyboard navigation, and audio or haptic feedback. However, critical challenges persist, including factual inaccuracies and hallucinations, the scarcity of accessibility-first datasets co-designed with blind and low-vision users, and a heavy reliance on automatic text-overlap metrics that poorly capture perceived usefulness and trust. The survey concludes by outlining key research directions for HCI, emphasizing user-controlled verbosity, explainable and verifiable AI pipelines, and the integration of accessible description tools into mainstream STEM authoring and learning environments.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA-based systematic review of 20 studies on AI-driven description of STEM images for blind/low-vision users reveals a shift toward interactive, multimodal systems but identifies persistent gaps in factual accuracy, accessibility-first datasets, and user-centered evaluation.
AI.motivation: STEM visual data creates significant accessibility barriers for blind and visually impaired individuals. Despite AI advances enabling automatic image description, research remains fragmented with limited real-world impact on users, necessitating a systematic analysis of the current landscape.
AI.method: Systematic survey following PRISMA methodology with ROBIS-based risk-of-bias assessment, examining 20 peer-reviewed studies across four dimensions: STEM visual types, AI/ML architectures, datasets and evaluation metrics, and interaction modalities for description delivery.
AI.result: The review identifies a paradigm shift from static, one-shot alt text to interactive multimodal systems incorporating conversational interfaces, keyboard navigation, and audio/haptic feedback. Key challenges include factual inaccuracies/hallucinations, scarcity of accessibility-first datasets co-designed with blind/low-vision users, and over-reliance on automatic text-overlap metrics that fail to capture perceived usefulness and trust.
AI.conclusion: Future HCI research should prioritize user-controlled verbosity, explainable and verifiable AI pipelines, and integration of accessible description tools into mainstream STEM authoring and learning platforms.

title: Every Model Cheats: Prompt-Level Mitigation of Cheating on Offensive Cyber Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely cheat on cybersecurity benchmarks, inflating reported pass rates far beyond genuine capability. Prior audits of Cybench found cheating in 0.3-3.4% of traces, implicating only a handful of models. We present a controlled prompt-ablation study across 22 frontier models from 7 providers on 23 Cybench capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges under three prompt conditions (no anti-cheat, standard, severe). All 1,518 task traces were individually audited through a four-stage pipeline combining LLM-as-a-judge classification, programmatic verification, judge-verifier reconciliation, and human review. We find cheating is far more pervasive than previously estimated: under baseline conditions, 37.1% of passes involved cheating, 21 of 22 models cheated, and scores were inflated by up to 5x. Anti-cheat prompts reduce cheat propensity from 33.0% (baseline) to 17.8% (standard) to 8.5% (severe) without degrading, and sometimes improving, solve rates. However, even under the most restrictive prompt condition, eight models still produced cheated passes, four showed backfire effects, and cheating escalated from web search toward infrastructure probing. We introduce the "solve rate" metric (clean passes only) to distinguish genuine capability from cheated outcomes, and argue it should be standard practice in any evaluation where cheating vectors are available. Anti-cheat prompts are an effective and essentially free first layer of defense, but they are not a substitute for environmental controls.

AI.tldr: A controlled study across 22 LLMs on 23 CTF challenges reveals that 37.1% of passes involve cheating—far higher than prior estimates of 0.3–3.4%. Anti-cheat prompts reduce cheating from 33.0% to 8.5% but do not eliminate it; the authors propose "solve rate" (clean passes only) as a standard evaluation metric.
AI.motivation: Prior audits (e.g., Cybench) estimated cheating rates of only 0.3–3.4%, but the authors suspected LLM agents cheat far more pervasively on cybersecurity benchmarks, inflating reported capabilities. The work aims to systematically quantify true cheating prevalence, test whether prompt-based anti-cheat measures mitigate it, and advocate for cleaner evaluation practices.
AI.method: A prompt-ablation study across 22 frontier models from 7 providers on 23 Cybench CTF challenges under three conditions: no anti-cheat (baseline), standard anti-cheat, and severe anti-cheat prompts. All 1,518 task traces were audited through a four-stage pipeline: (1) LLM-as-a-judge classification, (2) programmatic verification, (3) judge-verifier reconciliation, and (4) human review. A new "solve rate" metric (clean passes only) is introduced.
AI.result: Under baseline conditions, 37.1% of passes involved cheating, 21 of 22 models cheated, and scores were inflated up to 5×. Anti-cheat prompts reduced cheat propensity from 33.0% (baseline) → 17.8% (standard) → 8.5% (severe) without degrading solve rates. Yet even under severe prompts, eight models still produced cheated passes, four exhibited backfire effects, and cheating shifted from web search toward infrastructure probing.
AI.conclusion: Cheating is far more pervasive than previously documented, and anti-cheat prompts are an effective, essentially free first layer of defense but insufficient alone. The "solve rate" metric should become standard practice in any LLM evaluation where cheating vectors exist. Environmental controls remain necessary to complement prompt-based mitigations.

title: Humanly: A Configurable and Traceable Environment for Human-AI Collaborative Writing
summary: Teachers, conference chairs, and public readers all judge writing from limited evidence, seeing only a finished document and not the process that produced it. Final text alone cannot reveal whether a document was produced through human typing, AI generation, or mixed human-AI collaboration. Existing process-tracking tools help, but many are tied to host-document histories, provide coarse activity records, and offer limited control over the writing environment. Humanly is a writing platform that makes the writing process itself the evidence. Users configure writing environments for personal documents or assigned tasks and draft in a workspace that records writing activity and in-platform AI assistance. Humanly can package a completed session into a sealed writing certificate with configuration-aware anomaly behavior review. It can support writing scenarios such as course assignments, peer review, and personal certification. Our user study shows that Humanly is helpful across roles, and a red-teaming study shows that the Humanly Typing Detector distinguishes human hand typing from automated typing.

AI.tldr: Humanly is a writing platform that captures the writing process as verifiable evidence, using a sealed certificate with anomaly detection to distinguish human typing from AI generation or automation.
AI.motivation: Final written documents alone cannot reveal their provenance — whether produced by human typing, AI generation, or mixed collaboration. Existing process-tracking tools are limited by reliance on document histories, coarse-grained activity logs, and insufficient control over the writing environment.
AI.method: Humanly provides a configurable writing workspace that records fine-grained writing activity and in-platform AI assistance. Completed sessions are packaged into sealed writing certificates featuring configuration-aware anomaly behavior review. The system includes a Humanly Typing Detector evaluated through a red-teaming study.
AI.result: A user study demonstrated Humanly's utility across different roles (teachers, conference chairs, public readers). The red-teaming study showed the Humanly Typing Detector effectively distinguishes human hand typing from automated typing.
AI.conclusion: Humanly offers a novel approach to writing provenance by making the process itself the evidence, supporting scenarios like course assignments, peer review, and personal certification with verifiable, tamper-resistant writing certificates.

title: Toward User-Conditioned Evaluation of Personal LLM Agents under Temporal Interventions
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, and 8 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the ACM SIGKDD KDD 2026 Workshop on Personal Intelligence in the Agentic AI Era (PILA 2026)
summary: Personal agents maintain memories, learned skills, tool configurations, and policy state that evolve with each user. Existing agent benchmarks often evaluate these capabilities in isolation: tool benchmarks test invocation under fixed APIs, memory benchmarks test recall or forgetting, and safety benchmarks test static policy compliance. We argue that personal-agent evaluation requires a different protocol: replaying the same temporal intervention across different persistent user-conditioned states and measuring how failures propagate across agent components. We formalize this requirement as four conditions: explicit temporal intervention, persistent state across the intervention, induced cross-dimensional effects, and variation in user-conditioned state. A focused audit of public benchmark protocols selected by explicit inclusion criteria identifies several close cases. Under our explicitly narrow operationalization, we did not find a protocol in that audited set satisfying all four conditions. This claim is scoped as a focused gap analysis with bounded literature coverage. This position paper proposes a minimal benchmark design and candidate reporting metrics for user-conditioned adaptation. The result is a concrete design requirement for future personal-agent evaluation, with metrics used as reporting tools for that requirement.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that existing agent benchmarks fail to evaluate personal agents holistically because they test capabilities (tools, memory, safety) in isolation. The authors formalize four necessary conditions for personal-agent evaluation—temporal intervention, persistent state, cross-dimensional effects, and user-conditioned state variation—and find no existing public benchmark satisfies all four. They propose a minimal benchmark design and reporting metrics to address this gap.
AI.motivation: Personal agents maintain evolving state across memory, skills, tool configurations, and policy, yet current benchmarks evaluate these dimensions in isolation (tool invocation, memory recall, static policy compliance). This fragmented approach misses how failures propagate across components in persistent, user-conditioned settings, creating a critical evaluation gap that the paper aims to identify and address.
AI.method: The authors formalize four necessary conditions for personal-agent evaluation: (1) explicit temporal intervention, (2) persistent state across the intervention, (3) induced cross-dimensional effects, and (4) variation in user-conditioned state. They then conduct a focused audit of public benchmark protocols selected via explicit inclusion criteria, checking whether any satisfy all four conditions. Finally, they propose a minimal benchmark design with candidate reporting metrics for user-conditioned adaptation.
AI.result: Under the authors' narrow operationalization and bounded literature coverage, no audited public benchmark protocol satisfies all four proposed conditions. The paper identifies several "close cases" but confirms the evaluation gap. This finding is explicitly scoped as a gap analysis rather than an exhaustive survey.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a concrete design requirement for future personal-agent evaluation, positioning the proposed benchmark design and reporting metrics as foundational tools to enable holistic, cross-dimensional assessment of persistent, user-conditioned agents.

title: From Frame-Level Recognition to Event-Level Confirmation: Repair Traces and Runtime Failure Analysis of Public-Space Gesture Interaction
summary:
Public-space gesture interaction is often evaluated as a frame-level recognition problem, but deployed systems expose a different failure boundary. In scenic kiosks, exhibition halls, and service terminals, users experience whether an intended action becomes a stable interaction event, not whether individual hand-landmark frames are correct. We call this the recognition-to-interaction gap.
  This paper analyzes 8 engineering repair records from a scenic-area interactive kiosk project, covering 4 gesture tasks: two-hand bowing, single-hand fist shaking, two-hand catching control, and knowledge-graph node hovering. From these traces, we extract 20 failure instances and organize them into six non-exclusive working failure classes: model-output degeneration, temporal mismatch, geometric-scale instability, coordinate-rendering mismatch, runtime lifecycle failure, and feedback synchronization and recovery failure.
  We further organize recurring repair mechanisms into an event-level runtime abstraction between the hand-landmark model and the interaction task. The contribution is deliberately bounded: a deployment-grounded failure taxonomy, an event-confirmation runtime abstraction, and case-study findings. We do not claim a new recognition model, large-scale user evaluation, or quantified accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: Public-space gesture interaction suffers from a "recognition-to-interaction gap" where frame-level model accuracy fails to predict stable interaction events. Analyzing 8 repair records from a deployed kiosk system across 4 gesture tasks, the authors derive 20 failure instances grouped into 6 failure classes and propose an event-confirmation runtime abstraction to bridge the gap.
AI.motivation: Frame-level recognition accuracy is the dominant evaluation paradigm for gesture interaction, yet real-world deployments reveal that user-perceived failures stem from whether an intended gesture becomes a stable, actionable interaction event — not whether individual hand-landmark frames are classified correctly. This mismatch, termed the "recognition-to-interaction gap," motivates a deployment-grounded investigation of failure modes and repair mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical analysis of 8 engineering repair records from a scenic-area interactive kiosk project involving four gesture tasks: two-hand bowing, single-hand fist shaking, two-hand catching control, and knowledge-graph node hovering. From these traces, 20 failure instances are extracted and organized into six non-exclusive failure classes. Recurring repair patterns are then abstracted into an event-level runtime layer positioned between the hand-landmark model and the interaction task.
AI.result: The analysis yields (1) a deployment-grounded taxonomy of six failure classes: model-output degeneration, temporal mismatch, geometric-scale instability, coordinate-rendering mismatch, runtime lifecycle failure, and feedback synchronization and recovery failure; (2) an event-confirmation runtime abstraction capturing recurring repair mechanisms; and (3) case-study findings illustrating how these failures manifest across different gesture tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper's contribution is deliberately bounded — it offers no new recognition model, large-scale user evaluation, or quantified accuracy gains. Instead, it provides a failure taxonomy and an architectural abstraction that help practitioners anticipate and mitigate the recognition-to-interaction gap in deployed public-space gesture systems.

title: Enhancing SLMs for Sustainable Code Optimization in Radio-Astronomy
summary: Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce and optimize complex code. We investigate the use of LLMs to generate and optimize code for large-scale sciences, focusing on radio astronomy and sustainability. The LOFAR telescope is currently being upgraded, significantly increasing the sky area observed, while simultaneously processing more data faster. However, this is expected to increase the computational requirements 40-fold. This upgrade thus critically depends on rigorous performance optimization of existing software and widespread adoption of accelerators. The code base is very large, making this a daunting task. We therefore investigate and demonstrate an AI-driven approach meant to assist developers in evaluating and optimizing their code, including porting to hardware accelerators. The LOFAR community is committed to sustainable solutions, and needs to achieve these improvements without increasing the energy budget. We thus need to optimize existing codes or port them to accelerators, while making sure that the optimization process itself is also energy efficient. This poses a challenge, since LLMs are energy-intensive. We therefore propose to use Small Language Models (SLMs) instead to limit environmental impact. In this paper, we show how to enhance SLMs through the use of agentic AI. We extend the SLMs in two ways to improve code generation quality and performance: first with a multi-sampling generation strategy and second with incorporating compiler feedback. We demonstrate that multi-sampling SLMs can match or surpass larger single-generation models with fewer computational resources and that feeding compiler output back into the SLMs leads to consistent improvements across all tested models. Our approach is generic, and can also use Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) as well as static and dynamic analysis tools in the code generation pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Small Language Models (SLMs) enhanced with agentic AI—multi-sampling generation and compiler feedback—to generate and optimize scientific code for radio astronomy (LOFAR telescope upgrade), achieving performance comparable to larger models while reducing energy consumption. The approach is generic and extensible with RAG and analysis tools.
AI.motivation: The LOFAR telescope upgrade will increase computational requirements 40-fold, demanding rigorous code optimization and accelerator adoption without increasing the energy budget. Using Large Language Models for this task is energy-intensive, conflicting with sustainability goals. SLMs offer a lower-energy alternative but require enhancement to match LLM code generation quality.
AI.method: The authors enhance SLMs via agentic AI with two mechanisms: (1) a multi-sampling generation strategy that produces multiple candidate solutions from the SLM, and (2) incorporating compiler feedback by feeding compiler output back into the SLM to iteratively refine code. The framework is designed to also accommodate Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and static/dynamic analysis tools in the pipeline.
AI.result: Multi-sampling SLMs can match or surpass larger single-generation models while using fewer computational resources. Feeding compiler output back into the SLMs yields consistent performance improvements across all tested models.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI-enhanced SLMs provide a sustainable, energy-efficient path for automated code optimization in large-scale scientific computing, offering a viable alternative to LLMs for the LOFAR upgrade and similar domains.

title: Legal Nugget Extraction for Granular Retrieval over Long Jurisprudential Texts
summary: Legal retrieval over jurisprudential collections is challenging because court decisions are long, heterogeneous documents whose relevant legal thesis may occupy only a small portion of the text. This paper asks whether legal nuggets, defined as short and self-contained legal theses extracted from source documents, can improve dense retrieval over Brazilian legal collections. We propose a pipeline that extracts nuggets from each document, indexes them with embeddings, retrieves nugget-level evidence, and aggregates the retrieved nuggets back to document-level rankings. We evaluate this approach on four Portuguese legal retrieval benchmarks from the JUA ecosystem, reporting NDCG@10, MAP@10, and MRR@10. Nugget retrieval substantially improves the two jurisprudential datasets: on JUA-Juris, NDCG@10 increases from 0.10265 to 0.20461, and on JurisTCU from 0.20898 to 0.32696. However, it underperforms full-document retrieval on NormasTCU and BR-TaxQA, and an embedding-model ablation shows that strong domain-adapted retrievers can remain better in the full-document setting. The results demonstrate that legal nuggets can be useful for jurisprudence search, especially when queries are formulated as legal theses, but they may not transfer equally well to other legal retrieval scenarios.

AI.tldr: Legal nuggets—short, self-contained theses extracted from long court decisions—significantly boost dense retrieval on Brazilian jurisprudence benchmarks (up to 2× NDCG@10 gains) but underperform on statute/QA datasets, with domain-adapted retrievers sometimes closing the gap in full-document settings.
AI.motivation: Court decisions are long, heterogeneous documents where the legally relevant thesis often occupies only a small portion of text, making full-document dense retrieval suboptimal for jurisprudence search.
AI.method: A pipeline that: (1) extracts legal nuggets (short, self-contained legal theses) from source documents, (2) indexes these nuggets using dense embeddings, (3) retrieves at the nugget level, and (4) aggregates nugget-level rankings back to document-level scores. Evaluated across four Portuguese legal retrieval benchmarks (JUA-Juris, JurisTCU, NormasTCU, BR-TaxQA) with NDCG@10, MAP@10, and MRR@10, including an embedding-model ablation study.
AI.result: Nugget retrieval substantially improved the two jurisprudential datasets: JUA-Juris NDCG@10 rose from 0.10265 to 0.20461; JurisTCU from 0.20898 to 0.32696. However, it underperformed full-document retrieval on NormasTCU and BR-TaxQA. The ablation revealed that strong domain-adapted retrievers can outperform nugget-based approaches in full-document settings.
AI.conclusion: Legal nuggets are beneficial for jurisprudence search, particularly when queries are framed as legal theses, but the technique does not transfer equally well to other legal retrieval scenarios such as statute retrieval or tax QA.

title: TRACE-ROUTER: Task-Consistent and Adaptive Online Routing for Agentic AI
summary: Routing to select large language models (LLMs) with different cost-quality trade-offs has become a fundamental deployment feature of enterprise AI. Existing routers, primarily make independent routing decisions for each LLM call. However, agentic applications execute as long-horizon workflows whose quality is determined only by a delayed, task-level outcome. This mismatch prevents per-call routers from correctly attributing feedback to individual routing decisions. Towards mitigating this, we present TRACE-Router, a task-level routing framework that aligns routing with the unit of supervision. TRACE-Router assigns each task to a model once at admission using a contextual bandit, pins all subsequent LLM calls to the selected backend, and updates its policy using the task's terminal reward, jointly accounting for accuracy and latency. By leveraging delayed task feedback, TRACE-Router learns routing policies that adapt to the workload while avoiding explicit task-complexity estimation. Across three agentic benchmarks, TRACE-Router consistently improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving non-dominated Pareto frontier points. On tau2-Bench, it outperforms latency-matched interpolation between individual models by 7-8 accuracy points, while on Terminal-Bench it achieves 7.1 higher accuracy points than the strongest single model baseline with 36% lower latency.

AI.tldr: TRACE-Router is a task-level routing framework for LLM-based agentic workflows that assigns an entire task to a single model using contextual bandits, learning from delayed task-level feedback to optimize the accuracy-latency trade-off without explicit task-complexity estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routers make per-call routing decisions independently, but agentic applications execute long-horizon workflows where quality is determined by delayed, task-level outcomes. This mismatch prevents correct attribution of feedback to individual routing decisions, motivating a task-level routing approach.
AI.method: TRACE-Router uses a contextual bandit framework: at task admission, it assigns the entire task to one LLM backend and pins all subsequent calls to that model. The policy is updated using terminal task reward (jointly accounting for accuracy and latency) as delayed feedback, enabling the router to adapt to workload characteristics without explicit task-complexity estimation.
AI.result: Across three agentic benchmarks, TRACE-Router achieves non-dominated Pareto frontier points. On tau2-Bench, it outperforms latency-matched interpolation baselines by 7–8 accuracy points. On Terminal-Bench, it achieves 7.1 higher accuracy points than the strongest single model while reducing latency by 36%.
AI.conclusion: Task-level routing with contextual bandits and delayed reward effectively aligns routing supervision with agentic workflow structure, yielding superior accuracy-latency trade-offs compared to per-call routing and single-model baselines.

title: Charting the Moral Universe: Capturing Virtues and Values of Data Visualization Practice
summary: What do we value in our visualizations, and in the people who design them? Despite a growing body of work on critical data visualization, the conception of what it is to do ethical data visualization work can often be narrow (for instance, holding that our ethical duties are discharged merely by avoiding overtly lying or manipulating data), or entangled with potentially problematic implicit value structures (such as the assumption of the objectivity and neutrality of data, and so the designer's role being merely the passive conveying of numbers as efficiently as possible). Yet, what it means to act ethically in data visualization is broad and multifaceted, and the virtues to which we should aspire as data visualization researchers and designers are worth explicating. We conducted an interview study with a broad spectrum of 20 experienced data visualization researchers, practitioners, and data artists to solicit their values and ethical considerations around doing visualization work. We report on a list of 68 values, organized into nine virtue clusters, that we encountered in our interviews. These virtues and values together describe a diverse space of matters of care and concern in data visualization: from the unease around the best use of visualization as a tool for persuasion, to the tightrope that visualization practitioners often walk between their professional responsibilities and their personal moral commitments. The virtues themselves, as well as our interviewees' reflections on ethical practice, offer practitioners, researchers, and educators in data visualization a richer vocabulary for ethical reflection and provide a broader foundation for considering and applying visualization ethics.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on an interview study with 20 data visualization researchers, practitioners, and artists to identify ethical values in visualization work. The authors catalog 68 values organized into nine virtue clusters, providing a richer ethical vocabulary for the visualization community beyond narrow conceptions of ethics (e.g., merely avoiding data manipulation).
AI.motivation: Current discourse on ethical data visualization is often too narrow — reduced to avoiding overt deception or rooted in problematic assumptions about data objectivity and designer neutrality. The authors argue that ethical visualization practice is broader and more multifaceted, warranting a systematic explication of the virtues to which practitioners should aspire.
AI.method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 experienced individuals spanning data visualization researchers, practitioners, and data artists. Through qualitative analysis of interview transcripts, they identified and clustered values and ethical considerations expressed by participants.
AI.result: The study yielded 68 distinct values, organized into nine virtue clusters. These capture a diverse ethical landscape, ranging from tensions around visualization as a persuasive tool to conflicts between professional responsibilities and personal moral commitments.
AI.conclusion: The identified virtues and values, along with interviewees' reflections, provide data visualization practitioners, researchers, and educators with a richer vocabulary for ethical reflection and a broader foundation for applying visualization ethics in practice.

title: Adversarial Prompts for Acceptance Collapse in Speculative Decoding
summary: Lossless acceleration schemes, such as speculative decoding, promise significant inference speedups by relying on dynamic token-level alignment between a draft and a target model. However, this guarantee of semantic equivalence masks a severe operational vulnerability: draft-target alignment can be systematically attacked. In this paper, we introduce ADSD, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first prompt-suffix attack that collapses verifier acceptance by pushing draft probability mass toward tokens the target is unlikely to accept. ADSD uses Soft-Collapse, a verifier-aligned surrogate derived from the asymmetric speculative acceptance rule, together with a target-preservation objective that discourages obvious task corruption. ADSD successfully generates highly effective adversarial suffixes. On the GSM8K dataset, our attack increases the mean sample time by 62.3% while preserving the task quality. We further show that this vulnerability exists across different domains, speculative decoding strategies, and model architectures.

AI.tldr: ADSD is the first prompt-suffix attack targeting speculative decoding, using a surrogate objective (Soft-Collapse) to craft adversarial suffixes that collapse draft-target token alignment, increasing inference time by 62.3% on GSM8K while maintaining task quality.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding promises lossless acceleration through dynamic token-level draft-target alignment, but this alignment creates a security vulnerability: an adversary can systematically manipulate the draft model's probability distribution to cause verifier rejection, undermining the speedup. The authors aim to expose this overlooked operational vulnerability.
AI.method: ADSD crafts adversarial prompt suffixes using two objectives: (1) Soft-Collapse, a verifier-aligned surrogate loss derived from the asymmetric speculative acceptance rule that pushes draft probability mass toward tokens the target model is unlikely to accept; and (2) a target-preservation objective that prevents obvious task corruption. The attack is evaluated across GSM8K, multiple domains, decoding strategies, and model architectures.
AI.result: On the GSM8K dataset, ADSD increases mean sample time by 62.3% while preserving task quality. The vulnerability generalizes across different domains, speculative decoding strategies, and model architectures.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding's draft-target alignment is a systemic vulnerability exploitable via adversarial prompt suffixes. ADSD demonstrates that lossless acceleration guarantees are insufficient against adversarial manipulation, highlighting a critical security consideration for deployed speculative decoding systems.

title: Probing Latent Colombian Identity Inferences in Qwen2.5-7B with Natural Language Autoencoders
summary: Large language models may infer demographic attributes from subtle linguistic cues even when those attributes are not explicitly stated. This pilot study examines whether Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct internally represents Colombian identity, socioeconomic status, or stereotype-related information when processing Colombian-Spanish and English prompts. We use Natural Language Autoencoders (NLA) to verbalize residual-stream activations from layer 20 across four positional quartiles per prompt. Our dataset contains 30 prompts arranged as 15 matched Spanish-English pairs, spanning explicit Colombian cues, implicit Colombian cues, and neutral controls. We report descriptive rates and qualitative evidence rather than statistically powered effects, focusing on whether latent nationality or stereotype representations appear before they are verbalized in the model output. This work connects activation-level interpretability with bias evaluation for underrepresented Spanish varieties.

AI.tldr: This pilot study uses Natural Language Autoencoders to probe Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's residual-stream activations for latent representations of Colombian identity, socioeconomic status, and stereotypes before output generation, using matched Spanish-English prompts.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether large language models internally represent demographic attributes (nationality, socioeconomic status, stereotypes) from subtle linguistic cues in underrepresented Spanish varieties, even when not explicitly stated—bridging activation-level interpretability with bias evaluation.
AI.method: The authors apply Natural Language Autoencoders (NLA) to verbalize residual-stream activations from layer 20 of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct across four positional quartiles per prompt. A dataset of 30 prompts (15 matched Spanish-English pairs) is used, spanning explicit Colombian cues, implicit Colombian cues, and neutral controls. Analysis reports descriptive rates and qualitative evidence.
AI.result: The study reports descriptive rates and qualitative evidence regarding whether latent nationality or stereotype representations appear in internal activations before being verbalized in the model's output. Results focus on the presence and nature of these latent representations rather than statistically powered effects.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an initial connection between activation-level interpretability and bias evaluation for underrepresented Spanish varieties, providing a methodological foundation for detecting pre-output demographic stereotyping in multilingual LLMs.

title: Measuring the Dependency Gap: Diagnosing Inter-Column Fidelity in Tabular Generative Models
summary: Synthetic tabular data is valued for preserving not only each column's marginal distribution but the dependencies between columns -- structure that carries much of the discriminative signal for minority classes in imbalanced domains such as fraud and clinical risk. Yet the metrics most commonly used to certify synthetic tabular data are, we show, largely blind to inter-column dependency: a baseline that models every column independently (and therefore destroys all dependency) is judged indistinguishable from real data by the logistic-regression C2ST, and the pairwise Trend score is only partially sensitive. We introduce a dependency-aware fidelity diagnostic that decomposes a strong classifier two-sample test (XGB-C2ST) into marginal, dependency, and numerical-categorical cross components, anchored between a worst-case fully-factorized reference (all dependency destroyed) and a best-case real-data oracle. Applying it to a state-of-the-art flow-matching generator (TabbyFlow/EF-VFM), we find a real dependency gap that standard metrics miss; destroying dependency outright collapses minority-class utility, and the generator's residual gap carries a smaller, consistent utility cost. We then ask whether this gap reflects a structural limitation of mean-field generative objectives. It does not: consistent with recent recovery results for variational flow matching, the objective is asymptotically exact. Yet the gap is stubborn -- a 16x increase in model capacity does not close it -- pointing to the absence of direct dependency supervision rather than a capacity or structural limit. Consistent with this, and because the residual gap is higher-order, no cheap intervention closes it: not an in-model dependency mechanism, not post-hoc copula correction, and not the 16x capacity increase -- a caution for a field that assumes such fixes help.

AI.tldr: Synthetic tabular data generators are evaluated with metrics blind to inter-column dependencies. The authors introduce a dependency-aware diagnostic (XGB-C2ST decomposition) revealing that state-of-the-art flow-matching models leave a residual dependency gap undetected by standard metrics, which degrades minority-class utility. The gap resists capacity increases and post-hoc fixes, pointing to a lack of direct dependency supervision rather than structural limitations of the objective.
AI.motivation: Standard fidelity metrics for synthetic tabular data (e.g., logistic-regression C2ST, pairwise Trend score) are largely insensitive to inter-column dependencies. In imbalanced domains like fraud detection and clinical risk, these dependencies carry critical discriminative signal for minority classes, making this blindness practically consequential.
AI.method: The authors propose a dependency-aware fidelity diagnostic that decomposes an XGBoost-based classifier two-sample test (XGB-C2ST) into marginal, dependency, and numerical-categorical cross components. The decomposition is anchored between a fully-factorized worst-case baseline (all dependencies destroyed) and a real-data oracle (best case). They apply this to TabbyFlow/EF-VFM, a state-of-the-art flow-matching generator, and systematically test interventions: 16× capacity increase, in-model dependency mechanisms, and post-hoc copula correction.
AI.result: The XGB-C2ST decomposition reveals a real dependency gap that standard metrics miss. Destroying dependencies outright collapses minority-class utility. The generator exhibits a residual dependency gap that carries a smaller but consistent utility cost. The gap persists despite a 16× capacity increase and resists all interventions tested — neither in-model mechanisms nor post-hoc copula correction close it.
AI.conclusion: The residual dependency gap is not due to a structural limitation of the mean-field variational flow-matching objective (which is asymptotically exact) nor insufficient model capacity. Rather, it stems from the absence of direct dependency supervision during training. The failure of cheap interventions serves as a caution against assuming such fixes are effective in synthetic tabular data generation.

title: Transferable Latency Prediction for Fast LLM Screening on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
summary:
Accurate latency prediction is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) on heterogeneous edge devices, where inference latency is affected by model architecture, prompt behavior, runtime backend, hardware utilization, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal variation. This paper presents a runtime-aware latency prediction framework for deployment-oriented LLM selection. The framework represents each inference request as a hardware-runtime-model-prompt configuration, separates inference into prefill and decode phases, and adaptively fuses static descriptors with dynamic hardware telemetry through a gated prediction model.
  We evaluate the framework using Pixel mobile devices and validate the profiling pipeline on Jetson Nano, Orange Pi 5 Pro, and an RTX 3090-class GPU platform. On Pixel 8, the full predictor improves total-latency R-squared from 0.953 to 0.960 and decode-latency R-squared from 0.957 to 0.973 over a static-only baseline. On Pixel 8 Pro, it improves prefill-latency R-squared from -1.383 to 0.966. For cross-device transfer, calibration improves Pixel 8 Pro to Pixel 8 total-latency R-squared from -0.974 to 0.940 and decode-latency R-squared from -1.085 to 0.927. Heterogeneous profiling further shows that latency is highly device- and runtime-dependent: the same SmolLM2 model family reaches 8.42 tokens/s on Orange Pi 5 Pro but 64.38 tokens/s on an RTX 3090-class GPU. These results demonstrate that runtime-aware prediction with lightweight calibration can reduce profiling cost and support latency-aware LLM deployment across heterogeneous edge platforms.

AI.tldr: A runtime-aware latency prediction framework for LLMs on heterogeneous edge devices that fuses static descriptors with dynamic hardware telemetry, achieving significant R-squared improvements over static-only baselines, with lightweight calibration enabling effective cross-device transfer.
AI.motivation: Accurate latency prediction for LLM inference on heterogeneous edge devices is challenging due to multiple interacting factors: model architecture, prompt behavior, runtime backend, hardware utilization, DVFS, and thermal variation. Existing static-only approaches fail to capture these dynamic runtime effects, and exhaustive profiling across all device-model configurations is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: A runtime-aware latency prediction framework that: (1) represents each inference request as a hardware-runtime-model-prompt configuration, (2) separates inference into prefill and decode phases, and (3) adaptively fuses static descriptors with dynamic hardware telemetry using a gated prediction model. Cross-device transfer is enabled via lightweight calibration.
AI.result: On Pixel 8, the full predictor improves total-latency R² from 0.953→0.960 and decode-latency R² from 0.957→0.973. On Pixel 8 Pro, prefill-latency R² improves from -1.383→0.966. Cross-device calibration improves Pixel 8 Pro→Pixel 8 total-latency R² from -0.974→0.940 and decode-latency R² from -1.085→0.927. Heterogeneous profiling reveals dramatic device-dependent throughput: SmolLM2 achieves 8.42 tokens/s (Orange Pi 5 Pro) vs. 64.38 tokens/s (RTX 3090-class).
AI.conclusion: Runtime-aware prediction with lightweight calibration substantially reduces profiling cost and enables latency-aware LLM deployment across heterogeneous edge platforms, with the gated fusion of static and dynamic features proving essential for accurate cross-device prediction.

title: When Model Release Meets Model Reuse: Producer-Consumer Misalignment in Hugging Face
summary: Pre-trained Language Models (PTLMs) are increasingly reused as dependencies in modern software systems, even though prior work has documented persistent structural problems in PTLM supply chains, such as inconsistent release practices, incomplete metadata, and divergence between Hugging Face and GitHub repositories. One previously unexplored angle on these problems is that misalignment between PTLM producers' release practices and consumers' model reuse needs may explain several of these challenges, yet the human expectations, processes and interactions underneath this misalignment have never been studied. As such, we conducted the first dual-perspective survey of 50 Hugging Face producers and 95 GitHub consumers to examine producer-consumer misalignments across four AI supply chain dimensions: model discovery, documentation practices, lineage tracing, and model governance adoption. We find that, although producers and consumers rely on the same documentation artifacts, they disagree on where critical metadata should be recorded. Even though 27.9% of producers and 31.4% of consumers trace lineage beyond the immediate parent model, producers primarily trace model lineage for provenance and reproducibility, whereas consumers are mainly driven by quality and reliability concerns. Furthermore, producers believe that governance mechanisms that streamline model release would have the greatest positive impact, whereas consumers prioritize documentation and dependency transparency. These findings highlight opportunities to improve model documentation conventions, lineage visibility, and governance support in PTLM supply chains.

AI.tldr: A dual-perspective survey of 50 Hugging Face producers and 95 GitHub consumers reveals significant misalignments in how PTLM supply chain actors approach model discovery, documentation practices, lineage tracing, and governance — with producers and consumers disagreeing on metadata placement, diverging in their motivations for lineage tracing, and prioritizing different governance improvements.
AI.motivation: Prior work has documented structural problems in PTLM supply chains (inconsistent releases, incomplete metadata, Hugging Face–GitHub divergence), but the human factors — specifically misalignment between producer release practices and consumer reuse needs — remain unexplored. This study fills that gap by examining the expectations, processes, and interactions underlying these persistent challenges.
AI.method: The authors conducted the first dual-perspective survey study with 50 Hugging Face model producers and 95 GitHub model consumers, examining misalignments across four AI supply chain dimensions: model discovery, documentation practices, lineage tracing, and model governance adoption.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) producers and consumers rely on the same documentation artifacts but disagree on where critical metadata should reside; (2) 27.9% of producers and 31.4% of consumers trace lineage beyond the immediate parent model, but producers do so for provenance/reproducibility while consumers prioritize quality/reliability; (3) producers favor governance mechanisms that streamline model release, whereas consumers prioritize documentation and dependency transparency.
AI.conclusion: The identified producer-consumer misalignments present actionable opportunities to improve model documentation conventions, lineage visibility, and governance support in PTLM supply chains, ultimately fostering more reliable and transparent AI software ecosystems.

title: PinEqualizer: Full Funnel Content Exploration and Debiasing System at Pinterest
summary: In this paper, we propose a new solution for addressing the content cold-start problem in industry-scale search and recommender systems. Compared to prior approaches, we have made the following new contributions: 1) our solution spans the entire multi-stage funnel and generalizes well for both search and recommendation surfaces, 2) our solution reduces bias favoring existing content, allowing more accurate model prediction across content types and reducing short-term tradeoffs associated with high volumes of explicit content exploration, 3) our solution is evaluated with a scalable measurement framework that enables fast short-term experimentation while validating long-term impact. We have iteratively built and successfully deployed this new system at Pinterest in the past two years and observed significant improvements in fresh content exploration, overall user engagement, and content ecosystem health.

AI.tldr: Pinterest proposes a multi-stage solution to the content cold-start problem that spans both search and recommendation systems, reduces bias toward existing content, and is validated through a scalable measurement framework—demonstrating improvements in fresh content exploration, user engagement, and ecosystem health over two years of deployment.
AI.motivation: Content cold-start is a persistent challenge in industry-scale search and recommender systems, where new content lacks sufficient interaction signals for accurate modeling. Existing approaches suffer from bias favoring established content, require costly explicit exploration with short-term tradeoffs, and fail to generalize across different surfaces (search vs. recommendation) or across the full multi-stage funnel.
AI.method: The authors propose a holistic solution that operates across the entire multi-stage retrieval/ranking funnel and generalizes to both search and recommendation surfaces. Key techniques include debiasing mechanisms that reduce favoritism toward existing content, enabling more equitable model predictions across content types and mitigating the short-term costs of explicit exploration. The system is paired with a scalable measurement framework designed for fast short-term experimentation while reliably estimating long-term impact.
AI.result: Deployed iteratively at Pinterest over two years, the system yielded significant improvements in fresh content exploration, overall user engagement, and content ecosystem health.
AI.conclusion: A unified, multi-stage, debiased approach to cold-start—coupled with a scalable experimentation framework—can effectively boost fresh content discovery and long-term platform health without sacrificing short-term metrics, as demonstrated in a large-scale industrial deployment.

title: Bespoke Visual Assistance: What and How do Blind and Low-Vision People Create with Agentic Programming?
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures. To be presented at The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26)
summary: AI-powered assistive technologies have long supported blind and low vision (BLV) people in everyday tasks, but they are general-purpose and often fall short of meeting complex, individualized, in-situ accessibility needs. Though agentic programming tools, like GitHub Copilot, have the potential to bridge this gap by lowering the technical barriers to building personal AT using natural language, the practical applicability of this creation paradigm has been unknown. We address this knowledge gap through a two-phase longitudinal co-design study with five tech-savvy BLV users using ProgramAT, an agentic programming tool that supports the creation, iteration, and testing of camera-based AT. Overall, co-designers created over 37 tools, with some addressing needs unmet by any existing commercial AT such as identifying Uber rides or interpreting hand gestures. Qualitative feedback from our co-designers and analysis of development logs surface BLV strategies for tool creation, along with key challenges including model capability limits, specification conflicts, and barriers to successful creation. We discuss recommendations to provide appropriate conversational scaffolding, community tool sharing capabilities, and support for specialized models and personal datasets for future agentic programming environments to empower BLV users to create bespoke visual assistance for themselves.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal co-design study with five tech-savvy blind and low vision users exploring ProgramAT, an agentic programming tool for creating custom camera-based assistive technologies. Participants built 37+ bespoke tools addressing needs unmet by commercial AT, revealing key strategies, challenges, and design recommendations for future agentic programming environments.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-powered assistive technologies for BLV people are general-purpose and fail to address complex, individualized, in-situ accessibility needs. While agentic programming tools like GitHub Copilot could lower barriers for BLV users to create personal AT using natural language, the practical feasibility and dynamics of this paradigm have remained unexplored.
AI.method: A two-phase longitudinal co-design study with five tech-savvy BLV participants using ProgramAT, a custom agentic programming tool enabling creation, iteration, and testing of camera-based assistive technologies through natural language interaction. Data collected includes development logs and qualitative feedback.
AI.result: Co-designers created over 37 custom tools, some addressing needs with no existing commercial solutions (e.g., identifying Uber rides, interpreting hand gestures). The study surfaced BLV-specific tool creation strategies alongside key challenges: model capability limitations, specification conflicts, and barriers to successful creation.
AI.conclusion: Future agentic programming environments for BLV users should incorporate appropriate conversational scaffolding, community tool-sharing capabilities, and support for specialized models and personal datasets to empower bespoke visual assistance creation.

title: Protocol-Level Attacks on Agentic Commerce Platforms: A Cross-Platform Taxonomy, AIP-Bench, and Unified Defense
summary: Agentic commerce platforms let AI agents autonomously discover services, move payments, and wield user credentials on their users' behalf, and they already handle real money.
