Their security has so far been studied almost entirely at the level of the AI model, through prompt injection and misalignment. We show that the more consequential risks lie one layer down, in the protocol between agents and commerce services. There, vulnerabilities are structural : exploitation is deterministic and ndependent of which model an agent runs, so no model improvement removes them. Across three leading platforms we identify 33 such vulnerabilities, each succeeding deterministically regardless of the deployed model, at a 100% attack-success rate (ASR) wherever live-measured. The same failure modes recur across independently built codebases, a systemic pattern rather than isolated bugs. Three of them chain into an end-to-end payment hijack. We contribute a taxonomy separating these structural attacks from model-dependent semantic ones. We also build two artifacts: AIP-Bench (Agent Interaction Protocol Benchmark), to our knowledge the first deterministic benchmark for agentic commerce security, and PCAT (Protocol-level Commerce Agent Trust), a platform-agnostic defense that drives the structural attack-success rate to zero for four of the five structural classes (RC-1, RC-2, RC-4, RC-5), with RC-3 (observable credential channels) reduced to warn-only, without modifying any platform. Agentic commerce must be secured at the protocol layer, not only the model.

AI.tldr: Agentic commerce platforms face critical security vulnerabilities at the protocol layer between AI agents and commerce services—not just the model layer. The authors identify 33 structural vulnerabilities across three platforms with 100% attack-success rates, demonstrate an end-to-end payment hijack, and provide a taxonomy plus two artifacts (AIP-Bench and PCAT) to address these flaws.
AI.motivation: Prior security research on agentic commerce has focused almost exclusively on model-level threats like prompt injection and misalignment. The authors argue that protocol-layer vulnerabilities are more consequential because they are structural (platform-independent), deterministic (not probabilistic), and cannot be fixed by model improvements—yet they have been largely ignored.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyzed three leading agentic commerce platforms at the protocol layer. They identified recurring vulnerability patterns across independently built codebases, measured attack-success rates live, and classified vulnerabilities into a taxonomy separating structural (protocol-level) attacks from semantic (model-dependent) ones. They also built AIP-Bench, the first deterministic benchmark for agentic commerce security, and PCAT, a platform-agnostic defense.
AI.result: Thirty-three structural vulnerabilities were identified across three platforms, all achieving 100% attack-success rate (ASR) regardless of the deployed AI model. Three vulnerabilities chained into a complete end-to-end payment hijack. The PCAT defense reduced structural ASR to zero for four of five structural classes (RC-1, RC-2, RC-4, RC-5), with RC-3 reduced to warn-only, without modifying any underlying platform.
AI.conclusion: Agentic commerce must be secured at the protocol layer, not only at the model layer. Structural vulnerabilities are systemic—recurring across independently developed platforms—and model-agnostic improvements cannot eliminate them. Protocol-level defenses like PCAT are both necessary and demonstrably effective.

title: Khondo: A Multimodal Benchmark for Document Packet Splitting of Bangla Forms
summary: Document packets, multiple documents concatenated into a single file, are common in government and administrative workflows, yet splitting them into their constituent documents is difficult, especially for low-resource languages. We introduce Khondo (Bangla for split/segment), the first benchmark for document packet splitting on Bangladeshi government forms. Unlike prior English and OCR-text-based datasets, Khondo is bilingual (Bangla--English) and vision-native; where models operate directly on page images. It spans five concatenation schemes, from sequential to fully shuffled, across 14 administrative domains, with ground-truth boundaries, domain types, and page order. Zero-shot evaluation of MLLMs shows they cluster pages into their source documents fairly well but struggle in restoring the original page order once shuffled. To isolate what drives this difficulty, we run two controlled analyses, varying the prompt instruction and then the packet language. Both primarily affect ordering rather than clustering: (a) explicit page-order instructions are necessary but insufficient, and (b) English packets are ordered more reliably than Bangla, making page arrangement the dominant challenge and language a secondary but consistent factor. Khondo establishes page-order reconstruction as a key open problem in vision-based, low-resource document understanding, and provides a controlled benchmark for measuring progress toward solving it. Our dataset and code is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mausul/khondo

AI.tldr: Khondo is the first vision-native, bilingual (Bangla-English) benchmark for splitting concatenated government form packets, revealing that MLLMs cluster pages well but struggle with page-order reconstruction, especially in Bangla.
AI.motivation: Document packets (multiple documents concatenated into one file) are prevalent in government/administrative workflows, but splitting them is challenging, particularly for low-resource languages. Prior datasets are English-only and OCR-text-based, leaving a gap for vision-native, low-resource language evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Khondo, a benchmark of Bangladeshi government forms spanning 14 administrative domains with five concatenation schemes (sequential to fully shuffled). They evaluate MLLMs in a zero-shot setting and conduct two controlled analyses: varying prompt instruction specificity (with/without explicit page-order instructions) and varying packet language (Bangla vs. English).
AI.result: MLLMs cluster pages into source documents reasonably well but fail significantly at restoring original page order after shuffling. Explicit page-order instructions are necessary but insufficient for ordering. English packets are ordered more reliably than Bangla ones, making page arrangement the dominant challenge and language a secondary but consistent factor.
AI.conclusion: Page-order reconstruction is identified as a key open problem in vision-based, low-resource document understanding. Khondo provides a controlled benchmark for measuring progress on this task.

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo Initialization for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
summary: This paper explores the efficacy of quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) weight initialization for meta-reinforcement learning within modern benchmark environments. Various sampling methods are used to bound a population-based search and aggregate an optimal prior from a baseline set of tasks. The QMC meta-priors show improvements in training convergence compared to modern orthogonal (SB3) defaults when extrapolated to similar unseen continuous control environments. In dissimilar tasks, the orthogonal orientation was globally superior for an unbiased search.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) weight initialization for meta-reinforcement learning, showing that QMC-based meta-priors improve training convergence over orthogonal defaults in similar continuous control tasks, while orthogonal initialization remains superior for dissimilar, unbiased search scenarios.
AI.motivation: Standard weight initialization schemes (e.g., orthogonal defaults in SB3) may not optimally leverage prior knowledge across a distribution of related tasks. The authors aim to determine whether QMC-based population sampling can construct better meta-priors that accelerate meta-RL convergence.
AI.method: The authors employ quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) sampling methods to bound a population-based search, aggregating an optimal prior weight initialization from a baseline set of tasks. These QMC-derived meta-priors are then evaluated in modern continuous control benchmark environments, comparing convergence against standard orthogonal initialization (SB3 defaults). Performance is assessed under both similar (extrapolated) and dissimilar task distributions.
AI.result: QMC meta-priors yield improved training convergence over orthogonal defaults when evaluated on similar unseen continuous control tasks. However, for dissimilar tasks, the orthogonal initialization proves globally superior, providing a more unbiased search.
AI.conclusion: QMC-based meta-priors offer a valuable inductive bias for meta-RL when task distributions share structural similarity, but orthogonal initialization remains the safer, more general-purpose choice for diverse or dissimilar task sets. The choice of initialization strategy should thus be conditioned on the expected task similarity.

title: AgentKVShift: Efficient KV Cache Reuse for Agentic Memory Systems
summary: Memory-augmented LLM agents maintain context across hundreds of interactions through agentic memory systems that actively curate retrieved content with LLM-generated metadata such as summaries, keywords, and tags. From an inference cost standpoint, every retrieval triggers a full re-encoding of these structured memory units into Key-Value (KV) states, which dominates prefill latency. Existing training-free KV reuse methods mitigate this by selectively recomputing a small fraction of tokens, but were designed for RAG-style raw passages and degrade on structured agentic memories. We present AgentKVShift, a training-free, probe-guided KV residual correction method that operates per retrieved memory unit. One of the crucial insights we demonstrate is that the per-memory KV reuse residual decomposes into a shared memory-level offset plus small token-wise fluctuations. Estimating this offset from a small probe set allows us to correct every reused token by a single weighted correction. Unlike prior reuse methods which decide which tokens to recompute and leave the rest of the cache stale, AgentKVShift also corrects the tokens it does not recompute, turning the refresh budget into useful signal across the entire chunk. Across four open-source LLMs spanning 3B to 32B parameters and two long-horizon agentic memory benchmarks (long-term dialogue and agentic applications), AgentKVShift achieves near full recompute performance while refreshing only 10-30% of the cache, outperforming baselines at the same recompute ratio. It requires up to 5x lower recompute to reach this near-full performance, which prior reuse methods only attain at 45-55% refresh. In this regime, AgentKVShift delivers prefill speedups of 2-3.5x over no-KV-reuse on a single A100. AgentKVShift orthogonally composes with KV cache quantization, retaining over 2x the F1 of prior reuse methods under aggressive 2- and 4-bit settings.

AI.tldr: AgentKVShift is a training-free KV cache reuse method for memory-augmented LLM agents that applies probe-guided residual corrections per retrieved memory unit, achieving near full-recompute performance while refreshing only 10–30% of tokens, yielding 2–3.5× prefill speedups.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented LLM agents use structured metadata (summaries, keywords, tags) to curate retrieved content. Every retrieval triggers full re-encoding of these memory units into KV states, dominating prefill latency. Existing training-free KV reuse methods (designed for RAG-style raw passages) degrade on structured agentic memories because they selectively recompute only a fraction of tokens while leaving the rest of the cache stale.
AI.method: AgentKVShift operates per retrieved memory unit. The key insight is that the per-memory KV reuse residual decomposes into a shared memory-level offset plus small token-wise fluctuations. A small probe set estimates this offset, which is then used to correct every reused token via a single weighted correction. Crucially, unlike prior methods that only decide which tokens to recompute, AgentKVShift also corrects tokens it does not recompute, converting the refresh budget into useful signal across the entire chunk.
AI.result: Across four open-source LLMs (3B–32B parameters) and two long-horizon agentic memory benchmarks, AgentKVShift achieves near full-recompute performance while refreshing only 10–30% of the cache. It requires up to 5× lower recompute to reach near-full performance compared to prior methods (which need 45–55% refresh). This yields 2–3.5× prefill speedups over no-KV-reuse on a single A100. It also composes orthogonally with KV cache quantization, retaining over 2× the F1 of prior reuse methods under 2- and 4-bit settings.
AI.conclusion: AgentKVShift demonstrates that per-memory KV reuse residuals have exploitable structure (shared offset + token-wise noise), enabling a probe-guided correction approach that significantly outperforms prior selective-recompute methods on structured agentic memories, with strong compatibility with KV cache quantization.

title: How Do AI Coding Agents Contribute to Software Development? an Empirical Study of Agentic Pull Requests
summary: Recent advances in large language models and their rapid adoption across software engineering tasks have made Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding agents an integral component of modern software development workflows. While developers increasingly benefit from these coding agents, their impact on software quality remains insufficiently understood. In particular, how agentic contributions evolve across the software development lifecycle has not been thoroughly investigated. This study aims to characterize agentic pull requests (PR) in comparison to human generated PRs and to examine how their properties change across different stages of the development lifecycle. Using the AIDev dataset, we first analyze how differences in merge rates between agentic and human generated PRs vary over time. We then identify the types of development tasks where AI coding agents are predominantly applied and investigate how these task distributions evolve across development quarters. Finally, we compare a set of key characteristics of agentic and human generated PRs, focusing on their implications for software quality and their temporal dynamics. Overall, our findings provide an empirical and longitudinal perspective on the role of AI coding agents in software development, offering a more nuanced understanding of their benefits and limitations in real-world practices.

AI.tldr: This study provides a longitudinal empirical analysis comparing AI-generated (agentic) pull requests to human-generated ones across the software development lifecycle, examining merge rates, task distributions, and quality-related characteristics to understand how AI coding agents impact software quality in real-world development practices.
AI.motivation: Despite the rapid adoption of AI coding agents in software engineering, their impact on software quality remains poorly understood. Specifically, no prior work has thoroughly investigated how agentic contributions evolve across different stages of the software development lifecycle, leaving a gap in understanding the temporal dynamics of AI-assisted development.
AI.method: Using the AIDev dataset, the authors conduct a comparative analysis between agentic and human-generated pull requests across three dimensions: (1) merge rate differences over time, (2) predominant development task types where AI agents are applied and their quarterly distribution shifts, and (3) key PR characteristics related to software quality, all examined through a longitudinal lens.
AI.result: The paper reports empirical findings on how agentic and human PRs differ in merge rates across development quarters, which task categories AI coding agents are most frequently employed for, and how temporal dynamics affect key quality-related PR characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The study offers a nuanced, empirical, and longitudinal perspective on AI coding agents' role in software development, delineating both benefits and limitations. It underscores that agentic contributions are not static but evolve across the development lifecycle, which has practical implications for how teams integrate AI tools into their workflows.

title: From Grasping to Speaking: Generative AI-Based Environment-Grounded VR Communication Training for Autistic Individuals
summary: Autistic individuals often face barriers in workplace communication, where soft skills are embedded within ongoing tasks and surrounding environment context, not in isolated verbal exchange. Recent work has introduced LLM-driven agents into VR-based communication training and proposed prompting schemas that let agents generate dialogue grounded in the VR environment and the user's hand-based interactions. Building on this work, we explore how different levels of environmental grounding influence the training experience of autistic trainees and job coaches. We conducted an exploratory study with 9 autistic trainees and 7 job coaches across three modalities: conversation-only (C), conversation with environmental objects (C+O), and conversation with objects and grasp interactions (C+O+G). Usability and workload were comparable across modalities, while both trainees and coaches preferred the more interactive and environment-grounded condition (C+O+G). Participants viewed C+O+G as helpful for sustaining engagement and integrating communication practice into task performance. We discuss design considerations for more flexible, interactive, and workplace-relevant VR communication training for autistic individuals.

AI.tldr: The study explores how varying degrees of environmental grounding in VR-based communication training affect autistic trainees and job coaches. Across three modalities—conversation-only, conversation with objects, and conversation with objects plus grasp interactions—the most interactive condition (C+O+G) was preferred for engagement and integrating communication with task performance, despite comparable usability and workload across all conditions.
AI.motivation: Autistic individuals face workplace communication challenges because soft skills are embedded in environmental context and ongoing tasks rather than isolated verbal exchanges. Prior work introduced LLM-driven agents in VR for communication training with environment-grounded prompting, but it was unclear how different levels of environmental grounding influence the training experience.
AI.method: An exploratory study was conducted with 9 autistic trainees and 7 job coaches comparing three modalities: conversation-only (C), conversation with environmental objects (C+O), and conversation with objects and grasp interactions (C+O+G). Usability, workload, and participant preferences were assessed across conditions.
AI.result: Usability and workload were comparable across all three modalities. Both trainees and job coaches preferred the C+O+G condition, finding it more engaging and effective for integrating communication practice into task performance.
AI.conclusion: Greater environmental grounding (C+O+G) enhances engagement and contextual integration of communication training without increasing usability burden or workload. The authors offer design considerations for more flexible, interactive, workplace-relevant VR communication training systems for autistic individuals.

title: ToolGuardian: Declarative Security for AI Agent-Tool Interactions
summary:
LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools, expanding capability while creating a new security boundary: third-party tools may appear benign at the interface level while embedding unsafe behavior in implementation. Existing defenses rely on weak metadata, collapse characterization and policy judgment into a single decision, or use heuristic/LLM enforcement that lacks deterministic, auditable reasoning over task context and multi-tool composition.
  This paper presents ToolGuardian, a policy-driven framework for securing agent-tool interactions through pre-admission vetting and task-aware runtime authorization. ToolGuardian uses progressive characterization to convert evidence into structured facts: descriptions capture declared intent, system-call traces expose coarse behavior, mock execution reveals observed effects, and source analysis identifies latent behavior. ToolGuardian's core contribution is an Answer Set Programming (ASP)-based declarative policy layer that reasons explicitly over capabilities, effects, task context, and composition. We compare ASP against heuristic and LLM-based policy realizations using identical inputs and output contracts.
  We evaluate ToolGuardian on 16 MCP-style tools, including 8 malicious variants derived from real open-source tools, and 20 runtime scenarios. For vetting, ASP reaches a deny-class F1 of 0.86 and 88% accuracy using description, syscall, and observed-effect evidence. For runtime authorization, fully specified realizations classify all scenarios correctly, while ablations show that removing compositional and conformance rules substantially degrades performance.

AI.tldr: ToolGuardian is a policy-driven framework that secures LLM agent-tool interactions using pre-admission vetting and task-aware runtime authorization, with an ASP-based declarative policy layer that reasons over capabilities, effects, task context, and multi-tool composition, outperforming heuristic and LLM-based baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly use external tools, but third-party tools can embed unsafe behavior hidden behind benign interfaces. Existing defenses are inadequate: they rely on weak metadata, conflate characterization with policy decisions, or lack deterministic, auditable reasoning over task context and tool composition.
AI.method: ToolGuardian employs progressive characterization (descriptions, syscall traces, mock execution, source analysis) to produce structured facts, then uses an Answer Set Programming (ASP) declarative policy layer for explicit reasoning over capabilities, effects, task context, and composition. ASP is compared against heuristic and LLM-based policy realizations.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 MCP-style tools (8 malicious variants) and 20 runtime scenarios: ASP vetting achieves deny-class F1 of 0.86 and 88% accuracy using description, syscall, and observed-effect evidence. Fully specified runtime authorization classifies all scenarios correctly; ablations removing compositional and conformance rules significantly degrade performance.
AI.conclusion: The ASP-based declarative policy approach provides deterministic, auditable, and high-accuracy security decisions for agent-tool interactions, with compositional and conformance reasoning proving essential to robust performance.

title: Agentic Evaluation of Copyright Law Compliance
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform commercial tasks that involve retrieving external content such as images and, where appropriate, reproducing that content. LLM agents should comply with the law, including copyright law. Presently, however, we lack adequate frameworks to assess whether they do so in practice. To that end, we introduce \textbf{Copyright-Bench}, a benchmark designed to evaluate \textit{LLM agents' compliance with} \emph{copyright law}. Copyright-Bench is comprised of realistic commercial tasks---website development, merchandise design, and pitch deck production---that involve agents selecting between public-domain content (the use of which is \textit{legal}) and copyrighted content (the use of which is \textit{infringing} in this setting).The evaluation introduces prompt variations that simulate different user preferences, as well as time pressure.Comparing state-of-the-art LLM agents against a human baseline, we find that: (1) agents select copyrighted works despite the availability of public-domain alternatives; and (2) for open-weights models, violation rates increase in response to certain user preferences and simulated time pressure.

AI.tldr: Copyright-Bench is a benchmark evaluating whether LLM agents comply with copyright law in realistic commercial tasks (web development, merchandise design, pitch decks). Tests reveal that state-of-the-art agents frequently select copyrighted content over available public-domain alternatives, and open-weights models show increased infringement under certain user preferences and time pressure.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in commercial tasks involving retrieval and reproduction of external content (e.g., images), yet no adequate frameworks exist to assess whether these agents comply with copyright law in practice.
AI.method: The authors construct Copyright-Bench, comprising three realistic commercial tasks: website development, merchandise design, and pitch deck production. Agents must choose between public-domain (legal) and copyrighted (infringing) content. Prompt variations simulate different user preferences, and time pressure is introduced as an additional variable. State-of-the-art LLM agents are compared against a human baseline.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) LLM agents select copyrighted works despite the availability of public-domain alternatives; (2) for open-weights models, copyright violation rates increase under certain user preferences and simulated time pressure.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents exhibit systematic non-compliance with copyright law in commercial task settings, with open-weights models showing particular vulnerability to situational factors like user preferences and time pressure. This highlights a significant gap in legal compliance that warrants attention from developers and policymakers.

title: Toward Goal-Agnostic Joint-Embedding Predictive Control of Partial Differential Equations
comment: Associated code will be open sourced alongside the V2 submission
summary: We present a goal-agnostic control framework for partial differential equations (PDEs) built around a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). The small 2D ViT encoder and action-conditioned latent dynamics are trained offline without a reward or downstream goal, frozen, and reused by a model-predictive path integral (MPPI) controller. We find that when available, the control objective is better applied to an explicit physical observable (provided injectivity) than to minimizing raw Euclidean distance ($L^2$) in the learned latent space. For a learned linear kinetic-energy (KE) probe on frozen latent rollouts we can reproduce held-out trajectories with $R^2=0.989$, while requiring no change to the underlying world model. On the PDE Control Gym 2D Navier--Stokes benchmark, using KE-probe planning improves the matched 50-episode native reward from $-12.08\pm0.86$ for latent-$L^2$ planning to $-10.90\pm0.91$ (95\% CI), while lowering last-quarter velocity-field RMSE from $0.0765$ to $0.0692$. Across three intentionally withheld, dissimilar, aperiodic targets, KE planning lowers late field RMSE by $53\%$ relative to latent-$L^2$ planning ($0.0220$ versus $0.0469$), winning all 30 paired episodes. The same frozen model also supports controls targeting stabilization around a steady configuration via direct regulation of KE achieving $2.7\%$ mean relative error. While the latent probe is brittle to measurement noise and missing pixels, we believe the results support the claim that latent dynamics can remain both dynamic and goal-agnostic while calibrated observables (granted they guarantee unique continuation) may be a better objective for state control

AI.tldr: A frozen, goal-agnostic JEPA-based world model for 2D Navier–Stokes PDE control is paired with MPPI; planning against a learned kinetic-energy probe significantly outperforms latent L² planning in trajectory matching and stabilization, but the latent probe is brittle to sensor degradation.
AI.motivation: Standard model-based RL for PDE control ties the world model to a specific reward, limiting reusability. The authors investigate whether a frozen, goal-agnostic latent dynamics model (JEPA) can be repurposed for diverse control tasks and whether control objectives are better applied in a physically meaningful observable space rather than raw latent space.
AI.method: A small 2D ViT encoder and action-conditioned latent dynamics are trained offline via a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) without any reward signal. The model is then frozen. Control is performed by model-predictive path integral (MPPI) optimization. Two planning objective variants are compared: (1) minimizing L² distance in the learned latent space, and (2) minimizing error against a separately learned linear kinetic-energy (KE) probe applied to latent rollouts. The framework is evaluated on the PDE Control Gym 2D Navier–Stokes benchmark with trajectory following, aperiodic target tracking, and steady-state stabilization tasks.
AI.result: The KE probe reconstructs held-out trajectories with R²=0.989. On the standard benchmark, KE-probe planning improves native reward from −12.08±0.86 (latent-L²) to −10.90±0.91 and reduces last-quarter velocity-field RMSE from 0.0765 to 0.0692. On withheld aperiodic targets, KE planning reduces late field RMSE by 53% (0.0220 vs 0.0469) and wins all 30 paired episodes. For stabilization, direct KE regulation achieves 2.7% mean relative error. However, the latent probe is brittle under measurement noise and missing pixels.
AI.conclusion: Goal-agnostic latent dynamics models can effectively serve multiple downstream control tasks when frozen, but control objectives should be applied to calibrated physical observables (with injectivity/unique continuation guarantees) rather than raw latent L² distance, which yields inferior performance.

title: TILT: Improving Compositional Generation in Diffusion Models with a Model-Intrinsic Reward
summary: Recent advances in powerful text-to-image generation models have made it increasingly important to develop test-time methods that modify the sampling trajectory to produce images more faithful to complex compositional prompts. We present TILT, a training-free framework for compositional text-to-image generation via test-time reward alignment. We interpret compositional failures as overlap modes between joint and single-concept distributions, and define a reward that favors samples where all concepts are jointly present. This reward is intrinsic to the base model and does not require any external supervision or reward models. This yields a KL-constrained objective with a closed-form tilted target distribution and principled guiding steps for diffusion sampling. The interaction of concept distributions together with the above reward naturally leads to two different guidance strategies while a hybrid approach that balances their respective benefits produces stronger performance. Experiments on prompts from T2ICompBench show that our method improves compositional alignment while preserving image quality compared to previous baselines.

AI.tldr: TILT is a training-free framework that improves compositional text-to-image generation by defining an intrinsic reward favoring joint concept presence, leading to a principled KL-constrained diffusion sampling strategy with hybrid guidance.
AI.motivation: Powerful text-to-image models often fail on complex compositional prompts (e.g., multiple objects with specific attributes/relations). The authors frame these failures as the model collapsing to single-concept distributions rather than the desired joint distribution, and aim to address this at test time without external supervision.
AI.method: The authors interpret compositional failures as overlap modes between joint and single-concept distributions. They define an intrinsic reward (no external reward model needed) that favors samples where all concepts are jointly present. This yields a KL-constrained optimization objective with a closed-form tilted target distribution. The interaction of concept distributions with the reward naturally produces two guidance strategies, which are combined into a hybrid approach balancing their respective benefits during diffusion sampling.
AI.result: Experiments on T2ICompBench prompts demonstrate that TILT improves compositional alignment while preserving image quality compared to previous baselines.
AI.conclusion: TILT offers a principled, training-free method for improving compositional faithfulness in text-to-image generation by leveraging intrinsic rewards and KL-constrained tilted sampling, with a hybrid guidance strategy that outperforms existing approaches.

title: No Snake Oil: Verifying Python Package Builds
summary: Python has become the default language for interacting with AI, with packages being distributed through registries like the Python Package Index (PyPI). This creates a need to analyse supply chains comprising such packages. One such analysis is to rebuild packages in order to identify compromised builds injecting malware. Independent rebuilds in hardened environments have the added advantage that they can generate and record provenance in order to increase the trustworthiness of packages. Two tools that are designed to automate such rebuilds and run them at scale are macaron and oss-rebuild. We study 12,180 popular releases from PyPI and find that the byte-for-byte equivalence rate is generally low. We analyse the reasons why they produce different wheels, and find that equivalence between the original and rebuilt wheels can often still be established, preserving most of the guarantees users expect from rebuildable releases. We present and evaluate daleq4py, a tool to establish the equivalence of Python wheels through the kernel of a normalisation function that is based on provenance-preserving datalog rules. Experimental results show that daleq4py substantially expands the set of rebuilds that can be accepted as equivalent. Although only 15.4% of macaron rebuilds and 19.1% of oss-rebuild rebuilds are byte-for-byte identical to the published PyPI wheels, daleq4py establishes wheel equivalence for 60.2% and 78.9% of source-equivalent rebuilds, respectively.

AI.tldr: Only 15–19% of PyPI package rebuilds are byte-for-byte identical to originals, but the daleq4py tool uses datalog-based normalization to establish equivalence for 60–79% of rebuilds, preserving trust guarantees.
AI.motivation: Rebuilding Python packages in hardened environments can detect compromised builds and generate provenance metadata, but byte-for-byte comparisons yield low equivalence rates. There is a need to understand why rebuilds differ and to develop methods that still establish equivalence, preserving the security guarantees of reproducible builds.
AI.method: The authors study 12,180 popular PyPI releases rebuilt using macaron and oss-rebuild. They analyze root causes of byte differences, then introduce daleq4py — a tool that normalizes Python wheels using provenance-preserving datalog rules to establish semantic equivalence beyond strict byte-for-byte matching.
AI.result: Byte-for-byte rebuild rates are 15.4% (macaron) and 19.1% (oss-rebuild). However, daleq4py establishes wheel equivalence for 60.2% and 78.9% of source-equivalent rebuilds respectively, substantially expanding the set of accepted rebuilds.
AI.conclusion: Byte-for-byte identity is an overly strict criterion for rebuild verification. Semantic equivalence via normalization (as implemented in daleq4py) recovers most of the trust guarantees while dramatically increasing the proportion of verifiable rebuilds in PyPI supply chains.

title: AI-Integrated Scientific Inquiry: A Practice-Centered Vision for Science Education
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of scientific inquiry. Scientists use AI to observe and measure phenomena, to identify patterns in data, and to build models. As AI moves into scientific inquiry, it gains relevance for science education: students should learn how AI is changing scientific practices, ideally by engaging in AI-integrated scientific inquiry themselves. How to design such instruction, grounded in authentic scientific practice rather than taught as a standalone topic, remains an open question. In our vision, which we describe in this article, AI is treated as a set of scientific instruments that students use within the scientific practices described by the Next Generation Science Standards. Each instrument is a genuine scientific tool, pedagogically bounded: its controls are simplified while its core scientific function is preserved. The approach has two aims: engaging students in authentic scientific inquiry, and building an understanding of how AI is used in science and where it can mislead (discipline-based AI literacy, DAIL). In the article, we focus on the investigative core of inquiry, namely observing, analyzing, and modeling, and describe one exemplary AI instrument for each: computer vision for observing, clustering for analyzing, and generative modeling for modeling. We argue that every AI instrument in science education should carry a distinct reflection point that prompts critical evaluation of the AI instrument itself. Finally, we describe how agentic AI, operating across the whole inquiry rather than a single practice, could be represented, arguing that students should first build a foundational understanding of scientific inquiry and AI instruments before relying on agentic AI.

AI.tldr: Proposes integrating AI into science education as a set of bounded scientific instruments aligned with NGSS practices (observing, analyzing, modeling), with built-in reflection points for critical AI literacy, and advocates for foundational inquiry skills before introducing agentic AI.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly used in authentic scientific research, yet science education lacks a principled framework for integrating AI that preserves genuine inquiry rather than teaching AI as an isolated topic. The authors aim to develop discipline-based AI literacy (DAIL) through authentic, practice-based instruction.
AI.method: The authors propose treating AI tools as pedagogically bounded scientific instruments — simplifying controls while preserving core scientific functions. They map three AI instruments to NGSS scientific practices: computer vision (observing), clustering (analyzing), and generative modeling (modeling). Each instrument includes a distinct "reflection point" prompting critical evaluation. Agentic AI is positioned as a later-stage tool requiring prior foundational understanding.
AI.result: This is a conceptual/vision paper; it does not report empirical results. The contribution is a design framework for AI-integrated science instruction grounded in authentic scientific practices, with concrete exemplars and pedagogical principles.
AI.conclusion: AI should be integrated into science education as scientific instruments within established inquiry practices, not as a standalone subject. Critical reflection on AI's limitations must be embedded into each tool's use. Students need foundational competence in both scientific inquiry and AI instruments before engaging with agentic AI systems.

title: Certified in Theory, Broken in Practice: Assumption Gaps in Cryptographic Model Certification
summary:
Privacy-preserving machine learning auditing protocols allow auditors to assess models for properties such as accuracy or fairness, without revealing their internals or training data. This makes them especially attractive for auditing models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare or finance. For these protocols to be meaningful in real-world audit settings, though, their guarantees must reflect how the model will behave once deployed, rather than merely certifying its behavior during an audit. Existing security definitions often miss this mark: most certify model behavior only on a fixed audit dataset, without ensuring that the same guarantees generalize to other datasets drawn from the same distribution.
  As we show, this gap allows a model provider to attack many cryptographic model certification (CMC) schemes built on secure zero knowledge proofs (ZKP) by carefully engineering training data, resulting in models that exhibit benign behavior during an audit, but pathological behavior in practice. For example, we empirically demonstrate that an attacker can certify that a model achieves over 99% accuracy on an audit dataset, but less than 30% accuracy on fresh samples from the same distribution.
  To address this gap, we formalize rigorous cryptographic security notions tailored to CMC frameworks, introduce a generic protocol template, and prove that it satisfies these requirements. Our results thus offer both cautionary evidence about existing approaches and constructive guidance for designing secure, privacy-preserving ML auditing protocols.

AI.tldr: Existing cryptographic model certification (CMC) schemes fail to guarantee that model behavior certified during an audit generalizes to deployment. The authors demonstrate attacks exploiting this gap (99% audit accuracy vs. 30% real accuracy) and propose formal security definitions plus a generic protocol template to fix it.
AI.motivation: Privacy-preserving ML auditing protocols are critical for sensitive domains, but current security definitions only certify model behavior on a fixed audit dataset. This creates a dangerous generalization gap: a malicious model provider can engineer training data so the model performs well during the ZKP-based audit but fails catastrophically on real-world samples from the same distribution.
AI.method: The authors first empirically demonstrate an attack where a model achieves >99% accuracy on the audit set but <30% on fresh in-distribution samples. They then formalize rigorous cryptographic security notions specifically tailored to CMC frameworks, capturing generalization guarantees. Finally, they introduce a generic protocol template and prove it satisfies these strengthened requirements.
AI.result: The paper provides both negative and positive results: (1) an empirical demonstration that existing CMC schemes are vulnerable to training-data engineering attacks that break generalization, and (2) constructive cryptographic definitions and a provably secure protocol template that closes this gap.
AI.conclusion: Existing CMC schemes offer insufficient guarantees for real-world audit settings because they fail to ensure generalization. The paper offers both cautionary evidence about current approaches and constructive guidance for designing secure, privacy-preserving ML auditing protocols with meaningful deployment-relevant guarantees.

title: Data Quality over Capacity: Internalizing Documents into LoRA Adapters for Closed-Book QA
summary: We study baking documents directly into the weights of a 4-bit Gemma-4-e4b model via LoRA, so a system can answer questions about a corpus closed-book: no retrieval and no context-window budget. Across roughly 100 training runs from single documents to a 99-document corpus, we find that once adapter capacity is adequate, training-data quality is the dominant lever on closed-book accuracy, outweighing LoRA rank, learning rate, and two alternative architectures combined; capacity itself is a hard gate below which no data intervention helps. A single curation pass (shortening gold answers to canonical 1-6 word spans and dropping trivia) moved closed-book accuracy from 57.7% to 85.7% on a 15-document corpus, a larger jump than any architectural change. We confirm a capacity trend (rank must grow with corpus size) entangled with a coupling between rank and learning rate that we initially misdiagnosed. On a 15-document slice we add a real retrieval baseline: the internalized adapter (84.2% recall) beats a BM25-RAG pipeline with a base reader (58.9%) and even a realistic gold-chunk oracle (65.6%) at lower latency. We report the full arc, including three misdiagnoses, as a case study in debugging LLM training empirically.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates "baking" document knowledge directly into model weights via LoRA fine-tuning on a 4-bit Gemma model, enabling closed-book QA without retrieval. Key finding: data quality (curation) is the dominant accuracy lever, outweighing architectural choices. A curated 15-doc adapter beats BM25-RAG and a gold-chunk oracle in recall with lower latency.
AI.motivation: To explore whether knowledge can be internalized into model weights via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), eliminating the need for retrieval-based pipelines and context-window constraints, and to systematically identify what factors most influence closed-book QA accuracy in this setting.
AI.method: LoRA fine-tuning of a 4-bit quantized Gemma-4-e4b model across ~100 training runs, varying corpus size (single doc to 99 docs), LoRA rank, learning rate, and architecture. A key intervention is data curation: shortening gold answers to 1–6 word canonical spans and removing trivia. Baselines include BM25-RAG and a gold-chunk oracle retriever.
AI.result: Data curation raised closed-book accuracy from 57.7% to 85.7% on a 15-doc corpus — a larger gain than any architectural change. Capacity acts as a hard gate: below a rank threshold, no data intervention helps. Rank must scale with corpus size, and rank–learning rate coupling was initially misdiagnosed. The internalized adapter (84.2% recall) outperformed BM25-RAG (58.9%) and a gold-chunk oracle (65.6%) at lower latency.
AI.conclusion: For closed-book knowledge internalization via LoRA, training-data quality is the dominant lever once adapter capacity is sufficient. The work also serves as a case study in debugging LLM training empirically, documenting three misdiagnoses encountered during the investigation.

title: Multi-Horizon Consistency as Geometry: When Latent Dynamics Contract, and When They Do Not
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures. Diagnostic study of multi-horizon latent consistency, expansion proxies (L20), and a stochastic-forcing law for world-model geometry. Code and experiment logs to be released publicly
summary: Multi-horizon latent consistency is a common training knob in video predictors and world models, but practitioners rarely know what it does to transition geometry. We treat lambda, the weight on multi-step latent agreement, as a diagnostic control and measure an empirical expansion proxy L20,q95 together with horizon-20 prediction error E20. On Moving-MNIST (n=6 seeds at the critical pair), raising lambda from 0 to 0.8 cuts L20 from 4.96 +/- 2.01 to 1.01 +/- 0.06 (paired t p=0.005, Wilcoxon p=0.031) and halves E20 (0.365 to 0.177, paired t p=1.1e-13). Four of six seeds cross L<1 at lambda=0.8. The same loss does not produce population L<1 on action-conditioned Pendulum-v1 or CartPole-v1, nor on KTH Actions video, even when E20 improves. An associational mediation analysis on MMNIST gives r-hat=0.94 (95% CI [0.88, 1.00], n=27, B=2000); lambda was not randomized. Defensive checks (architectural baselines, exogenous stress, WorldTest, MPC, scaling) mostly support a narrow claim: soft consistency can push passive video toward a near-contractive band, and that band is domain-limited. A stochastic-forcing law L20 ~ 1.23 + 1.82 eta at lambda=0.8 (bootstrap slope CI [1.73, 1.92], R^2=0.96) unifies control domains on the same curve via calibrated eta_eff. Complete joint slices at lambda in {0.4, 1.2} (30/30 cells, 5 eta x 3 seeds) show comparable linear L20(eta) slopes (~1.69 and ~2.00); we do not fit a continuous (lambda, eta) surface. We do not report DreamerV3 or TD-MPC2 returns.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how the multi-horizon latent consistency weight λ affects transition geometry in video predictors, finding that higher λ can push passive video toward a near-contractive regime (L<1) on Moving-MNIST but not on action-conditioned control domains, with a stochastic-forcing law unifying results across domains.
AI.motivation: Practitioners routinely use multi-horizon latent consistency as a training knob in video predictors and world models without understanding its geometric effects on transitions. The authors aim to characterize what λ does to transition geometry, treating it as a diagnostic control variable.
AI.method: The authors measure an empirical expansion proxy L20 (q95 of per-step Jacobian spectral norms over horizon 20) alongside horizon-20 prediction error E20. They sweep λ values (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2) across four domains: Moving-MNIST, Pendulum-v1, CartPole-v1, and KTH Actions video. Statistical tests include paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, associational mediation analysis (r-hat with bootstrap CIs), and a stochastic-forcing law fitted via bootstrap. Defensive checks include architectural baselines, exogenous noise stress tests, WorldTest, MPC evaluation, and scaling experiments.
AI.result: On Moving-MNIST (n=6 seeds), raising λ from 0 to 0.8 reduces L20 from 4.96±2.01 to 1.01±0.06 (paired t p=0.005) and halves E20 from 0.365 to 0.177 (p=1.1e-13). Four of six seeds achieve L<1 at λ=0.8. Control domains (Pendulum-v1, CartPole-v1, KTH) do not achieve population L<1 despite improved E20. Mediation analysis yields r-hat=0.94 [0.88, 1.00]. A stochastic-forcing law L20 ~ 1.23 + 1.82·η at λ=0.8 (R²=0.96, slope CI [1.73, 1.92]) unifies control domains. Complete joint slices at λ∈{0.4, 1.2} (30 cells) show comparable linear slopes (~1.69 and ~2.00). DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 returns are not reported.
AI.conclusion: Soft multi-horizon consistency can push passive video predictors toward a near-contractive regime, but this effect is domain-limited — it succeeds on Moving-MNIST but fails on action-conditioned control environments. The stochastic-forcing law provides a unified characterization across domains, and the authors explicitly restrict their claims to this narrow finding without extending to full world-model returns.

title: Spectral Flow Certificates for Depth-Aware Long-Range Propagation in Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Neural Networks propagate information through local message passing, but the graph topologies themselves can silently prevent any amount of training from solving long-range tasks. When we deploy GNNs on new graphs, there is currently no inexpensive way to know, before training begins, whether the graphs' structures will allow information to travel far enough between distant nodes. We address this gap by proposing Spectral Flow Certificates (SFCs), single scalars computed from the graphs' normalised Laplacians in seconds, requiring no model training and no labelled data. An SFC fuses a graph's algebraic connectivity with the chosen message-passing depth into one number that measures how much of the critical spectral bottleneck can be traversed within the available depth budget. Unlike raw spectral gaps, which are static and depth-agnostic, SFCs adapt as the number of layers increases and therefore carry strictly more diagnostic information when depths vary. Compared with classical structural statistics such as average effective resistance and graph diameter, SFCs explain more than twice as much variance in trained GNN long-range accuracy. Across twenty-five synthetic graph families spanning paths, cycles, grids, regular graphs, and random graphs, SFCs predict trained accuracy before any gradients are computed, achieving explanatory power above ninety percent at all tested depths. The same predictive relationships hold on one hundred fifty real molecular graph topologies drawn from three independent benchmark datasets, confirming that the findings are not artefacts of their synthetic construction. Taken together, these results show that a single eigenvalue computation is sufficient to flag topology-limited graphs before committing to expensive training pipelines, providing a principled first filter for GNN deployments.

AI.tldr: Spectral Flow Certificates (SFCs) are single scalars computed from a graph's normalized Laplacian that predict, before any training, whether a GNN's message-passing depth can overcome spectral bottlenecks. SFCs explain >90% of variance in long-range accuracy across synthetic graphs and generalize to real molecular datasets, offering a cheap, principled pre-training diagnostic.
AI.motivation: Graph topologies can silently prevent GNNs from solving long-range tasks regardless of training, yet no inexpensive, pre-training method exists to diagnose whether a given graph's structure permits sufficient information flow across distant nodes given a fixed message-passing depth budget.
AI.method: Proposes Spectral Flow Certificates (SFCs), scalars computed from the normalized Laplacian's eigenvalues, that fuse algebraic connectivity with the chosen number of GNN layers. Unlike static spectral gaps, SFCs adapt with depth, quantifying how much of the critical spectral bottleneck is traversable. Validated on 25 synthetic graph families (paths, cycles, grids, regular, random graphs) and 150 real molecular graphs from three benchmark datasets.
AI.result: SFCs explain more than twice the variance in trained GNN long-range accuracy compared to classical statistics (average effective resistance, graph diameter). They achieve >90% explanatory power across all tested depths on synthetic graphs and maintain predictive relationships on real molecular topologies.
AI.conclusion: A single eigenvalue computation suffices to flag topology-limited graphs before expensive training, providing a principled first filter for GNN deployment on new graphs.

title: Claim Plane: Enforceable Change Intents and Dynamic Scope for Parallel Coding Agents
summary: Parallel coding agents can independently produce locally valid changes while still interfering at integration time, expanding beyond planned scope, or relying on premises invalidated by concurrent work. Existing responses emphasize communication, isolated workspaces, late merge-time repair, continuous supervision, or post-hoc runtime recovery. This paper presents Claim Plane, a model-agnostic coordination architecture that treats concurrent software change as a pre-write admission problem. Before implementation, each worker declares a versioned ChangeIntent containing an exact base commit, typed resources, dependencies, and operations marked as committed or contingent. A deterministic control plane atomically admits compatible intents, constrains same-file parallelism to declared regions, serializes unresolved overlap, tracks dependency invalidation, and fails closed on ambiguous authority. During execution, a contingent mutation does not reserve write ownership initially; the first attempted mutation triggers atomic scope promotion and re-admission against the current active set. Brokered execution binds capabilities to intent versions, leases, OS-level worktree locks, monotonic fencing tokens, and Git-tree provenance, while integration verifies immutable patches and evidence. A preliminary six-pair CooperBench mechanism check is reported only as feasibility evidence: static Claim Plane achieved 6/6 pair passes with full serialization, while dynamic scope retained parallel admission on half of the pairs, performed seven successful scope promotions, and failed closed on two undeclared mutations. The sample is intentionally too small for comparative claims. We argue that separating probabilistic planning from deterministic authority provides a foundation for a future learned semantic-dependency model and frontier-model escalation only on unresolved cases.

AI.tldr: Claim Plane introduces a deterministic coordination architecture for parallel coding agents that treats concurrent changes as a pre-write admission problem, requiring workers to declare versioned ChangeIntents before implementation. A control plane atomically admits compatible intents, manages scope promotion for contingent mutations, and binds execution to leases, fencing tokens, and provenance tracking.
AI.motivation: Parallel coding agents produce locally valid changes that still conflict at integration time due to scope expansion, invalidated premises, and undeclared interference. Existing approaches (communication, isolated workspaces, merge-time repair, supervision, runtime recovery) fail to prevent these conflicts before they occur.
AI.method: A model-agnostic architecture where each worker declares a ChangeIntent (base commit, typed resources, dependencies, committed/contingent operations). A deterministic control plane atomically admits compatible intents, constrains same-file parallelism to declared regions, serializes unresolved overlap, and tracks dependency invalidation. Contingent mutations use atomic scope promotion on first attempted mutation with re-admission. Brokered execution binds capabilities via intent versions, leases, OS-level worktree locks, monotonic fencing tokens, and Git-tree provenance. Integration verifies immutable patches and evidence.
AI.result: A preliminary CooperBench mechanism check with six pairs: static Claim Plane achieved 6/6 passes with full serialization; dynamic scope retained parallel admission on half the pairs, performed seven successful scope promotions, and failed closed on two undeclared mutations. Sample size is acknowledged as too small for comparative claims.
AI.conclusion: Separating probabilistic planning from deterministic authority establishes a foundation for future learned semantic-dependency models, with frontier-model escalation reserved for unresolved cases only.

title: Adaptive Driving Style for SAE Level-2 Driving Automation: Minimizing Preference Mismatch
comment: Published in the 2026 American Control Conference (ACC), May 26-29, 2026, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
summary: Driving style is a key factor in the comfort and acceptance of automated vehicle (AV) features. In SAE Level-2 automation, where the driver must supervise the system and remain ready to intervene, mismatches between the automation's driving style and the driver's preference can reduce trust and trigger takeovers. This paper proposes an adaptive driving-style control framework that minimizes such preference mismatch. In a driving-simulator study, we compare fixed, trust-based, and preference-based adaptation heuristics and analyze their effects on preference mismatch and trust. We then train a driving-preference prediction model and use it in an implicit adaptation policy that selects among bounded driving styles for upcoming events. A validation study shows that the predictive policy achieves equal or lower preference mismatch than comparison baselines, particularly when starting from a less defensive style, while also yielding higher average trust. The results provide a step toward developing human-aware driving automation that can implicitly adapt its driving style to the driver's preferences.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive driving-style control framework for SAE Level-2 automated vehicles that minimizes mismatch between the automation's driving style and the driver's preferences. Using a driving-preference prediction model within an implicit adaptation policy, the approach achieves equal or lower preference mismatch and higher trust compared to fixed, trust-based, and preference-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Mismatches between automated vehicle driving style and driver preferences in Level-2 automation reduce trust and trigger unnecessary takeovers. Existing adaptation heuristics (fixed, trust-based, preference-based) have limitations, motivating the need for a predictive, implicit adaptation approach.
AI.method: The authors conducted a driving-simulator study comparing fixed, trust-based, and preference-based adaptation heuristics. They then trained a driving-preference prediction model and integrated it into an implicit adaptation policy that selects among bounded driving styles for upcoming events. A validation study evaluated the predictive policy against baselines.
AI.result: The predictive policy achieved equal or lower preference mismatch than all comparison baselines, especially when starting from a less defensive style. It also yielded higher average trust scores across participants.
AI.conclusion: Predictive, implicit adaptation of driving style based on learned driver preferences represents a promising step toward human-aware driving automation that enhances both comfort and trust in Level-2 systems.

title: Decentralized Compute on Untrusted Hardware Using Intel TDX and Encrypted CVMs
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Prior version at Intel Community Blog and manifold.inc
summary:
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence workloads has generated an unprecedented demand for secure and scalable compute resources. However, centralized cloud providers continue to dominate both pricing and security models. In an increasingly competitive AI landscape, where the compromise of training data or model weights can confer a significant advantage, there is a critical need for a computing infrastructure that safeguards data at rest, in transit, and in use, while remaining affordable and broadly accessible. Furthermore, existing GPU cluster offerings (e.g., 8xH100s, 8xH200s, 8xB200s) create financial barriers that limit access for organizations, startups, and independent researchers seeking secure, high-performance computing environments.
  This paper introduces a decentralized, confidential computing platform that leverages Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX), Intel Trust Authority (ITA) and NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) to establish a distributed ecosystem of fully encrypted Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs). The proposed architecture incentivizes hardware providers to contribute Intel TDX capable compute resources. Each participating provider is provisioned with a freshly instantiated, uniquely encrypted Ubuntu 24.04 CVM, providing data protection across all stages, at rest, in transit, and in use.
  By decentralizing the confidential computing stack and leveraging confidential computing across independently operated nodes, this work demonstrates a viable alternative to traditional cloud-based infrastructures. The proposed system offers enhanced security assurances, transparent cost structures, and democratized access to enterprise-grade secure compute capabilities, paving the way for a more open, secure, and equitable foundation for next-generation AI development.

AI.tldr: A decentralized confidential computing platform using Intel TDX, Intel Trust Authority, and NVIDIA CC to create encrypted CVMs, incentivizing independent hardware providers and offering secure, affordable GPU compute as an alternative to centralized cloud.
AI.motivation: Centralized cloud providers dominate pricing and security for AI workloads, creating financial barriers and security risks (data/model weight compromise). There is a critical need for affordable, broadly accessible compute infrastructure that protects data at rest, in transit, and in use.
AI.method: A decentralized platform using Intel TDX, Intel Trust Authority (ITA), and NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) to provision encrypted Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs) across independently operated nodes. Hardware providers are incentivized to contribute TDX-capable resources, each receiving a freshly instantiated, uniquely encrypted Ubuntu 24.04 CVM.
AI.result: The system demonstrates a viable alternative to traditional cloud infrastructure with enhanced security assurances and transparent cost structures, enabling democratized access to enterprise-grade secure compute.
AI.conclusion: Decentralizing the confidential computing stack across independent nodes paves the way for a more open, secure, and equitable foundation for next-generation AI development.

title: Leveraging External Knowledge for Historical Document Restoration via Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
summary: Historical documents act as invaluable knowledge archives but often suffer from illegibility due to physical deterioration and damage. While existing restoration methods based on masked language modeling effectively utilize local context, they struggle to restore named entities that require external historical knowledge. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework for historical document restoration that leverages large language models with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). By combining the implicit knowledge of pre-trained LLMs with explicitly retrieved external context, our model ARI effectively mitigates the challenge of inferring context-dependent proper nouns. Extensive experiments on Korean historical documents demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms baselines, achieving substantial gains in restoring both general characters and named entities. Furthermore, comprehensive evaluations including expert assessments confirm that ARI serves as a practical tool for domain experts, promising to accelerate the analysis of historical records.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework named ARI is proposed for restoring illegible text in historical documents, combining LLM implicit knowledge with explicit external context to better handle named entities, outperforming baselines on Korean historical documents.
AI.motivation: Existing masked language modeling methods for historical document restoration leverage local context effectively but fail to restore named entities requiring external historical knowledge. There is a need for a method that can infer context-dependent proper nouns by incorporating broader historical knowledge.
AI.method: The authors introduce ARI, a framework that combines pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It integrates the implicit knowledge encoded in LLMs with explicitly retrieved external historical context to restore damaged text, particularly targeting named entities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Korean historical documents show that ARI significantly outperforms baselines, achieving substantial gains in restoring both general characters and named entities. Expert assessments further validate ARI as a practical tool for domain experts.
AI.conclusion: ARI effectively mitigates the challenge of restoring context-dependent proper nouns in historical documents and promises to accelerate the analysis of historical records for domain experts.

title: Adjustment Speed as a Safety Constraint for Nonstationary Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Ensuring safety in reinforcement learning under nonstationarity requires determining whether a learning system can safely adapt to forecasted environmental change within the required recovery horizon. Existing safe reinforcement learning methods typically assume stationary environments and do not explicitly consider adaptation speed as a safety concern. However, when environments evolve over time, delayed adaptation may result in transient unsafe behavior.
  This paper proposes adjustment speed as a safety constraint for nonstationary reinforcement learning. The central idea is to define safety in terms of adaptation feasibility: future states or regions may become unsafe when the adaptation required to remain safe exceeds the learning system's calibrated recovery capacity. The proposed framework uses learned context representations and short-horizon context forecasts to estimate adaptation demand and compare it with the agent's achievable adaptation capacity.
  When predicted adaptation demand exceeds the calibrated recovery capacity, the framework proactively tightens the admissible action set and activates an action-level shield to reduce unsafe behavior before violations occur.
  Experiments in a nonstationary driving environment show that the proposed approach primarily reduces safety violations in short-horizon windows aligned with context changes. Ablation studies further show that shielding is more conservative for peak- and tail-risk suppression, while optimization-level adjustment provides additional reductions in short-horizon switch-conditioned violations.
  These results support adaptation feasibility as a practical safety principle for reinforcement learning under nonstationarity and demonstrate that proactive intervention can improve safety during periods of environmental change.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a safety framework for nonstationary reinforcement learning that proactively constrains actions when the required adaptation to environmental changes exceeds the agent's calibrated recovery capacity, reducing transient unsafe behavior during context shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing safe RL methods assume stationary environments and ignore adaptation speed as a safety concern. In nonstationary settings, delayed adaptation to environmental changes can cause transient unsafe behavior. The paper addresses the gap by explicitly considering whether a learning system can adapt fast enough to forecasted changes.
AI.method: The framework uses learned context representations and short-horizon context forecasts to estimate adaptation demand (how much the policy must change) and compares it against the agent's calibrated recovery capacity. When predicted demand exceeds capacity, the framework proactively tightens the admissible action set via an action-level shield. Two intervention mechanisms are employed: shielding (conservative, for peak- and tail-risk suppression) and optimization-level adjustment (for reducing short-horizon switch-conditioned violations).
AI.result: Experiments in a nonstationary driving environment show the approach primarily reduces safety violations in short-horizon windows aligned with context changes. Ablation studies reveal shielding is more conservative for peak- and tail-risk, while optimization-level adjustment provides additional reductions in switch-conditioned violations.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation feasibility is a practical safety principle for RL under nonstationarity. Proactive intervention based on comparing adaptation demand to recovery capacity can meaningfully improve safety during periods of environmental change.

title: Coupled Hierarchical Search over Topology and Execution for Agentic Workflow Synthesis
summary: Although structured workflows empower Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex problems, automating their creation is severely hindered by a vast combinatorial search space, frequently resulting in inflexible and resource-heavy offline training dependencies. To address this, we conceptualize workflow generation as an intertwined topology-and-execution search paradigm, where the broader topological layer dictates subtask boundaries and lower-level execution outcomes actively reshape the topology itself. Building on this foundation, we introduce HierFlow, a training-free, test-time hierarchical search architecture that automates agentic workflow design by merging feedback-guided topology adjustments with a fast, MCTS-inspired tree search for sub-workflow optimization. HierFlow maximizes efficiency through an intelligent gating module that selectively triggers execution-level searches based on contextual necessity, a mechanism we further support with an in-depth analysis detailing how varying degrees of cross-task coupling impact the effectiveness of hierarchical splitting. Comprehensive testing across question answering, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks confirms that HierFlow consistently outperforms strong baselines, delivering an optimal balance of high-quality results and computational efficiency without any additional training overhead.

AI.tldr: HierFlow is a training-free, test-time hierarchical search architecture that automates LLM workflow generation by jointly optimizing task topology and subtask execution via feedback-guided adjustments and MCTS-inspired tree search, outperforming baselines across QA, math, and code benchmarks without extra training.
AI.motivation: Automating workflow creation for LLMs is hindered by a vast combinatorial search space, leading to inflexible, resource-heavy solutions dependent on offline training. Existing methods fail to capture the dynamic interplay between high-level task topology and low-level execution outcomes.
AI.method: HierFlow treats workflow generation as an intertwined topology-and-execution search paradigm. It employs a training-free hierarchical architecture with two levels: (1) feedback-guided topology adjustments at the macro level to define subtask boundaries, and (2) a fast MCTS-inspired tree search at the micro level for sub-workflow optimization. An intelligent gating module selectively triggers execution-level search based on contextual necessity, supported by analysis of cross-task coupling effects on hierarchical splitting.
AI.result: Comprehensive testing across question answering, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks shows HierFlow consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving an optimal balance of high-quality results and computational efficiency without additional training overhead.
AI.conclusion: HierFlow demonstrates that jointly optimizing workflow topology and execution in a training-free, test-time framework is both effective and efficient, offering a scalable solution for automated agentic workflow design in LLMs.

title: Leveraging Resolved Incident History for LLM-Assisted Software Bug Diagnosis
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, accepted at IEEE SMC 2026
summary: Effective software bug diagnosis requires two ingredients: the right knowledge source (operational failure history, not just system documentation) and the right retrieval structure (structured records, not unstructured chunks). Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches fall short on one or both dimensions. We propose Operational Memory RAG (OM-RAG), which indexes resolved issues as structured symptom-root cause-resolution triples and retrieves the most similar historical precedent via single-hop embedding. OM-RAG powers a purpose-built large language model (LLM) administrator that has operated a production Dataverse instance for over six months, operationalizing the Knowledge component of the Monitor-Analyze-Plan-Execute-Knowledge (MAPE-K) feedback loop with the system's own resolved failure history. In a controlled four-configuration ablation, LLM-based judging covers all 1,172 issues and manual verification a 123-issue subset. OM-RAG achieves Diagnosis Accuracy of 0.931 and Fix Correctness of 0.809, outperforming chunk-based retrieval (+186%) and a documentation-anchored concept graph (+77%). Model-free retrieval metrics (mean similarity 0.880) independently corroborate the ranking.

AI.tldr: OM-RAG indexes resolved software issues as structured triples (symptom–root cause–resolution) and uses single-hop embedding retrieval, achieving 0.931 diagnosis accuracy and 0.809 fix correctness, outperforming chunk-based RAG (+186%) and documentation-graph baselines (+77%) on 1,172 production issues over six months.
AI.motivation: Current RAG approaches for software bug diagnosis fail in two ways: they rely on static system documentation rather than operational failure history (wrong knowledge source), and they use unstructured text chunks rather than structured records (wrong retrieval structure). Both deficiencies degrade diagnostic accuracy.
AI.method: OM-RAG constructs a structured index of historical resolved issues as symptom–root cause–resolution triples. Retrieval uses single-hop embedding to match a new issue against the most similar historical precedent. The system powers an LLM administrator within a MAPE-K (Monitor-Analyze-Plan-Execute-Knowledge) loop on a production Dataverse instance, operationalizing the Knowledge component with the system's own failure history. Evaluation uses LLM-based judging on all 1,172 issues and manual verification on a 123-issue subset, with four ablation configurations.
AI.result: OM-RAG achieved Diagnosis Accuracy of 0.931 and Fix Correctness of 0.809. It outperformed chunk-based retrieval by +186% and a documentation-anchored concept graph by +77%. Model-free retrieval metrics (mean similarity 0.880) independently corroborated the ranking quality.
AI.conclusion: Structured, history-anchored retrieval is critical for operational bug diagnosis. OM-RAG demonstrates that indexing resolved issues as structured triples within a MAPE-K self-healing loop yields substantial accuracy gains and represents a validated path toward autonomic system administration.

title: Filtering Offensive Content Changes Its Visibility but Not User Behavior: Two Randomized Controlled Trials with 200,000 Users on Nextdoor
summary: We investigate the effectiveness of interventions that reduce the visibility of offensive content on the local social platform Nextdoor. Content filtering -- hiding or downranking offensive content that brushes against a platform's rules without clearly breaking them -- is deployed across virtually every major platform, yet almost no field evidence exists on whether it changes user behavior. We report two large-scale randomized controlled trials, each involving 100,000 users. Study 1 (2022) tested a report-triggered filter applied to comments in post threads and produced a modest 12% reduction in views of offensive comments; across eleven further measures of platform behavior we found no significant effects. Study 2 (2023-2024) remedied Study 1's central limitation -- a weak manipulation driven by slow, report-based eligibility -- by proactively scoring posts and comments at creation with Google Jigsaw's Perspective API and filtering them from the newsfeed. This produced a near-complete (95%) reduction in views of offensive posts, yet across thirteen further measures we again found no significant effects. Across two independent trials spanning different content types, filtering mechanisms, classifiers, and countries -- and despite manipulation strength rising from 12% to 95% -- filtering reliably reduced the visibility of offensive content without altering platform visitation, content consumption, or content production. These convergent null results provide rare field evidence on a ubiquitous intervention and underscore the complexity of effectively moderating online platforms.

AI.tldr: Two large-scale RCTs on Nextdoor found that content filtering (hiding/downranking offensive content) reliably reduced visibility of offensive material (12% and 95% reductions) but produced no significant effects on user behavior — no changes in platform visitation, consumption, or production — challenging assumptions about the behavioral efficacy of this ubiquitous moderation tool.
AI.motivation: Despite content filtering being deployed across virtually every major online platform to reduce visibility of borderline-offensive content, almost no field evidence exists on whether it actually changes user behavior. The authors aimed to fill this gap with rigorous causal evidence.
AI.method: Two large-scale randomized controlled trials on Nextdoor (~100,000 users each). Study 1 (2022) used a report-triggered filter on post comments. Study 2 (2023–2024) remedied Study 1's weak manipulation by using Google Jigsaw's Perspective API to proactively score and filter posts/comments at creation, directly from the newsfeed. Both measured effects across multiple behavioral outcomes (11–13 measures).
AI.result: Study 1 achieved a modest 12% reduction in views of offensive comments with no significant effects across 11 behavioral measures. Study 2 achieved a near-complete 95% reduction in views of offensive posts, yet again found no significant effects across 13 measures — including platform visitation, content consumption, and content production.
