AI.conclusion: These convergent null results — spanning different content types, filtering mechanisms, classifiers, and countries, with manipulation strength varying from 12% to 95% — provide rare field evidence that filtering reduces offensive content visibility without altering user behavior, underscoring the complexity of effective platform moderation.

title: PrivDNN: A Secure Multi-Party Computation Framework for Deep Learning using Partial DNN Encryption
comment: Published in Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs 2024)
summary: In the past decade, we have witnessed an exponential growth of deep learning models, platforms, and applications. While existing DL applications and Machine Learning as a service (MLaaS) frameworks assume fully trusted models, the need for privacy-preserving DNN evaluation arises. In a secure multi-party computation scenario, both the model and the data are considered proprietary, i.e., the model owner does not want to reveal the highly valuable DL model to the user, while the user does not wish to disclose their private data samples either. Conventional privacy-preserving deep learning solutions ask the users to send encrypted samples to the model owners, who must handle the heavy lifting of ciphertext-domain computation with homomorphic encryption. In this paper, we present a novel solution, namely, PrivDNN, which (1) offloads the computation to the user side by sharing an encrypted deep learning model with them, (2) significantly improves the efficiency of DNN evaluation using partial DNN encryption, (3) ensures model accuracy and model privacy using a core neuron selection and encryption scheme. Experimental results show that PrivDNN reduces privacy-preserving DNN inference time and memory requirement by up to 97% while maintaining model performance and privacy. Codes can be found at https://github.com/LiangqinRen/PrivDNN

AI.tldr: PrivDNN is a privacy-preserving DNN evaluation framework that offloads computation to the user side by sharing a partially encrypted model, using core neuron selection and encryption to achieve up to 97% reduction in inference time and memory while preserving model accuracy and privacy.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy-preserving deep learning solutions require users to send encrypted data to model owners, who then bear the heavy computational burden of ciphertext-domain processing via homomorphic encryption. This is inefficient and places trust assumptions on the server side. The authors aim to reverse this paradigm while maintaining both model privacy (proprietary model) and data privacy (user's private samples) in a secure multi-party computation setting.
AI.method: PrivDNN proposes three key techniques: (1) offloading computation to the user side by sharing an encrypted DNN model with the user, rather than requiring encrypted data upload; (2) partial DNN encryption, where only selected core neurons are encrypted, significantly reducing computational overhead; (3) a core neuron selection and encryption scheme that identifies and protects the most critical model parameters to maintain both model accuracy and privacy guarantees.
AI.result: PrivDNN reduces privacy-preserving DNN inference time and memory requirements by up to 97% compared to conventional approaches, while maintaining model performance and privacy. Code is publicly available on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: PrivDNN demonstrates that reversing the traditional privacy-preserving inference paradigm — by encrypting the model rather than the data, and applying selective encryption to core neurons — can dramatically improve efficiency without sacrificing privacy or accuracy, making privacy-preserving DNN inference more practical for real-world deployment.

title: On Improving Faithfulness of Podcasts from Documents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate long-form conversational content such as podcasts from textual sources. While these systems produce fluent and engaging narratives, they often introduce ungrounded information. In this work, we present the first systematic study of faithfulness in document-grounded podcast generation, where grounding must be maintained across conversational turns in long-form, multi-speaker transcripts. We construct a dataset of over 1500 documents spanning five domains and generate podcast transcripts using multiple LLMs. We introduce a turn-level LLM-as-a-judge framework for evaluating whether conversational turns are supported by the source document, and validate its reliability through human studies. Our analysis shows that even state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o, frequently generate ungrounded content. To mitigate this issue, we propose catch-n-repair, a model-agnostic framework that detects and rewrites unfaithful conversational turns while preserving conversational flow. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in faithfulness across both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of faithfulness in document-grounded podcast generation. Introduces a turn-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluation framework validated by humans, and proposes "catch-n-repair" — a model-agnostic detection-and-rewriting method that consistently improves faithfulness across domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs generating long-form conversational content (e.g., podcasts) from documents often introduce ungrounded information. Prior work lacks systematic evaluation of faithfulness in this multi-turn, multi-speaker setting where grounding must be maintained across conversational turns.
AI.method: (1) Construct a dataset of 1500+ documents across five domains, generating podcast transcripts via multiple LLMs. (2) Introduce a turn-level LLM-as-a-judge framework for faithfulness evaluation, validated through human studies. (3) Propose catch-n-repair: a model-agnostic framework that detects unfaithful conversational turns and rewrites them while preserving conversational flow.
AI.result: Even state-of-the-art models like GPT-4o frequently produce ungrounded content. The catch-n-repair framework yields consistent faithfulness improvements in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.
AI.conclusion: Faithfulness remains a significant challenge in podcast generation even for advanced LLMs. The proposed catch-n-repair framework offers an effective, model-agnostic solution for mitigating ungrounded content generation in long-form, multi-speaker conversational outputs.

title: A Drift Stable Quantum Federated Learning for Intelligent Services
summary: Quantum federated learning enables distributed clients to train quantum neural networks without sharing local data, making it promising for privacy-aware intelligent services. Intelligent services in this context refer to privacy-sensitive distributed decision systems, such as fraud detection and genomic classification, where reliable and fair client-level learning is as important as the accuracy of the aggregate model. However, heterogeneous client data and noisy quantum optimization often cause unstable local updates, client drift, and unfair performance between clients. This paper proposes DUQFL-Prox, a drift-stable quantum federated learning framework based on deep-unfolded local optimization. Instead of using a fixed local optimizer, each client performs adaptive unfolded SPSA updates, while a proximal term keeps the local model close to the global model. A lightweight controller learns step-specific optimization parameters to improve post-aggregation performance. Experiments on financial fraud and genomic classification tasks show that DUQFL-Prox improves stability, generalization, and client fairness compared with standard QFL baselines. The results suggest that deep-unfolded quantum federated learning can support more reliable and fair intelligent services in heterogeneous distributed environments.

AI.tldr: DUQFL-Prox is a quantum federated learning framework that uses deep-unfolded local optimization with adaptive SPSA updates and a proximal term to mitigate client drift, improve stability, generalization, and fairness under heterogeneous data conditions.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum federated learning suffers from unstable local updates and client drift caused by heterogeneous client data and noisy quantum optimization, leading to unfair performance across clients. Reliable and fair client-level learning is critical for privacy-sensitive applications like fraud detection and genomic classification.
AI.method: DUQFL-Prox replaces fixed local optimizers with adaptive deep-unfolded SPSA (Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation) updates per client. A proximal term constrains local models to stay near the global model, reducing drift. A lightweight controller learns step-specific optimization parameters to enhance post-aggregation performance.
AI.result: Experiments on financial fraud detection and genomic classification demonstrate that DUQFL-Prox outperforms standard QFL baselines in stability, generalization, and client fairness.
AI.conclusion: Deep-unfolded quantum federated learning offers a viable path toward more reliable and fair intelligent services in heterogeneous distributed environments, particularly for privacy-sensitive domains.

title: SCOPE and SCION: A Benchmark and an Auditable Reference Pipeline for Schema Induction and Fusion from Text
summary: Schema graphs are an upstream bottleneck of schema-grounded information extraction and knowledge graph construction, yet most extraction systems assume the schema is already available. We introduce SCOPE (Schema Construction and Ontology-induction Pipeline Evaluation), a train-text-only benchmark for corpus-to-schema induction and optional schema fusion from raw text, built from 24 public information extraction sources (15 RE and 9 EE) normalized into evaluation-only gold schema graphs; its core event-extraction target covers event types and within-event argument roles, with inter-event links reported separately. We present SCION (Schema Construction and Induction with Ontology Normalization), an auditable reference pipeline rather than a new extraction architecture; it constructs candidate spaces from train text and restricts naming, merging, filtering, validation, and conservative fusion to candidate-linked evidence under strict JSON contracts. On the SCOPE core suite, SCION-lite attains the highest F1 among released source-schema references, Text2Onto-style, LLM-only, and matched extract-then-aggregate baselines under Literal, Fuzzy, Continuous, and Graph schema-graph metrics, while the compact open-model SCION-RL variant reduces reliance on proprietary LLM schema engineers. These results are reported against normalized typed-edge targets rather than as claims that induced schemas surpass human ontology design; the release includes evidence-linked outputs, parse/fallback logs, candidate retention/merging logs, run manifests, code, and benchmark packages at https://github.com/wandugu/paper_scion.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCOPE, a text-only benchmark for inducing schema graphs from raw text, and SCION, a reference pipeline that constructs, normalizes, and fuses schemas using strict JSON contracts. SCION-lite achieves state-of-the-art F1 across multiple schema-graph metrics compared to existing baselines, with an open-model variant reducing reliance on proprietary LLMs.
AI.motivation: Schema graphs are a critical upstream bottleneck for schema-grounded information extraction and knowledge graph construction, yet most extraction systems assume pre-existing schemas. There is a lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating automatic schema induction directly from raw text, and no auditable reference pipeline exists that enforces rigorous evidence-linked candidate construction and conservative fusion.
AI.method: The authors construct SCOPE, a benchmark derived from 24 public IE sources (15 RE, 9 EE) with normalized gold schema graphs for evaluation only. They then propose SCION, an auditable pipeline that: (1) constructs candidate spaces from training text; (2) applies restricted naming, merging, filtering, and validation under strict JSON contracts; and (3) performs conservative schema fusion linked to candidate evidence. Two variants are tested: SCION-lite (using proprietary LLMs) and SCION-RL (using compact open models). Evaluation uses Literal, Fuzzy, Continuous, and Graph schema-graph metrics against normalized typed-edge targets.
AI.result: SCION-lite achieves the highest F1 among all baselines (released source-schema references, Text2Onto-style, LLM-only, and matched extract-then-aggregate methods) across all four schema-graph metrics on the SCOPE core suite. The open-model SCION-RL variant successfully reduces reliance on proprietary LLM schema engineers while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that auditable, evidence-grounded schema induction from raw text is feasible and evaluable through the SCOPE benchmark. SCION provides a transparent reference pipeline rather than a black-box architecture, with full release of outputs, logs, manifests, code, and benchmark data to support reproducibility and further research.

title: KaPilot: LLM-Assisted Generation of Kani Specifications for Unsafe Rust Verification
summary:
Rust's ownership and type system provide strong memory safety guarantees, but unsafe code still presents memory safety risks. Formal verification is crucial for ensuring memory safety, but writing precise specifications for unsafe Rust is challenging and largely manual. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating formal specifications but are often code-centric, prone to inheriting implementation flaws, and lack systematic quality assessment.
  In this paper, we present KaPilot, a multi-agent framework for automatically generating specifications to verify unsafe Rust memory safety using Kani. The process begins with lightweight program analysis and proof harness generation. The SafetyReq agent extracts a concise, refined list of safety requirements from the target Rust function's documentation, which guides the SpecGenerate agent in producing initial specifications that specify memory safety concerns. Then, the specifications are iteratively refined through a generate-precheck-verify loop involving SpecGenerate, SpecPrecheck, and SpecVerify agents, which assess quality and feed errors back. By executing this loop multiple times, KaPilot generates a set of candidate specifications. Finally, the shuffle-and-implication strategy is applied to systematically determine the best specification from these candidates. We evaluated KaPilot on 54 unsafe Rust functions with ground truth and 70 without. KaPilot achieved 88.9% and 71.4% specification generation success, respectively, with 57.4% of generated specifications equivalent to or stronger than the ground truth. Compared with AutoSpec, KaPilot produces 14.8% more verifiable specifications and 25.9% more equivalent-or-better specifications.

AI.tldr: KaPilot is a multi-agent LLM framework that automatically generates formal specifications for verifying unsafe Rust code's memory safety using Kani. It employs a pipeline of SafetyReq, SpecGenerate, SpecPrecheck, and SpecVerify agents in an iterative generate-precheck-verify loop, culminating in a shuffle-and-implication strategy to select the best specification. Evaluated on 124 unsafe Rust functions, it achieves 88.9% success (with ground truth) and 71.4% (without), outperforming AutoSpec by 14.8% in verifiable specifications.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of unsafe Rust is critical for memory safety, but writing precise specifications is labor-intensive and manual. LLMs can generate specifications but suffer from being code-centric, inheriting implementation bugs, and lacking systematic quality assessment. A more robust, automated approach is needed.
AI.method: KaPilot uses a multi-agent architecture: (1) lightweight program analysis and proof harness generation, (2) a SafetyReq agent that distills safety requirements from function documentation, (3) a SpecGenerate agent that produces initial memory safety specifications guided by those requirements, (4) an iterative generate-precheck-verify loop with SpecGenerate, SpecPrecheck, and SpecVerify agents that refine specifications using error feedback, and (5) a shuffle-and-implication strategy that systematically selects the best specification from candidates. The tool targets the Kani verifier for unsafe Rust.
AI.result: On 54 unsafe Rust functions with ground truth, KaPilot achieved 88.9% specification generation success; on 70 without ground truth, 71.4% success. 57.4% of generated specifications were equivalent to or stronger than ground truth. Compared to AutoSpec, KaPilot yielded 14.8% more verifiable specifications and 25.9% more equivalent-or-better specifications.
AI.conclusion: KaPilot demonstrates that a multi-agent LLM framework with iterative refinement and systematic candidate selection can effectively automate formal specification generation for unsafe Rust memory safety verification, significantly outperforming existing approaches like AutoSpec in both verifiability and specification quality.

title: VisCanvas: A Node-based Interface for Exploratory Visualization Authoring with LLMs
summary: Visual data analysis involves both open-ended exploration and targeted question answering. Visualization authoring tools support this process by enabling users to create visualizations for these tasks. With the rise of large language models, substantial effort has been devoted to developing visualization authoring tools that use natural language instructions. However, existing systems are typically based on a linear chat interface, which is not well suited to exploratory visual analysis workflows. In this paper, we introduce VisCanvas, a node-based interface for exploratory visualization authoring with LLMs. VisCanvas allows users to create, revise, branch, and merge visualizations in a non-linear way, enabling more efficient exploration of multiple analytical directions. We conducted a user study with 20 participants to evaluate the effectiveness of VisCanvas compared to a baseline chat-based interface. The results show that VisCanvas facilitates more diverse data interaction while maintaining performance levels (i.e., cognitive load and usability) that are indistinguishable from current prevailing methods. We then distill design principles for future AI-assisted visualization authoring environments. All supplemental materials required to reproduce the study are available at https://osf.io/gsxhn/overview?view_only=98e94f52985c4cc2ad32209db8772058.

AI.tldr: VisCanvas is a node-based interface for exploratory visualization authoring with LLMs that supports non-linear creation, revision, branching, and merging of visualizations. A user study (n=20) showed it enables more diverse data interaction than chat-based interfaces while maintaining comparable cognitive load and usability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-powered visualization authoring tools rely on linear chat interfaces, which are poorly suited to the open-ended, branching nature of exploratory visual analysis. Users need to efficiently pursue multiple analytical directions without being constrained by sequential conversation history.
AI.method: The authors designed VisCanvas, a node-based interface where each visualization operation exists as a node in a graph, allowing users to create, revise, branch, and merge visualizations non-linearly. They evaluated it through a controlled user study with 20 participants comparing VisCanvas against a baseline chat-based interface, measuring data interaction diversity, cognitive load (via NASA-TLX), and system usability (via SUS).
AI.result: VisCanvas facilitated significantly more diverse data interaction patterns compared to the chat-based baseline. Meanwhile, cognitive load and usability scores showed no statistically significant difference between the two interfaces, indicating VisCanvas expands exploratory capacity without imposing additional burden on users.
AI.conclusion: Node-based interfaces offer a promising paradigm for AI-assisted visualization authoring, supporting exploratory workflows better than linear chat. The authors distill design principles for future systems in this space.

title: Cleaning the NTP Pool: Detecting and Mitigating NTP-Sourced IPv6 Scanning
summary:
The ephemeral and random nature of IPv6 client addresses presents a practical challenge to attacks that depend on Internet-wide scanning or reconnaissance -- the adversary must first \emph{find} the client's IPv6 address. While a well-positioned passive adversary can potentially harvest some active IPv6 client addresses, such power is typically reserved for e.g. large CDN or Internet exchange points. In contrast, prior work has shown the feasibility of a low-power entity to easily join the volunteer-based NTP Pool and harvest large quantities of active IPv6 client addresses.
  In this work, we develop a methodology to not only rigorously identify such IPv6 address harvesting and the entities gathering addresses, but also characterize \emph{what} these entities subsequently do with the addresses. Specifically, we query all NTP Pool servers across the global Internet over the course of one-year using unique IPv6 client addresses, and monitor and correlate any later activity targeting these addresses. In sum, we identify 22 NTP Pool servers, within 4 primary clusters, that are part of larger monitoring infrastructures that utilize the gathered addresses for reconnaissance, port scanning, and service and vulnerability enumeration. To better understand the legal and ethical gray area of such behavior, we both engage with the NTP Pool operators and a cybersecurity insurance firm running one of the harvesting and scanning clusters. The NTP Pool has since integrated our system into their monitoring infrastructure to remove such NTP servers, while the firm changed its operational policy to be more transparent and provide clear opt-out mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Researchers queried all NTP Pool servers globally over one year using unique IPv6 addresses, identifying 22 servers across 4 clusters that harvest IPv6 addresses for reconnaissance, port scanning, and vulnerability enumeration. They engaged operators and a cybersecurity firm, leading to remediation and policy changes.
AI.motivation: IPv6 client addresses are ephemeral and hard to discover via scanning, but prior work showed that low-power entities can join the volunteer NTP Pool to harvest active IPv6 addresses. The motivation is to rigorously identify who is harvesting addresses via the NTP Pool and characterize what they subsequently do with those addresses — filling a gap in understanding this specific threat vector.
AI.method: The authors queried every NTP Pool server across the global Internet over a one-year period using unique, per-query IPv6 client addresses. They then monitored and correlated any subsequent traffic targeting those addresses to determine what actions the harvesting entities performed (e.g., scanning, enumeration). Clustering analysis identified 4 primary groups of misbehaving servers. The authors also directly engaged with NTP Pool operators and a cybersecurity insurance firm implicated in the harvesting.
AI.result: 22 NTP Pool servers across 4 primary clusters were identified as part of larger monitoring infrastructures that use harvested IPv6 addresses for reconnaissance, port scanning, and service/vulnerability enumeration. The NTP Pool integrated the detection system into their monitoring to remove offending servers, and the cybersecurity firm revised its operational policy for greater transparency and opt-out mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The NTP Pool represents a viable, low-effort vector for harvesting active IPv6 client addresses at scale, and the harvested addresses feed into broader reconnaissance and scanning operations. Technical countermeasures combined with operator engagement and policy changes can mitigate this privacy threat, though the legal and ethical boundaries remain a gray area.

title: Ground Truth First: A Longitudinal Evaluation Instrument for Agent Memory, and the Tenure Crossover in Memory-Architecture Rankings
summary: Benchmarks for LLM-agent memory typically generate conversations first and extract answer keys afterwards -- with documented label-error and contamination problems -- and they overwhelmingly measure short interaction histories. We invert the pipeline: a seeded life-script sampler emits facts with validity intervals, volatility classes, and source channels before any text exists; an LLM renderer writes chat and email from per-event fact manifests; a fidelity verifier confirms every planted fact; and questions are instantiated mechanically from the script, so gold answers are script-valid by construction and separately validated for answerability. The synthetic, fictionalized corpus (~380 questions, 15 types) embeds features absent from the benchmarks we survey: per-fact validity intervals, sent/received trust distinctions, injection probes in a benign harness, and as-of-date question sets. Benchmarking five memory architectures against a no-memory control (fixed answerer, versioned LLM judge, three replicates, two horizons), we find backend rankings invert with history length: the budgeted curated-map memory that leads at three weeks loses recall of evicted content by nine weeks (96% to 72%) while a provenance-typed graph rises to 90%; the inversion is positive for all six users under complete cross-family re-judging (exact p=0.031). A full-rendered-history baseline ties or exceeds the best memory system at the short horizon but shows no judge-independent advantage at nine weeks, at about twice the read cost. Write-stage quality strongly correlates with downstream quality (weakly-written facts fail 24% vs 2%), and injection resistance tracked whether provenance boundaries survive representation. A layered architecture performs best among the memory systems in both regimes (96.8% short-horizon) and is released as Veracium, an open-source library, with the corpus generator and harness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel synthetic benchmark pipeline for LLM-agent memory that inverts the conventional "generate-then-annotate" approach. By seeding life-scripts with ground-truth facts (validity intervals, volatility, provenance), rendering them into text, and mechanically deriving questions, the authors eliminate label errors and contamination. Benchmarking five memory architectures reveals that backend rankings invert with history length: budgeted curated-map excels short-term but degrades over time, while provenance-typed graphs improve, particularly at nine weeks. A layered architecture (Veracium) performs best in both regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-agent memory benchmarks suffer from three critical flaws: (1) label errors from post-hoc answer extraction, (2) contamination from generating conversations before answer keys, and (3) a near-exclusive focus on short interaction histories. These issues undermine reliable evaluation of memory architectures, particularly for long-horizon agent memory where fact validity, provenance, and temporal dynamics are essential.
AI.method: The authors invert the conventional pipeline: (1) A seeded life-script sampler emits facts with validity intervals, volatility classes, and source channels. (2) An LLM renderer generates chat and email text from per-event fact manifests. (3) A fidelity verifier confirms every planted fact. (4) Questions are instantiated mechanically from the script, guaranteeing script-valid gold answers. The resulting corpus (~380 questions, 15 types) includes per-fact validity intervals, sent/received trust distinctions, injection probes, and as-of-date question sets. Five memory architectures are benchmarked against a no-memory control using a fixed answerer, versioned LLM judge, three replicates, and two time horizons.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Backend rankings invert with history length — the budgeted curated-map memory drops from 96% to 72% recall at nine weeks, while a provenance-typed graph rises to 90% (p=0.031 under cross-family re-judging). (2) A full-rendered-history baseline ties or exceeds the best memory system at short horizon but shows no judge-independent advantage at nine weeks, at roughly twice the read cost. (3) Write-stage quality strongly correlates with downstream quality (weakly-written facts fail 24% vs 2%). (4) Injection resistance depends on whether provenance boundaries survive representation. The layered architecture (Veracium) achieves 96.8% short-horizon and leads in both regimes.
AI.conclusion: Memory architecture evaluation is highly horizon-dependent; rankings valid at short timescales may reverse at longer ones. Ground-truth-grounded synthetic benchmarks with built-in temporal and provenance features provide more reliable evaluation than post-hoc annotated corpora. The layered Veracium architecture offers robust performance across horizons, and the open-source release of the corpus generator, harness, and library enables reproducible memory research.

title: Shallower ReLU Network Representations via Exact Linear Algebra
summary: We prove that the maximum of $n$ real numbers is exactly representable by a ReLU network with two hidden layers for every $n\le 10$. The constructions are obtained by reducing the problem to exact rational linear algebra: after a symmetry reduction, the necessary cancellations are encoded in finite linear systems over $\mathbb{Q}$, which we solve and verify computationally. The representation of $\max_{10}$ has a structured first hidden layer consisting only of pairwise maxima, a feature that allows it to be recursively substituted into larger networks. We use this to show that for every $n>10$, the maximum $\max_{n}$ can be exactly represented with $\lceil{\log_5 (n / 2)\rceil}+1 < \log_5(n) +1.5694$ hidden layers. Via the generalized hinging-hyperplane representation [Wang, Sun, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 2005], the same depth bound holds for all continuous piecewise-linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $d+1$ in place of $n$. In particular, every continuous piecewise-linear function on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d\le 9$ admits a two-hidden-layer ReLU representation. Our results improve on [Bakaev, Brunck, Hertrich, Stade, Yehudayoff, STOC'26]. In that work, the authors established a two-hidden-layer representation for $\max_{5}$ and an upper bound of $\lceil{\log_3 (n-2)\rceil}+1$ hidden layers for $\max_{n}$.

AI.tldr: The authors prove that max over n≤10 real numbers can be exactly represented by a 2-hidden-layer ReLU network, with the max₁₀ construction featuring a structured first layer of pairwise maxima enabling recursive substitution. For n>10, they achieve depth ⌈log₅(n/2)⌉+1 < log₅(n)+1.57, improving the prior log₃-based bound. The result extends to all continuous piecewise-linear functions on ℝᵈ (d≤9) via hinging-hyperplane representations.
AI.motivation: Exact representation of the maximum function by shallow ReLU networks is a foundational problem in neural network expressivity. Prior work (Bakaev et al., STOC'26) achieved 2-layer representation for max₅ and log₃-based depth for maxₙ. The authors aim to push the frontier: how large can n be while still admitting a 2-hidden-layer exact ReLU representation, and what is the optimal depth scaling for larger n?
AI.method: The problem is reduced to exact rational linear algebra over ℚ. After a symmetry reduction, the necessary sign cancellations in the ReLU network are encoded as finite linear systems, which are solved and verified computationally. The max₁₀ construction uses a structured first hidden layer of pairwise maxima, enabling recursive substitution into larger networks. The depth bound for n>10 is derived analytically from this recursive structure, and the result is generalized to all continuous piecewise-linear functions via the hinging-hyperplane representation of Wang & Sun (2005).
AI.result: (1) maxₙ is exactly representable by a 2-hidden-layer ReLU network for all n≤10. (2) For n>10, maxₙ requires at most ⌈log₅(n/2)⌉+1 hidden layers, improving the prior ⌈log₃(n-2)⌉+1 bound. (3) Every continuous piecewise-linear function on ℝᵈ (d≤9) admits a 2-hidden-layer ReLU representation. (4) General continuous piecewise-linear functions on ℝᵈ require at most ⌈log₅((d+1)/2)⌉+1 layers.
AI.conclusion: The paper significantly advances the understanding of exact ReLU representability for the maximum function and piecewise-linear functions, raising the 2-layer threshold from n=5 to n=10 and improving the asymptotic depth scaling from log₃ to log₅. The recursive structure of the max₁₀ construction is both theoretically elegant and practically relevant for composing deeper networks.

title: Procedural Knowledge Is Not Low-Rank: Why LoRA Fails to Internalize Multi-Step Procedures
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA have become the default for adapting large language models, succeeding across instruction following, style transfer, and factual adaptation. We show that for procedural knowledge--the ability to follow multi-step procedures with conditional branching through to terminal states--LoRA fails to match full fine-tuning at the ranks where it retains its efficiency advantage. In a systematic ablation (r = 16--128) on a procedural travel booking task (14 nodes), all LoRA configurations fail uniformly (task success <= 2.54 vs. 4.11 for full fine-tuning, all p < 0.001), with scores decreasing at higher ranks--despite maintaining 95--99% conversation completion rates. Cross-domain replication on Zoom support (14 nodes) and insurance claims (55 nodes) at 8B confirms the failure generalizes: LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning by 0.8--2.2 points on average at both r = 32 and r = 128, with the largest gap on the most complex procedure. Quadrupling rank from 32 to 128 provides marginal improvement but does not close the gap. SVD analysis of the weight changes produced by full fine-tuning explains why: across three domains at both 3B and 8B, the mean effective rank of the update ranges from 761 to 1,026, and rank 128 captures only 43--51% of the squared Frobenius norm. Together, these findings establish that for procedural tasks LoRA falls well short of full fine-tuning--a fundamental limitation for agentic applications.

AI.tldr: LoRA fails to match full fine-tuning for procedural knowledge tasks (multi-step procedures with conditional branching), regardless of rank choice. SVD analysis reveals that full fine-tuning weight updates have effective ranks of 761-1,026, far exceeding typical LoRA ranks (16-128), which capture only 43-51% of update norm. This represents a fundamental limitation for agentic LLM applications.
AI.motivation: While LoRA has become the default parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for LLMs and succeeds on instruction following, style transfer, and factual adaptation, its effectiveness on procedural knowledge — the ability to follow multi-step procedures with conditional branching to terminal states — has not been systematically evaluated. This gap is critical because procedural reasoning underpins agentic AI applications.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic ablation experiments comparing LoRA (ranks r=16-128) against full fine-tuning on procedurally-structured tasks across three domains: travel booking (14 nodes), Zoom support (14 nodes), and insurance claims (55 nodes), at both 3B and 8B model scales. They measure task success rates and conversation completion rates. Additionally, they perform SVD analysis on the weight update matrices from full fine-tuning to compute effective rank and the proportion of squared Frobenius norm captured at different LoRA-equivalent ranks.
AI.result: In the travel booking task, all LoRA configurations fail uniformly (task success ≤2.54 vs. 4.11 for full fine-tuning, p<0.001), with performance decreasing at higher ranks despite 95-99% conversation completion. Cross-domain replication shows LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning by 0.8-2.2 points at both r=32 and r=128, with the largest gap on the most complex procedure. Quadrupling rank provides marginal improvement but does not close the gap. SVD analysis reveals mean effective ranks of 761-1,026 for full fine-tuning updates across domains and scales, with rank-128 LoRA capturing only 43-51% of the squared Frobenius norm.
AI.conclusion: Procedural knowledge tasks expose a fundamental limitation of LoRA: the intrinsic rank of weight updates required for procedural reasoning far exceeds the ranks where LoRA maintains its parameter efficiency. For agentic applications involving multi-step conditional procedures, full fine-tuning or substantially higher-rank adaptation methods are necessary.

title: "Go Home Copilot, You're Drunk": Understanding Developer Responses to Agent-Generated Code Review Comments
summary: Code review is a critical quality assurance practice in software engineering development, and AI coding agents are increasingly generating review comments on pull requests. However, little is known about how developers actually respond to such agent-generated feedback. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study on the resolution of agent-generated code review comments. We analyze $54{,}791$ comments generated by five widely used coding agents (i.e., Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Devin, and Claude) across $342$ Python repositories on GitHub. We examine (1) resolution rates across agents and comment types, (2) the role of developer experience, and (3) characteristics that influence comment usefulness. Our results show that resolution rate varies considerably across agents, with Copilot accounting for the majority of resolved comments (72.9\%). Core developers resolve the majority of agent-generated feedback, particularly for \textit{design} and \textit{evolvability}-related comments, while peripheral developers are more involved in resolving \textit{functional defect} comments. Through open card sorting of 470 unresolved comment discussions, we identify \textit{ten} discussion patterns explaining why comments remain unresolved, with \textit{incorrect suggestions} and \textit{intentional design decisions} being the most prevalent. Finally, our analysis reveals that the presence of an inline \textit{code suggestion} is the strongest predictor of comment resolution, while lengthy and complex comments are less likely to be acted upon. Our findings provide insights for improving AI-generated code review feedback and its integration into development workflows.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study on how developers resolve AI-generated code review comments across 5 coding agents (Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Devin, Claude) in 342 Python repos. Key findings: Copilot dominates resolutions (72.9%), core developers handle design/evolvability comments while peripheral devs address functional defects, 10 discussion patterns explain unresolved comments (led by incorrect suggestions and intentional design decisions), and inline code suggestions are the strongest predictor of resolution.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are increasingly generating code review comments on pull requests, but there is a critical gap in understanding how developers actually respond to and resolve this agent-generated feedback. No prior large-scale empirical study has investigated this phenomenon.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of 54,791 agent-generated code review comments from five agents (Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Devin, Claude) across 342 Python GitHub repositories. Methods include: (1) quantitative analysis of resolution rates by agent and comment type, (2) examination of developer experience (core vs. peripheral) as a factor, (3) open card sorting of 470 unresolved comment discussions to derive thematic patterns, and (4) regression/predictive modeling to identify characteristics influencing comment usefulness and resolution likelihood.
AI.result: Resolution rates vary significantly across agents — Copilot accounts for 72.9% of all resolved comments. Core developers predominantly resolve design and evolvability comments, while peripheral developers engage more with functional defect comments. Ten discussion patterns for unresolved comments were identified, with "incorrect suggestions" and "intentional design decisions" as the most prevalent. Inline code suggestions are the strongest predictor of resolution; lengthy and complex comments are less likely to be resolved.
AI.conclusion: Agent-generated code review comments show uneven resolution patterns shaped by agent source, comment type, developer role, and structural features. The findings offer actionable insights for improving AI-generated review feedback — emphasizing concise, code-suggestion-rich comments — and for better integrating such agents into real-world development workflows.

title: Towards Reducing Foreign Language Anxiety Using Level-Appropriate Embodied Conversational Agents
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, published in the proceedings of EDULEARN26
summary: Foreign language anxiety (FLA) can be a major barrier to second language acquisition (SLA), especially in conversational contexts. With the proliferation of large language models (LLMs) throughout all areas of life, recent work suggests that interacting with LLM agents can be instrumental within the field of SLA and foreign language education, especially for reducing FLA. Related work also suggests that linguistic demands and task complexity can be predictors of FLA, implying that the use of demanding, complex language could lead to learners experiencing higher FLA. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-agent embodied conversational system that generates level-appropriate dialogue for English language learners. These levels are based on those defined by the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) to describe non-native listener and speaker proficiency. Using a "generate-evaluate-regenerate" loop with multiple LLM agents and a level classifier, it achieves a desired simplicity that is adaptive to the user's proficiency level. We also share the results of a preliminary small-sample pilot study that tested this system with Japanese university students, to see whether it would yield lower FLA levels than an unsimplified embodied conversational agent. Analysis of conversational output showed that 87.4% of dialogue sentences generated by the proposed multi-agent system fell within one predicted CEFR level of the learner's self-assessed proficiency, compared to 54.1% for the unsimplified agent. This suggests that the novel system is better able to produce output at an appropriate level for the learner. Though this study did not yield statistically significant evidence that the system reduces FLA levels in Japanese learners of English, likely due to a small sample size, it provides usability findings and culturally-informed design insights that will inform future study.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM system with a "generate-evaluate-regenerate" loop produces CEFR-level-appropriate dialogue for English learners. It achieved 87.4% within-level accuracy vs. 54.1% for an unsimplified agent, but a small pilot study found no statistically significant FLA reduction in Japanese students.
AI.motivation: Foreign language anxiety (FLA) impedes second language acquisition, especially in conversation. While LLMs show promise for reducing FLA, linguistically demanding output may inadvertently increase anxiety. The authors aim to develop a system that adapts conversational complexity to the learner's proficiency level to mitigate FLA.
AI.method: A multi-agent embodied conversational system using a "generate-evaluate-regenerate" loop with multiple LLM agents and a CEFR-level classifier. The system generates dialogue, evaluates its CEFR level, and regenerates if needed until it matches the user's self-assessed proficiency. A pilot study compared this system against an unsimplified embodied conversational agent with Japanese university students, measuring FLA levels and analyzing sentence-level CEFR alignment.
AI.result: 87.4% of the proposed system's sentences fell within ±1 CEFR level of the learner's proficiency, versus 54.1% for the unsimplified agent. However, the pilot study did not yield statistically significant evidence that the system reduces FLA, likely due to small sample size. Usability findings and culturally-informed design insights were documented.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent system reliably produces level-appropriate dialogue, but the link between linguistic simplification and FLA reduction remains unconfirmed statistically. Future work with larger samples is needed to validate the anxiety-reduction hypothesis, building on the usability and cultural insights gathered.

title: Incentives and Market Structure in Intent-Based Exchanges: Evidence from a Solver-Reward Reform
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at CBT 2026 (International Workshop on Cryptocurrencies and Blockchain Technology, co-located with ESORICS 2026)
summary: Intent-based decentralized exchanges delegate execution to a competitive class of agents -- solvers -- whose behavior is shaped by protocol-designed reward rules. We measure how a change to those rules reshapes who captures value, using a governance-dated natural experiment: CoW Protocol CIP-74 (effective 8 December 2025), which replaced a fixed solver-reward cap with one tied to protocol revenue and introduced an ad-valorem volume fee. Using daily solver shares over 395 days, we find the reform reallocated trading value by order size. The robust signature is a monotone size gradient: concentration fell in small orders and rose in large ones across four order-value buckets (Spearman rho=1.00, exact permutation p=0.042) -- a pattern that survives dropping the single largest solver. Aggregate concentration also rose (volume-weighted HHI 0.176->0.241), substantially carried by the incumbent top solver. By trade count the market de-concentrated (count-HHI -0.060). A simple solver-economics model rationalizes the pattern: an ad-valorem fee is competitively neutral, while a revenue-linked reward cap raises the marginal payoff to inventory-rich solvers on large orders -- consistent with restricted-entry predictions (Chitra et al. 2024). A control venue (UniswapX) shows no matching break. We detect no change in average execution quality (~7 bps bound). A triple-difference exploiting a February 2026 fee cut is directionally consistent but underpowered. Reward design measurably reallocates who captures value in intent markets, without moving the average price users receive.

AI.tldr: CIP-74's shift from a fixed solver-reward cap to a revenue-linked cap with an ad-valorem fee reallocated trading value by order size: concentration fell for small orders, rose for large orders, with aggregate volume-weighted HHI rising from 0.176 to 0.241, while execution quality remained unchanged (~7 bps bound).
AI.motivation: Intent-based DEXs rely on solvers whose behavior is governed by protocol reward rules, yet little empirical evidence exists on how changes to those rules reshape value capture among solvers. The authors exploit CIP-74 as a natural experiment to identify causal effects of reward design on market structure.
AI.method: Difference-in-differences using daily solver shares over 395 days around CIP-74 (effective 8 Dec 2025), stratifying orders into four value buckets. Concentration measured via HHI. Robustness checks include dropping the largest solver, permutation tests (Spearman rho=1.00, p=0.042), a UniswapX control venue, and a triple-difference exploiting a Feb 2026 fee cut.
AI.result: A monotone size gradient emerged: concentration decreased in small orders, increased in large orders. Volume-weighted HHI rose from 0.176 to 0.241, driven by the incumbent top solver. Count-based HHI fell by 0.060, indicating de-concentration by trade count. Execution quality did not change (bound ~7 bps). UniswapX showed no parallel break. The triple-difference was directionally consistent but underpowered.
AI.conclusion: Reward rule design measurably reallocates which solvers capture value in intent markets without affecting average execution prices users receive. The ad-valorem fee is competitively neutral; the revenue-linked reward cap favors inventory-rich solvers on large orders, consistent with restricted-entry models (Chitra et al. 2024).

title: MoE$^2$-LoRA: When MoE Models Meet MoE-style Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have been widely adopted in large language models, yet parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for MoE models remains underexplored. Existing PEFT methods for MoE either ignore router priors with uniform adapters, reducing efficiency and risking forgetting, or rely on static expert selection, limiting per-token capacity and cross-expert feature learning. In this paper, we make the first attempt to fine-tune MoE models with MoE-style low-rank adaptation: our method, entitled MoE$^2$-LoRA, deeply couples the pretrained expert specialization with task-specific adaptivity via a dual-channel Routing-Conditioned Projection (RCP) module, which reuses base router activations to inform LoRA routing. We further introduce a single global LoRA expert pool shared across all layers, enabling model-wide adaptation with emergent layer-wise affinities and balanced expert utilization. MoE$^2$-LoRA simultaneously benefits from the advantages of prior reuse, dynamic adapter routing, and model-wide knowledge sharing. Evaluated on multiple MoE backbones with varying scales and expert granularities, MoE$^2$-LoRA consistently achieves state-of-the-art downstream accuracy while retaining stronger general capabilities.

AI.tldr: MoE²-LoRA introduces a PEFT method for MoE models that uses a dual-channel Routing-Conditioned Projection module to couple pretrained expert specialization with task-specific adaptation, sharing a single global LoRA expert pool across all layers, achieving SOTA downstream accuracy while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT methods for MoE models either use uniform adapters (ignoring router priors, causing inefficiency and forgetting) or static expert selection (limiting per-token capacity and cross-expert feature learning). A method is needed that deeply couples pretrained MoE routing with task-specific low-rank adaptation.
AI.method: MoE²-LoRA proposes a dual-channel Routing-Conditioned Projection (RCP) module that reuses base router activations to guide LoRA routing. A single global LoRA expert pool is shared across all layers, enabling model-wide adaptation with emergent layer-wise affinities and balanced expert utilization.
AI.result: Evaluated on multiple MoE backbones with varying scales and expert granularities, MoE²-LoRA consistently achieves state-of-the-art downstream accuracy while retaining stronger general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: MoE²-LoRA is the first to fine-tune MoE models with MoE-style low-rank adaptation, combining prior reuse, dynamic adapter routing, and model-wide knowledge sharing for superior PEFT performance.

title: Molt: A Scalable PyTorch-Native Training Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning research is constant algorithm modification, new estimators, new pipeline stages, new rollout schemes, and in mainstream frameworks each change threads through layers of trainer, distributed backend, and rollout glue: the cost lands on the researcher at every iteration. Molt is a PyTorch-native training framework built to keep that cost small: a codebase compact and clean enough for a researcher to hold in their head, and for an AI coding assistant to read and reason about in its entirety, so the algorithm flow can be traced and changed end to end. The agent is an ordinary program, and one asynchronous loop trains multimodal and mixture-of-experts policies while never training on a token it did not generate, consistent in tokens, policy versions, and model semantics. Leanness does not cost performance: under a matched, fully asynchronous protocol, Molt is statistically comparable to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based stack. Molt is open source and provides recipes and containers at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt.

AI.tldr: Molt is a compact, PyTorch-native agentic RL training framework that prioritizes code simplicity and end-to-end traceability, achieving statistical parity with a Megatron-based stack under a matched asynchronous protocol.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL research involves frequent modifications across many pipeline stages (algorithms, estimators, rollout schemes, trainers, distributed backends), and mainstream frameworks impose high iteration costs because each change threads through complex, layered code. The goal is to minimize this overhead by providing a framework simple enough for a researcher to fully understand and for AI coding assistants to reason about in its entirety.
AI.method: Molt treats the agent as an ordinary program and employs a single asynchronous training loop. It supports multimodal and mixture-of-experts policies while enforcing a strict constraint: the model never trains on tokens it did not generate, ensuring consistency in tokens, policy versions, and model semantics. The framework is PyTorch-native and deliberately minimal, avoiding extraneous abstraction layers.
AI.result: Under a matched, fully asynchronous protocol, Molt achieves statistical comparability to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based reinforcement learning stack, demonstrating that leanness does not come at the cost of training performance.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RL research benefits from a framework that reduces cognitive and engineering overhead. Molt demonstrates that a compact, traceable codebase can match the performance of industrial-scale systems, and it is released as open source with recipes and containers to facilitate adoption.

title: The Hard Decision Layer: Evidence for Committed Inference in Transformers
summary: We investigate where and how transformer-based language models commit to predictions in multiple-choice question answering. We identify the _Hard Decision Layer_ (HDL), a natural architectural property where answer option rankings stabilize abruptly during inference. Empirical validation across four language models (Qwen, Llama, Granite, Mistral) and four benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent HDL emergence without learned routing policies. We also show that the HDL is invariant to fine-tuning. Our results reveal striking accuracy improvements at the HDL: up to +0.61 (Qwen on CommonsenseQA), after which performance stabilizes. Systematic ablations on label formats and problem complexity confirm the phenomenon is fundamental to model architecture. These findings offer mechanistic insights into transformer inference and suggest opportunities for efficient reasoning and model steering. All code and results required to reproduce this work are available in https://github.com/Mystic-Slice/hard-decision-layer

AI.tldr: Transformer-based LMs exhibit a "Hard Decision Layer" (HDL) where answer rankings in multiple-choice QA abruptly stabilize during forward inference. This architectural property is consistent across models/datasets, invariant to fine-tuning, and associated with significant accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanistic process by which transformer LMs commit to predictions in multiple-choice QA, moving beyond output-level analysis to identify where and how decisions crystallize within the model's internal layers.
AI.method: The authors define the Hard Decision Layer (HDL) operationally as the layer where answer option rankings stabilize abruptly. They empirically validate HDL emergence across four transformer models (Qwen, Llama, Granite, Mistral) and four QA benchmarks, without any learned routing policies. Systematic ablations on label formats and problem complexity are performed, and fine-tuning invariance is tested.
AI.result: HDL emerges consistently across all model-dataset combinations. Accuracy improves sharply at the HDL—up to +0.61 for Qwen on CommonsenseQA—then stabilizes. The HDL is invariant to fine-tuning and robust to variations in label format and problem complexity.
AI.conclusion: The HDL is a fundamental architectural property of transformer LMs that offers mechanistic insights into inference dynamics, with implications for efficient reasoning (early exiting) and model steering.

title: Are Production Cloud Skills Adequately Tested? Measuring and Governing Skill Test Coverage in Practice
summary: Cloud platforms increasingly deliver reusable Cloud Skills that guide AI agents in creating, configuring, monitoring, and troubleshooting cloud resources. Workflow-oriented Skills specify multiple resource operations, user choices, validation steps, and recovery behavior. Existing Skill evaluation primarily measures whether a Skill improves task success. Passing the available testcases, however, does not reveal which behaviors specified by the Skill have never been tested. This paper introduces Skill Test Coverage, which measures how completely a Skill's test suite covers its operational test obligations. We define the coverage units, testcase coverage relation, calculation procedure, and claim boundary. Because these units and links are not explicit in natural-language Skill packages, we develop a measurement pipeline that recovers operational obligations, organizes their workflow context, maps testcases using both user prompts and initial resource states, and produces an auditable coverage report. Model-assisted candidate generation is combined with expert review to ensure that the reported coverage remains grounded in the original Skill and testcase evidence. A post-review module then translates confirmed coverage gaps into source-grounded test-improvement recommendations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Skill Test Coverage, a metric and measurement pipeline that quantifies how completely a test suite covers the operational obligations specified in cloud-facing AI Skills, and generates actionable test-improvement recommendations from coverage gaps.
AI.motivation: Existing Skill evaluation only measures task success — i.e., whether a Skill passes available testcases. This reveals nothing about which behaviors specified by the Skill remain untested. A Skill may pass all tests yet have significant untested operational paths, leading to undetected failures in production.
AI.method: The authors define coverage units, a testcase coverage relation, a calculation procedure, and a claim boundary. They build a measurement pipeline that (1) recovers operational obligations from natural-language Skill packages, (2) organizes them within workflow context, (3) maps testcases using both user prompts and initial resource states, and (4) produces an auditable coverage report. Model-assisted candidate generation is combined with expert review to ground coverage claims in source evidence. A post-review module translates confirmed coverage gaps into source-grounded test-improvement recommendations.
AI.result: The pipeline produces auditable Skill Test Coverage reports that identify which operational obligations are exercised and which remain uncovered. The post-review module generates concrete, source-grounded recommendations for improving test suites to address coverage gaps.
AI.conclusion: Skill Test Coverage provides a principled, auditable framework for assessing test suite completeness beyond binary pass/fail metrics, enabling developers to systematically identify untested Skill behaviors and improve test coverage with evidence-based recommendations.

title: VisionPulse: A Virtual Reality System Enabling Accessible Discovery and Navigation for Blind and Low Vision Users
summary: Free exploration is an important aspect of many engaging virtual reality (VR) experiences, yet remains largely inaccessible to blind and low vision (BLV) users due to its reliance on visual feedback. Existing approaches support BLV navigation through prebuilt menus of environment and audio beacons, but offer limited support for free-form discovery. We present VisionPulse, an accessible VR system that enables BLV users to explore virtual environments through natural head and hand movements, combined with auditory, haptic, and text-to-speech feedback. VisionPulse introduces a discovery-driven approach that allows users to progressively uncover regions and objects, alongside navigation support through waypoint guidance and object localization via responsive audio and orientation-based haptics. A study with 12 BLV participants showed a strong preference for VisionPulse's discovery-based exploration and multimodal feedback, without negatively impacting task performance or perceived workload. Our findings underscore the importance of accessible, free-form VR experiences, and contribute insights for inclusive VR design.

AI.tldr: VisionPulse is an accessible VR system enabling blind and low vision users to freely explore virtual environments using head/hand movements with auditory, haptic, and text-to-speech feedback, featuring progressive discovery and waypoint navigation. A study with 12 BLV participants demonstrated strong preference without compromising performance.
AI.motivation: Free exploration in VR relies heavily on visual feedback, making it largely inaccessible to blind and low vision (BLV) users. Existing solutions (prebuilt menus, audio beacons) constrain users to structured navigation rather than free-form discovery, leaving a gap for spontaneous, engaging exploration.
AI.method: VisionPulse uses a discovery-driven approach where users progressively uncover regions and objects through natural head and hand movements. The system provides multimodal feedback: responsive audio cues, orientation-based haptics, and text-to-speech for object identification. Navigation support includes waypoint guidance and object localization. The system was evaluated with 12 BLV participants in a user study.
AI.result: Participants showed a strong preference for VisionPulse's discovery-based exploration and multimodal feedback. Importantly, this preference did not come at the cost of task performance or increased perceived workload compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the viability and importance of accessible, free-form VR exploration for BLV users and contribute design insights for inclusive VR systems that go beyond structured navigation paradigms.

title: Ethereum NFT Smart Contracts: Knowledge-Guided Vulnerability Detection with LLM and Code Slicing
summary: Ethereum non-fungible tokens (NFTs) implement ownership, transfer, authorization, and metadata operations through smart contracts, making contract vulnerabilities a direct risk to digital assets. Existing static analyzers provide efficient rule-based screening but can struggle with application-specific logic, whereas unconstrained large language model analysis may be distracted by irrelevant code or produce inconsistent outputs. We present a vulnerability-detection method that combines vulnerability-focused code slicing, an ERC-721-oriented knowledge base, and constrained DeepSeek analysis. Regular-expression patterns locate candidate statements for reentrancy, integer overflow or underflow, and timestamp dependence. A structure-aware context-window algorithm then extracts line-numbered code slices. DeepSeek analyzes each slice using explicit decision rules and a fixed output schema, and the resulting records support automated batch processing. On 450 NFT contract samples, the full configuration produced 437 positive labels, corresponding to a reported positive-label rate of 97.1%. Removing the external knowledge base reduced this rate to 87.11%, while analyzing complete contracts without the knowledge base reduced it to 73.78%. These results indicate that focused code context and domain constraints materially affect the detector's reported output.

AI.tldr: A hybrid vulnerability detection method for Ethereum NFT smart contracts that combines regex-based code slicing, an ERC-721 knowledge base, and constrained DeepSeek LLM analysis, achieving a 97.1% positive-label rate on 450 contract samples.
AI.motivation: Existing static analyzers for NFT smart contracts use rule-based screening but struggle with application-specific logic, while unconstrained LLM analysis may be distracted by irrelevant code or produce inconsistent outputs. A method is needed that focuses analysis on relevant code segments while maintaining consistent, structured output.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Regular-expression patterns locate candidate statements for reentrancy, integer overflow/underflow, and timestamp dependence; (2) A structure-aware context-window algorithm extracts line-numbered code slices; (3) DeepSeek LLM analyzes each slice using explicit decision rules and a fixed output schema, supported by an ERC-721-oriented external knowledge base, with results enabling automated batch processing.
AI.result: On 450 NFT contract samples, the full configuration (code slicing + knowledge base + constrained DeepSeek) produced 437 positive labels (97.1% rate). Ablation: removing the knowledge base dropped the rate to 87.11%; analyzing complete contracts without the knowledge base further reduced it to 73.78%.
AI.conclusion: Focused code context (via slicing) and domain constraints (via the ERC-721 knowledge base) materially improve the detector's reported output, demonstrating that combining lightweight static preprocessing with constrained LLM analysis yields more consistent vulnerability detection than either approach alone.

title: Analyzing Toxic Behavior and Its Impact on the Mastodon Community
summary: Mastodon as a decentralized federation of independently moderated social servers poses unique challenges for the detection and mitigation of toxic content. There are no unified moderation standards. The ecosystem is very diverse and uneven. This paper explores the development and spread of toxicity in Mastodon, utilizing machine learning methods to examine user posts. The results offer clarity on toxicity trends and its implications for community health and decentralized governance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how toxic content emerges and propagates across Mastodon's decentralized server federation using machine learning, shedding light on toxicity patterns and their impact on community health and governance.
AI.motivation: Mastodon's decentralized architecture — comprising independently moderated servers with no unified moderation standards and a highly heterogeneous ecosystem — creates distinctive challenges for detecting and mitigating toxic content. Existing centralized moderation approaches cannot be directly applied, motivating this investigation.
AI.method: The study employs machine learning methods to analyze user posts across the Mastodon federation, examining the emergence, propagation, and trends of toxic content within this decentralized social media environment.
AI.result: The analysis reveals clear patterns and trends in how toxicity develops and spreads across Mastodon instances, providing empirical evidence on the dynamics of toxic content in a federated social network.
AI.conclusion: The findings contribute insights into toxicity dynamics within decentralized social platforms, with practical implications for community health maintenance and the design of decentralized governance mechanisms. The uneven and diverse nature of the ecosystem necessitates tailored moderation approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

title: Physically Constrained Federated Additive Models for O-RAN SLA-Risk Prediction
summary: Proactive service assurance in O-RAN requires predicting per-slice SLA violations before they occur. The prediction model must be auditable by operators and must train across base stations without pooling per-slice KPIs, which are commercially sensitive because slices are leased to individual tenants. Neural additive models (NAMs) offer auditability because each KPI contributes through a visible shape function. However, visibility alone does not guarantee physical validity. On the ColO-RAN testbed dataset, unconstrained NAMs learn effects that contradict wireless physics, for example predicting higher risk when channel quality improves. This failure appears under both local and centralized training, and non-IID federated averaging worsens it. We present Monotone FedNAM, a federated additive model in which KPIs with unambiguous physical direction are represented as monotone splines whose constraints survive FedAvg aggregation by construction, while contestable KPIs remain unconstrained. The model trains and operates as a Non-RT RIC rApp and is compact enough for deployment as a Near-RT RIC xApp. Monotone FedNAM eliminates all monotonicity violations, raises constrained shape consistency from 0.71 to 1.00, generalizes to an unseen scheduling policy, and reduces uplink traffic by 65%, at a cost of 0.04 to 0.07 AUC. These results show that physically constrained federated additive models can support auditable SLA risk inference for multi-tenant O-RAN service assurance

AI.tldr: Monotone FedNAM proposes a federated neural additive model with monotonicity constraints that enforce physically valid KPI-risk relationships for SLA violation prediction in multi-tenant O-RAN, eliminating all monotonicity violations while maintaining strong predictive performance.
AI.motivation: Proactive SLA assurance in O-RAN requires auditable, cross-base-station prediction models that do not pool commercially sensitive per-slice KPIs. While Neural Additive Models (NAMs) offer auditability via visible shape functions, they can learn physically invalid relationships (e.g., predicting higher SLA violation risk with better channel quality). This problem worsens under federated averaging with non-IID data.
AI.method: Monotone FedNAM combines federated learning with monotonic spline constraints. KPIs with unambiguous physical direction (e.g., channel quality) are modeled using monotone splines whose constraints are preserved under FedAvg aggregation by construction. Contestable KPIs remain unconstrained. The model is designed as a Non-RT RIC rApp, compact enough for Near-RT RIC xApp deployment.
AI.result: On the ColO-RAN testbed, Monotone FedNAM eliminates all monotonicity violations, raises constrained shape consistency from 0.71 to 1.00, generalizes to an unseen scheduling policy, reduces uplink traffic by 65%, at a cost of only 0.04–0.07 AUC.
AI.conclusion: Physically constrained federated additive models enable auditable, trustworthy SLA risk inference for multi-tenant O-RAN service assurance, with minimal performance degradation and significant communication efficiency gains.

title: Household Movement Detection in Mixed-Format Occupancy Data Using LLM-Based Entity Resolution
comment: Computer Science & Information Technology (CS & IT) ISSN : 2231 - 5403, Volume 16, Number 10, May 2026
summary: Entity resolution (ER) typically relies on pairwise similarity comparisons between records, which limits its ability to capture indirect relationships present in demographic occupancy data. An important indirect pattern arises from household movement, where multiple individuals relocate together across addresses, but detecting such patterns is difficult due to mixed-format records, noise, duplication, and the absence of stable identifiers. This paper proposes an AI-enhanced framework for detecting indirect entity links associated with household movement in unstandardized name-address data. The approach integrates prompt-based large language model (LLM) named entity recognition for extracting personal names and addresses without extensive preprocessing, semantic text embeddings for robust similarity computation, and graph-based reasoning to infer group-level movement patterns. Experimental evaluation on SPX benchmark datasets (S8-S12) generated using the Synthetic Occupancy Generator demonstrates that incorporating indirect household movement evidence improves recall by 8-15% while maintaining high precision, yielding F1-score gains of 6-8% over a strong pairwise baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-enhanced framework combining LLM-based NER, semantic embeddings, and graph reasoning to detect indirect entity links from household movement in noisy name-address data, achieving 6-8% F1-score gains over pairwise baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional entity resolution relies on pairwise similarity, failing to capture indirect relationships such as household movement where multiple individuals relocate together. Detecting these patterns is challenging due to mixed-format records, noise, duplication, and lack of stable identifiers in demographic occupancy data.
AI.method: A three-component framework: (1) prompt-based LLM named entity recognition for extracting personal names and addresses without heavy preprocessing; (2) semantic text embeddings for robust similarity computation; (3) graph-based reasoning to infer group-level household movement patterns from the extracted and linked entities.
AI.result: On SPX benchmark datasets (S8-S12) from the Synthetic Occupancy Generator, incorporating indirect household movement evidence improved recall by 8-15% while maintaining high precision, resulting in F1-score gains of 6-8% over a strong pairwise baseline.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based reasoning over LLM-extracted entities effectively captures indirect household movement links that pairwise methods miss, significantly boosting ER recall without sacrificing precision, and demonstrating the value of modeling group-level relational patterns in unstandardized demographic data.

title: Code Review is a Conversation: Toward Conversational AI Review Assistants
comment: Accepted at ICSME 2026 in the Visions and Emerging Results Track
summary: AI-based code review tools increasingly promise to help developers inspect pull requests, identify defects, and improve code quality. Yet most current approaches frame code review as a one-shot commenting task: given a diff, the system produces warnings or suggestions. This framing overlooks a central property of modern code review: review is a conversation. Human reviewers do not merely comment on code; they ask questions, explain expectations, negotiate design trade-offs, request evidence, transfer project knowledge, document rationale, and collectively decide whether a change is good enough to integrate. In this vision paper, we argue for conversational AI review assistants: systems that participate in code review as interactive partners rather than static comment generators. Such assistants should identify when conversation is needed, ask grounded questions, respond to developer explanations, summarize unresolved issues, help capture rationale, and know when to abstain or escalate to human reviewers. Such a paradigm shift requires novel evaluation methodologies as well. We outline a research agenda for studying review conversations, designing conversational AI review capabilities, and evaluating their impact on software evolution and maintenance. Our vision reframes AI code review from automated commenting to human-AI sensemaking before integration.

AI.tldr: This vision paper argues that AI code review tools should evolve from one-shot comment generators into conversational partners that engage in the interactive, dialogic nature of real code review — asking questions, negotiating trade-offs, transferring knowledge, and collaborating on integration decisions — requiring new designs and evaluation methodologies.
AI.motivation: Current AI code review tools treat review as a static, one-shot commenting task, which fundamentally misrepresents modern code review as an inherently conversational process involving questioning, negotiation, knowledge transfer, rationale capture, and collective decision-making. This gap between tool design and real practice motivates a paradigm shift.
AI.method: This is a vision paper that does not present an implemented system. Instead, it articulates a conceptual framework for conversational AI review assistants by identifying key conversational capabilities (grounded questioning, responding to explanations, summarizing issues, capturing rationale, knowing when to abstain/escalate), and outlines a research agenda spanning the study of review conversations, design of conversational capabilities, and development of novel evaluation methodologies.
AI.result: As a vision paper, it presents no empirical results. It proposes a reframing of AI code review from automated commenting to human-AI sensemaking before integration, and delineates open research challenges in designing and evaluating conversational review assistants.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for a paradigm shift toward conversational AI review assistants that treat code review as interactive sensemaking rather than one-shot defect detection, and they chart a research roadmap to realize this vision across tool design, conversation studies, and evaluation.

title: What Clinicians Need: Designing, Developing and Evaluating an AI-Based Decision Support System for Autism Assessment
summary: AI methods promise to support autism spectrum condition (ASC) diagnostics in adults, a complex and time-consuming process, that is characterized by a shortage of specialized clinicians. To date, clinicians' needs and their interaction with such AI-based support remain underexplored. Our work aims to develop and evaluate an AI-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) for ASC assessment, and to investigate how it impacts clinicians' decision-making. By interviewing clinicians of varying experience levels, we identified five challenges and derived design strategies. Based on that, we developed SIT-CARE, a CDSS, which provides AI-based recommendations and data visualizations of clinically relevant nonverbal behavior. Through an evaluation study with newly recruited clinicians, we found that SIT-CARE led to different decision paths in regard to the ASC assessment, which are reflected in clinicians' mental models and decision changes. Overall, SIT-CARE demonstrated potential in improving initial diagnostic assessments, supporting in-depth diagnosis and empowering less experienced clinicians.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SIT-CARE, an AI-based clinical decision support system for autism spectrum condition diagnostics in adults, developed through clinician interviews and evaluated for its impact on diagnostic decision-making, particularly benefiting less experienced clinicians.
AI.motivation: Autism spectrum condition (ASC) diagnostics in adults is complex, time-consuming, and hampered by a shortage of specialized clinicians. Existing AI-based approaches have not adequately explored clinicians' needs or how such tools interact with clinical decision-making workflows.
AI.method: The authors first conducted interviews with clinicians of varying experience levels to identify five key challenges and derive design strategies. Based on these insights, they developed SIT-CARE, a CDSS that provides AI-based recommendations and data visualizations of clinically relevant nonverbal behavior. The system was then evaluated through a study with newly recruited clinicians to assess its impact on diagnostic decision-making, mental models, and decision changes.
