AI.result: SIT-CARE led to different decision paths in ASC assessment, reflected in changes to clinicians' mental models and diagnostic decisions. The system showed potential for improving initial diagnostic assessments, supporting in-depth diagnosis, and empowering less experienced clinicians.
AI.conclusion: AI-based CDSS tools like SIT-CARE can positively influence ASC diagnostic processes by augmenting clinician decision-making, particularly for those with less experience, suggesting a promising direction for addressing the clinician shortage in adult ASC diagnostics.

title: Practical Graph Optimisation and AI-Driven Models for Active Directory Security Hardening
summary: Microsoft's Active Directory (AD) is a directory service that enables the IT admin to manage security permissions and control access within a Windows domain network. As a core management system in many of organisation, AD has become a primary target for adversaries. While many solutions for hardening attack graphs exist, these efforts fall short in addressing several key practical challenges specific to the AD attack graph. First, existing models often assume the graph is static, whereas a real-world AD environment is highly dynamic. Second, most proposed solutions are limited to the defensive measure of revoking vulnerabilities (edge removal), while more active defence mechanisms are largely unstudied. Third, because not all remediations are implementable, a practical end-to-end model must incorporate system admin feedback into the prioritisation process. This thesis aims to address these limitations by studying and proposing a number of game-theoretic and optimisation-based decision-making models. First, we propose a honeypot/decoy placement model based on the principle of minimising the number of shortest paths and the number of Domain Admin-reachable nodes. Second, building on this model, we introduce a defence strategy that considers the dynamic/temporal nature of the AD graph, where the objective is to find the location to deploy decoys that maximises the worst-case incident response time. Third, we introduce an adaptive prioritisation model that queries each high-risk attack path to the IT administrator for mediation. Finally, we introduce an end-to-end adaptive prioritisation model that minimises the approval effort of the system admin by finding a general adaptive edge-removal policy that generalises the system admin's decisions to edges with similar risk features. We show that the problems underlying all of the contributed models are computationally intractable.

AI.tldr: This thesis addresses practical limitations in Active Directory attack graph defense by proposing four game-theoretic and optimization-based models: honeypot placement, dynamic decoy deployment for incident response, adaptive prioritization with admin feedback, and an end-to-end adaptive edge-removal policy that generalizes admin decisions across similar risk features.
AI.motivation: Existing AD attack graph hardening solutions suffer from three key gaps: (1) they treat the AD graph as static rather than dynamic, (2) they focus solely on edge removal (revoking vulnerabilities) while neglecting active defense mechanisms like decoys, and (3) they lack practical end-to-end models that incorporate system administrator feedback for prioritization, since not all remediations are implementable in practice.
AI.method: The thesis proposes four game-theoretic and optimization-based decision-making models: (1) a honeypot/decoy placement model minimizing shortest paths and Domain Admin-reachable nodes; (2) a dynamic defense model that deploys decoys to maximize worst-case incident response time under temporal graph changes; (3) an adaptive prioritization model that queries system admins on high-risk attack paths; and (4) an end-to-end adaptive prioritization model that learns a general edge-removal policy by generalizing admin feedback to edges with similar risk features.
AI.result: The underlying computational problems for all four contributed models are proven to be computationally intractable.
AI.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that practical AD defense requires moving beyond static edge-removal models toward dynamic, active-defense, and admin-in-the-loop approaches. While the resulting optimization problems are intractable, the formulations highlight critical design considerations and motivate the need for efficient heuristic or approximate solution methods in real-world deployments.

title: J-CoT: Chain-of-Thought in J-Space
summary: Chain-of-thought prompting improves language-model reasoning by carrying intermediate states across successive computation steps. However, relying on natural language as the only recurrent interface is overly restrictive, since many transient computations do not need to be fully verbalized. Existing latent-reasoning methods remove this constraint by recurrently propagating continuous hidden states. However, these methods pass a dense hidden vector as a whole, without an explicit mechanism for selecting and organizing the information needed by the next reasoning step. This motivates an intermediate interface that remains linguistically grounded without requiring a decoded sentence. We introduce \textbf{J-CoT}, a recurrent reasoning framework built on \emph{J-space}, a vocabulary-indexed coordinate system within the model's hidden representations. Within each cycle, the model computes in its full hidden space. At the cycle boundary, J-CoT expresses the intermediate state as vocabulary-indexed coefficients, carries these coefficients forward as a \emph{J-thought}, and maps them back into the model's hidden representation for the next cycle. J-CoT therefore requires neither a fluent intermediate rationale nor recurrence over the complete hidden state. Under matched backbone and inference settings, J-CoT-Zero matches or exceeds the strongest evaluated latent-reasoning baseline on every benchmark, while J-CoT-Train obtains the highest score across the evaluated mathematical, scientific, coding, and structured path-reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: J-CoT introduces a vocabulary-indexed coordinate system (J-space) within hidden representations, enabling recurrent reasoning that carries linguistically-grounded but non-verbalized intermediate states (J-thoughts) across computation steps, outperforming both chain-of-thought and latent-reasoning baselines.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought is constrained by requiring fully verbalized natural-language intermediates, while existing latent-reasoning methods pass dense hidden vectors without explicit mechanisms to select and organize information for the next step. An intermediate interface is needed that remains linguistically grounded but does not require decoded sentences.
AI.method: J-CoT is a recurrent reasoning framework operating in J-space — a vocabulary-indexed coordinate system in the model's hidden representations. Each cycle computes in full hidden space, then at cycle boundaries expresses the intermediate state as vocabulary-indexed coefficients (J-thoughts), carries them forward, and maps them back into hidden representations for the next cycle, avoiding both fluent rationale decoding and full hidden-state recurrence.
AI.result: J-CoT-Zero matches or exceeds the strongest latent-reasoning baseline on every benchmark under matched settings. J-CoT-Train achieves the highest scores across mathematical, scientific, coding, and structured path-reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: J-CoT effectively bridges the gap between fully verbalized chain-of-thought and dense latent reasoning by using vocabulary-indexed coordinates, achieving state-of-the-art reasoning performance while maintaining linguistic grounding without requiring decoded intermediate sentences.

title: Neural Feature Governance: Extending Atom Prevalence
summary: Neural network compression and interpretability remain open challenges in modern deep learn- ing, where billion-parameter architectures deliver impressive accuracy at the cost of trans- parency, computational efficiency, and reliable uncertainty quantification. This paper introduces Neural Atom Prevalence (NAP), a principled Bayesian framework for structured node-level model selection in feedforward neural networks. NAP introduces the neural atom (activation unit) and functions as a hybrid method operating through a four-phase pipeline: Bayesian Lottery Ticket (BLT) identification via Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), soft variational training of the Spike and Slab Independent Gaussian (SS-IG) model, Poisson-Binomial (PB) optimal layer-size selection, and Bayesian fine-tuning to produce a sparse, stable, interpretable, and accurate model. Extensive empirical validation across simulated nonlinear regression, two UCI benchmark datasets (Concrete, YearPredictionMSD), and the MNIST image classification task demonstrates that NAP achieves state-of-the-art structural sparsity, reducing active nodes to as few as 8% of the original dense architecture on MNIST, while well-calibrated probabilisti- cally: the aleatoric-epistemic uncertainty decomposition reveals that model ignorance accounts for only 3 to 4% of total predictive variance across all experiments, and regression reliability diagrams confirm a near-nominal predictive interval coverage (93.4% observed against a 95% target). These results establish NAP as a reliable, theoretically grounded, and computation- ally tractable solution to the simultaneous pursuit of sparsity, accuracy, interpretability, and uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks.

AI.tldr: Neural Atom Prevalence (NAP) is a Bayesian framework for structured node-level pruning in feedforward networks. It combines Lottery Ticket pruning, Spike-and-Slab variational training, Poisson-Binomial layer-size selection, and Bayesian fine-tuning to produce sparse, well-calibrated models. On MNIST, NAP reduces active nodes to 8% while maintaining accuracy and achieving near-nominal predictive interval coverage (93.4% vs. 95% target).
AI.motivation: Modern deep learning models with billions of parameters suffer from opaqueness, high computational cost, and unreliable uncertainty quantification. There is a pressing need for methods that simultaneously deliver sparsity, interpretability, accuracy, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates within a principled probabilistic framework.
AI.method: NAP is a four-phase pipeline: (1) Bayesian Lottery Ticket identification via Iterative Magnitude Pruning, (2) soft variational training under a Spike-and-Slab Independent Gaussian (SS-IG) prior, (3) Poisson-Binomial optimal layer-size selection to determine which nodes to retain, and (4) Bayesian fine-tuning of the resulting sparse architecture. The framework treats each activation unit as a "neural atom" and performs structured node-level model selection.
AI.result: On MNIST, NAP reduced active nodes to 8% of the original dense architecture. Across all experiments (simulated nonlinear regression, UCI Concrete and YearPredictionMSD, MNIST), aleatoric-epistemic uncertainty decomposition showed model ignorance accounts for only 3–4% of total predictive variance. Regression reliability diagrams confirmed 93.4% observed predictive interval coverage against a 95% target, indicating near-nominal calibration.
AI.conclusion: NAP provides a theoretically grounded, computationally tractable solution that jointly achieves structural sparsity, maintained accuracy, enhanced interpretability via node-level selection, and reliable uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks. It advances the state of the art in simultaneous neural network compression and calibration.

title: FrED: External Data Influence Estimation via Domain Knowledge Graph Grounding
summary: The rapid deployment of generative AI has amplified the critical need for Training Data Attribution to ensure transparency and accountability. However, current parametric approaches require computationally prohibitive access to model weights, while similarity-based methods ignore deep structural context. We propose a novel probabilistic framework that operates entirely in a black-box setting. Our method fuses continuous feature similarities with discrete, domain-specific Knowledge Graphs (KGs). This approach ensures the attribution is grounded in structural reality, explicitly rewarding highly specific historical samples while preventing generic background data from dominating the results. We evaluate our framework across two distinct domains where linking outputs to data and domain context is inherently complex: abstract artistic image synthesis and high-dimensional physical weather forecasting. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the robust efficacy of our approach. In the artistic domain, it achieves a strong Linear Datamodeling Score that exceeds standard black-box similarity baselines, while closing much of the gap to gradient-based estimators. We additionally present a cross-domain feasibility case study in environmental forecasting, where we use domain KGs to retrieve physically consistent historical analogs for regional flood forecasts, improving geographic localisation over a latent-only baseline. Operating entirely without internal model access, our approach provides an efficient, interpretable mechanism for post-hoc influence analysis and domain-grounded retrieval.

AI.tldr: A black-box, probabilistic framework for training data attribution that fuses continuous feature similarities with domain-specific Knowledge Graphs, grounding attribution in structural reality. Demonstrated on artistic image synthesis and weather forecasting, it outperforms similarity baselines and narrows the gap to gradient-based methods—all without requiring model weights.
AI.motivation: Current training data attribution is bottlenecked: parametric methods demand prohibitive model weight access, while similarity-based methods ignore deep structural/domain context. With the proliferation of generative AI, there is an urgent need for transparent, accountable attribution that works in black-box settings without sacrificing structural grounding.
AI.method: A probabilistic black-box framework that integrates (1) continuous feature similarities derived from model outputs or embeddings with (2) discrete, domain-specific Knowledge Graphs. The KG component enforces structural constraints, rewarding highly specific, historically relevant training samples while suppressing generic background data from dominating attribution results.
AI.result: In artistic image synthesis, the method achieves a strong Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), exceeding standard black-box similarity baselines and substantially closing the gap to gradient-based estimators. In a cross-domain feasibility study on environmental weather forecasting, domain KGs retrieved physically consistent historical analogs for regional flood forecasts, improving geographic localization over a latent-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an efficient, interpretable, and fully black-box mechanism for post-hoc influence analysis and domain-grounded retrieval. By operating without internal model access, it offers a practical path to transparency and accountability across diverse generative AI application domains.

title: No Edges, No Verdict: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Declared Dependency Graphs in 78K SBOMs in the Wild
summary: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) are consumed not only as component inventories but as dependency graphs: vulnerability triage, reachability filtering, and impact analysis all traverse the edges an SBOM declares. We present the first large-scale characterization of the declared dependency graph across 78,612 real-world SBOM files from the Wild SBOMs dataset (77,092 parseable). We find that the population splits into three regimes: 52.9% of SBOMs declare no edges at all (failing the NTIA minimum-elements requirement of dependency relationships), 8.8% declare a dependency block yet leave the majority of components isolated (degenerate regime; among such SBOMs with at least 50 components the median orphan share is 93%, and our 11 Syft-generated container-image SBOMs fall in this regime at 95-98% orphans), and 38.3% form well-connected graphs. Edge emission is determined by the generator, not the described software (0%-100% no-edge rates across tools), and the specification-level mechanism for declaring graph incompleteness (CycloneDX compositions) is used by 0.10% of the population. We argue that in the first two regimes, the common consumer inference "no path implies unreachable" is an unsound closed-world conclusion drawn from a demonstrably incomplete artifact; in a production vulnerability-prioritization system, replacing the resulting veto with an explicit "unknown" level guarded by a degeneracy detector recovered KEV recall from 0.600 to 0.950 (controlled re-scoring; 0.957 in a live end-to-end run) without alert flooding. We release our streaming scanner and the full per-SBOM topology dataset.

AI.tldr: First large-scale study of SBOM dependency graphs (78K+ files) reveals most SBOMs are structurally deficient: 52.9% declare no edges, 8.8% are "degenerate" with mostly orphan components. Only 38.3% are well-connected. Edge emission depends on the generator tool, not the software itself. Using "no path → unreachable" inference on incomplete SBOMs cripples vulnerability detection (0.600→0.950 KEV recall with degeneracy-aware approach).
AI.motivation: SBOMs are increasingly used for security tasks (vulnerability triage, reachability analysis, impact assessment) that critically depend on dependency graph edges. However, no prior study has characterized whether real-world SBOMs actually contain complete dependency graphs, raising the risk that downstream consumers make unsound closed-world inferences from incomplete data.
AI.method: Large-scale empirical analysis of 78,612 SBOMs from the Wild SBOMs dataset (77,092 parseable). Classified SBOMs into three topological regimes: no-edge (no dependencies declared), degenerate (some edges but majority of components isolated), and well-connected. Analyzed edge emission rates by generator tool and software type. Assessed real-world impact by modifying a production vulnerability-prioritization pipeline to replace binary reachability veto with an "unknown" signal guarded by a degeneracy detector, measuring KEV recall changes.
AI.result: Three regimes emerged: 52.9% no-edge SBOMs (failing NTIA minimum requirements), 8.8% degenerate (median 93% orphan share for SBOMs ≥50 components; Syft container-image SBOMs at 95-98%), 38.3% well-connected. Edge emission is tool-dependent (0-100% no-edge rates across generators). Only 0.10% use CycloneDX compositions to signal incompleteness. Degeneracy-aware approach recovered KEV recall from 0.600 to 0.950 (controlled) and 0.957 (live end-to-end). Dataset and scanner released.
AI.conclusion: The majority of real-world SBOMs lack adequate dependency edges, making closed-world "no path implies unreachable" inferences unsound and dangerous. Generators, not software properties, drive edge completeness. A degeneracy detector with explicit "unknown" handling dramatically improves vulnerability recall without flooding alerts, offering a practical path forward while the ecosystem matures.

title: The machine can say it but cannot hear it. Designed affective patterns and the expressive-sensing asymmetry in human-machine communication
summary: Affect-adaptive systems increasingly act as communicators that sense a user's emotion and respond with events meant to change it, closing an affective loop. This vision assumes both that a machine's affective messages are received and that the bodily channel it monitors carries an intelligible reply-assumptions rarely tested together. In a within-subjects virtual-reality study (N = 20), an autonomous system delivered six empirically derived affective patterns-scripted emotional events distilled from 104 practitioners' (first responders') critical incidents-while we recorded the human reply across felt emotion, felt arousal, and autonomic (electrodermal and cardiac) activity. Acting only as an author of designed messages, the machine reliably evoked strong, differentiated emotions: valence fell sharply for every pattern (|dz| = 1.1-1.7), and the patterns produced distinguishable, individually classifiable signatures of anger, fear, and sadness, functioning as a vocabulary of machine-to-human affective messages. Yet the channel the machine would read stayed largely silent. Self-reported arousal did not change, with Bayesian and equivalence evidence for no effect; sympathetic and cardiac arousal moved only for the most perceptually salient events, not for the messages experienced as most powerful; and within individuals, felt valence was decoupled from both bodily registers. This valence-arousal dissociation reveals an expressive-sensing asymmetry: machine agency extends to expression but not perception, and closed-loop designs regulate on a variable their messages neither reliably move nor are legible in. We draw out implications for theories of machine agency and for affect-adaptive design.

AI.tldr: A VR study tested whether an autonomous system could evoke distinct emotions (expression) while simultaneously reading users' bodily signals (perception). The machine reliably produced differentiable anger, fear, and sadness, but self-reported arousal and autonomic responses showed little to no change. This reveals an expressive-sensing asymmetry that challenges the core assumption of closed-loop affect-adaptive systems.
AI.motivation: Affect-adaptive systems are designed on the assumption that machines can both send affective messages that alter user emotion and read the bodily response to close the loop. These two assumptions are rarely tested simultaneously, threatening the validity of closed-loop affective computing.
AI.method: Within-subjects VR study (N=20) where an autonomous system delivered six empirically derived affective patterns, scripted from 104 first responders' critical incidents. Researchers measured felt emotion (valence), felt arousal, electrodermal activity, and cardiac activity as the human reply.
AI.result: The machine reliably evoked strong, differentiated emotions (valence drops |dz| = 1.1–1.7) with individually classifiable signatures of anger, fear, and sadness. However, self-reported arousal showed no effect (Bayesian/equivalence evidence), sympathetic and cardiac arousal responded only to perceptually salient events—not the most powerful messages—and within individuals, felt valence was decoupled from bodily registers.
AI.conclusion: A valence-arousal dissociation reveals an expressive-sensing asymmetry: machine agency extends to expression but not perception. Closed-loop affect-adaptive designs regulate on a variable their messages neither reliably move nor can legibly read, carrying implications for machine agency theory and system design.

title: Agent Security Needs Redefinition through a Holistic Framework
summary:
Agent security is widely treated as a question about action content. Defenses ask whether an instruction looks malicious. Benchmarks ask whether an agent performs a harmful sounding action. \textbf{We argue that agent security is fundamentally a contextual problem, and that the current content based framing systematically misdefines it.} A command to ``delete user data'' might be a routine administrative request or a prompt injection attacking production systems, and the content alone cannot distinguish the two. Authorization context can. Across every injection task in AgentDojo and WASP, the same action is one an authenticated user would plausibly request in a routine workflow, which makes the conflation a structural property of evaluating security through content.
  We operationalize contextual security through four properties that must hold jointly and be evaluated continuously across the agent's trajectory. Source Authorization asks who issued the command. Task Alignment specifies the agent's authorized objective. Action Alignment evaluates whether each action serves that objective. Data Isolation governs information flows across privilege boundaries. Under this reframing, indirect prompt injection becomes a Source Authorization violation. Snapshot benchmarks are structurally incapable of evaluating Data Isolation. Existing defenses are reorganized around the property they actually approximate. The contextual reframing changes which defenses are coherent, which evaluations measure something useful, and which attack patterns evaluation can see at all.

AI.tldr: Agent security is fundamentally a contextual problem, not a content-based one. The same action (e.g., "delete user data") can be benign or malicious depending on authorization context. The paper proposes four contextual properties — Source Authorization, Task Alignment, Action Alignment, and Data Isolation — that must be continuously evaluated across an agent's trajectory, reframing how defenses, evaluations, and attacks are understood.
AI.motivation: Current agent security research misdefines the problem by treating it as a content-based question — asking whether an instruction *looks* malicious or whether an action *sounds* harmful. The authors argue this framing is structurally flawed because the same action can be either legitimate or an attack depending on authorization context. This conflation is systemic: across AgentDojo and WASP benchmarks, every injection task involves actions an authenticated user could plausibly request, making content-based evaluation incapable of distinguishing benign from malicious.
AI.method: The authors operationalize contextual security through four properties that must hold jointly and be evaluated continuously across an agent's entire trajectory: (1) Source Authorization — who issued the command; (2) Task Alignment — the agent's authorized objective; (3) Action Alignment — whether each action serves that objective; and (4) Data Isolation — information flows across privilege boundaries. They then use this framework to reclassify known attack patterns (e.g., indirect prompt injection becomes a Source Authorization violation), reorganize existing defenses around which property they actually approximate, and demonstrate that snapshot benchmarks are structurally incapable of evaluating Data Isolation.
AI.result: The contextual reframing reveals that snapshot benchmarks (like AgentDojo and WASP) are structurally incapable of evaluating Data Isolation, as this property requires continuous trajectory-level assessment. Existing defenses map unevenly onto the four properties, and the reframing changes which defenses appear coherent, which evaluations measure something useful, and which attack patterns are even visible to evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Agent security must be reframed from content-based to context-based evaluation. The four-property framework (Source Authorization, Task Alignment, Action Alignment, Data Isolation) provides a more structurally sound foundation for building defenses, designing benchmarks, and understanding attack surfaces in agent systems.

title: Analysing Self-Harm Representations in Language Models: a Cross-Architecture Study
summary: Self-harm content is particularly challenging to detect using NLP techniques, and is also a high-stakes task which requires the highest accuracy to enable timely intervention or flagging at-risk users. We therefore present an analysis of how LLMs represent such self-harm content, which has downstream applications in self-harm detection, LLM intervention and governance and policing. In this paper, we focus on two datasets and four models, and perform two main experiments: (1) We train and evaluate linear probes across all layers of each model on two self-harm datasets: X-Sensitive and SH-Detection. Across both corpora, self-harm information crystallizes in the final 3 - 7% of network layers (93 to 97% depth). (2) We extract contrastive self-harm directions and, after performing a normaliation step, we find that the most accurate probes are not necessarily the most linearly separable. In particular, we find Gemma-3-4B to represent this \textit{contrastive self-harm direction} in a slightly different, more intricate way than the other LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how large language models internally represent self-harm content, finding that such information crystallizes in the final 3–7% of network layers and that the most accurate linear probes do not always correspond to the most linearly separable self-harm directions, with Gemma-3-4B exhibiting a distinct representational pattern.
AI.motivation: Self-harm content detection is both technically challenging for NLP and a high-stakes task requiring maximal accuracy for timely intervention. Understanding how LLMs internally represent self-harm content can improve detection systems, inform LLM governance, and enable better intervention mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors use two self-harm datasets (X-Sensitive and SH-Detection) and four LLMs. They conduct two experiments: (1) training linear probes across every layer of each model to locate where self-harm information emerges; (2) extracting contrastive self-harm directions via a normalization step to assess linear separability and probe accuracy relationships.
AI.result: Self-harm information consistently crystallizes in the final 3–7% of network layers (93–97% depth) across both corpora. Additionally, the most accurate probes are not necessarily the most linearly separable. Gemma-3-4B represents the contrastive self-harm direction in a more intricate, distinct manner compared to the other LLMs studied.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode self-harm content in late layers with surprising consistency, and linear separability alone is an insufficient proxy for probe accuracy. Architectural differences (as seen in Gemma-3-4B) can yield qualitatively different internal representations of sensitive content, with implications for detection system design and model governance.

title: Self-Poisoning in Adaptive Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Sharp-Threshold Theory and Certified Label-Free Calibration
summary: Test-time adaptive out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors update a memory bank from the unlabelled stream. We show this adaptation obeys a provable dynamical law. Modelling bank impurity as a generalized Pólya urn, we prove almost-sure convergence to a mean-field equilibrium whose slope acts as a reproduction number. Below one, impurity stays benign. Above one, the bank is fully poisoned and the detector collapses. The measured admission kernel is affine ($R^2 \ge 0.996$) with slope just below one in every encoder family (a protocol signature), so this detector class is near-critical by design, and across 96 settings the predicted threshold matches the empirical collapse, where ungated dictionaries lose up to $0.163$ AUROC. We then prove that a certified admission gate, reading only a frozen reserve, severs the feedback loop and removes the transition at every contamination rate, even adversarially, while controlling false positives label-free. For the complementary static-calibration failure under drift we give CDC, which restores nominal FPR label-free on all tested drift-affected cells. Finally we prove a two-world impossibility theorem. Drift and contamination are indistinguishable without labels, forcing a closed-form power ceiling our procedure approaches. Together these give a complete possibility/impossibility characterization of label-free adaptive OOD detection.

AI.tldr: Test-time adaptive OOD detectors that update a memory bank from unlabeled streams follow a provable dynamical law modeled as a generalized Pólya urn. The system has a critical reproduction number: below one, impurity stays benign; above one, the bank is fully poisoned. The authors prove this theoretically, validate it across 96 settings, propose a certified admission gate that severs the feedback loop, introduce CDC to handle drift-induced calibration failure, and prove an impossibility theorem showing drift and contamination are indistinguishable without labels, yielding a complete characterization of label-free adaptive OOD detection.
AI.motivation: Test-time adaptive OOD detectors lack theoretical understanding of how unlabeled-stream adaptation can degrade via impurity accumulation. There is no formal characterization of when and why such detectors collapse, and no principled solution that simultaneously handles both contamination and distribution drift without labels.
AI.method: The authors model memory bank impurity dynamics as a generalized Pólya urn process, proving almost-sure convergence to a mean-field equilibrium governed by a reproduction number (admission kernel slope). They propose a certified admission gate using a frozen reserve to break the feedback loop, and introduce CDC (Calibration under Drift Correction) to restore nominal FPR under drift. Finally, they prove a two-world impossibility theorem establishing a power ceiling for any label-free method.
AI.result: The admission kernel is affine (R² ≥ 0.996) with slope just below one across all tested encoder families, confirming near-critical design. Predicted collapse thresholds match empirical collapse across 96 settings, with ungated dictionaries losing up to 0.163 AUROC. The certified admission gate removes the phase transition at every contamination rate, even adversarially. CDC restores nominal FPR label-free. The impossibility theorem yields a closed-form power ceiling that the proposed procedure approaches.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete possibility/impossibility characterization of label-free adaptive OOD detection: adaptive memory banks are inherently near-critical and prone to collapse above a sharp threshold, but a certified gate + CDC can provably handle both contamination and drift, approaching the theoretical power ceiling dictated by the fundamental indistinguishability of drift and contamination without labels.

title: Lost in Context: Addressing Context Anxiety in Large Language Models
summary: Conventional wisdom suggests that reasoning models fail when problems exceed their capabilities. However, we find that frontier reasoning models sometimes possess the necessary capabilities to solve problems but fail due to premature self-doubt -- a phenomenon informally known as context anxiety. We provide the first systematic study of context anxiety, demonstrating that it arises, in part, from a model's inability to accurately estimate the tokens required to complete a task. We also show that context anxiety leads to material efficiency losses when models operate under perceived constraints. Building on this analysis, we further show that models can learn alternative strategies for solving long-horizon problems without exhibiting context anxiety, suggesting that performance improvements may be achievable not through scaling model capabilities, but by improving models' ability to accurately assess and adapt to their own limitations.

AI.tldr: Frontier reasoning models can fail not from lack of capability but from "context anxiety" — premature self-doubt driven by inaccurate estimation of required token lengths. The paper systematically studies this phenomenon, shows it causes efficiency losses under perceived constraints, and suggests that improving self-assessment rather than scaling capabilities may boost performance.
AI.motivation: The conventional assumption is that reasoning models fail when tasks exceed their capabilities. The authors challenge this by investigating whether failures sometimes occur despite adequate capabilities, specifically due to a psychological analog called "context anxiety" — where models prematurely abandon problem-solving due to erroneous self-assessment of task demands.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical study of context anxiety in frontier reasoning models. They analyze how models estimate required token budgets for task completion, examine behavior under perceived constraints, and explore whether alternative reasoning strategies can mitigate context anxiety without scaling model size or training data.
AI.result: Context anxiety is shown to arise partly from models' inability to accurately estimate the tokens needed to complete a task. This leads to material efficiency losses when models operate under perceived constraints. However, models can learn alternative strategies for long-horizon problems that do not exhibit context anxiety, indicating a path to improvement without scaling capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Performance improvements in reasoning models may be achieved not through scaling model capabilities, but by improving models' ability to accurately assess and adapt to their own limitations. This reframes the challenge from capability enhancement to metacognitive accuracy.

title: HarnessLLM: Rust Verification Harness Generation with Large Language Models
summary:
Rust's ownership model and type system offer strong memory safety guarantees, but unsafe code and runtime panics still present significant risks. Formal verification is essential to ensure memory safety, but developing verification harnesses remains a challenging and manual task. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in various code analysis tasks, directly applying them to harness generation often results in inaccurate API invocations, inefficient nondeterministic data generation, and fabricated fixes.
  In this paper, we present HarnessLLM, an automated workflow that leverages LLMs to generate verification harnesses for Rust code directly from existing test suites. HarnessLLM automatically extracts calling scenarios from test cases, generates nondeterministic arguments based on dependency analysis, and incrementally synthesizes harnesses. It then iteratively refines the harnesses, preserving critical code regions and reporting fabricated types or functions to LLMs for correction. In our evaluation on 9 real-world Rust codebases, HarnessLLM extracted 294 calling scenarios from 494 test cases with 94.66% precision and generated harnesses for all scenarios in an average of 145 seconds each. It outperformed the existing approach, Autoharness, which succeeded on only 41% of those scenarios. Finally, 6 real-world memory safety bugs were detected using the generated harnesses, demonstrating the practical utility of our approach in verification. To our knowledge, this is the first work to use LLMs for generating harnesses aimed at memory safety verification in real-world Rust projects.

AI.tldr: HarnessLLM is an LLM-powered automated workflow that generates verification harnesses for Rust code from existing test suites, achieving 94.66% precision in extracting calling scenarios and outperforming Autoharness by detecting 6 real-world memory safety bugs.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of Rust code is essential for memory safety but developing verification harnesses is challenging and manual. LLMs, while capable in code analysis, struggle with accurate API invocations, nondeterministic data generation, and tend to fabricate fixes when applied directly to harness generation.
AI.method: HarnessLLM automatically (1) extracts calling scenarios from existing test cases, (2) generates nondeterministic arguments via dependency analysis, (3) incrementally synthesizes harnesses, and (4) iteratively refines them by preserving critical code regions and reporting fabricated types/functions back to the LLM for correction.
AI.result: Evaluated on 9 real-world Rust codebases: extracted 294 calling scenarios from 494 test cases with 94.66% precision; generated harnesses for all scenarios at ~145 seconds each; Autoharness succeeded on only 41% of those scenarios; 6 real-world memory safety bugs were detected.
AI.conclusion: HarnessLLM demonstrates the first successful application of LLMs to harness generation for memory safety verification in real-world Rust projects, showing both high precision and practical bug-finding utility.

title: An AI-Driven Virtual Patient for Breaking Bad News: An Expert Formative Study on Facial Expression Intensity
summary: Interactive virtual patients driven by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable solutions for medical communication training, such as breaking bad news. However, designing their emotional expressiveness remains a challenge. This paper presents an AI-driven virtual patient framework combining LLM dialogue with real-time facial animation in virtual reality (VR). We conducted an exploratory, formative evaluation with seven medical experts to gather early feedback and elicit design requirements. The evaluation focused on how variations in facial expression intensity affect perceived realism and the virtual patient's emotion intelligibility. While descriptive quantitative ratings remained baseline across conditions, qualitative interviews provided deep insights into how experts perceive virtual emotional cues. The findings suggest that experts evaluate emotional realism holistically through multiple verbal and non-verbal channels; isolated facial adjustments are easily overshadowed by dialogue nuances and vocal prosody. Based on these insights, we present a roadmap for future medical training simulators, highlighting the need for synchronized, multi-modal pipelines incorporating body gestures, conversational pauses, and vocal dynamics.

AI.tldr: An AI-driven VR virtual patient using LLMs was tested with seven medical experts to assess how facial expression intensity affects perceived realism. While quantitative ratings showed no significant differences, qualitative feedback revealed that emotional realism is evaluated holistically—facial cues are overshadowed by dialogue and vocal prosody. A roadmap for multi-modal training simulators is proposed.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven virtual patients offer scalable medical communication training (e.g., breaking bad news), but designing appropriate emotional expressiveness remains an open challenge. The study aims to understand how facial expression variations influence perceived realism and emotion intelligibility in VR-based virtual patients.
AI.method: An exploratory, formative evaluation was conducted with seven medical experts interacting with an AI-driven virtual patient framework that combines LLM dialogue with real-time facial animation in VR. The study manipulated facial expression intensity across conditions, collecting both quantitative ratings and qualitative interview data on perceived realism and emotion intelligibility.
AI.result: Quantitative ratings remained at baseline across conditions with no significant differences. Qualitative interviews revealed that experts assess emotional realism holistically through multiple verbal and non-verbal channels; isolated facial adjustments were easily overshadowed by dialogue nuances and vocal prosody.
AI.conclusion: Effective virtual patient design requires synchronized, multi-modal emotional pipelines integrating body gestures, conversational pauses, and vocal dynamics—not merely facial expression adjustments. A roadmap for future medical training simulators is proposed based on these findings.

title: BioZKFHE: Scalable Encrypted Biometric Identification via Verifiable Homomorphic Similarity Evaluation
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing. 28 pages, including supplementary material
summary: Large-scale biometric identification in outsourced settings requires two properties simultaneously: biometric templates and queries must remain protected during computation, and the encrypted similarity outputs produced by an untrusted compute node must be verifiably correct before any application result is released. Existing FHE-based biometric systems primarily address confidentiality, while practical verifiability introduces two bottlenecks in the underlying encrypted 1:N matching layer: rotation- and bandwidth-heavy similarity evaluation and the high cost of proving repeated homomorphic similarity traces. We present BioZKFHE, a framework for scalable encrypted biometric identification via verifiable homomorphic similarity evaluation that combines BGV homomorphic computation with committee-mediated proof opening/decryption and smart-contract verification of opened proof batches. To reduce encrypted storage and avoid rotation-heavy encrypted 1:N matching, we propose Single-Coefficient Multi-Value (SCMV) packing, which binds multiple quantized embedding values into each plaintext entry through base-T expansion. To make proof generation practical, we propose Parallelizable and Verifiable Similarity Computation (PVSC), which exploits the Double-CRT execution structure of BGV to decompose each blockwise similarity trace into parallel proof instances that are opened and checked before result release. Under standard lattice assumptions and explicit committee/verifier assumptions, we analyze recoverability, noise growth, confidentiality, encrypted-output integrity, and finalized-result integrity. Experiments on FaceNet and MobileFaceNet show near-lossless biometric utility, up to 67 percent encrypted-storage reduction, and about 22 to 44 seconds end-to-end proof-verified runtime for 10k to 40k templates.

AI.tldr: BioZKFHE is a framework for scalable encrypted biometric identification that combines BGV homomorphic encryption with committee-mediated proof verification and smart contracts, introducing SCMV packing to reduce storage/rotation overhead and PVSC to enable parallelizable verifiable similarity computation, achieving near-lossless utility and practical end-to-end verified runtime.
AI.motivation: Outsourced biometric identification requires both confidentiality of templates/queries and verifiable correctness of encrypted similarity outputs. Existing FHE-based systems address privacy but face two bottlenecks for verifiability: rotation-heavy, bandwidth-intensive similarity evaluation and the prohibitive cost of proving repeated homomorphic similarity traces at scale.
AI.method: The framework uses BGV homomorphic computation with committee-mediated proof opening/decryption and on-chain smart-contract verification of batched proofs. Two key innovations: (1) Single-Coefficient Multi-Value (SCMV) packing, which packs multiple quantized embeddings into one plaintext coefficient via base-T expansion, reducing storage and avoiding rotation-heavy 1:N matching; (2) Parallelizable and Verifiable Similarity Computation (PVSC), which leverages BGV's Double-CRT structure to decompose blockwise similarity traces into parallel proof instances that are opened and verified before result release.
AI.result: Experiments on FaceNet and MobileFaceNet demonstrate near-lossless biometric utility, up to 67% reduction in encrypted storage, and end-to-end proof-verified runtime of approximately 22–44 seconds for 10k to 40k templates. Security is analyzed under standard lattice assumptions with explicit committee/verifier trust assumptions, covering recoverability, noise growth, confidentiality, encrypted-output integrity, and finalized-result integrity.
AI.conclusion: BioZKFHE makes verifiable encrypted biometric identification practical at scale by jointly addressing storage, computational, and proof-generation bottlenecks, achieving a favorable trade-off among privacy, verifiability, and efficiency for real-world outsourced biometric systems.

title: DWT-Fusion: A Signal-Based Framework for Training-Free LLM-Generated Text Detection
summary: Detecting LLM-generated text remains challenging under zero-shot and training-free conditions, especially when detectors must generalize across datasets, domains, and unseen generators. While existing training-free approaches exploit language-model statistics as detection signals, they typically characterize a text through global measures that summarize overall model behavior. Consequently, potentially informative local and multiscale variations in token-level predictability may remain underutilized. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DWT-Fusion, a training-free signal-based framework for detecting LLM-generated text using discrete wavelet analysis of token-level log-probability sequences produced by a proxy causal language model. The proposed framework analyzes these sequences through wavelet-based multiresolution signal representations and derives detection signals from localized probability dynamics. We further evaluate four training-free voting variants, including equal-weight hard voting, equal-weight soft voting, calibration-weighted hard voting, and calibration-weighted soft voting, to combine multiple wavelet configurations without training a supervised meta-classifier. We evaluate the framework on HC3, M4, and MAGE using GPT-Neo-2.7B, GPT-J-6B, Falcon-7B, and LLaMA-3-8B as proxy models. The best single wavelet configurations achieve AUROC values of 0.9872, 0.8185, and 0.7138 on HC3, M4, and MAGE, respectively. With calibration-weighted voting, the best ensemble variants further improve AUROC to 0.9919, 0.8477, and 0.7471. These findings show that DWT-based multiresolution scoring and calibration-guided voting fusion provide effective and interpretable signals for training-free LLM-generated text detection.

AI.tldr: DWT-Fusion introduces a training-free detection method for LLM-generated text using discrete wavelet transform on token-level log-probability sequences, achieving strong AUROC scores across multiple datasets and proxy models, with further gains from calibration-weighted voting ensembles.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free LLM-text detectors rely on global summary statistics of language-model signals, neglecting localized and multiscale variations in token-level predictability that could improve detection. The authors aim to exploit these fine-grained, multiresolution probability dynamics without requiring training.
AI.method: The proposed DWT-Fusion framework applies discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to sequences of token-level log-probabilities from a proxy causal LLM, producing multiresolution signal representations. Detection signals are derived from localized probability dynamics across wavelet subbands. Four training-free voting variants (equal-weight hard/soft and calibration-weighted hard/soft) combine multiple wavelet configurations without a supervised meta-classifier. Proxy models include GPT-Neo-2.7B, GPT-J-6B, Falcon-7B, and LLaMA-3-8B.
AI.result: Best single wavelet configurations achieved AUROC of 0.9872 (HC3), 0.8185 (M4), and 0.7138 (MAGE). Calibration-weighted soft voting ensembles improved these to 0.9919, 0.8477, and 0.7471, respectively.
AI.conclusion: DWT-based multiresolution scoring combined with calibration-guided voting fusion yields effective, interpretable, and training-free signals for detecting LLM-generated text, with robust generalization across datasets and proxy models.

title: Encoding Invisible Causation for Bridge Diagnostic Agents: Triple-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning with QLoRA
summary: Bridge infrastructure deteriorates gradually, yet its root causes---salt intrusion, freezing, fatigue cracking, and others---remain invisible to the naked eye. Expert diagnosis relies on tacit knowledge built over years of practice. We address the challenge of automating this latent causal reasoning by proposing a Damage Cause Encoder that classifies 10-class damage causes from visible damage descriptions $S_i$ for use in autonomous bridge diagnostic agents. Our approach chains three components: (i)Knowledge Triple Extraction---a large language model extracts causal triples of the form (damage $\xrightarrow{\mathtt{caused\_by}}$ cause) from 15--35 diagnostic PDF manuals and indexes them in a FAISS vector store; (ii)Retrieval-Augmented Context---at training and inference time, relevant causal triples $\mathcal{C}_i$ are retrieved and concatenated with $S_i$, converting implicit domain knowledge into explicit Encoder context; (iii)Systematic Fine-tuning Comparison---we conduct a rigorous comparison of LoRA, QLoRA, and QA-LoRA on a fixed Golden Testset (116 stratified samples), demonstrating that QLoRA achieves the optimal trade-off: identical test accuracy (87.07%) to full-precision LoRA, 11% faster inference, 72% lower GPU memory, and superior generalization across diverse unseen inputs. A controlled Golden Testset---stratified, deduplicated, and difficulty-tagged---is introduced as a reusable benchmark contribution. QLoRA further outperforms LoRA by 13 percentage points on a 100-sample diverse evaluation spanning all 10 damage cause classes.These findings enable memory-efficient, high-accuracy diagnostic agents on consumer-grade hardware for edge deployment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Damage Cause Encoder that classifies 10 bridge damage causes by chaining LLM-based knowledge triple extraction from diagnostic manuals, retrieval-augmented context, and QLoRA fine-tuning, achieving 87.07% test accuracy with 72% less GPU memory than full-precision LoRA while introducing a reusable stratified Golden Testset benchmark.
AI.motivation: Bridge deterioration root causes (salt intrusion, freezing, fatigue cracking, etc.) are invisible to the naked eye, and expert diagnosis depends on tacit knowledge accumulated over years. Automating this latent causal reasoning for autonomous bridge diagnostic agents is an unsolved challenge, particularly under edge-deployment constraints where GPU memory and inference speed are limited.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Knowledge Triple Extraction — an LLM extracts (damage → caused_by → cause) triples from 15–35 diagnostic PDF manuals, indexed in a FAISS vector store; (2) Retrieval-Augmented Context — at train/inference time, relevant triples C_i are retrieved and concatenated with damage descriptions S_i to make implicit domain knowledge explicit; (3) Systematic Fine-tuning Comparison — LoRA, QLoRA, and QA-LoRA are rigorously compared on a fixed, stratified, deduplicated, difficulty-tagged 116-sample Golden Testset, with additional evaluation on a 100-sample diverse set spanning all 10 classes.
AI.result: QLoRA achieves the optimal trade-off: 87.07% test accuracy (identical to full-precision LoRA), 11% faster inference, 72% lower GPU memory consumption, and superior generalization. QLoRA also outperforms LoRA by 13 percentage points on the 100-sample diverse evaluation set. The Golden Testset is contributed as a reusable benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables memory-efficient, high-accuracy bridge diagnostic agents deployable on consumer-grade hardware at the edge. QLoRA is identified as the superior fine-tuning strategy for this domain, and the structured Golden Testset provides a foundation for reproducible future work in automated infrastructure diagnostics.

title: Do VLMs Read or Rewrite? On Transcription Faithfulness in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used in place of traditional OCR pipelines for document understanding. In this paper, we show they do not always act as faithful transcribers: when text is imperfect, they often tend to rewrite it into a more plausible form - a behavior that clean-text OCR benchmarks cannot detect. We introduce FaithC4, a multilingual perturbation benchmark of 1,455 single-page documents (English, Chinese, Korean) with three perturbation families: scramble, random substitution, and visually similar substitution. We use the benchmark to evaluate 15 systems spanning general-purpose VLMs, OCR-specialized VLMs, and traditional OCR pipelines. These three categories differ in WER degradation under perturbation: general-purpose VLMs degrade by up to 4.5 points, OCR-specialized VLMs by 0.2-2 points, and traditional OCR by less than 0.6 points on English. Probing Qwen3-VL-4B layer-by-layer, we identify a consistent pattern: rewriting fires only when a perturbed word's final layer FFN representation stays close to the original encoding; when the representation diverges sufficiently, the model transcribes faithfully. Word length affects rewriting rate: short words (4-6 characters) are rewritten up to 10% of the time, with a sharp cutoff at 8 characters above which rewriting drops to 0%.

AI.tldr: VLMs tend to "rewrite" imperfect text into plausible forms rather than faithfully transcribing it, a failure mode invisible to clean-text benchmarks. The FaithC4 benchmark quantifies this, revealing that general-purpose VLMs degrade most under perturbation, and that rewriting behavior is linked to how closely a perturbed word's FFN representation stays near the original encoding.
AI.motivation: VLMs are increasingly deployed for document understanding, but existing OCR benchmarks only evaluate on clean text. The authors identify a hidden failure mode: VLMs sometimes "hallucinate" corrections to imperfect or perturbed text, rewriting it to be more plausible rather than transcribing faithfully. This behavior is undetectable with standard clean-text benchmarks, motivating the need for a perturbation-based evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors introduce FaithC4, a multilingual (English, Chinese, Korean) benchmark of 1,455 single-page documents perturbed using three families: character scrambling, random substitution, and visually similar substitution. They evaluate 15 systems across three categories (general-purpose VLMs, OCR-specialized VLMs, traditional OCR pipelines) by measuring Word Error Rate (WER) degradation. They also probe Qwen3-VL-4B layer-by-layer, analyzing FFN representations to determine when rewriting occurs versus faithful transcription.
AI.result: Under perturbation, general-purpose VLMs show the largest WER degradation (up to 4.5 points), OCR-specialized VLMs degrade moderately (0.2–2 points), and traditional OCR pipelines remain robust (<0.6 points on English). Probing reveals that rewriting fires when a perturbed word's final-layer FFN representation remains close to the original's encoding; when it diverges sufficiently, transcription becomes faithful. Short words (4–6 characters) are rewritten up to 10% of the time, with a sharp cutoff at 8 characters where rewriting drops to 0%.
AI.conclusion: VLMs exhibit a systematic "plausibility rewriting" bias when transcribing imperfect text, a failure mode tied to representational similarity in FFN layers and modulated by word length. Traditional OCR pipelines remain more faithful under perturbation. FaithC4 provides a new lens for evaluating and diagnosing this behavior in document understanding systems.

title: Integrating Energy Efficiency into Software Development: Developer Perspectives and Requirements
summary: In the context of the growing energy footprint of information and communication technology, industry optimization efforts have primarily focused on hardware, while the impact of software on energy consumption is often overlooked. Although technical approaches for optimizing software energy consumption have been developed in research, their adoption in everyday development practice remains limited. This study investigates how software developers perceive energy efficiency in their daily work and which requirements and barriers they formulate for AI-assisted tools supporting energy-aware development. As part of the European GreenCode project, ten semi-structured interviews with professional software developers were conducted and analyzed using qualitative content analysis following Mayrings methodology. The identified requirements were subsequently partly interpreted through the lens of the Technology Acceptance Model. The results indicate that energy efficiency rarely plays an explicit role in daily development activities. Instead, energy savings are typically achieved indirectly through performance optimization. Identified barriers to the explicit consideration of energy efficiency include limited awareness and a strong focus on timely delivery. The interviews further revealed requirements for practical tool support, such as actionable optimization suggestions and seamless integration into common development environments. Furthermore, the acceptance of AI-assisted optimization tools strongly depends on transparency regarding the use of data, the actual energy savings compared to the energy consumption of the tool itself, and the disclosure of the training data used. This study contributes a developer-centered perspective on requirements for energy-aware software development tools and provides insights for designing AI-assisted solutions that align with real-world development practices.

AI.tldr: This study explores how professional developers perceive energy efficiency in software development, finding that energy savings are mostly achieved indirectly via performance optimization rather than explicit energy-aware practices. Through ten interviews, the authors identify barriers (limited awareness, deadline pressure) and requirements for AI-assisted energy optimization tools (actionable suggestions, IDE integration, transparency about data usage and tool energy overhead).
AI.motivation: Despite growing ICT energy consumption, software-level energy optimization remains under-adopted in practice, with research tools failing to transition into everyday development workflows. The study aims to understand developer perceptions, requirements, and barriers regarding energy-aware development and AI-assisted tooling.
AI.method: Ten semi-structured interviews with professional software developers were conducted within the European GreenCode project. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis following Mayring's methodology, with identified requirements subsequently interpreted through the lens of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM).
AI.result: Energy efficiency is rarely an explicit concern in daily development; it is pursued indirectly through performance optimization. Key barriers include limited developer awareness and pressure for timely delivery. Developers require actionable optimization suggestions, seamless IDE integration, and transparency regarding data usage, net energy savings versus tool energy cost, and training data provenance for AI-assisted tools.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a developer-centered perspective on requirements for energy-aware development tools and offers design insights for AI-assisted solutions aligned with real-world practices. Tool acceptance hinges critically on transparency and demonstrable net energy benefits.

title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
comment: 8 pages. Voice-first, offline-capable learning companion for visually-impaired children with multi-signal struggle detection and cross-language answer matching. Prototype built at the Half Baked hackathon (English and Tamil)
summary: Most educational technology for children is built around visual interfaces, which excludes the many children worldwide who live with visual impairment -- an estimated 1.4 million children are blind and many more have low vision. We present Kutti AI, a voice-first learning companion designed so that audio is the primary and sufficient interface: children learn curriculum concepts through spoken conversation, respond by speaking, and receive spoken feedback, with no reliance on visual elements. The system contributes three practical mechanisms for accessible, adaptive learning on commodity mobile hardware: (1) a multi-signal struggle-detection engine that combines response-latency analysis, wrong-attempt tracking, and keyword-based hesitation detection to decide, in real time, when to offer hints or simplify a question; (2) a multi-layered cross-language answer-matching pipeline that combines language-aware translation/transliteration, Levenshtein-based fuzzy matching, and text normalization so that children are not penalized for code-switching or pronunciation variation; and (3) an offline-first speech pipeline using an on-device automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, enabling use in low-connectivity settings common in underserved communities. We describe the architecture, the interaction flow, and the design decisions that prioritize accessibility, and we report qualitative observations from a hackathon prototype supporting English and Tamil. We discuss lessons learned and outline a path toward formal evaluation with target users. Kutti AI illustrates how a small, carefully-engineered voice-first system can lower both accessibility and financial barriers to early education.

AI.tldr: Kutti AI is a voice-first learning companion for visually impaired children that uses audio as the sole interface, featuring struggle detection, cross-language answer matching, and offline speech recognition to enable accessible education on low-cost mobile devices.
AI.motivation: Most educational technology relies on visual interfaces, excluding an estimated 1.4 million blind children and many more with low vision worldwide. There is a need for accessible, adaptive learning tools that function without visual elements and operate in low-connectivity, underserved settings.
AI.method: The system employs three core mechanisms: (1) a multi-signal struggle-detection engine analyzing response latency, wrong-attempt counts, and keyword-based hesitation to trigger hints or question simplification; (2) a cross-language answer-matching pipeline using translation/transliteration, Levenshtein-based fuzzy matching, and text normalization to accommodate code-switching and pronunciation variation; (3) an offline-first speech pipeline with on-device ASR for low-connectivity environments. A hackathon prototype was built supporting English and Tamil.
AI.result: The paper reports qualitative observations from a hackathon prototype demonstrating the feasibility of the voice-first approach. Formal evaluation with target users has not yet been conducted.
AI.conclusion: Kutti AI demonstrates that a small, carefully-engineered voice-first system can lower both accessibility and financial barriers to early education for visually impaired children. The authors outline a path toward formal evaluation with target users.

title: PoCEvolve: Generating Proof-of-Concept Exploits from Security Patches with Vulnerability-Aware Prompt Evolution
summary: Ideally, the detailed information about a vulnerability should be made available together with the fixing commit. In practice, however, such details often become available only long after the commit, even when a CVE has already been published. During this window, the patch is already public, so attackers can reverse-engineer it, yet defenders lack the details needed to assess exposure, prioritize, and validate the fix. Executable evidence, such as a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, could fill this gap. Prior work has automated PoC generation, but the state-of-the-art approach, PoCGen, assumes that a detailed vulnerability report is already available, which is precisely what is missing during this window. In this paper, we first present an empirical study quantifying the long delay between the fixing commit and the availability of a detailed vulnerability report. We then introduce PoCEvolve, a vulnerability-aware prompt-evolution framework that generates PoCs directly from vulnerability-fixing commits. Given a vulnerability-fixing commit, PoCEvolve synthesizes a corresponding PoC exploit. To learn from unsuccessful generation attempts, PoCEvolve assesses the usefulness of different dimensions of vulnerability-related context, including the inferred vulnerable API and code-coverage information. These assessments guide prompt evolution towards more effective exploit-generation prompts. We evaluate PoCEvolve on SecBench.VFC.js, where PoCEvolve achieves a PoC generation success rate of 58.4%, corresponding to relative improvements of 20.7% over PoCGen and 200.0% over the LLM baseline with GPT-4o-mini. With a recent model, Qwen3.7-Plus, PoCEvolve achieves a higher success rate of 85.3%. When detailed vulnerability reports are available, PoCEvolve achieves a success rate of 71.7%, improving over PoCGen by 11.1%.

AI.tldr: PoCEvolve is a framework that generates proof-of-concept exploits directly from vulnerability-fixing commits without requiring detailed vulnerability reports. It uses a vulnerability-aware prompt-evolution mechanism that learns from failed generation attempts. It achieves 58.4% success on SecBench.VFC.js (20.7% improvement over PoCGen) and 85.3% with Qwen3.7-Plus.
AI.motivation: There exists a significant time gap between when a vulnerability-fixing commit is published and when detailed vulnerability information (e.g., CVE reports) becomes available. During this window, attackers can reverse-engineer the public patch while defenders lack sufficient details to assess exposure, prioritize, and validate fixes. Executable evidence like PoC exploits could bridge this gap, but existing automated PoC generation tools (e.g., PoCGen) assume detailed vulnerability reports are already available — which is precisely what is missing.
AI.method: The authors first conduct an empirical study quantifying the delay between fixing commits and detailed vulnerability report availability. They then propose PoCEvolve, a vulnerability-aware prompt-evolution framework that synthesizes PoC exploits directly from vulnerability-fixing commits. PoCEvolve works by (1) inferring vulnerability-related context such as the vulnerable API and code-coverage information, (2) assessing the usefulness of these contextual dimensions after failed generation attempts, and (3) using these assessments to iteratively evolve prompts toward more effective exploit-generation prompts. The framework is evaluated on the SecBench.VFC.js benchmark using GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.7-Plus.
AI.result: On SecBench.VFC.js, PoCEvolve achieves a PoC generation success rate of 58.4% with GPT-4o-mini, representing relative improvements of 20.7% over PoCGen and 200.0% over a vanilla LLM baseline. Using Qwen3.7-Plus, success rate rises to 85.3%. When detailed vulnerability reports are available, PoCEvolve achieves 71.7% success, improving over PoCGen by 11.1%.
AI.conclusion: PoCEvolve demonstrates that effective PoC generation is feasible directly from vulnerability-fixing commits, mitigating the vulnerability window problem. The prompt-evolution strategy, which learns from failed attempts by evaluating contextual dimensions, proves effective across different LLM backends. The approach outperforms prior work both with and without detailed vulnerability reports.

title: Enough is as good as a feast: A Comprehensive Analysis of How Reinforcement Learning Mitigates Task Conflicts in LLMs
summary: Model merging plays a crucial role in consolidating multiple specialized models into a single, unified model, especially in the era of large language models (LLMs). Recent research has primarily focused on developing strategies to enhance merging performance with the trained models, while the impact of training paradigms, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), on the effectiveness of model merging remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically explore the merging behavior of RL-trained LLMs compared to those trained with traditional SFT. Through comprehensive evaluations across five representative tasks, we find that RL significantly reduces task conflicts and results in less performance degradation after merging, making RL-trained models particularly well-suited for this process. To unearth the reasons behind the superior suitability of RL for model merging, we conduct extensive empirical experiments and theoretical analyses. Our findings highlight three key factors: (1) On-policy training data in RL control the gradient updates in a smaller magnitude, reducing the risk of overwriting existing knowledge for other tasks in the model. (2) The RL optimization objective, which favors ``\textit{enough is as good as a feast}", progressively reduces the magnitude and the number of conflict parameter updates as the model converges. (3) Joint optimization of positive and negative examples in RL steers the model towards an unbiased task-specific parameter subspace, ensuring robust performance while further preventing parameter conflicts.

AI.tldr: RL-trained LLMs exhibit significantly less task conflict and performance degradation during model merging compared to SFT-trained models, due to smaller gradient updates from on-policy data, a satisficing optimization objective, and joint optimization of positive/negative examples that steers parameters into unbiased task-specific subspaces.
AI.motivation: The impact of training paradigms (RL vs. SFT) on model merging effectiveness is underexplored. The authors aim to systematically investigate why RL-trained models may be more amenable to merging than SFT-trained ones.
AI.method: Comprehensive empirical evaluations across five representative tasks comparing merging behavior of RL-trained and SFT-trained LLMs, supplemented by theoretical analysis. The study examines three mechanistic factors: gradient update magnitudes under on-policy data, the satisficing nature of RL objectives, and the effect of joint positive/negative example optimization on parameter subspaces.
AI.result: RL-trained models show reduced task conflicts and less performance degradation after merging. Three key mechanisms identified: (1) on-policy training yields smaller-magnitude gradient updates, reducing knowledge overwriting; (2) RL's "enough is as good as a feast" objective progressively diminishes conflict-causing parameter updates during convergence; (3) joint positive/negative optimization directs parameters toward unbiased task-specific subspaces, mitigating inter-task parameter conflicts.
AI.conclusion: RL training is inherently better suited for downstream model merging than SFT, and the identified mechanisms provide both empirical and theoretical grounding for this advantage, offering guidance for future multi-model consolidation strategies.

title: CARNet Cycle-Conditioned Core Aggregation and Redistribution for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
comment: Accepted at ECML PKDD 2026 (Research Track). Shortlisted for Best Research Track Student Paper Award
summary: Accurately modeling cross-variate dependencies remains a key challenge in multivariate time series forecasting, particularly in the presence of strong periodic patterns. Many existing approaches rely on attention-based mechanisms that incur quadratic complexity and scale poorly with increasing numbers of variates. Recent attention-free aggregation models address this issue through linear-complexity core-based interactions, but they do not explicitly leverage the global periodic structure present in the data. To overcome this limitation, we propose CARNet, a Cycle-Conditioned Core Aggregation and Redistribution framework that integrates global recurrent cycle information into efficient core based interaction modeling via Multihead Core Aggregation. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world multivariate forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CARNet consistently outperforms strong transformer and non-attention baselines across diverse prediction horizons while preserving linear-complexity modeling of cross-variate dependencies.

AI.tldr: CARNet introduces a linear-complexity framework for multivariate time series forecasting that integrates global periodic cycle information into core-based cross-variate interaction modeling, outperforming both transformer and non-attention baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing attention-based models for multivariate forecasting suffer from quadratic complexity, while attention-free core aggregation models fail to explicitly leverage global periodic structures in the data. There is a need for an efficient model that combines linear complexity with explicit periodic modeling.
AI.method: CARNet employs a Cycle-Conditioned Core Aggregation and Redistribution framework. It uses Multihead Core Aggregation to efficiently model cross-variate dependencies in linear time while integrating global recurrent cycle information to capture strong periodic patterns in the data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world multivariate forecasting benchmarks show that CARNet consistently outperforms strong transformer and non-attention baselines across diverse prediction horizons.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating global periodic cycle information into core-based cross-variate interaction modeling yields state-of-the-art forecasting performance while maintaining linear complexity, making it scalable to high-dimensional multivariate settings.

title: LeafData: An Agentic System for Data Migration
summary: Modern data migration relies on JSON configuration to define data connection, pipeline logic, and orchestration behavior. This requires domain knowledge from users and is time-consuming and error-prone. In this paper, we present LeafData, an agentic system that converts user intent into validated and executable JSON configuration for data migration. Specifically, LeafData comprises a frontend chatbot and the backend service. The chatbot incrementally collects required information from users and performs schema-driven validation, while the backend service processes validated inputs and generates JSON configuration artifacts. These artifacts are directly consumable by orchestration platforms, enabling end-to-end pipeline generation and execution without manual coding. LeafData supports heterogeneous data migration across various data sources and connectors including relational databases, file-based systems, document-oriented databases, and REST APIs.

AI.tldr: LeafData is an agentic system that converts user intent into validated, executable JSON configuration for data migration, using a chatbot frontend for incremental information gathering and schema-driven validation, and a backend service that generates directly consumable configuration artifacts for orchestration platforms.
AI.motivation: Modern data migration requires users to manually author JSON configurations for data connection, pipeline logic, and orchestration behavior — a process that demands domain expertise, is time-consuming, and is error-prone.
AI.method: LeafData employs a two-component architecture: (1) a frontend chatbot that incrementally gathers required information from users and performs schema-driven validation, and (2) a backend service that processes validated inputs and generates JSON configuration artifacts consumable by orchestration platforms, supporting heterogeneous sources including relational databases, file systems, document databases, and REST APIs.
AI.result: The system enables end-to-end pipeline generation and execution without manual coding, producing validated JSON configuration artifacts directly usable by orchestration platforms across diverse data sources and connectors.
AI.conclusion: LeafData demonstrates that an agentic, intent-driven approach can effectively abstract away the complexity of JSON configuration authoring for data migration, reducing both the domain knowledge barrier and the potential for human error.

title: Comparing and Conceptualizing Data Protection Requirements Worldwide for Privacy Regulatory Compliance
summary: The growing digitalization of society has intensified the collection, processing, and sharing of personal data, increasingly moving across national borders and regulatory jurisdictions, prompting a proliferation of data protection frameworks worldwide.
