These transborder personal data flows (TPDF) are essential to today's economy, but organizations managing them must reconcile data protection requirements that differ, sometimes subtly, across jurisdictions. For requirements engineering, this is the central challenge: regulatory data protection requirements (RDPRs) are complex and not directly translatable into software requirements, especially when frameworks impose similar, non-identical, or contradictory obligations. Identifying which requirements are shared and which diverge is therefore critical to managing TPDF, and addressing them late in the software development lifecycle (SDLC) causes costly rework, making early identification essential for compliance and stakeholder communication. This paper identifies and conceptualizes common RDPRs worldwide from the perspective of data protection legal experts, answering: (SQ1) which requirements are common across regulations and how are they conceptualized, and (SQ2) which requirements diverge and how do they differ conceptually. We combine deductive qualitative analysis of interviews with 70 legal experts from G20 economies and other countries and systematic content analysis of these economies' data protection regulations. We identify common requirements, such as consent, and divergent ones, such as the right to be forgotten. Given their impact across the SDLC and enterprise architecture, we translate these findings into a set of Data Protection Officer DPO (DPO) stories, using the user story notation, classified by SDLC phase and enterprise architecture layer, to help organizations manage TPDF compliance.

AI.tldr: Analyzing 70 legal expert interviews and G20 data protection regulations, this paper identifies common and divergent regulatory data protection requirements (RDPRs) for transborder personal data flows (TPDF). Findings are translated into "DPO stories" using user story notation, classified by SDLC phase and enterprise architecture layer, to facilitate early compliance integration.
AI.motivation: Organizations managing transborder personal data flows face complex, fragmented data protection frameworks across jurisdictions. RDPRs often appear similar but contain subtle, non-identical, or contradictory obligations. Addressing these late in the SDLC causes costly rework, yet no systematic identification of common versus divergent requirements exists from the legal expert perspective. Early requirements engineering intervention is essential.
AI.method: A two-pronged qualitative approach: (1) deductive qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews with 70 data protection legal experts from G20 economies and other countries, and (2) systematic content analysis of data protection regulations from those economies. Findings are synthesized and operationalized into "DPO stories" using the user story notation, classified by SDLC phase and enterprise architecture layer.
AI.result: Identified common RDPRs (e.g., consent requirements) shared across jurisdictions and divergent RDPRs (e.g., the right to be forgotten) that vary conceptually. These were codified into DPO stories mapped to SDLC phases and enterprise architecture layers to support early compliance engineering and stakeholder communication.
AI.conclusion: Early identification of shared and divergent RDPRs is critical for cost-effective TPDF compliance. Translating legal expert insights into structured DPO stories bridges the gap between legal interpretation and software requirements engineering, enabling organizations to embed data protection by design across the entire development lifecycle.

title: Universal BCI Personalization: One API for Frozen EEG Trunks and Foundation Models
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures. Companion paper on the control layer forthcoming
summary: Frozen EEG encoders proliferate; per-model fine-tune defaults do not scale. We present Nimbus Personalizer: one contract encode to Bayesian head to BrainState (optional affine mid-tier) that sits on heterogeneous frozen trunks without a new personalization stack per architecture. Thesis (systems): the contribution is the trunk-agnostic API - not LDA-on-embeddings as an ML novelty - so OEMs integrate once and swap trunks. Evidence: the same surface runs on five classical trunks EEGNet, Shallow, Deep, Conformer, ATCNet x four MI datasets (18 cells) and on a foundation encoder (REVE) under the same Personalizer. Where embedding capacity exists, the head is a cheap default mid-point versus warm-start fine-tune or PEFT, costing orders of magnitude less adaptation wall time while recovering much of the fine-tune accuracy gain; calibration-only-when-clean holds in 12/18 cells. Head gains are supporting evidence that the API is useful where capacity exists. Subject-level confidence intervals identify the clearest dataset and span zero elsewhere. All results are exploratory (subject-level bootstrap, no confirmatory tests); the decision logic for when to escalate adaptation is addressed in our companion work on the control layer.

AI.tldr: Nimbus Personalizer introduces a trunk-agnostic API that attaches a Bayesian head (with optional affine mid-tier) to frozen EEG encoders, enabling a single personalization stack to serve across heterogeneous architectures without per-model fine-tuning, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a fraction of adaptation cost across multiple encoder–dataset combinations.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of frozen EEG encoders creates a scalability problem: per-model fine-tuning defaults require a separate personalization stack for each architecture. The authors argue for a trunk-agnostic API that OEMs can integrate once and swap encoder trunks freely, rather than treating the machine learning contribution (e.g., LDA-on-embeddings) as the novelty.
AI.method: The Nimbus Personalizer consists of a contract encoder feeding into a Bayesian head (BrainState), with an optional affine mid-tier. This surface runs identically on five classical EEG trunks (EEGNet, Shallow, Deep, Conformer, ATCNet) across four motor imagery datasets (yielding 18 cells), and also on a foundation encoder (REVE). The head serves as a cheap default mid-point versus warm-start fine-tuning or PEFT, drastically reducing adaptation wall time. Subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals are used for evaluation (no confirmatory tests).
AI.result: Where embedding capacity exists, the Bayesian head recovers much of the fine-tune accuracy gain at orders of magnitude lower adaptation wall time. Calibration-only-when-clean holds in 12 out of 18 cells. Subject-level confidence intervals clearly identify the best-performing dataset but span zero elsewhere. All results are exploratory.
AI.conclusion: The trunk-agnostic API is viable and useful where embedding capacity is sufficient, offering a scalable approach to EEG decoder personalization. The decision logic for escalating adaptation is deferred to companion work on the control layer.

title: Transforming Keystroke Noise to Text: Self-Supervised Acoustic Eavesdropping Attacks on Keyboards
summary: We present a self-supervised acoustic eavesdropping attack that reconstructs typed text solely from keystroke sounds, without requiring labeled data for the target device. The proposed attack enables stealthy eavesdropping in two real-world scenarios-physical spaces (public and semi-public) and online meetings. Our method combines unsupervised acoustic clustering with Transformer-based language model inference and iterative self-training, enabling stable character inference under highly uncertain acoustic-to-character mappings. We demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 99% reconstruction accuracy with only 100-150 observed keystrokes under a close-proximity recording setup using a smartphone placed near the target device, significantly outperforming prior unsupervised baselines in low-data regimes. We further evaluate robustness across multiple laptop platforms and in realistic acquisition channels, including distance recording from approximately 3 meters away on the same desk, through-the-wall eavesdropping with a contact microphone, and background keyboard noise in online conferencing systems. Across these scenarios, the proposed method achieves high reconstruction accuracy (often exceeding 90%) with approximately 150-250 observed keystrokes. These results indicate that accurate text reconstruction from keystroke sounds is feasible in practice under an audio-only setting, even with limited observed keystrokes and without requiring device-specific labeled data, highlighting a realistic and previously underestimated privacy risk.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised acoustic side-channel attack that reconstructs typed text from keystroke sounds using unsupervised clustering, Transformer-based language models, and iterative self-training, achieving >99% accuracy with 100-150 keystrokes in close-proximity and >90% in realistic eavesdropping scenarios, all without device-specific labeled data.
AI.motivation: Prior acoustic eavesdropping attacks on keyboards require labeled training data from the target device, limiting their practicality. This paper addresses the open problem of reconstructing typed text from keystroke sounds in a fully unsupervised, self-supervised manner — eliminating the need for device-specific labeled data while operating effectively in the low-data regime typical of real-world eavesdropping.
AI.method: The attack pipeline combines three components: (1) unsupervised acoustic clustering to group keystroke sounds into pseudo-classes without labels; (2) Transformer-based language model inference that leverages linguistic context to resolve the ambiguous mapping between acoustic clusters and actual characters; and (3) iterative self-training that refines cluster-to-character assignments by bootstrapping from high-confidence predictions. The system operates on raw keystroke audio across multiple realistic recording setups.
AI.result: In close-proximity smartphone recording, the method achieves >99% reconstruction accuracy with only 100–150 observed keystrokes, dramatically outperforming prior unsupervised baselines. In realistic scenarios — 3-meter distance recording, through-the-wall contact microphone eavesdropping, and online conference background noise — accuracy remains high (>90%) with 150–250 keystrokes. Robustness is demonstrated across multiple laptop platforms.
AI.conclusion: Accurate text reconstruction from keystroke sounds is practically feasible in audio-only settings without device-specific labeled data and with limited observations. This reveals a significant and previously underestimated privacy risk, as the attack requires only commodity hardware and works across diverse real-world eavesdropping scenarios.

title: Developing and Validating the Spanish Version of the Large Language Models Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-SP)
summary: There is a growing need for reliable and culturally validated instruments to assess psychological dependency on large language models (LLMs), particularly as LLMs are increasingly used for task execution, decision-making, and communication in organizational and work-related settings. This need is especially relevant for Spanish-speaking populations, where LLM adoption is rapidly expanding, yet validated psychometric tools remain scarce. The present study reports the first validation of the Spanish version of the Large Language Model Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-SP), extending prior validations conducted in English- and Arabic-speaking samples. The LLM-D12 is a two-dimensional instrument assessing Instrumental Dependency (reliance on LLMs for performing tasks and supporting decisions) and Relationship Dependency (psychological reliance on LLMs for companionship and social interaction). A total of 386 Spanish-speaking participants (M = 28.0 years, SD = 6.1; 55% male) completed the LLM-D12-SP. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original two-factor structure. The scale demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89 total; 0.86 Instrumental; 0.85 Relationship). Discriminant validity analyses indicated that the two subscales represent related but distinct constructs. External validation showed that both dependency dimensions were positively associated with internet addiction and perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, while showing weak or no association with need for cognition. Together with prior English and Arabic validations, these findings establish cross-linguistic support for the scale's structure and provide a psychometrically sound tool for investigating psychological aspects of LLM use in organizational contexts.

AI.tldr: First Spanish-language validation of the Large Language Model Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-SP) confirms the original two-factor structure (Instrumental and Relationship Dependency) with strong psychometric properties in 386 participants, establishing cross-linguistic support alongside prior English and Arabic validations.
AI.motivation: Rapidly expanding LLM adoption in Spanish-speaking populations lacks culturally validated psychometric tools to assess psychological dependency on LLMs, particularly in work-related and organizational contexts where LLMs are used for task execution, decision-making, and communication.
AI.method: 386 Spanish-speaking participants (M=28.0 years, SD=6.1; 55% male) completed the LLM-D12-SP. Confirmatory factor analysis tested the two-factor structure. Internal consistency was assessed via Cronbach's alpha. Discriminant validity examined the distinctiveness of the two subscales. External validation correlated dependency dimensions with internet addiction, perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, and need for cognition.
AI.result: Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original two-factor model. Internal consistency was good (total α=0.89; Instrumental α=0.86; Relationship α=0.85). The two subscales were related but distinct constructs. Both dependency dimensions positively correlated with internet addiction and perceived LLM trustworthiness, and showed weak/no association with need for cognition.
AI.conclusion: The LLM-D12-SP is a psychometrically sound instrument for assessing LLM dependency in Spanish-speaking populations. Combined with prior English and Arabic validations, the findings provide robust cross-linguistic support for the scale's structure and its utility in organizational research on psychological aspects of LLM use.

title: Learning What Matters: Supervising Sparse Attention Routing with Causal Evidence Sets
summary: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long contexts by allowing each query to read only selected parts of the input. These selectors are often trained by distilling the attention patterns of a dense teacher, assuming that attention reveals which context the teacher actually uses. We test that assumption on retrieval tasks where the evidence for each answer is known exactly. By masking parts of the context and measuring whether the answer changes, we find that attention and causal dependence often disagree, and distilled selectors inherit the mismatch. Teachers attend to outdated facts they have learned to ignore, and their attention can vary across training runs even when they rely on the same evidence. In a two-step reference task, attention at the answer skips the intermediate step because it was resolved earlier in the forward pass: a selector trained on attention achieves 41% accuracy, while the same selector trained on causal evidence reaches 99% and matches the teacher. These evidence sets require no annotation: recovered from a frozen teacher by masking alone, they train selectors to the same accuracy. We find the same conflict in pretrained models: Qwen2.5-3B gives more attention to an outdated fact than the current one on 58% of conflicting-fact examples despite answering correctly, while Gemma-2-9B rises from 56% to 99% accuracy when restricted to the two relevant sentences. Attention shows where a model looks, not necessarily what its answer depends on; across the regimes we tested, that dependence matched or outperformed attention as a training target.

AI.tldr: Sparse attention selectors are commonly trained by distilling dense teacher attention patterns, but this paper shows that attention does not reliably indicate which context the teacher's answer actually depends on. Using retrieval tasks with known ground-truth evidence, the authors demonstrate that attention and causal dependence frequently diverge, and selectors trained on causal evidence (recovered via masking) consistently match or outperform those trained on attention.
AI.motivation: Sparse attention mechanisms reduce computational cost for long contexts by selectively attending to parts of the input. The standard training approach distills attention patterns from a dense teacher model, operating under the assumption that attention weights reveal which context is actually used. This paper directly tests that foundational assumption.
AI.method: The authors use retrieval tasks where the supporting evidence for each answer is known exactly. They intervene by masking parts of the context and measuring whether the teacher's answer changes — this identifies which context causally determines the output. They compare these causal dependence patterns against the teacher's attention distributions. They then train sparse attention selectors on both signals (attention-based vs. causal-evidence-based) and compare downstream accuracy. The causal evidence requires no manual annotation: it is recovered from a frozen teacher purely through masking. Experiments extend to pretrained models (Qwen2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B) using conflicting-fact examples.
AI.result: Attention and causal dependence frequently disagree. Teachers attend to outdated facts they have learned to ignore, and attention patterns vary across training runs even when models rely on identical evidence. In a two-step reference task, an attention-trained selector achieves only 41% accuracy, while a causal-evidence-trained selector reaches 99%, matching the teacher. On conflicting-fact examples, Qwen2.5-3B allocates more attention to outdated facts than current ones on 58% of examples despite answering correctly. Gemma-2-9B improves from 56% to 99% accuracy when restricted to only the two relevant sentences.
AI.conclusion: Attention reveals where a model looks, not what its answer depends on. Causal dependence, recoverable from a frozen teacher via masking without annotation, matched or outperformed attention as a training target for sparse attention selectors across all tested regimes.

title: From Profiles to Steering Vectors: Global Sparse Priors and Local Semantic Calibration for Personalized Text Generation
summary: Personalized text generation requires models to capture user-specific writing styles from historical data. Existing approaches based on retrieval, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or activation steering either introduce inference and storage overhead or struggle to separate stylistic signals from semantic content. We propose GLASS, a training-free framework for personalized generation via Global-Local Activation Steering with Sparse priors. GLASS uses sparse autoencoders to extract a global user-style prior from historical responses and constructs local contrastive style vectors over clustered interaction scenarios. During inference, it jointly injects global and local vectors into different model layers, enabling context-aware personalization without retrieval or parameter updates. Experiments on LaMP and LongLaMP show that GLASS outperforms retrieval-, fine-tuning-, and steering-based baselines across ROUGE metrics and LLM-as-judge evaluations. Further analyses show that SAE-based representations are more robust to topic and length shifts, suggesting better disentanglement of stylistic information from semantic residue.

AI.tldr: GLASS is a training-free framework for personalized text generation that uses sparse autoencoders to extract global user-style priors and local contrastive style vectors, then jointly injects them into model layers during inference—outperforming retrieval, fine-tuning, and steering baselines without parameter updates or retrieval overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized text generation methods (retrieval-based, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, activation steering) suffer from inference/storage overhead or fail to disentangle stylistic signals from semantic content. A training-free approach is needed that cleanly separates style from semantics while avoiding parameter updates and retrieval costs.
AI.method: GLASS (Global-Local Activation Steering with Sparse priors) uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to derive a global user-style prior from historical responses and constructs local contrastive style vectors over clustered interaction scenarios. During inference, both global and local vectors are jointly injected into different transformer layers, enabling context-aware style personalization without any training or retrieval.
AI.result: On LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks, GLASS outperforms retrieval-based, fine-tuning-based (e.g., LoRA), and steering-based baselines across ROUGE metrics and LLM-as-judge evaluations. SAE-based representations also show stronger robustness to topic and length shifts, indicating better stylistic disentanglement from semantic residue.
AI.conclusion: GLASS demonstrates that training-free activation steering with SAE-derived sparse style representations can effectively personalize text generation, offering a lightweight, context-aware alternative to existing methods with superior style–content disentanglement.

title: Vibe Coding: An Experiment with Test-Driven Development
summary:
Context: Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration can lead to poor quality output.
  Objective: This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can collaborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration.
  Method: We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the collaborative model (human-CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously performed by the MetaGPT~X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corresponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated exploratory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks to obtain complementary evidence.
  Results: Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and functionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity. However, they may also introduce additional implementation decisions that are not explicitly required by the functional specifications, resulting in untested decision points. In contrast, collaborative workflows produce higher-quality, better-organized test suites.
  Conclusions: Our work explored how...

AI.tldr: This exploratory study investigates four interaction models for human-CLLM collaboration in software development — solo, collaborative, fully automated, and agentic (MetaGPT~X) — implemented via TDD workflows. A controlled pre-experiment with professionals found that agentic workflows excel at rapid, functionally correct code production but introduce untested implementation decisions, while collaborative workflows yield higher-quality test suites.
AI.motivation: Conversational LLMs can generate code via natural language collaboration, but poor collaboration leads to low-quality output. The study aims to understand how humans and CLLMs can collaborate as peers through "vibe coding" — integrating prompt engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation principles.
AI.method: Four interaction models were designed (solo, collaborative, fully automated, agentic via MetaGPT~X) and implemented as TDD workflows using structured prompts and Python scripts. A controlled pre-experimental study compared solo vs. collaborative workflows with TDD professionals, complemented by repeated exploratory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on identical tasks.
AI.result: The choice of interaction model should depend on development objectives. Agentic workflows are best for rapid development and functionally correct production code but introduce additional, untested implementation decisions beyond functional specifications. Collaborative workflows produce higher-quality, better-organized test suites.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that different interaction models suit different development goals, with agentic models favoring speed and functional correctness versus collaborative models favoring test suite quality and organization. (The abstract appears truncated.)

title: Unboxing Diffusion Models for the Arts: Interactive Model Bending and Practice-Based Explainability
comment: Under review for "Explainable AI for the Arts" (N. Bryan-Kinns, Ed.), Springer
summary: Explainable AI (XAI) in creative practice can be less about technocentric explanation and more about enabling artists to inspect modify and debug models as part of making Yet largescale texttoimage diffusion systems are typically presented as opaque endtoend tools limiting this kind of material engagement We argue that even large models can function as creative materials when their internal structure is made visible and manipulable To support this we propose a handson approach to explainability centred on experimentation and intervention We instantiate this approach with a model bending and an interactive (inspection) interface integrated into ComfyUIs nodebased workflow including interactive layer selection and intervention controls Through qualitative and quantitative analysis of bending interventions in Stable Diffusion 15 we show how manipulating specific components of a diffusion pipeline produces relatively consistent families of visual effects allowing artists to build practical layerlevel intuition about how different parts of the model shape generated images

AI.tldr: The paper argues that explainable AI for artists should emphasize hands-on experimentation and intervention rather than technical explanations. The authors present a model-bending approach with an interactive inspection interface integrated into ComfyUI, enabling layer-level manipulation of Stable Diffusion 1.5. Their analysis shows that targeted component interventions produce consistent visual effect families, helping artists build practical intuition about how model internals shape outputs.
AI.motivation: Large-scale text-to-image diffusion models are typically deployed as opaque, end-to-end tools, which prevents artists from materially engaging with—inspecting, modifying, and debugging—the model's internal structure. The authors argue that XAI in creative contexts should prioritize enabling artistic agency through direct manipulation rather than providing passive, technocentric explanations.
AI.method: The authors propose a hands-on explainability framework centered on experimentation and intervention. They instantiate this via two mechanisms: (1) **model bending**—targeted manipulation of specific components within the diffusion pipeline, and (2) an **interactive inspection interface** integrated into ComfyUI's node-based workflow, featuring interactive layer selection and intervention controls. They conduct both qualitative and quantitative analyses of bending interventions applied to Stable Diffusion 1.5.
AI.result: Manipulating specific components of the diffusion pipeline yields relatively consistent families of visual effects. The quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate that different layers and components govern distinct, predictable aspects of image generation, enabling artists to develop practical, layer-level intuition about the model's internal behavior.
AI.conclusion: Even large-scale generative models can function as creative materials when their internal structure is made visible and manipulable. The proposed intervention-based approach to explainability empowers artists to experiment with and debug models as part of their creative process, bridging the gap between opaque AI systems and material artistic practice.

title: DeFiScreener: Efficient DeFi Attack Pre-screening in Smart Contracts via Historical Case Matching
summary:
Blockchain and its killer applications, particularly decentralized finance (DeFi), are gaining widespread adoption, with over 5,200 DeFi projects deployed on mainstream blockchains as of January 2026. At the same time, security risks in DeFi are becoming increasingly serious. However, existing DeFi detection tools usually cover only specific attack types, exhibiting severely limited detection coverage.
  In this paper, we argue that an effective way to address this gap is to pre-screen vulnerable instances from large volumes of smart contract functions and call sequences. This is motivated by a key phenomenon we term "perilous temporal asymmetry". Inspired by this, we propose DeFiScreener, the first automated pre-screening framework for DeFi attacks that uses historical exploit cases to identify potentially vulnerable functions and call sequences. Given the full source code of a target project, DeFiScreener builds Function Call Trees (FCTs) and generates semantic embeddings for each function using a large language model (LLM), allowing both program structure and function intent to be analyzed together. It then applies a dual-level screening process. At the function level, function embeddings are matched against an Attack Pattern Library of historically exploited functions. At the sequence level, the proposed Attack Pattern Oriented Monte Carlo Tree Search (APO-MCTS) efficiently explores the FCTs and screens vulnerable call sequences. The identified candidates are ultimately passed to an LLM for further interpretive and security analysis.
  We empirically evaluate the DeFiScreener over datasets comprising 207 real-world DeFi attack incidents. Experimental results demonstrate that DeFiScreener achieves a remarkable 98.55% recall and 84.30% precision in attack pre-screening.

AI.tldr: DeFiScreener is an automated pre-screening framework that identifies potentially vulnerable DeFi smart contract functions and call sequences by combining LLM-generated semantic embeddings, Function Call Trees, and a novel Attack Pattern Oriented Monte Carlo Tree Search, achieving 98.55% recall and 84.30% precision on 207 real-world DeFi attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing DeFi detection tools suffer from severely limited coverage, targeting only specific attack types. The authors identify "perilous temporal asymmetry" as a key phenomenon and argue that pre-screening vulnerable instances from large volumes of smart contract functions and call sequences is an effective way to bridge this detection gap.
AI.method: DeFiScreener constructs Function Call Trees (FCTs) from full source code, generates semantic embeddings for each function via LLM, and maintains an Attack Pattern Library from historical exploits. A dual-level screening process is applied: (1) function-level matching of embeddings against the Attack Pattern Library, and (2) sequence-level screening using Attack Pattern Oriented Monte Carlo Tree Search (APO-MCTS) to efficiently explore FCTs for vulnerable call sequences. Flagged candidates are then passed to an LLM for interpretive security analysis.
AI.result: Evaluated on 207 real-world DeFi attack incidents, DeFiScreener achieves 98.55% recall and 84.30% precision in attack pre-screening, demonstrating strong effectiveness in identifying vulnerable functions and call sequences.
AI.conclusion: DeFiScreener demonstrates that historical exploit patterns combined with LLM-based semantic analysis and structured program exploration can provide broad-coverage, high-recall pre-screening for DeFi vulnerabilities, significantly outperforming tools limited to specific attack types.

title: Scaling Native Multimodal Pre-Training From Scratch
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, their reliance on text-only pre-training restricts the perception of the multimodal physical world. Native multimodal pre-training avoids this limitation by training models from scratch on multimodal inputs, thereby achieving deep cross-modal integration and mitigating optimization asymmetries inherent to traditional late-fusion architectures. Despite these advantages, the scaling properties of this paradigm remain systematically uncharacterized. To address this gap, we investigate the optimal model size and token count for training a transformer-based vision-language model under a fixed computational budget. We demonstrate that minimal objective loss adheres to a predictable compute law, whereas compute-optimal model sizes and token counts scale as power laws. Notably, language and multimodal objectives manifest distinct scaling behaviors. The language allocation law is largely invariant to the composition of the data, indicating stable language learning regardless of the multimodal data ratio. Conversely, the multimodal allocation law is highly sensitive to this composition. Specifically, text-heavy mixtures become compute-efficient only at larger model scales, shifting the optimal resource allocation toward greater model capacity. Additionally, by modeling the influence of data composition on compute laws and allocation exponents, we derive an efficiency frontier specifying precise configurations of model size, token count, and data mixture. Downstream evaluations further reveal that native multimodal pre-training induces positive cross-modal transfer, thereby enhancing pure-text spatial reasoning and enabling robust multimodal in-context learning. In summary, this empirical research establishes the essential groundwork for predictably scaling multimodal foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically characterizes the scaling laws of native multimodal pre-training (training from scratch on multimodal inputs), revealing that language and multimodal objectives follow distinct power-law scaling behaviors with different sensitivities to data composition, and deriving an efficiency frontier for optimal model size, token count, and data mixture under fixed compute budgets.
AI.motivation: LLMs are limited by text-only pre-training for perceiving the multimodal physical world. While native multimodal pre-training offers advantages (deep cross-modal integration, avoiding late-fusion optimization asymmetries), its scaling properties remain uncharacterized, creating a critical knowledge gap for efficiently scaling multimodal foundation models.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate scaling laws for transformer-based vision-language models under fixed computational budgets. They analyze how minimal objective loss relates to compute (compute law), how optimal model size and token count scale (allocation laws), how data composition (text vs. multimodal ratios) modulates these laws, and derive an efficiency frontier. Downstream evaluations test cross-modal transfer and multimodal in-context learning.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Minimal loss follows a predictable compute law; (2) Compute-optimal model size and token count scale as power laws; (3) Language allocation law is invariant to data composition, while multimodal allocation law is highly sensitive — text-heavy mixtures become compute-efficient only at larger model scales; (4) An efficiency frontier can be derived specifying optimal model size, token count, and data mixture; (5) Native multimodal pre-training yields positive cross-modal transfer (improving pure-text spatial reasoning) and robust multimodal in-context learning.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes essential empirical groundwork for predictably scaling multimodal foundation models, providing principled guidance on compute-optimal resource allocation across model size, token count, and data mixture.

title: An Introduction to Bayesian and Frequentist Simulation-Based Inference with Machine Learning
summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) with machine learning is an increasingly important tool for solving inverse problems in science and engineering, including parameter inference and the inversion of detector effects. We provide an overview of the Bayesian and frequentist statistical frameworks, describe how machine-learning-based SBI methods, such as neural posterior estimation and neural likelihood estimation, can be used for parameter estimation within these frameworks, and show that the same methods can also be applied to Empirical Bayes or unfolding tasks. We also discuss how to validate inference results and the limitations of SBI with machine learning.

AI.tldr: An overview of simulation-based inference (SBI) using machine learning for inverse problems, covering Bayesian and frequentist frameworks, neural posterior/likelihood estimation methods, applications to Empirical Bayes and unfolding, plus validation and limitations.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of how machine-learning-based simulation-based inference can address inverse problems in science and engineering, unifying parameter inference, detector effect inversion, Empirical Bayes, and unfolding under a common methodological framework.
AI.method: The paper surveys SBI methods including neural posterior estimation (NPE) and neural likelihood estimation (NLE), situating them within both Bayesian and frequentist statistical frameworks. It describes how these amortized inference techniques replace costly simulations with learned surrogates for posterior or likelihood functions, and extends their applicability to Empirical Bayes and detector unfolding tasks.
AI.result: The review demonstrates that ML-based SBI methods can be applied across a range of inference tasks — parameter estimation, model comparison, Empirical Bayes, and unfolding — within both Bayesian and frequentist paradigms, while also identifying key validation strategies and inherent limitations.
AI.conclusion: Machine-learning-based SBI is a versatile and powerful approach for inverse problems, but requires careful validation and awareness of its limitations, including simulation fidelity, amortization gaps, and potential misspecification issues.

title: FBLayout: Optimizing Memory Layout for Efficient LLM Finetuning on Mobile GPUs
summary:
Transformer-based models have enabled unprecedented capabilities across language, vision, and multimodal tasks. On-device fine-tuning of transformer models offers a privacy-preserving path to personalized AI, yet remains inefficient on mobile GPUs due to severe memory constraints and frequent layout transformations in attention mechanism during training. Existing mobile training frameworks either use unified layouts for forward and backward passes -- leading to fragmented memory access and poor GPU utilization during backpropagation -- or rely on explicit layout conversions, which introduce significant transformation overhead.
  To overcome this, we propose FBLayout, a layout-aware framework that co-designs tensor organization with mobile GPU platforms. FBLayout introduces: (1) a unified R-Tile layout for multi-dimensional reductions across forward/backward passes; (2) tile-based index transformation to eliminate physical data movement; and (3) activation-guided layout selection to propagate efficient layouts globally. Evaluations on seven transformer models across different mobile phones (including ARM Mali and Qualcomm Adreno GPUs) show that FBLayout achieves 2.2-5.7x speedup over MNN, TFLite, and TVM, while significantly improving cache efficiency and reducing memory footprint, enabling practical on-device large model fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: FBLayout is a layout-aware framework that co-designs tensor organization with mobile GPU architectures to accelerate on-device transformer fine-tuning, achieving 2.2–5.7× speedup over MNN, TFLite, and TVM through unified R-Tile layout, tile-based index transformation, and activation-guided layout selection.
AI.motivation: On-device fine-tuning of transformers enables privacy-preserving personalization but is inefficient on mobile GPUs due to severe memory constraints and frequent layout transformations in the attention mechanism during training. Existing frameworks either use unified layouts causing fragmented memory access and poor GPU utilization, or incur significant overhead from explicit layout conversions.
AI.method: FBLayout introduces three key techniques: (1) a unified R-Tile layout that optimizes multi-dimensional reductions across both forward and backward passes; (2) tile-based index transformation that eliminates physical data movement by manipulating logical-to-physical mappings; and (3) activation-guided layout selection that propagates efficient layouts globally throughout the model graph.
AI.result: Evaluated on seven transformer models across ARM Mali and Qualcomm Adreno mobile GPUs, FBLayout achieves 2.2–5.7× speedup over MNN, TFLite, and TVM, while significantly improving cache efficiency and reducing memory footprint.
AI.conclusion: FBLayout demonstrates that layout-aware co-design with mobile GPU hardware enables practical on-device fine-tuning of large transformer models, overcoming the key memory and layout transformation bottlenecks that plague existing mobile training frameworks.

title: MineValiCoder: Reliable Code Generation with Test Case Quality Mining and Bipartite Graph-Based Mutual Validation
summary:
Large Language Model (LLM)-based Test-Driven Development (TDD) has advanced automated code generation. However, existing approaches depend heavily on human-crafted test cases and cannot operate effectively when only natural-language requirements are available. Although recent work enables automatic test generation, it often overlooks the inherent stochasticity of LLMs, leading to two key defects: faulty tests generate misleading feedback that distorts code optimization, while mixed-quality test cases produce conflicting evaluation signals that hinder reliable code selection.
  To address these challenges, we propose MineValiCoder, a collaborative closed-loop TDD framework based on the mutual reinforcement of test-case quality and code quality. MineValiCoder comprises three modules. The Test Case Quality Mining (TCQM) module filters faulty test cases through self-validation, providing reliable optimization supervision. The Parallel TDD Refinement module iteratively optimizes code and generates diverse high-quality code candidates using validated test-case feedback. The Bipartite Graph-Based Code-Test Mutual Validation (BiCoTeV) module dynamically models code-test interactions and performs mutual validation scoring for stable and reliable optimal-code selection.
  Extensive evaluations across four LLMs and mainstream benchmarks show that MineValiCoder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieves Pass@1 scores of 96.34% on HumanEval, 87.40% on MBPP, 64.00% on APPS, and 51.33% on LiveCodeBench. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MineValiCoder in mitigating LLM stochasticity and improving the reliability of automated code generation.

AI.tldr: MineValiCoder is a closed-loop TDD framework that mitigates LLM stochasticity by mutually reinforcing test-case quality and code quality through faulty test filtering, parallel iterative refinement, and bipartite graph-based mutual validation, achieving state-of-the-art Pass@1 scores across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based TDD relies heavily on human-crafted tests and fails with only natural-language requirements. Automatic test generation neglects LLM stochasticity, causing faulty tests to produce misleading optimization feedback and mixed-quality tests to yield conflicting signals for code selection.
AI.method: MineValiCoder consists of three modules: (1) Test Case Quality Mining (TCQM) filters faulty tests via self-validation; (2) Parallel TDD Refinement iteratively optimizes code using validated test feedback to generate diverse high-quality candidates; (3) Bipartite Graph-Based Code-Test Mutual Validation (BiCoTeV) dynamically models code-test interactions for stable mutual validation scoring and optimal-code selection.
AI.result: MineValiCoder achieves Pass@1 scores of 96.34% on HumanEval, 87.40% on MBPP, 64.00% on APPS, and 51.33% on LiveCodeBench, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods across four LLMs and mainstream benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MineValiCoder effectively mitigates LLM stochasticity and improves the reliability of automated code generation by establishing a mutual reinforcement loop between test-case quality and code quality.

title: Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education
summary: Generative AI is reshaping programming education, yet educators often infer students' AI-supported learning from classroom observations alone. This experience report presents a trio-ethnography involving two computing educators with different teaching philosophies and one undergraduate computer science student to examine how these interpretations evolve through dialogue. Across three conversations, the educators reflected on students' AI use, discussed changes to programming pedagogy, and revisited their assumptions after engaging with the student's lived experiences. Rather than simply confirming or contradicting the educators' perspectives, the student's narratives revealed learning processes that were largely invisible in the classroom, prompting both educators to reconsider assumptions about AI use, assessment, transparency, and programming instruction. We argue that trio-ethnography offers a valuable reflective approach for helping computing educators move beyond observable student behaviors toward a richer understanding of AI-supported learning and for informing instructional adaptation in the era of generative AI.

AI.tldr: A trio-ethnography involving two computing educators and one CS student reveals that student AI-supported learning processes are often invisible in the classroom, prompting educators to reconsider their assumptions about AI use, assessment, and pedagogy.
AI.motivation: Educators typically rely on classroom observations alone to infer students' AI-supported learning, yet these surface-level observations may miss critical, invisible learning processes. The authors aim to demonstrate how structured dialogue between educators and students can surface these hidden dynamics and challenge educator assumptions.
AI.method: The authors employed trio-ethnography, a collaborative reflective method involving three participants: two computing educators with contrasting teaching philosophies and one undergraduate CS student. The study unfolded across three structured conversations in which educators reflected on students' AI use, debated pedagogical changes, and ultimately revisited their assumptions after engaging with the student's lived experiences.
AI.result: The student's narratives revealed learning processes largely invisible in the classroom. Rather than simply validating or refuting educator beliefs, these accounts prompted both educators to fundamentally reconsider their assumptions regarding AI use, assessment design, transparency expectations, and programming instruction strategies.
AI.conclusion: Trio-ethnography offers a valuable reflective approach for helping computing educators move beyond observable student behaviors toward a richer, more nuanced understanding of AI-supported learning, and for informing instructional adaptation in the generative AI era.

title: trasgoDP: An Open Source Framework for Releasing Noised Tabular Microdata under Local Differential Privacy
summary: trasgoDP is a modular, open-source, and easy-to-use Python framework for releasing tabular microdata under ε-local differential privacy guarantees, as well as location data under geo-indistinguishability assumptions, designed to be installed and integrated within standard data science workflows. The software enables systematic exploration of privacy-utility trade-offs across multiple mechanisms, data types, and ε values. While differential privacy has been extensively studied for aggregate data, its application to row-wise microdata release remains underexploited in terms of reusable software tools, a gap that is even more pronounced in the case of metric privacy and location-based data. trasgoDP implements local-DP mechanisms for numerical and categorical attributes (Laplace, Gaussian, Exponential, and Randomized Response), a geo-indistinguishability mechanism for location data, and a set of utility metrics, including a novel correlation-loss measure, to quantify information loss as a function of the allocated privacy budget. The objective of this work is to provide the research community with a reproducible, open-source baseline for evaluating tabular and location-based data publication methodologies under formal local differential privacy guarantees.

AI.tldr: trasgoDP is an open-source Python framework for releasing tabular microdata and location data under local differential privacy and geo-indistinguishability, providing mechanisms, utility metrics, and a reproducible baseline for privacy-utility trade-off exploration.
AI.motivation: While differential privacy is well-studied for aggregate data, reusable software tools for row-wise microdata release under local DP remain scarce, and this gap is even wider for metric privacy and location-based data. The authors aim to fill this void with a modular, easy-to-use framework integrable into standard data science workflows.
AI.method: trasgoDP implements multiple local-DP mechanisms (Laplace, Gaussian, Exponential, Randomized Response) for numerical and categorical attributes, a geo-indistinguishability mechanism for location data, and a suite of utility metrics including a novel correlation-loss measure to quantify information loss against the privacy budget ε.
AI.result: The framework enables systematic, reproducible exploration of privacy-utility trade-offs across different mechanisms, data types, and ε values, serving as a baseline for evaluating tabular and location-based data publication under formal local DP guarantees.
AI.conclusion: trasgoDP provides the research community with a much-needed open-source, reproducible baseline for local differential privacy research on microdata and location data, addressing a clear tooling gap in the field.

title: Benchmarking Fine-tuning and Retrieval Strategies for a Multimodal Language Model on the NRC Reactor Operator Licensing Examination
summary: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into the nuclear power industry requires outputs grounded in domain-specific knowledge. This study evaluates a 31-billion-parameter open-weight multimodal model (Gemma 4 31B-IT) on its capacity to apply nuclear knowledge by benchmarking eight model-retrieval configurations against the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Reactor Operator licensing examination. We evaluate 14 Generic Fundamentals Examinations (GFE) from the 2015-2021 March sittings (seven pressurized and seven boiling water reactor exams) using the standard 80% human passing criterion. The base model is compared against configurations utilizing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Gemini-distilled chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with BM25 sparse retrieval over the U.S. Department of Energy Fundamentals Handbook, and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning (RAFT). Within the retrieval pipeline, we compare fixed-size sliding-window chunking against structure-aware chunking. The SFT configuration with fixed-size chunking RAG met the criterion on 8 of the 14 examinations, outperforming all alternatives, whereas no configuration without fine-tuning passed any. Aggregate accuracy reached 79.7%, with a confidence interval spanning the threshold, and 80.2% on PWR items specifically. Furthermore, two regularities emerged: the preferred chunking strategy reverses depending on the model's training state, and RAFT underperforms compared to standard SFT in matching search environments. These results demonstrate which combination of fine-tuning and search approaches achieves operator-level capabilities.

AI.tldr: A 31B-parameter multimodal model was benchmarked on U.S. NRC Reactor Operator licensing exams across 8 configurations. Only supervised fine-tuning with RAG (fixed-size chunking) passed the 80% threshold on 8/14 exams. No non-fine-tuned configuration passed any exam. Aggregate accuracy was 79.7% (80.2% on PWR items). RAFT underperformed standard SFT, and optimal chunking strategy depended on training state.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in the nuclear power industry must produce outputs grounded in domain-specific knowledge. This study investigates whether open-weight multimodal models can achieve operator-level competency on NRC licensing exams, identifying which combination of fine-tuning and retrieval strategies meets the 80% human passing criterion.
AI.method: The study evaluates Gemma 4 31B-IT across 8 configurations: base model (no fine-tuning), SFT on Gemini-distilled chain-of-thought rationales, RAG with BM25 sparse retrieval over the DOE Fundamentals Handbook, and RAFT. Retrieval used either fixed-size sliding-window chunking or structure-aware chunking. Evaluation used 14 GFE exams (7 PWR, 7 BWR) from 2015–2021 March sittings, with the standard 80% passing criterion.
AI.result: SFT with fixed-size chunking RAG passed on 8/14 exams — the only configuration to meet the criterion. No non-fine-tuned configuration passed any exam. Aggregate accuracy was 79.7% (CI spanning 80%) and 80.2% on PWR items. Two key regularities: optimal chunking strategy reversed depending on training state, and RAFT underperformed standard SFT in matched search environments.
AI.conclusion: Operator-level nuclear knowledge capability in open-weight LLMs requires both supervised fine-tuning on CoT rationales and retrieval augmentation. The interaction between chunking strategy and training state is non-trivial (reversal effect), and RAFT offers no advantage over standard SFT when search environments match. These findings provide a blueprint for deploying LLMs in high-stakes nuclear domain applications.

title: A Defense of the Quadratic Model
summary: Due to the complexity of neural network loss landscapes, optimization theory is forced to rely on idealized models, and there is generally a tradeoff between how theoretically tractable the model is, and how accurately it describes the true optimization dynamics. In this work, we stress test the simplest possible model of optimization -- the quadratic model -- and show that it can be surprisingly predictive in an LLM setting with 150M parameters and 3B training tokens. Specifically, we show that Taylor expanding the model and the loss function at intermediate checkpoints through training can accurately predict the optimization dynamics over windows that can last up to 10\% of training. Having established this agreement, we then turn to analyzing the structure of these local quadratic optimization problems through two lenses: the Hessian spectrum and local stability. Using Lanczos quadrature with extremely deep probes, we are able to estimate the Hessian spectrum deep into the tail, and we find a surprising amount of structure in both the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which depends on the batch size, preconditioner, and training time. We also empirically test local linear stability at intermediate checkpoints and compare it to theoretical predictions to demonstrate that optimization in LLMs typically occurs at a stochastic edge of stability, whose nature is also determined by batch size. Our results indicate the quadratic model may be a theoretically tractable proxy for pretraining optimization dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a simple quadratic approximation of the loss landscape can surprisingly predict LLM optimization dynamics over ~10% of training. Using deep Lanczos quadrature, it reveals structured Hessian spectra and demonstrates that LLM optimization operates at a stochastic edge of stability, influenced by batch size and preconditioning.
AI.motivation: There is a fundamental tradeoff in optimization theory between tractability and realism. The authors aim to stress-test whether the simplest possible model — the quadratic (second-order Taylor) approximation — can capture real optimization dynamics in large-scale LLM pretraining, bridging the gap between idealized theory and empirical practice.
AI.method: The authors Taylor-expand both the model and loss at intermediate checkpoints during LLM pretraining (150M parameters, 3B tokens). They evaluate predictive accuracy of the quadratic model over training windows. They then analyze the local quadratic problems via (1) Hessian spectrum estimation using Lanczos quadrature with deep probes to characterize eigenvalue/eigenvector structure, and (2) empirical tests of local linear stability compared against theoretical predictions.
AI.result: The quadratic model accurately predicts optimization dynamics over windows spanning up to 10% of training. The Hessian spectrum exhibits rich structure in both eigenvalues and eigenvectors, modulated by batch size, preconditioner, and training time. LLM optimization consistently operates at a stochastic edge of stability, with its nature determined by batch size.
AI.conclusion: The quadratic model is a viable, theoretically tractable proxy for understanding pretraining optimization dynamics in large language models, enabling deeper theoretical analysis without sacrificing empirical fidelity.

title: Trajectory-Aware Retrieval Agents for Temporal Decision- Making
summary: We study the problem of decision-making from long-form, temporally structured text using large language model (LLM) agents. Standard retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) pipelines fragment chronological context into isolated snippets, discarding the temporal structure that is often critical for correct downstream decisions. We introduce TLM (Trajectory Language Model), a closed-loop agentic framework that iteratively refines the evidence set using SHAP-guided feedback. The key technical contribution is the latent growth curve model (LGCM) over retrieved chunk embeddings, which provides an interpretable mechanism for detecting trajectory trends, turning points, and information gaps. We show that, under a scorer-calibration assumption (which holds approximately in practice), the iterative refinement procedure is monotonically non-decreasing in the probability assigned to the correct label. Empirically, TLM is evaluated on three temporally grounded decision tasks: medical question answering, earnings call surprise prediction, and overnight stock gap prediction. TLM substantially outperforms both zero-shot LLM baselines and standard retrieval-augmented approaches on the medical task, and yields consistent, economically meaningful gains on the two financial tasks.

AI.tldr: TLM is a closed-loop agentic framework that uses SHAP-guided feedback and a latent growth curve model over chunk embeddings to iteratively refine evidence for decision-making from temporally structured text, outperforming RAG baselines on medical QA and financial prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG pipelines fragment chronological context into isolated snippets, discarding temporal structure critical for downstream decisions. There is a need for an agentic framework that preserves and leverages temporal coherence when making decisions from long-form, temporally structured text.
AI.method: TLM operates as a closed-loop agentic framework with two key components: (1) a latent growth curve model (LGCM) over retrieved chunk embeddings that detects trajectory trends, turning points, and information gaps in an interpretable manner; and (2) a SHAP-guided iterative refinement procedure that, under a scorer-calibration assumption, is monotonically non-decreasing in probability assigned to the correct label.
AI.result: TLM substantially outperforms zero-shot LLM baselines and standard RAG approaches on medical question answering, and yields consistent, economically meaningful gains on earnings call surprise prediction and overnight stock gap prediction.
AI.conclusion: TLM demonstrates that preserving temporal structure via latent growth curve modeling and SHAP-guided evidence refinement enables LLM agents to make significantly better decisions on temporally grounded tasks compared to standard retrieval-based methods.

title: A Preliminary Search for Evidence on Government Software Engineering Practices: Results from Three Rapid Reviews
summary: Government agencies are major software developers and drivers of digital transformation, yet empirical evidence on their software engineering (SE) practices remains largely unexplored. This paper reports three rapid reviews of 2024 peer reviewed publications to assess the availability of evidence on government SE practices. We examined a subset of top tier international SE venues, regional South American SE conferences, and a curated newsletter on public sector digitalization. Across 984 screened papers, we identified only four studies reporting on SE practices conducted by, for, or in collaboration with government bodies, most published in regional venues as experience reports or case studies. Our findings are consistent with practitioners' perceptions that academic evidence on government SE practices has low visibility in mainstream SE venues. We discuss implications including the need for dedicated publication venues, incentives for government academia collaboration, and improved methods for evaluating grey literature, currently a key information source for government agencies. This work provides a preliminary study for understanding the evidence landscape and identifies directions for future research to better support evidence based software engineering in the public sector.

AI.tldr: A rapid review of 984 papers from top SE venues, regional conferences, and public sector newsletters found only four studies on government software engineering practices, revealing a critical evidence gap between academia and public sector SE.
AI.motivation: Government agencies are major software developers driving digital transformation, yet empirical evidence on their software engineering practices is largely absent from academic literature. The authors seek to systematically assess the availability of such evidence.
AI.method: Three rapid reviews were conducted across: (1) top-tier international SE venues, (2) regional South American SE conferences, and (3) a curated newsletter on public sector digitalization. A total of 984 papers were screened for studies reporting SE practices conducted by, for, or in collaboration with government bodies.
AI.result: Only 4 out of 984 papers reported on government SE practices, mostly appearing in regional venues as experience reports or case studies. Mainstream SE venues contained virtually no such evidence, confirming practitioners' perceptions of low academic visibility.
AI.conclusion: A significant evidence gap exists in government SE research. The authors recommend dedicated publication venues, stronger government-academia collaboration incentives, and improved methods for evaluating grey literature to support evidence-based software engineering in the public sector.

title: Gridnberg: A Topography-Aware Pedestrian Routing Dataset for New York City
summary: Cities are rarely flat, yet urban network analysis usually represents streets as planar graphs. This simplification affects modeled impedance, route choice, and the interpretation of accessibility, particularly where alternative paths differ in grade. This paper introduces Gridnberg ('grid-n-berg', grid and mountain), a topography-aware pedestrian routing dataset for New York City. The dataset enriches the NYCWalks network with vertex-level elevations derived from the New York City Planimetric Database. For each pedestrian-network geometry vertex, the workflow averages selected elevation observations within a 50 m radius, retains segments with complete vertex support, and uses direction-specific cumulative ascent and descent to calculate three routing costs: horizontal distance, a comfort-oriented slope score, and an accessibility-sensitive slope score. The release retains 313184 of 315577 source segments (99.24%). Gridnberg supports reproducible terrain-aware analysis, transparent scenario comparison, and improved pedestrian-network representations in New York and other cities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Gridnberg, a topography-aware pedestrian routing dataset for New York City that enriches the NYCWalks street network with vertex-level elevation data, enabling three slope-sensitive routing cost metrics beyond simple horizontal distance.
AI.motivation: Urban network analysis typically models streets as planar graphs, ignoring topography. This simplification distorts impedance calculations, route choice, and accessibility interpretations, especially where alternative paths differ significantly in grade. The authors aim to correct this by incorporating elevation into pedestrian network models.
AI.method: The workflow enriches NYCWalks network geometry vertices with elevations from the New York City Planimetric Database. Elevation observations within a 50 m radius are averaged per vertex. Only segments with complete vertex support are retained. Three routing costs are computed: horizontal distance, a comfort-oriented slope score, and an accessibility-sensitive slope score, using direction-specific cumulative ascent and descent.
AI.result: The final dataset retains 313,184 of 315,577 source segments (99.24% retention). Gridnberg supports reproducible terrain-aware analysis and transparent scenario comparison for pedestrian-network representations.
AI.conclusion: Gridnberg demonstrates that incorporating elevation into pedestrian network models is both feasible at scale and retains near-complete network coverage, enabling improved pedestrian accessibility analysis in New York and serving as a transferable methodology for other cities.

title: Kalyna Block Cipher: From Design Space Exploration to ASIC Design
summary: The Kalyna block cipher is a Ukrainian cryptography standard, selected through a national competition held between 2007 and 2010 and approved in 2015. Although its software implementations have been introduced, hardware-efficient implementations of the algorithm, i.e., accelerators, do not exist. In this paper, we explore various design architectures to implement its encryption, decryption, and unified encryption/decryption functions, considering the trade-off between area and latency. We present hardware reduction techniques and introduce alternative designs with low area, latency, and energy consumption, targeting an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). We present hardware-efficient designs that include countermeasures against side-channel analysis (SCA) and fault injection (FI) attacks, such as hiding, masking, and duplication techniques. We validate these implementations in a 65\;nm ASIC chip. Experimental results confirm the need for alternative designs that explore the design search space for different requirements. The proposed architectures enable hiding the power SCA leakage by randomizing the execution of operations, and the temporal duplication in designs with countermeasures against the SCA attacks can mitigate the FI attacks. The functionality of the ASIC test chip, including various Kalyna designs, is validated through measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first hardware-efficient ASIC implementations of the Ukrainian Kalyna block cipher, exploring area-latency trade-offs and incorporating side-channel analysis (SCA) and fault injection (FI) countermeasures such as hiding, masking, and duplication, validated on a 65nm ASIC test chip.
AI.motivation: Kalyna is Ukraine's national block cipher standard (approved 2015), but prior work only addressed software implementations. No hardware accelerators existed, nor had any hardware implementations with SCA/FI countermeasures been explored, creating a gap for resource-constrained, security-critical applications.
AI.method: The authors explore multiple hardware architectures (encryption-only, decryption-only, unified encryption/decryption) targeting ASIC. They apply hardware reduction techniques to optimize area, latency, and energy. SCA countermeasures use hiding (randomized execution order) and masking, while FI protection employs temporal duplication. All designs are fabricated and validated on a 65nm ASIC test chip with real measurements.
AI.result: Experimental measurements from the 65nm ASIC chip confirm that the proposed architectures successfully enable exploration of the design space across different constraints. Randomized execution of operations effectively hides power SCA leakage, and temporal duplication in SCA-protected designs simultaneously mitigates FI attacks.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-efficient Kalyna accelerators are feasible with tunable area-latency-energy trade-offs. Integrating combined SCA and FI countermeasures (hiding, masking, duplication) into low-area designs is practical and validated in silicon, establishing a foundation for secure Kalyna hardware deployment.

title: FSE: Continual Learning for Named Entity Recognition by Fast-Slow Experts
comment: Preprint submitted to Pattern Recognition Letters
summary: Continual Learning for Named Entity Recognition (CLNER) enable models to incrementally learn new entity types without forgetting previously acquired ones. However, existing methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and insufficient exploitation of shared information across tasks. This paper proposes FSE, a Fast-Slow Experts enhanced span-based NER model for CLNER. The shared fast expert learns token-level links to efficiently filter out unlikely spans, while the task-specific slow expert performs span classification only on the remaining candidates. It stabilizes learning by promoting knowledge sharing across tasks and maintains plasticity by reducing learning burden at each task. A length-decay negative sampling strategy to mitigate span imbalance is also introduced. Extensive experiments on OntoNotes and FewNERD synthestic datasets demonstrate that FSE achieves state-of-the-art performance in CLNER scenarios, with effectiveness of each component, empirical evidence of faster convergence and expected functionality of both experts.

AI.tldr: FSE is a span-based continual NER model using a dual-expert architecture: a shared fast expert filters candidate spans via token-level links, while task-specific slow experts classify only the remaining spans, achieving SOTA on CLNER benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing CLNER methods suffer from (1) catastrophic forgetting of previously learned entity types and (2) insufficient exploitation of shared information across incremental tasks.
AI.method: The FSE model combines: (1) a shared fast expert that learns token-level links to efficiently filter out unlikely spans across all tasks; (2) task-specific slow experts that perform span classification only on remaining candidates, reducing per-task learning burden; (3) a length-decay negative sampling strategy to mitigate span imbalance.
AI.result: FSE achieves state-of-the-art performance on OntoNotes and FewNERD synthetic CLNER datasets, with empirical evidence of faster convergence and confirmation that both experts function as designed.
AI.conclusion: The dual-expert design effectively addresses both catastrophic forgetting and knowledge sharing in CLNER, with the fast expert providing cross-task efficiency and the slow expert maintaining task-specific plasticity.

title: RED-PIM: Reducing Data Movement for Transformers using Processing-in-Memory
summary:
Transformers are widely used across many domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, web search, and DNA sequence analysis. Given their broad applicability, improving the performance of transformer models is critical. However, the high volume of data movement between processing units and memory during attention operations significantly limits their efficiency. Processing-In-Memory (PIM) mitigates this issue by performing computations directly inside memory. While prior work has proposed PIM-based transformer implementations, they suffer from costly inter-bank communication, and struggle to scale due to the limited capacity of memory banks. As a result, attention-related data must be split across banks, diminishing the potential benefits of PIM.
  In this work, we propose RED-PIM, an algorithm-architecture co-design that reduces attention latency by minimizing inter-bank data movement from O(N^2) to O(N) and shrinking intermediate attention matrices from N x N to d x d. By reorganizing matrix operations, performing computations locally, and employing an optimized data transfer strategy, RED-PIM significantly reduces computation cost and interconnect traffic. Compared to baseline PIM implementation, RED-PIM achieves inference time reductions ranging from 16.05% to 99.99% (geometric mean of 66.42%), with the largest gains on longer sequences. On real-world datasets, RED-PIM improves performance by 99.60% for long documents and 13.44% for shorter ones, while maintaining or improving accuracy. These results demonstrate RED-PIM's effectiveness for scalable and efficient transformer inference.

AI.tldr: RED-PIM proposes an algorithm-architecture co-design that reduces transformer attention latency in Processing-In-Memory systems by minimizing inter-bank data movement from O(N²) to O(N) and shrinking intermediate attention matrices from N×N to d×d, achieving inference time reductions of 16–99.99% with greatest gains on long sequences.
AI.motivation: Transformers suffer from high data movement between processing units and memory during attention operations. Existing PIM-based transformer implementations incur costly inter-bank communication and scale poorly because memory banks have limited capacity, forcing attention data to be split across banks and undermining PIM benefits.
AI.method: The authors propose RED-PIM, an algorithm-architecture co-design that (1) reorganizes matrix operations to reduce inter-bank data movement from O(N²) to O(N), (2) shrinks intermediate attention matrices from N×N to d×d, (3) performs computations locally within memory banks, and (4) employs an optimized data transfer strategy to reduce interconnect traffic and computation cost.
AI.result: Compared to a baseline PIM implementation, RED-PIM achieves inference time reductions ranging from 16.05% to 99.99% (geometric mean: 66.42%), with the largest gains on longer sequences. On real-world datasets, RED-PIM improves performance by 99.60% for long documents and 13.44% for shorter ones, while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.conclusion: RED-PIM demonstrates effective and scalable transformer inference by fundamentally addressing inter-bank communication bottlenecks in PIM architectures, making it particularly well-suited for long-sequence processing.

title: Discrete Action Space as a Prerequisite for GRPO Convergence in Small-Model Continuous Control
summary: We study whether Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can fine-tune small language models for simulated quadrotor continuous-control tasks. In our benchmark, vanilla GRPO fine-tuning of Qwen-0.5B for 25 Hz quadrotor velocity control collapses to the trivial zero action: 0 percent success rate, with entropy falling from 0.35 to 0.03 within 60 steps. Two ablations - removing the jerk-penalty term and removing the KL anchor to the pretrained prior - each prevent entropy collapse, yet neither enables learning. When the action interface is replaced by a 5-way categorical choice over PID presets, training converges. The resulting controller traces a smoothness-reliability Pareto frontier along training duration; both endpoints are reported: 98.6 percent success with 0.656 m/s3 jerk at 64 steps, and 100 percent success with 1.103 m/s3 jerk, or 0.796 under a matched velocity cap, at 256 steps. The recipe is evaluated across three pretrained language models. As context, a re-tuned classical baseline, PID with Ki = 0.30 and vmax = 2.5, reaches the same 100 percent success rate at jerk 0.736 m/s3. A high-fidelity simulation using Crazyflie 2.1 dynamics surfaces a hover-region training-distribution gap.

AI.tldr: GRPO fine-tuning of small LMs for continuous quadrotor control fails due to entropy collapse; switching to a categorical PID-preset action space enables successful learning, achieving up to 100% success with competitive jerk, comparable to a re-tuned classical PID baseline.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether GRPO can fine-tune small language models (specifically Qwen-0.5B) for simulated quadrotor continuous-control tasks, addressing the challenge of applying LLM-based reinforcement learning to low-level robotic control.
AI.method: GRPO fine-tuning of Qwen-0.5B for 25 Hz quadrotor velocity control, with ablations (removing jerk penalty, removing KL anchor), followed by a reformulated action interface using 5-way categorical selection over PID presets. Evaluated across three pretrained LMs, with a re-tuned PID baseline (Ki=0.30, vmax=2.5) and high-fidelity Crazyflie 2.1 simulation for distribution-gap analysis.
AI.result: Vanilla GRPO collapses to zero-action (0% success, entropy 0.35→0.03 in 60 steps). Ablations prevent collapse but don't enable learning. Categorical PID-preset approach yields a smoothness-reliability Pareto frontier: 98.6% success, 0.656 m/s³ jerk at 64 steps; 100% success, 1.103 m/s³ jerk (0.796 under matched velocity cap) at 256 steps. Re-tuned PID achieves 100% success at 0.736 m/s³ jerk. High-fidelity simulation reveals hover-region training-distribution gap.
AI.conclusion: GRPO with continuous actions fails for quadrotor control due to entropy collapse. A categorical PID-preset interface resolves this, yielding controllers competitive with classical PID. The approach generalizes across multiple pretrained LMs, though distribution gaps in hover regions remain a challenge for high-fidelity transfer.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization in the Wild: An Empirical Taxonomy from 100+ Bug Bounty Disclosures
summary: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) is consistently ranked the most critical API security vulnerability, yet the existing literature remains almost entirely conceptual. This paper presents one of the first large-scale empirical analyses of BOLA in publicly disclosed bug bounty reports. We constructed a reproducible sampling frame of 200 HackerOne disclosures tagged IDOR or Improper Access Control (2021-2026) and applied a three-criterion inclusion filter, yielding 107 fully classified reports. Classification used an LLM-assisted schema-completion procedure under constrained, human-adjudicated criteria against a six-family BOLA taxonomy.
