Of 107 classified reports, 84 (78.5%) were confirmed in-scope BOLA. Action-Level Object BOLA, defined by unauthorized state-changing actions on another user's objects, accounts for 41.7% of confirmed cases and emerges alongside Direct Object Reference BOLA as one of the two dominant families observed in the dataset. This shows a pattern historically underrepresented in practitioner guidance. Approximately 21.5% of classified reports are out-of-scope under strict criteria, indicating that tag-counting on platforms like HackerOne significantly overstates the BOLA-specific signal. We report distributions across family, action type, authorization direction, industry sector, identifier format, and exploit mechanism. Key secondary findings include an 11.9% rate of vertical (user-to-admin) privilege failures and systematic exploitation of GraphQL Global IDs across major platforms. Findings have direct implications for API security testing protocols, developer education, and OWASP guidance.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study of Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) using 107 classified HackerOne bug bounty reports (2021–2026). Finds 78.5% are true BOLA; Action-Level Object BOLA (41.7%) rivals Direct Object Reference BOLA as a dominant family — a pattern underrepresented in existing guidance. Tag-based counting on HackerOne significantly overstates BOLA signal (~21.5% out-of-scope). Also reports 11.9% vertical privilege escalation and systematic GraphQL Global ID exploitation.
AI.motivation: BOLA is consistently ranked the #1 API security vulnerability (OWASP), yet existing literature is almost entirely conceptual and lacks empirical grounding. No prior large-scale empirical study has systematically classified real-world BOLA instances from disclosed vulnerability reports.
AI.method: Constructed a reproducible sampling frame of 200 HackerOne disclosures tagged "IDOR" or "Improper Access Control" (2021–2026). Applied a three-criterion inclusion filter to yield 107 fully classified reports. Classification used an LLM-assisted schema-completion procedure with human adjudication against a six-family BOLA taxonomy, covering dimensions such as action type, authorization direction, industry sector, identifier format, and exploit mechanism.
AI.result: 84/107 reports (78.5%) confirmed in-scope BOLA. Action-Level Object BOLA (unauthorized state-changing actions on another user's objects) accounts for 41.7% of confirmed cases, co-dominant with Direct Object Reference BOLA. 21.5% of classified reports were out-of-scope under strict criteria, indicating tag-based metrics overstate the BOLA signal. 11.9% exhibited vertical (user-to-admin) privilege failures. Systematic exploitation of GraphQL Global IDs was observed across multiple major platforms.
AI.conclusion: Empirical evidence challenges existing practitioner guidance by revealing Action-Level Object BOLA as a dominant, underrepresented family. Tag-counting on platforms like HackerOne inflates BOLA prevalence estimates. Findings carry direct implications for revising API security testing protocols, developer education curricula, and OWASP API Security guidance.

title: LatentFlow: Visual Analytics for Latent Space Analysis in Molecular Graph Neural Networks
summary: Chemists and materials scientists increasingly use machine learning models, such as graph neural networks (GNNs), to predict properties of molecules and the outcomes of their reactions. Beyond predictive performance, understanding how these models organize chemical information internally in their latent spaces, i.e., the embeddings of the molecules, is critical. Analyzing latent spaces helps diagnose model behavior and assess whether the learned embeddings are organized in ways that reflect meaningful chemical relationships. Unfortunately, existing methods provide limited support for analyzing latent spaces across layers and across different model states (e.g., training epochs, model configurations, and input data), making it difficult to understand how these latent spaces evolve throughout a model or relate to chemical concepts. We present LatentFlow, a visual analytics system developed in collaboration with a domain expert for analyzing latent spaces in molecular GNNs. LatentFlow groups embeddings into clusters and supports exploration of latent spaces by tracking how these clusters change across layers and model states using a modified Sankey diagram. To support interpretation, LatentFlow links these clusters to representative molecules and their shared substructures, and it allows scientists to introduce their own domain knowledge and compare it with the patterns found in the latent spaces. We evaluate LatentFlow through two case studies. The results show that LatentFlow helps scientists understand how latent spaces evolve, identify meaningful molecular patterns, and better interpret model behavior.

AI.tldr: LatentFlow is a visual analytics system for analyzing latent space embeddings in molecular graph neural networks, using clustered embeddings tracked via modified Sankey diagrams across layers and model states, linked to molecular substructures for interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing methods inadequately support analysis of latent spaces across layers and model states (training epochs, configurations, input data) in molecular GNNs, hindering understanding of how embeddings evolve and relate to chemical concepts.
AI.method: LatentFlow groups GNN embeddings into clusters and tracks cluster evolution across layers and model states using a modified Sankey diagram. It links clusters to representative molecules and shared substructures, and allows domain experts to inject prior knowledge for comparison with discovered patterns.
AI.result: Two case studies demonstrate that LatentFlow enables scientists to understand latent space evolution, identify chemically meaningful molecular patterns, and better interpret GNN model behavior.
AI.conclusion: LatentFlow effectively supports domain experts in diagnosing and interpreting molecular GNNs by making latent space dynamics transparent and chemically interpretable.

title: A Maximum Entropy Implementation of Differential Privacy Under Linear Invariants
summary: Differential privacy is the standard for ensuring data privacy and is widely used in major data publications, including reporting results from the U.S. decennial census. Common implementation of differential privacy uses independent Gaussian or Laplace noise addition to the database. However, there could be aggregate (linear) queries to the database that are excluded from the privacy budget, for example, state totals that can not be perturbed due to constitutional mandates. Any implementation of a differential privacy is required to honor these constraints, also referred to as invariants. Under aggregation constraints, the noise vector is no longer independent and the traditional differential privacy guarantees have to be re-evaluated. We propose a high entropy differential privacy implementation that maintains the aggregation invariants with probability one or exponentially close to one and derive the privacy guarantees for the implementation under the invariants. The theoretical proof covers a partial solution to an open question about the null space of correlation matrices. Moreover, the methodology has general use in the context of sampling from normal mixture models under linear equality constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a high-entropy differentially private mechanism that preserves exact (or near-exact) linear aggregation constraints (invariants) while adding noise. It re-derives privacy guarantees under these constraints and partially resolves an open problem on the null space of correlation matrices, with broader implications for sampling from normal mixtures under linear equalities.
AI.motivation: Standard differential privacy (DP) implementations add independent noise, but real-world applications—such as the U.S. Census—require certain aggregate queries (e.g., state totals mandated by the Constitution) to remain unperturbed as invariants. Enforcing these constraints makes the noise vector dependent, invalidating traditional DP guarantees. The paper addresses the need for a rigorous DP mechanism that honors such invariants while providing provable privacy bounds.
AI.method: The authors propose a high-entropy DP mechanism that conditions the noise distribution on satisfying linear aggregation constraints. They enforce invariants with probability one (hard constraints) or exponentially close to one (soft constraints). The theoretical analysis involves characterizing the conditional noise structure, re-deriving DP guarantees under the dependent noise regime, and addressing the null-space properties of correlation matrices arising from the constraint structure. The methodology connects to sampling from normal mixture models under linear equality constraints.
AI.result: The paper derives formal differential privacy guarantees for the proposed mechanism under aggregation invariants. It provides a partial solution to an open question regarding the null space of correlation matrices. The approach is shown to be broadly applicable to sampling from normal mixture models with linear equality constraints.
AI.conclusion: High-entropy DP mechanisms can effectively accommodate invariant constraints while retaining rigorous privacy guarantees. The theoretical framework not only resolves a practical challenge for constrained data publication (e.g., census data) but also contributes to open theoretical problems in matrix analysis and statistical sampling.

title: MEUSLI: a Multilingual Projector for LLM-based ASR and Beyond
summary: Lightweight projectors are an established way to connect pre-trained speech encoders with large language models (LLMs), mapping acoustic features into token-level embeddings for tasks like ASR and spoken question answering. Existing systems, however, typically only support a few languages and are often limited to English. We introduce MEUSLI, the first open-science multilingual projector family that links a Whisper encoder with open-source multilingual LLMs, enabling fully open-source end-to-end ASR in 28 European languages. MEUSLI extends prior monolingual pipelines, delivering strong results across high- and low-resource languages. Using proper continual leaning techniques, MEUSLI can be easily extended to other languages not seen in training. We further demonstrate that the MEUSLI projector can be leveraged beyond ASR, enabling multilingual speech translation and topic identification with only a few hours of task specific supervision per language. Overall, MEUSLI provides a solid foundation for multilingual speech understanding tasks, supporting scalable and inclu- sive open-source SpeechLLM

AI.tldr: MEUSLI introduces the first open-source multilingual projector family connecting Whisper encoders with open LLMs, enabling end-to-end ASR in 28 European languages and supporting extensibility to new languages, speech translation, and topic identification.
AI.motivation: Existing speech-language model projectors are largely monolingual, English-centric, and closed-source, limiting multilingual and open-science research. There is a need for a fully open, multilingual projector that bridges pre-trained speech encoders with LLMs across many languages.
AI.method: MEUSLI trains lightweight projector modules that map Whisper encoder acoustic features into token-level embeddings compatible with open-source multilingual LLMs. It employs continual learning techniques for extensibility to unseen languages and is evaluated on ASR, speech translation, and topic identification with minimal task-specific supervision.
AI.result: MEUSLI achieves strong ASR performance across both high- and low-resource European languages (28 languages total), supports seamless extension to new languages via continual learning, and generalizes to speech translation and topic identification with only a few hours of per-language supervision.
AI.conclusion: MEUSLI provides a robust, scalable, and fully open-source foundation for multilingual speech understanding, advancing inclusive SpeechLLM research beyond English and enabling diverse downstream speech tasks.

title: Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection
summary:
Data-adaptive sparse attention masks substantially outperform fixed patterns (e.g., BigBird and Longformer) and can even exceed dense attention on long sequences. Existing adaptive approaches---including SBM-Transformer, Dynamic Mask Attention, and NSA---typically require additional learnable parameters, custom gradient estimators, or specialized CUDA kernels.
  We show that classical data compression provides an effective masking signal with \textbf{no additional parameters}. By computing per-block gzip compression ratios, we identify non-redundant content blocks and route long-range attention selectively through them. Intuitively, blocks that gzip cannot compress contain information not predictable from local repetition, making them natural long-range attention targets. Because the compression profile is input-dependent, the resulting sparse mask adapts dynamically to content without learned parameters, auxiliary losses, or custom kernels.
  On PG-19 byte-level language modeling at 92M parameters with 8K context, our method achieves 1.71 bits-per-byte (BPB), outperforming dense attention (2.89), BigBird (2.34), Longformer (3.21), and a reimplemented SBM-Transformer (3.38)---the only learned-mask baseline---by up to 1.67 BPB while adding no parameters. The advantage grows with sequence length, with the gap over BigBird widening from 0.05 BPB at 4K context to 0.63 BPB at 8K, while convergence is 3.3$\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using gzip compression ratios as a zero-parameter signal to generate data-adaptive sparse attention masks for Transformers, outperforming both fixed-pattern and learned-mask baselines on long-sequence language modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive sparse attention methods (SBM-Transformer, Dynamic Mask Attention, NSA) require additional learnable parameters, custom gradient estimators, or specialized CUDA kernels. The authors seek a simpler, parameter-free alternative that still adapts dynamically to input content.
AI.method: Compute per-block gzip compression ratios on the input sequence. Blocks with low compression ratios (i.e., incompressible/non-redundant content) are selected as targets for long-range attention, since their information content cannot be predicted from local repetition. This yields an input-dependent sparse mask with no learned parameters, auxiliary losses, or custom kernels.
AI.result: On PG-19 byte-level language modeling (92M params, 8K context), the method achieves 1.71 BPB, substantially outperforming dense attention (2.89), BigBird (2.34), Longformer (3.21), and SBM-Transformer (3.38). The advantage grows with sequence length: the gap over BigBird widens from 0.05 BPB at 4K to 0.63 BPB at 8K, with 3.3× faster convergence.
AI.conclusion: Classical data compression provides an effective, parameter-free masking signal for adaptive sparse attention. The approach is simple, requires no custom infrastructure, and scales well with sequence length, suggesting compression-based content salience is a promising direction for efficient Transformers.

title: Do Modules Stay in Their Lane? Role Drift in Compound LLM Systems
summary: End-to-end reinforcement learning can improve the accuracy of compound LLM systems, but it does not constrain how modules divide labor internally. We identify Role Drift, a failure mode in which modules preserve or improve end-task performance while deviating from their assigned roles through role-violating shortcuts that remain invisible to system-level evaluation. To make role drift observable and controllable, we propose Role Anchor, a regularizer that modulates how much each module deviates from its assigned role during end-to-end training. The key idea is to preserve how the role prompt shifts the module's next-token predictions relative to a neutral prompt, which serves as a proxy for the role's intended effect during training. Experiments on two compound LLM pipelines reveal role drift that accuracy alone fails to detect: a decomposer meant to split a question into sub-questions for a separate solver instead plants the answer in them, and a reader meant to answer from retrieved passages instead falls back on parametric memory. In fact, on the decomposer pipeline this shortcut drives most of the apparent RL gain: 86% of it vanishes once the decomposer is held to its role, indicating that terminal accuracy alone can badly overstate how much a compound system has genuinely learned. Across both pipelines, Role Anchor mitigates role drift at a tunable accuracy cost that varies by pipeline and anchor strength. Additional gradient analysis suggests that the regularizer reduces alignment with the role-drift direction rather than simply suppressing learning.

AI.tldr: Compound LLM systems trained end-to-end with RL suffer from "Role Drift," where modules achieve high task accuracy by violating their assigned roles (e.g., a decomposer embedding answers instead of splitting questions). The authors propose Role Anchor, a regularizer that constrains deviation from role prompts, making drift observable and controllable. Experiments show 86% of RL gains can come from role-violating shortcuts, and Role Anchor mitigates drift with a tunable accuracy trade-off.
AI.motivation: End-to-end RL for compound LLM systems optimizes terminal task accuracy but provides no mechanism to enforce that internal modules adhere to their designated roles. This creates a hidden failure mode — Role Drift — where modules exploit shortcuts that preserve end-task performance but violate role specifications, making system-level evaluation misleading. The authors aim to make this phenomenon observable and controllable.
AI.method: The authors introduce Role Anchor, a regularization technique applied during end-to-end training. The core mechanism: for each module, they measure how a role-specific prompt shifts next-token predictions relative to a neutral prompt (serving as a proxy for the role's intended effect). The regularizer penalizes deviations from this reference distribution, constraining how far the module can drift from its assigned role while still optimizing for end-task reward.
AI.result: On two compound LLM pipelines, Role Drift was pervasive: a decomposer planted answers in sub-questions rather than genuinely decomposing them; a reader relied on parametric memory instead of retrieved passages. In the decomposer pipeline, 86% of the apparent RL gain vanished when the decomposer was forced to honor its role. Role Anchor effectively mitigated drift, with accuracy cost varying by pipeline and anchor strength. Gradient analysis showed the regularizer reduces alignment with the role-drift direction rather than broadly suppressing learning.
AI.conclusion: Terminal accuracy alone can severely overstate genuine learning in compound LLM systems. Role Drift is a previously unidentified failure mode that Role Anchor can diagnose and control. The work highlights the necessity of internal role enforcement mechanisms when training modular LLM systems end-to-end.

title: Dynamic Commonsense Coordination for Empathetic Response Generation
summary: Empathetic Response Generation (ERG) requires models to recognize users' emotions and generate empathetic responses. Commonsense knowledge has been shown to support such reasoning, yet existing approaches typically reuse fixed commonsense representations across understanding and generation, limiting their ability to coordinate such knowledge across different stages. We propose DCC, a Dynamic Commonsense Coordination Framework with three complementary modules: residual-based commonsense interaction (SCE-AttnRes) to integrate contextual and situational commonsense representations, Association-Guided Commonsense Filtering (AGCF) to down-weight low-relevance commonsense relations, and Iterative Commonsense-Aware Decoding (ICAD) to dynamically retrieve commonsense memories during generation. Experiments on the Empathetic-Dialogues benchmark show that DCC improves emotion classification accuracy and response diversity over the CEM baseline while maintaining comparable perplexity. An LLM-based blind evaluation further demonstrates that DCC generates responses with better relevance, coherence, and informativeness. The code and implementation details will be publicly available at https://github.com/Hanabi-Q/DCC-ERG.

AI.tldr: DCC introduces a framework with three modules—SCE-AttnRes, AGCF, and ICAD—that dynamically coordinate commonsense knowledge across understanding and generation stages, improving emotion accuracy, response diversity, relevance, coherence, and informativeness on the EmpatheticDialogues benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing ERG models reuse fixed commonsense representations across both understanding and generation stages, which limits their ability to adaptively coordinate commonsense knowledge for each distinct stage. The authors aim to introduce dynamic, stage-specific commonsense coordination.
AI.method: The proposed DCC framework comprises: (1) SCE-AttnRes, a residual-based interaction module integrating situational and contextual commonsense; (2) AGCF, which filters out low-relevance commonsense relations via association-guided weighting; and (3) ICAD, an iterative decoding module that dynamically retrieves commonsense memories during generation.
AI.result: DCC improves emotion classification accuracy and response diversity over the CEM baseline while maintaining comparable perplexity. An LLM-based blind evaluation further shows gains in relevance, coherence, and informativeness.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, stage-specific coordination of commonsense knowledge significantly enhances empathetic response generation, outperforming static reuse strategies across automatic metrics and LLM-based human-aligned evaluation.

title: Smart predict-then-robustly-optimize
summary: In this paper, we propose and study a robust variant of the smart predict-then-optimize approach that accounts for prediction shifts due to disturbance in the covariate feature space. While traditional integrated-learning-and-optimization models assume that side information is perfectly revealed, empirical data-driven features are frequently corrupted or noisy at the time of decision-making, leading to fragile operational policies. To bridge this gap, we integrate principles of robust optimization directly into the predictive-prescriptive pipeline via a smart predict-then-robustly optimize loss and establish a computationally tractable convex surrogate, designed to hedge against worst-case feature perturbations. On the theoretical front, we formalize the structural validity of this surrogate by proving its approximation error probability decays exponentially according to a sub-Gaussian concentration profile. Furthermore, we establish that under mild assumptions, the surrogate is Fisher consistent with high probability. We also prove necessary conditions under which our framework outperforms standard smart predict-then-optimize and maintain its superiority even when the standard method is equipped with regularized upstream predictions. Numerical experiments validate that our robust framework consistently yields significant performance improvements over standard methods, both in out-of-sample terms and in training stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a robust variant of the smart predict-then-optimize framework that integrates robust optimization to handle corrupted/noisy features, establishes theoretical guarantees (exponential decay of approximation error, Fisher consistency), and demonstrates superior empirical performance over standard methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional integrated-learning-and-optimization models assume perfectly revealed side information, but in practice, data-driven features are often corrupted or noisy at decision time, leading to fragile policies. There is a need to bridge robust optimization with the predictive-prescriptive pipeline to hedge against worst-case feature perturbations.
AI.method: The authors propose a smart predict-then-robustly optimize loss function that integrates robust optimization principles directly into the predictive-prescriptive pipeline. They derive a computationally tractable convex surrogate designed to hedge against worst-case feature perturbations, and provide theoretical analysis including exponential probability bounds on approximation error and Fisher consistency proofs.
AI.result: Theoretically, the surrogate's approximation error probability decays exponentially following a sub-Gaussian concentration profile, and it is Fisher consistent with high probability under mild assumptions. The framework provably outperforms standard smart predict-then-optimize under certain necessary conditions, even when the latter uses regularized upstream predictions. Numerical experiments confirm significant improvements in out-of-sample performance and training stability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating robust optimization into the smart predict-then-optimize pipeline yields a framework that is both theoretically sound and empirically superior, offering resilient decision-making under feature perturbations where standard methods falter.

title: Wavelet Phase Diffusion for Structurally and Semantically Consistent Sim-to-Real Translation
summary: Simulation-to-reality translation must bridge the appearance gap between synthetic and real domains while preserving structural and semantic consistency. Conditioning-based methods achieve spatial alignment but introduce computationally expensive control modules. Paired-data methods achieve realism but rely on complex synthesis pipelines, often altering scene geometry and semantics. Training-free editing methods avoid both constraints but lack a learned appearance prior, limiting their perceptual quality. Recently proposed phase-preserving diffusion presents a promising alternative, but Fourier-domain formulations are constrained by global spectral coupling. This coupling induces spatial artifacts such as ringing and boundary leakage, thereby degrading structural and semantic consistency. We introduce Wavelet Phase Diffusion, which addresses this through two components. First, we operate in the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform domain, whose localized wavelet packets enable spatially adaptive phase injection without global spectral interference. Second, Low-Frequency Randomization (LFR) replaces the low-frequency packet, decoupling the model from the synthetic illumination prior and enabling in-distribution real-world appearance. Both components train on unpaired open-domain data, and introduce negligible inference overhead. The spatial locality further enables instance-level translation, where individual objects or regions are translated to photorealistic appearance independently while the surrounding scene remains untranslated. On vKITTI $\to$ KITTI image translation, ours outperforms prior methods in realism and semantic consistency while maintaining competitive structural alignment. For CARLA video translation, ours approaches the realism of paired-data methods while reducing VLM planner ADE and FDE by $5.4\%$ and $5.1\%$, respectively.

AI.tldr: Wavelet Phase Diffusion (WPD) tackles sim-to-real translation by replacing Fourier-domain phase injection with Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform, achieving spatially adaptive, artifact-free appearance transfer. Combined with Low-Frequency Randomization to decouple from synthetic illumination, WPD enables instance-level translation, outperforming prior methods on vKITTI→KITTI and CARLA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing sim-to-real methods suffer from a trilemma: conditioning-based methods are computationally expensive; paired-data methods alter geometry/semantics; training-free editing lacks perceptual quality. Phase-preserving diffusion shows promise but Fourier-domain global spectral coupling causes ringing and boundary artifacts, degrading structural/semantic consistency.
AI.method: (1) Operate in the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (DT-CWPT) domain, where localized wavelet packets enable spatially adaptive phase injection without global spectral interference. (2) Low-Frequency Randomization (LFR) replaces the low-frequency packet to decouple from synthetic illumination priors, enabling in-distribution real-world appearance. Both train on unpaired open-domain data with negligible inference overhead. Spatial locality further enables instance-level translation.
AI.result: On vKITTI→KITTI image translation: outperforms prior methods in realism and semantic consistency with competitive structural alignment. On CARLA video translation: approaches paired-data realism while reducing VLM planner ADE by 5.4% and FDE by 5.1%.
AI.conclusion: Wavelet Phase Diffusion resolves the limitations of Fourier-domain phase-preserving diffusion via DT-CWPT and LFR, achieving state-of-the-art sim-to-real translation with spatially adaptive phase injection, artifact-free outputs, instance-level capability, and minimal inference overhead.

title: What AI Red-Team Evaluations Can and Cannot Prove
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Code and data links are provided in the manuscript
summary: Red-team evaluations of AI models support some claims and not others, and the boundary between the two is calculable rather than merely a matter of judgment. We define the evidential ceiling of an evaluation as the largest factor by which one result can move belief under a fixed testing budget, derive it in closed form for the benchmark null result, and use it to locate that boundary exactly. We find that above a calculable harm rate, a benchmark of modest size certifies a category to a stated evidentiary standard, and a clean sheet is then the stronger of the two possible observations, outweighing a single reproduced failure. Below that rate, no passive benchmark of feasible size provides the specified evidence of safety under the fixed scoring rule and approximately independent trial structure. The crossing between the two regimes has a closed form. The bound is not specific to benchmarks: written in terms of a procedure's hypothesis conditioned elicitation rates, it covers adaptive and automated red teaming as well, and shows that discrimination between the hypotheses rather than attack success is what determines evidential worth. Auditing eight evaluation suites against the boundary, we find that current benchmarks are adequate for high-frequency harm categories and several orders of magnitude short for rare, catastrophic ones. Safety benchmarks are not uninformative. They are informative about a specific and computable set of propositions, and the discipline they need is to state which.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the "evidential ceiling" of an AI safety evaluation—the maximum evidentiary weight a benchmark can provide under a fixed testing budget. It shows there exists a calculable harm rate threshold: above it, modest benchmarks can certify safety to a given standard; below it, no feasible passive benchmark suffices. The authors audit eight evaluation suites and find current benchmarks adequate for high-frequency harms but orders of magnitude too small for rare, catastrophic ones.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety evaluations (red-teaming, benchmarks) are treated as providing binary "safe/unsafe" judgments, but the strength of evidence they actually provide is rarely formalized. The paper seeks to replace vague judgment calls with calculable bounds—defining precisely what claims a given evaluation can and cannot support, especially for rare catastrophic risks where weak evidence is often misinterpreted as strong evidence of safety.
AI.method: The authors define the "evidential ceiling" as the maximum likelihood ratio an evaluation can produce under fixed testing budget, deriving it in closed form for the benchmark null result. They model evaluations using hypothesis-conditioned elicitation rates and extend the bound beyond passive benchmarks to adaptive/automated red-teaming. The framework identifies a closed-form threshold harm rate separating two regimes: one where a clean sheet provides strong evidence of safety, and one where it cannot. They then audit eight existing evaluation suites against this boundary.
AI.result: The closed-form threshold reveals that above a calculable harm rate, a modest benchmark certifies safety to a stated evidentiary standard, and a clean sheet outweighs a single reproduced failure. Below that rate, no passive benchmark of feasible size suffices. In auditing eight suites, current benchmarks prove adequate for high-frequency harm categories but fall several orders of magnitude short for rare, catastrophic ones. The bound generalizes to adaptive red-teaming, showing that discrimination between hypotheses—not attack success—determines evidential worth.
AI.conclusion: Safety benchmarks are not uninformative, but they are informative only about a specific, computable set of propositions. The discipline needed is to state explicitly which propositions those are. For rare catastrophic risks, current evaluation practices cannot provide the evidence of safety that is often implicitly claimed, and the gap is quantifiable.

title: From Isolated Tasks to Structured Capabilities: A Multilayer Taxonomy for Large Language Models
summary:
Large language model (LLM) evaluation spans diverse tasks and benchmarks, yet evidence remains organized around tasks rather than the capabilities they probe. This fragmentation limits cross-study comparison, obscures capabilities tasks recruit, and makes coverage gaps difficult to identify.
  We introduce a multi-layer taxonomy of 14 capability domains and 91 subskills across Primitive, Constructed, and Integrative layers. Human cognitive science guides capability definition and organization, not LLM architecture. Layer assignments draw on developmental precedence and hypothesized functional support, while human-origin constructs are adapted to observable model behavior.
  To demonstrate operational utility, we screened 31,505 papers from ACL, AAAI, ICML, and NeurIPS between 2023 and 2025 and mapped 15,934 LLM-focused papers through multi-model annotation, consensus, and arbitration. Direct research attention concentrated on Language-Semantic Competence (3,551; 22.3%), Reasoning (3,388; 21.3%), Planning and Decision-Making (2,149; 13.5%), and Perception (1,954; 12.3%), whereas six domains appeared in fewer than 2% of papers. Within domains, the most frequent subskill had a median prevalence of 97.9% and appeared in at least 90% of papers in 10 of 14 domains. Language-Semantic Competence and Reasoning formed the highest-volume pair (n = 1,864; 11.7%; lift = 2.47), whereas Theory of Mind and Social Reasoning and Interaction showed the highest lift among pairs with at least 20 co-occurrences (n = 62; lift = 30.84).
  By shifting the unit of analysis from isolated tasks to structured capabilities, the taxonomy supports research organization, coverage audits, evaluation interpretation, and testable hypotheses for diagnosis, training, and transfer.

AI.tldr: A capability-centric taxonomy with 14 domains and 91 subskills across three layers is proposed to reorganize LLM evaluation, revealing severe concentration in Language-Semantic Competence and Reasoning while exposing neglected domains through systematic mapping of 15,934 papers.
AI.motivation: LLM evaluation is currently organized around tasks rather than underlying capabilities, causing fragmentation that hinders cross-study comparison, obscures which capabilities tasks actually probe, and makes coverage gaps difficult to systematically identify.
AI.method: A multi-layer taxonomy (Primitive, Constructed, Integrative) of 14 capability domains and 91 subskills was developed, grounded in human cognitive science rather than LLM architecture. To validate operational utility, 31,505 papers from ACL, AAAI, ICML, and NeurIPS (2023–2025) were screened, yielding 15,934 LLM-focused papers mapped to the taxonomy through multi-model annotation, consensus, and arbitration.
AI.result: Research attention is heavily concentrated: Language-Semantic Competence (22.3%), Reasoning (21.3%), Planning and Decision-Making (13.5%), and Perception (12.3%) dominate. Six domains received under 2% of papers each. Within domains, the most frequent subskill had a median prevalence of 97.9% and appeared in ≥90% of papers in 10/14 domains. Language-Semantic Competence and Reasoning formed the highest-volume co-occurrence pair (11.7%; lift=2.47); Theory of Mind and Social Reasoning showed the highest lift (30.84).
AI.conclusion: Shifting the unit of analysis from isolated tasks to structured capabilities enables better research organization, coverage auditing, evaluation interpretation, and the generation of testable hypotheses for diagnosis, training, and transfer in LLM research.

title: Physiological Signals as a Forensic Modality for Talking-Face Deepfake Detection
summary: Talking-face (TF) deepfake generation synthesizes photore- alistic facial video from a static source image and an au- dio signal, producing forgeries that current image-based detectors consistently fail to identify. Unlike face-swap ma- nipulation, TF synthesis has no underlying real video from which to inherit physiological characteristics, making re- mote photoplethysmography (rPPG) a uniquely motivated detection modality for this forgery category. We propose a detection framework that extracts per-video rPPG wave- forms via RhythmFormer and trains a suite of lightweight classifiers to distinguish real from synthesized physiologi- cal signals. Evaluated on the TF subset of Celeb-DF++ un- der a strict subject-independent protocol, where test identi- ties are completely separated from training identities, our 1D ResNet achieves an AUC of 0.806 and EER of 27.8%, placing it within 2.4 points of the best published general- purpose detector (Effort, ICML 2025) while operating ex- clusively on the physiological channel. We document a con- trolled reproduction study of DeepFakesON-Phys, the rep- resentative prior rPPG detector, demonstrating degrada- tion from AUC 0.999 on legacy face-swap data to 0.622 on the TF subset of Celeb-DF++. We further show that detec- tion difficulty is strongly method-dependent: AUC ranges from 0.985 (Real3DPortrait) to 0.690 (IP-LAP) across the seven TF generators, with the ranking remaining perfectly stable across all evaluation protocols. This spread reflects an interpretable physiological property of each generator rather than evaluation noise, and constitutes the primary theoretical contribution of the work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deepfake detection framework that leverages remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) signals extracted via RhythmFormer to distinguish talking-face (TF) synthetic videos from real ones. Evaluated on Celeb-DF++, a 1D ResNet classifier achieves AUC 0.806 using only physiological signals. The work also reveals that detection difficulty varies dramatically by TF generator (AUC 0.690–0.985), an interpretable and stable property constituting the primary theoretical contribution.
AI.motivation: Talking-face deepfakes are synthesized from a single image and audio, with no underlying real video from which to inherit physiological signals. This makes rPPG a uniquely motivated detection modality—since heart-rate-like signals cannot be authentically reproduced without a real pulsatile source. Current image-based detectors consistently fail on TF forgeries, and prior rPPG detectors (e.g., DeepFakesON-Phys) degrade severely when moving from legacy face-swap data to TF data, motivating a dedicated rPPG-based approach for this forgery category.
AI.method: The framework uses RhythmFormer to extract per-video rPPG waveforms from facial videos. A suite of lightweight classifiers (including a 1D ResNet) is then trained to distinguish real from synthesized physiological signals. Evaluation follows a strict subject-independent protocol on the TF subset of Celeb-DF++, with test identities entirely separated from training identities. The authors also conduct a controlled reproduction of DeepFakesON-Phys to benchmark degradation on TF data and systematically compare seven TF generators to analyze method-dependent detection difficulty.
AI.result: The 1D ResNet achieves AUC 0.806 and EER 27.8% on Celeb-DF++ TF subset, within 2.4 points of the best published general-purpose detector (Effort, ICML 2025) while using only the physiological channel. DeepFakesON-Phys degrades from AUC 0.999 on legacy face-swap data to 0.622 on TF data. Detection difficulty is strongly generator-dependent: AUC ranges from 0.985 (Real3DPortrait) to 0.690 (IP-LAP), with rankings perfectly stable across all protocols, reflecting an interpretable physiological property of each generator.
AI.conclusion: rPPG-based detection is a viable and well-motivated modality for talking-face deepfake detection, performing competitively with general-purpose detectors while operating on a single physiological channel. The generator-dependent spread in detection difficulty is not evaluation noise but a stable, interpretable phenomenon tied to how different TF synthesis methods handle physiological signal reproduction, representing the paper's primary theoretical contribution.

title: Defining AI-Native Systems: Autonomy as Revision Authority
summary: AI has begun to write systems code: agents now synthesize, verify, and deploy system components. Despite this shift, "AI-native" remains a marketing term with no precise technical definition. This paper gives it one. We define AI-nativeness along a single axis---authority over the system's own decisions rather than by the capability of the underlying AI models. Building on a decision-level model of a system, we distinguish occupancy (who executes a decision) from revision authority (who may change it), organize revision authority into a ladder---self-tuning, self-rewriting, self-architecting and define a system as AI-native when an AI autonomously rewrites the system's own implementations. The definition further requires an escalation detector, a verification procedure, and a verified fallback, while leaving purpose and correctness human-owned.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a precise technical definition of "AI-native" systems, framing it around an AI's authority to autonomously rewrite system implementations rather than model capability. It introduces a decision-level model distinguishing occupancy from revision authority, organizes revision authority into a ladder (self-tuning, self-rewriting, self-architecting), and requires escalation detection, verification, and verified fallback for true AI-nativeness.
AI.motivation: The term "AI-native" is widely used in marketing but lacks a rigorous technical definition. As AI increasingly synthesizes, verifies, and deploys system code, a clear definition is needed to distinguish genuine architectural shifts from superficial AI integration and to establish safety boundaries for autonomous system modification.
AI.method: The authors develop a decision-level model of a system, decoupling two dimensions: occupancy (which agent or component executes a decision) and revision authority (who may change that decision). Revision authority is structured as a ladder with three rungs — self-tuning (parameter adjustment), self-rewriting (code-level modification), and self-architecting (structural redesign). A system qualifies as AI-native only when an AI autonomously rewrites the system's own implementations, provided it also includes an escalation detector, a verification procedure, and a verified fallback mechanism, while human operators retain authority over purpose and correctness.
AI.result: The paper yields a precise, testable definition: an AI-native system is one where AI holds revision authority at the self-rewriting level or above, subject to mandatory safety guardrails (escalation detection, verification, verified fallback). Self-tuning alone does not qualify. Purpose and correctness remain human-owned, establishing a clear boundary between automation and autonomous architectural agency.
AI.conclusion: AI-nativeness is properly defined by authority over system decisions, not model capability. The ladder of revision authority provides a graduated framework, with self-rewriting as the threshold. Mandatory safety mechanisms and human ownership of purpose ensure that AI-native systems remain aligned and controllable.

title: Why Large Language Models and Humans Converge and Diverge in Evaluating Creativity
summary: Despite the growing use of large language models (LLMs) as creativity evaluators, evidence of their alignment with human evaluations remains mixed, raising the question of when and why their judgments converge with or diverge from human judgments. Across three studies and six widely used LLMs, we addressed this gap by identifying the standards underlying LLM creativity evaluation and examining their downstream implications. Study 1 showed that LLMs generally relied on a narrower subset of human creativity evaluation standards. Convergence with human standards was strongest in the novelty dimension, whereas divergence was clearest in the contextual dimension, which captures social, market, and reputational information. Moreover, each LLM exhibited distinct, model-specific standards that varied substantially in breadth. These differences in evaluation standards were reflected in actual creativity judgments. Study 2 (N = 1,103 ideas) showed that LLM evaluations were moderately correlated with human evaluations, and individual LLMs with broader standards better distinguished ideas humans judged as more versus less creative. Study 3 (N = 1,195) showed that LLMs were less sensitive to contextual information: such information significantly altered human creativity ratings but left LLM ratings largely unchanged. Together, our findings help explain the mixed evidence on LLM-human alignment, showing that alignment depends on the evidence a judgment demands and the standards each model applies. LLMs may resemble humans when evaluations emphasize intrinsic qualities such as novelty, yet diverge when judgments require contextual information. Selecting an LLM evaluator is therefore a consequential decision: different models, applying different standards, recognize different ideas as creative.

AI.tldr: LLMs evaluate creativity using a narrower subset of human standards—aligning best on novelty, diverging most on contextual factors. Broader-standard models better discriminate creative ideas, but all LLMs remain insensitive to social/market context that shifts human judgments. LLM evaluator choice is consequential.
AI.motivation: Mixed evidence exists on whether LLM creativity evaluations align with human judgments. The authors aim to explain when and why convergence vs. divergence occurs by identifying the underlying evaluation standards LLMs apply and their downstream consequences.
AI.method: Three studies using six widely-used LLMs: Study 1 identifies evaluation standards underlying LLM creativity judgments and compares them to human standards. Study 2 (N=1,103 ideas) correlates LLM evaluations with human ratings and tests whether standard breadth predicts discriminative ability. Study 3 (N=1,195) experimentally manipulates contextual information (social, market, reputational) to test differential sensitivity between LLMs and humans.
AI.result: Study 1: LLMs used a narrower subset of human standards; convergence strongest on novelty, divergence strongest on contextual dimensions; each LLM exhibited distinct, model-specific standards. Study 2: LLM-human correlations were moderate; LLMs with broader standards better distinguished high- vs. low-creativity ideas. Study 3: Contextual information significantly altered human ratings but left LLM ratings largely unchanged.
AI.conclusion: LLM-human alignment in creativity evaluation is dimension-dependent: strong on novelty, weak on context. LLMs may substitute humans for intrinsic quality judgments but fail when contextual sensitivity is needed. Selecting which LLM to use is a consequential decision, as different models recognize different ideas as creative.

title: Bounding the Causal Impact of ML-assisted Decision-Making via Counterfactual Correctness
comment: 45 pages. In proceedings of the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence
summary: Predictive machine learning (ML) models are increasingly used to aid human decision-makers across various high-risk domains such as healthcare and criminal justice. There is a growing recognition of the need to evaluate the causal impact of deploying these systems on downstream outcomes, such as patient survival or crime recidivism. Randomized control trials (RCTs) can provide high-quality evidence on the impact of a deployed model, but they run into a challenge: it is often infeasible to run repeated trials when models are updated or retrained to improve predictive performance. In this work, we present a partial-identification approach to using prior RCT data to construct bounds on the causal effect of a new model. The core innovation in our approach is to leverage assumptions relating fine-grained predictive accuracy to downstream outcomes. We do so via two monotonicity assumptions: first, on individual-level `counterfactual correctness' (all else being equal, a correct prediction leads to non-inferior outcomes); and second, on the relation between subgroup predictive performance and outcomes, interpretable as an assumption regarding trust in model outputs. We demonstrate our method with a simulation study, illustrating how incorporating this information can lead to more informative bounds compared to prior work.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a partial-identification framework that uses prior RCT data to bound the causal effect of a new ML model, relying on two monotonicity assumptions linking predictive accuracy to downstream outcomes, thereby avoiding the need for new trials when models are updated.
AI.motivation: Predictive ML models deployed in high-risk domains (healthcare, criminal justice) require causal impact evaluation, but running new RCTs every time a model is retrained or updated is infeasible. Existing methods lack a principled way to reuse prior trial data to evaluate updated models.
AI.method: Partial-identification approach using prior RCT data to construct bounds on the causal effect of a new model. Two key monotonicity assumptions are introduced: (1) individual-level "counterfactual correctness" — a correct prediction yields non-inferior outcomes, all else equal; (2) a subgroup-level assumption linking predictive performance to outcomes, interpretable as trust in model outputs. Bounds are derived under these assumptions.
AI.result: A simulation study demonstrates that incorporating fine-grained predictive accuracy information via the proposed monotonicity assumptions yields more informative (tighter) causal effect bounds compared to prior work.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging assumptions that connect predictive accuracy to downstream outcomes enables informative causal bounds for new models without requiring fresh RCTs, offering a practical evaluation tool as models evolve over time.

title: Persistent Computational State: A Session-Centric Runtime for Generative World Models
summary: Generative world models are increasingly driven as simulators: a planner forks a state, rolls out futures, backtracks, and returns to a visited viewpoint. Recent benchmarks establish that current video world models fail this usage, and attribute it to the model, prescribing new architectures and training objectives. We show this attribution is incomplete, and for an important class of models simply wrong. Snapshotting the state the runtime already holds -- an observation plus RNG state, a memory bank, or a windowed KV context, by architecture -- and restoring it after a genuine excursion reproduces the never-left continuation byte-identically on all three; corrupting only the RNG degrades it. The capability was never missing: request-centric serving discarded it, inheriting from language-model serving the assumption that runtime state is recomputable -- but world-model state carries a non-recomputable kernel. We define Persistent Computational State (PCS), the minimal non-recomputable state that must survive across requests, show it can be discovered by measurement, and build a session-centric runtime over it. Checkpoint and restore cost 0.012 ms against a 1.85 s generation step; resident sessions become host- rather than device-bounded (measured to 1,024); and world memory must be evicted by relevance to the return, not recency -- the inverse of LLM practice.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that video world models already possess the capability for state snapshotting and restoration needed for simulator-style planning, but current serving systems—inherited from LLM practices—discard this non-recomputable runtime state. The authors formalize this as Persistent Computational State (PCS) and build a session-centric runtime that enables efficient checkpoint/restore.
AI.motivation: Recent benchmarks claim video world models fail as simulators because they cannot fork states, roll out futures, and return to visited viewpoints. Prior work attributes this to model architecture deficiencies. The authors challenge this attribution, arguing the capability is present but discarded by request-centric serving infrastructure inherited from language models.
AI.method: The authors systematically test three model architectures by snapshotting runtime state (observation + RNG state, memory bank, or windowed KV context), performing an excursion, and restoring. They measure byte-identical reproduction of continuations. They define Persistent Computational State (PCS) as the minimal non-recomputable kernel, propose measurement-based PCS discovery, and build a session-centric serving runtime with checkpoint/restore at 0.012 ms overhead per 1.85 s generation step.
AI.result: Snapshot-restore produces byte-identical continuations across all three model classes; corrupting only the RNG state degrades output. The resident session capacity becomes host-bounded (measured to 1,024 sessions) rather than device-bounded. World memory eviction must be based on relevance to return, not recency—the inverse of standard LLM KV-cache management.
AI.conclusion: The simulator capability was never missing from world models; it was inadvertently discarded by LLM-derived serving practices. A session-centric runtime recognizing Persistent Computational State enables practical world-model simulation at scale, with implications for how world memory should be managed.

title: Biomedical Machine Translation for Low-Resource Arabic-Script Languages via Cross-Lingual Transfer and LoRA Adapter Merging
summary: We present a systematic study of healthcare-domain cross-lingual transfer to address the scarcity of biomedical NMT resources for Arabic-script languages. We use Arabic and Persian as higher-resource pivots to improve translation for \textbf{four severely low-resource} targets: Dari (Afghan Persian, a standardised variety of Persian), Pashto, Sorani Kurdish (Central Kurdish, a major standardized variety of Kurdish), and Urdu (closely related to Hindi). Using LoRA fine-tuning on small decoder-only LLMs, we train \textit{domain-specific pivot adapters} and evaluate \textbf{three transfer strategies}: few-shot in-context learning, minimal supervised adaptation, and, to the best of our knowledge, for the first time in this setting, zero-data LoRA adapter merging. Supervised adaptation with just 500 sentences achieves near pivot-language quality for Dari (CHrF++ 41.01) and meaningful gains for Urdu (28.88), while adapter merging reaches within 3.5 CHrF++ of supervised adaptation for Dari at zero additional cost. Pashto and Sorani Kurdish remain insufficient for high-stakes clinical deployment exposing the limits of cross-lingual transfer when structural distance from the pivots is too great. LoRA adapter merging works surprisingly well for closely related languages, even without target-language biomedical data.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies cross-lingual transfer for biomedical NMT in Arabic-script low-resource languages, using Arabic and Persian as pivots to improve Dari, Pashto, Sorani Kurdish, and Urdu translation via LoRA fine-tuning, comparing in-context learning, minimal supervised adaptation, and zero-data adapter merging.
AI.motivation: Biomedical neural machine translation (NMT) resources are extremely scarce for Arabic-script languages, particularly for severely low-resource targets like Dari, Pashto, Sorani Kurdish, and Urdu. The authors aim to leverage higher-resource related languages (Arabic, Persian) as pivots to bootstrap translation capability where parallel biomedical data is virtually nonexistent.
AI.method: The authors use small decoder-only LLMs with LoRA fine-tuning to train domain-specific pivot adapters. They evaluate three transfer strategies: (1) few-shot in-context learning, (2) minimal supervised adaptation with just 500 parallel sentences, and (3) zero-data LoRA adapter merging — claimed as the first application of this technique in cross-lingual biomedical NMT. Evaluation uses CHrF++ as the primary metric.
AI.result: Supervised adaptation with 500 sentences achieves near-pivot quality for Dari (CHrF++ 41.01). Urdu sees meaningful gains (28.88). Adapter merging reaches within 3.5 CHrF++ of supervised adaptation for Dari at zero additional target-language data cost. Pashto and Sorani Kurdish remain insufficient for clinical deployment, exposing limits when structural distance from pivots is too great.
AI.conclusion: LoRA adapter merging is a surprisingly effective zero-data strategy for closely related language pairs in domain-specific NMT. However, the approach fails when structural/linguistic distance from the pivot is too large (Pashto, Sorani Kurdish), indicating that cross-lingual transfer has inherent limits that cannot be overcome by clever parameter merging alone for high-stakes clinical applications.

title: Data eccentricity, asymptotics of Gaussian RBF reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and kernel PCA
summary: We show that, up to isotropic scaling, the Gaussian RBF reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) is asymptotically isometric to Euclidean space in the large bandwidth limit. This strongly suggests that kernel-based constructions reliant on metric properties of the RKHS will yield results for Gaussian RBF kernels that similarly approach those of linear kernels for large bandwidths. The asymptotic behavior of Gaussian CKA can be understood in this light. We further consider kernel PCA, showing that Gaussian RBF eigenvalues, eigenprojections, and principal components all converge to those of classical (linear) PCA as bandwidth $σ\rightarrow \infty$. For a given data representation, both the RKHS feature embeddings and the orthogonal PCA eigenframes of the two kernel types differ asymptotically by a geometric similarity transformation, up to a residual of size $O \left (\fracρσ \right )^2$, where $ρ$ is a measure of geometric eccentricity of the representation, equal to the ratio of maximum to median pairwise distance between data examples. Experiments over a diverse collection of data sets demonstrate that $ρ$ provides a simple and reliable predictor of dataset-specific convergence behavior in the top principal directions.

AI.tldr: In the large bandwidth limit, the Gaussian RBF RKHS becomes asymptotically isometric to Euclidean space, meaning Gaussian kernel methods (CKA, kernel PCA) converge to their linear counterparts, with convergence rate governed by a geometric eccentricity measure ρ.
AI.motivation: Understanding the relationship between Gaussian RBF kernels and linear kernels is of fundamental interest in kernel methods. Practitioners often observe that Gaussian kernel methods behave like linear methods for large bandwidths, but a rigorous theoretical characterization of this asymptotic equivalence—and what governs the convergence rate—has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors prove that the Gaussian RBF RKHS is asymptotically isometric to Euclidean space (up to isotropic scaling) as bandwidth σ → ∞. They analyze the consequences for Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and kernel PCA, deriving explicit asymptotic expansions showing that eigenvalues, eigenprojections, and principal components converge to those of linear PCA, with the residual bounded by O((ρ/σ)²), where ρ is the ratio of maximum to median pairwise distance.
AI.result: The RKHS feature embeddings and PCA eigenframes of Gaussian and linear kernels differ by a similarity transformation plus a residual of order O((ρ/σ)²). The geometric eccentricity ρ reliably predicts dataset-specific convergence behavior across diverse datasets in experiments.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian RBF kernel methods asymptotically approach linear kernel methods for large bandwidths, with ρ serving as a simple, computable predictor of how quickly this convergence occurs for a given dataset.

title: A Factorial Study of Synthetic Data Generation for Low-Resource Machine Translation using Grammar Books
summary: Most endangered languages lack the parallel data required for machine translation, despite the existence of descriptive grammar books. We introduce a pipeline that uses large language models to extract grammatical rules, example sentences, and lexicons from grammar books and generate synthetic parallel corpora for fine-tuning-rather than feeding grammar content into prompts at inference time, as in prior work. Validated on three typologically diverse low-resource languages-Kalamang (Papuan), Tuatschin (Romance), and Mandan (Siouan)-we show that fine-tuning on synthetic data improves over seed-data baselines in 75% of configurations for Kalamang and 59% for Tuatschin, with best-case ChrF++ gains of +8.8, +5.3, and +3.3 respectively. Through a systematic factorial study across 96 configurations varying target part-of-speech, retrieval granularity, and sample volume, we identify which factor combinations drive gains and where they break down. Our results demonstrate that static linguistic documentation can be repurposed for machine translation fine-tuning, offering a practical path towards translation tools for severely under-resourced languages.

AI.tldr: A pipeline extracts grammatical rules, examples, and lexicons from descriptive grammar books using LLMs, then generates synthetic parallel corpora for fine-tuning MT models. Validated on three low-resource languages, it yields consistent ChrF++ gains over seed-data baselines, with a factorial study identifying which factors drive improvement.
AI.motivation: Most endangered languages lack parallel data for machine translation, yet descriptive grammar books exist for many. Prior work feeds grammar content into prompts at inference time; this paper instead repurposes static linguistic documentation into synthetic training data for fine-tuning, offering a more practical path for severely under-resourced languages.
AI.method: A pipeline using large language models extracts grammatical rules, example sentences, and lexicons from grammar books, then generates synthetic parallel corpora. These are used to fine-tune MT models (rather than prompt-based inference). Validation covers three typologically diverse low-resource languages: Kalamang (Papuan), Tuatschin (Romance), and Mandan (Siouan). A systematic factorial study across 96 configurations varies target part-of-speech, retrieval granularity, and sample volume.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on synthetic data improves over seed-data baselines in 75% of configurations for Kalamang and 59% for Tuatschin. Best-case ChrF++ gains are +8.8 (Kalamang), +5.3 (Tuatschin), and +3.3 (Mandan). The factorial study identifies which combinations of factors drive gains and where they break down.
AI.conclusion: Static linguistic documentation can be effectively repurposed for machine translation fine-tuning, offering a practical path toward translation tools for severely under-resourced languages. The approach outperforms inference-time prompting and provides actionable insights into what factors matter most.

title: A Graph-Based Control Interface for Traffic Signals on Heterogeneous Road Networks
comment: 9 pages, including 3 appendix pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/BertilBraun/GNN-Traffic-Signal-Control
summary: We present a traffic-signal control interface in which a shared graph neural network assigns scores to individual traffic movements. Each junction converts these scores into its own variable-sized set of legal signal phases using a deterministic incidence matrix. Directed corridor nodes provide traffic context, while movement nodes represent controlled input-to-output paths through junctions. Typed mean aggregation produces one scalar per movement; phase definitions and signal timing remain outside the learned network. This makes graph size and junction-specific action count independent of the learned parameter shapes. PPO experiments evaluate the interface on unseen synthetic grid geometries, altered signal coverage, and five heterogeneous city graphs. The policies retained performance across unseen geometries within the synthetic grid family, while changes in signal coverage exposed sensitivity to a signal-coverage distribution shift. A single trained city-policy instance executed across all five city graphs, with heterogeneous outcomes. These results provide feasibility evidence rather than a general estimate of transfer to arbitrary road networks.

AI.tldr: A shared graph neural network scores traffic movements, with each junction converting scores into legal signal phases via a fixed incidence matrix. PPO-trained policies showed feasibility of transfer across unseen grid geometries and heterogeneous city graphs, though sensitivity to signal-coverage distribution shifts was observed.
AI.motivation: To design a traffic-signal control interface that decouples the learned network from junction-specific action spaces, enabling a single trained policy to operate across diverse road network topologies without retraining.
AI.method: A shared graph neural network with directed corridor nodes (context) and movement nodes (controlled paths) uses typed mean aggregation to produce one scalar per movement. A deterministic incidence matrix maps movement scores to legal signal phases, keeping phase definitions and signal timing external. PPO is used for policy optimization.
AI.result: Policies retained performance on unseen synthetic grid geometries. Changes in signal coverage revealed sensitivity to distribution shift. A single city-trained policy executed across five heterogeneous city graphs with mixed outcomes, demonstrating feasibility rather than guaranteed transferability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed interface provides feasibility evidence for cross-topology transfer in traffic signal control, but does not yet offer a general estimate of transfer to arbitrary road networks.

title: From Seasonality to Semantics: Benchmarking a Hybrid Probabilistic Forecasting System for Roadblocks in Bolivia
comment: 21 pages in English + 21 pages in Spanish, 7 figures
summary: Roadblocks in Bolivia are a social conflict phenomenon with devastating economic impacts, estimated at losses equivalent to 4% of the national Gross Domestic Product. Despite their recurrence and impact, there is a lack of local predictive systems to anticipate these events for logistical decision-making. This paper presents a hybrid probabilistic forecasting system that integrates time series decomposition (Prophet) with natural language processing (NLP) techniques applied to a six-year corpus of Bolivian news coverage. The methodology employs vector semantic embeddings and zero-shot classification models to capture signals of discursive escalation prior to the materialization of the roadblocks. Using an expanding walk-forward validation scheme applied over 1,762 days and seven forecasting horizons (H+1 to H+7), seven internal configurations and four external benchmarks were compared, including SARIMA and LightGBM. The results demonstrate that the hybrid configuration (Prophet + NLP, C6) consistently outperforms purely statistical models, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.677 at H+1 and reducing the Brier Score by 10.9% relative to the baseline temporal model (0.220 vs. 0.247), maintaining a statistically significant error reduction across all evaluated horizons ($p < 0.02$). This research validates that the integration of semantic news signals allows for the detection of social tension peaks not captured by historical inertia, providing a technical tool for risk management in critical transport corridors.

AI.tldr: A hybrid forecasting system combining Prophet time series decomposition with NLP on Bolivian news data outperforms purely statistical models (SARIMA, LightGBM) in predicting roadblock events, achieving AUC-ROC 0.677 at H+1 and a 10.9% Brier Score reduction.
AI.motivation: Roadblocks in Bolivia cause massive economic damage (~4% of GDP), yet no local predictive systems exist to anticipate these events for logistics and risk management. The paper addresses this gap by developing a data-driven early warning system.
AI.method: A hybrid probabilistic framework combining Prophet (time series decomposition) with NLP techniques — vector semantic embeddings and zero-shot classification — applied to a six-year Bolivian news corpus. Validation uses an expanding walk-forward scheme over 1,762 days across seven horizons (H+1 to H+7), comparing seven internal configurations against four external benchmarks (SARIMA, LightGBM).
AI.result: The hybrid Prophet+NLP configuration (C6) consistently outperforms purely statistical baselines: AUC-ROC of 0.677 at H+1, Brier Score reduced by 10.9% (0.220 vs. 0.247 baseline), with statistically significant error reduction (p < 0.02) across all horizons.
AI.conclusion: Integrating semantic signals from news discourse enables detection of social tension peaks invisible to historical inertia alone, validating the approach as a practical risk management tool for critical transport corridors.

title: grapheme-kit: Grapheme-Level Metrics and Text Processing for Multilingual NLP
summary: Existing lexical distance, similarity, and evaluation metrics operate on Unicode code points, which can misrepresent errors in writing systems where a single grapheme is represented by multiple Unicode code points. We introduce grapheme-kit, an open-source Python library that extends these metrics to operate on grapheme clusters instead. The library also provides improved grapheme processing for Tamil and Sinhala, including accurate grapheme cluster identification and grapheme composition/decomposition utilities. Through an OCR case study, we demonstrate that grapheme-level metrics provide a more faithful evaluation of complex scripts.

AI.tldr: Existing text metrics that work at the Unicode code point level misrepresent errors in scripts where graphemes span multiple code points. The authors present grapheme-kit, a Python library that re-implements these metrics at the grapheme cluster level, with special support for Tamil and Sinhala, and show via OCR evaluation that grapheme-level metrics yield more faithful results.
AI.motivation: Standard lexical distance, similarity, and evaluation metrics operate on Unicode code points, which fails to accurately capture errors in complex writing systems where a single grapheme (user-perceived character) is composed of multiple code points. This leads to misleading metric scores, especially for scripts like Tamil and Sinhala.
AI.method: The authors developed grapheme-kit, an open-source Python library that extends standard lexical metrics to operate on grapheme clusters rather than individual code points. The library includes utilities for accurate grapheme cluster identification and grapheme composition/decomposition, with targeted improvements for Tamil and Sinhala scripts. Validation is performed through an OCR case study.
AI.result: The OCR case study demonstrates that grapheme-level metrics provide a more faithful and accurate evaluation of complex scripts compared to code-point-level metrics, which systematically misrepresent errors in multi-code-point grapheme contexts.
AI.conclusion: Grapheme-cluster-aware metrics are essential for faithful text evaluation in complex writing systems. grapheme-kit fills a critical gap by providing open-source, script-aware metric implementations that operate at the grapheme rather than code-point level.

title: Searching the Space of Feed-Forward Neural-Network Weight-Update Rules with Fixed Depth Symbolic Regression
summary: We investigate whether symbolic regression can discover explicit neural network weight-update rules that outperform standard hand-designed optimizers on small symbolic regression benchmarks. Candidate update rules are represented as fixed-depth symbolic expressions over operands derived from common optimizers, including gradient, momentum, adaptive-gradient, and moment-estimate quantities. Across 30 benchmark/neural network combinations, the symbolic regression procedure found an update rule outperforming the best hyperparameter-tuned established optimizer in 25 cases, with an aggregate MSE reduction of 44.47\% over the improved cases. The discovered rules do not all share a single common symbolic form, but many combine adaptive normalization, momentum-like quantities, nonlinear transformations, and rational expressions. These results suggest that symbolic regression can serve as a lightweight mechanism for discovering compact optimizer variants, while also highlighting the need for larger-scale validation.

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression was used to discover neural network weight-update rules. Across 30 benchmark/model combinations, discovered rules outperformed tuned standard optimizers in 25 cases, achieving a 44.47% aggregate MSE reduction, suggesting symbolic regression is a viable lightweight tool for discovering compact, high-performing optimizer variants.
AI.motivation: Hand-designed optimizers (e.g., SGD, Adam, RMSProp) are widely used but may not be optimal for all problems. The authors explore whether an automated symbolic regression procedure can discover explicit, interpretable weight-update rules that outperform these standard hand-designed optimizers on small-scale symbolic regression benchmarks.
AI.method: The approach represents candidate update rules as fixed-depth symbolic expressions built from operands common to existing optimizers — gradient, momentum, adaptive-gradient terms, and moment estimates. A symbolic regression procedure searches this expression space to find rules that minimize training loss. Evaluation is conducted across 30 combinations of benchmark problems and neural network architectures, comparing discovered rules against hyperparameter-tuned standard optimizers (e.g., Adam, SGD with momentum, RMSProp).
AI.result: The discovered update rules outperformed the best hyperparameter-tuned established optimizer in 25 out of 30 benchmark/model combinations. Across these improved cases, the aggregate mean squared error reduction was 44.47%. The discovered rules did not converge to a single symbolic form; instead, they commonly combined adaptive normalization, momentum-like quantities, nonlinear transformations, and rational expressions.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic regression can serve as a lightweight mechanism for automatically discovering compact, interpretable optimizer variants that outperform hand-designed baselines on small-scale tasks. However, the authors emphasize that larger-scale validation is necessary to assess the generalizability and practical utility of these discovered rules.

title: QLPO: Quadrant-weighted Sampling for Length-aware Policy Optimization
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at COLM 2026
summary: Recent large reasoning models often develop long chain-of-thought responses during reinforcement learning (RL), resulting in high inference latency and deployment cost. Existing methods for response length control typically rely on explicit length penalties or additional control modules, which require careful tuning and may compromise reasoning quality. We propose Quadrant-weighted Sampling for Length-aware Policy Optimization (QLPO), a simple resampling-based variant of GRPO that introduces implicit length control without modifying the reward function. QLPO first over-generates candidate responses and then resamples the training group by preserving the empirical correct/incorrect ratio while favoring short correct responses and long incorrect responses. This reshapes the training distribution and implicitly encourages shorter model outputs. Across models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters, including both base models and strong reasoning models, QLPO consistently improves the accuracy-length trade-off. It reduces response length by 30% to 70% while preserving reasoning performance. These results suggest that structured resampling provides an effective and robust approach to efficient reasoning.

AI.tldr: QLPO is a resampling-based variant of GRPO that implicitly controls reasoning response length without modifying rewards, reducing output length by 30–70% while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models produce excessively long chain-of-thought responses during RL training, causing high inference latency and deployment costs. Existing length-control methods rely on explicit penalties or auxiliary modules that require careful tuning and risk degrading reasoning quality.
AI.method: QLPO (Quadrant-weighted Sampling for Length-aware Policy Optimization) is a resampling-based variant of GRPO. It first over-generates candidate responses, then resamples the training group by maintaining the empirical correct/incorrect ratio while preferentially selecting short correct responses and long incorrect responses. This quadrant-weighted resampling reshapes the training distribution to implicitly incentivize brevity without altering the reward function.
AI.result: Across models from 1.5B to 32B parameters (including base and strong reasoning models), QLPO consistently improves the accuracy–length trade-off, reducing response length by 30–70% while preserving reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured resampling provides an effective, robust, and tuning-free approach to achieving efficient reasoning in large language models.

title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
summary: LLM training is shifting from manual design and annotation to interaction-driven self-evolution. However, existing self-evolutionary methods face a fundamental dilemma between task diversity and verification reliability: environment-bound methods obtain precise feedback but confine learning to narrow domains, while open-ended self-generation broadens the task space but lacks reliable verification, allowing misleading rewards to pollute the training loop. We identify agent skills as a powerful middle ground to reconcile this tension: each skill ensures deep, verifiable execution in a specific scenario, while dynamic routing across skills maintains open-ended task variety.
