Leveraging this insight, we introduce Skill Self-Play (Skill-SP), a co-evolutionary framework comprising a proposer, a solver, and a dynamic skill controller. Orchestrated via a reinforcement learning loop, these components co-evolve in a continuous self-play loop: the proposer generates challenging tasks conditioned on dynamically sampled skills; the solver explores candidate solutions to push its capability boundaries; and the skill controller collects execution feedback to update and expand the skill library. This interactive co-evolution effectively bridges the gap between structured verification and open-ended exploration. Empirical evaluations on tool-use and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that Skill-SP, serving as a robust evolution engine, consistently pushes the performance ceiling of competent backbones while catalyzing striking turnarounds for initially misaligned models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/skill-self-play.

AI.tldr: Skill-SP introduces a co-evolutionary self-play framework where a proposer, solver, and dynamic skill controller co-evolve via RL, using agent skills as a middle ground to reconcile task diversity with reliable verification in LLM self-training.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM self-evolution methods face a dilemma: environment-bound approaches offer precise verification but narrow task diversity, while open-ended generation expands tasks but lacks reliable verification, risking reward hacking. The authors identify agent skills as a bridge between these extremes.
AI.method: Skill Self-Play (Skill-SP) is a co-evolutionary framework with three components: (1) a proposer that generates challenging tasks conditioned on dynamically sampled skills, (2) a solver that explores candidate solutions, and (3) a dynamic skill controller that collects execution feedback to update and expand a skill library. All components co-evolve through a reinforcement learning self-play loop.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on tool-use and reasoning benchmarks show Skill-SP consistently improves performance ceilings of competent models and enables striking turnarounds for initially misaligned models.
AI.conclusion: Skill-SP effectively bridges structured verification and open-ended exploration, serving as a robust self-evolution engine for LLMs.

title: LeAct: Learning to Reason from Expert Actions
summary: Modern reasoning models depend on reasoning data, today sourced from human annotations or distilled from stronger LLMs. However, a rich and largely untapped source of supervision lies in expert systems (e.g., game engines, classical planners, theorem provers), which routinely produce near-optimal actions across diverse domains. But these experts are silent: they commit to an action without writing down the chain of thought (CoT) behind it. Recovering that CoT as natural-language reasoning would distill expert knowledge into a student that generalizes beyond the demonstrated actions. We treat it as a latent variable and study how to recover it from the action alone. Our approach, LeAct (Learning to reason from Actions), optimizes this latent variable: the student samples candidate CoTs for each expert action, and we retain those that measurably improve its own probability of recovering the action. Across imperfect-information games at multiple scales and a simulated robotics benchmark, LeAct reaches the solver's numerical floor on small enumerable games. At larger scale, it is $5\times$ closer to the solver than the strongest expert-iteration baseline. At Flop Hold'em ($\sim 10^9$ infosets), LeAct wins head-to-head by $+60$ mbb/g, and on the robotics probe it is the only training recipe that improves on direct imitation. We present a principled framework and the result: expert systems become a categorically new source of reasoning teachers for foundation models.

AI.tldr: LeAct recovers latent chain-of-thought reasoning from expert system actions by treating CoT as a latent variable. The student generates candidate reasoning traces; those that improve the probability of recovering the correct action are retained. This turns silent expert systems (game engines, planners, theorem provers) into reasoning teachers, achieving solver-level performance on small games and significantly outperforming baselines on large-scale benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern reasoning models rely on expensive human-annotated or LLM-distilled reasoning data. Expert systems (game engines, classical planners, theorem provers) produce near-optimal actions but lack natural-language CoT, making them "silent" teachers. The authors aim to unlock this vast, untapped source of supervision by recovering the implicit reasoning behind expert actions.
AI.method: LeAct formulates CoT recovery as latent-variable optimization. For each expert action, the student model samples multiple candidate chain-of-thought explanations. Each candidate is scored by how much it increases the student's own probability of predicting the correct expert action. Only CoTs that measurably improve action recovery are retained for training, creating a self-reinforcing loop between reasoning generation and action prediction.
AI.result: On small enumerable imperfect-information games, LeAct reaches the solver's numerical floor. At larger scale, it achieves 5× closer distance to the solver than the strongest expert-iteration baseline. On Flop Hold'em (~10⁹ infosets), LeAct wins head-to-head by +60 mbb/g. On a simulated robotics benchmark, it is the only method that improves over direct imitation.
AI.conclusion: Expert systems constitute a categorically new source of reasoning teachers for foundation models. By recovering latent CoT from actions alone, LeAct provides a principled framework for distilling expert knowledge into generalizable natural-language reasoning without requiring human annotation or stronger LLMs.

title: DAGForge: Auditable Causal DAG Authoring with Biomedical Literature
summary: Constructing causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) is a core step in biomedical causal analysis, yet it remains a largely manual process. Analysts must connect study variables to prior literature, evaluate uncertain causal claims, and preserve sufficient provenance for expert review. We present DAGForge, a browser-based system for authoring causal DAGs as auditable, evidence-linked artifacts. Given free-text descriptions of study concepts, DAGForge creates a reproducible literature snapshot, uses an LLM-based reasoning module to generate structured pairwise causal judgments grounded in verbatim evidence excerpts, and assembles those judgments into a constraint-checked graph. Each proposed edge includes confidence estimates, provenance, and a reviewable rationale. The interface supports study specification, progress monitoring, evidence review, graph comparison, adjustment-set computation, and export. In evaluations against both compact benchmark DAGs and reference DAGs derived from published literature, DAGForge achieves high edge recall on the literature-based cohort while retaining verifiable evidence trails absent from LLM-only baselines. DAGForge thus reduces the burden of causal DAG curation while making the resulting assumptions auditable, supporting the design, analysis, and interpretation of biomedical studies.

AI.tldr: DAGForge is a browser-based system that uses LLMs with evidence grounding to semi-automate the construction of causal DAGs, producing auditable, provenance-tracked graphs for biomedical research.
AI.motivation: Constructing causal DAGs for biomedical studies is labor-intensive, manual, and requires linking variables to prior literature while maintaining provenance for expert review. Existing LLM-only approaches lack verifiable evidence trails, undermining trustworthiness.
AI.method: DAGForge takes free-text study concepts, creates a reproducible literature snapshot, and employs an LLM-based reasoning module to generate structured pairwise causal judgments anchored to verbatim evidence excerpts. These judgments are assembled into a constraint-checked graph with confidence estimates, provenance, and reviewable rationales. The interface supports study specification, progress monitoring, evidence review, graph comparison, adjustment-set computation, and export.
AI.result: Evaluated against compact benchmark DAGs and reference DAGs from published literature, DAGForge achieved high edge recall on the literature-based cohort while providing verifiable evidence trails that LLM-only baselines lacked.
AI.conclusion: DAGForge reduces the burden of causal DAG curation while ensuring assumptions remain auditable, thereby supporting design, analysis, and interpretation of biomedical studies.

title: Scaling Laws for Classical Machine Learning on Tabular Data: A Benchmark Study
summary: Prior classical-ML learning-curve work fits power laws to tree, linear, and kernel models on tabular data, but at small scale: typically one curve, one team, a handful of cells. We present a distributed classroom-scale replication: 127 students each ran a fixed protocol on 3 assigned datasets, drawn from 18 tabular classification and regression datasets and 6 model families (Boosting, Random Forest, SVM, Linear/Logistic, Ridge, Lasso), yielding 11,536 training runs and 1,648 fitted power-law curves of the form error(N) = a N^(-b) + c. Three findings. (1) Power laws fit: R^2 > 0.8 on 77.7% of cells, with tree ensembles dominating at full data (Boosting 50% of datasets, RandomForest 33%; linear models underperform on classification). (2) Approximate shared exponents within a model family: for 5 of 6 families, a single family-level exponent predicts each family's cross-dataset curves nearly as well as per-dataset exponents (R^2 gap < 0.011), though AIC favors the unconstrained fit and curve collapse is partial (32-58% of points within +/-0.5 dex). We frame this as approximate predictive compressibility, not dataset-independent universality; Lasso fails outright (negative control) and Ridge is fragile under leave-one-dataset-out. (3) Replicator-implementation variance: with random_state=42 fixed, independent re-implementations of the same protocol still differ by mean CV(b) = 0.144 on the fitted exponent -- not seed variance, but the spread induced by unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling). We release the aggregated curves, per-cell fits, and a practical data-requirement table for N* to reach target error 0.15.

AI.tldr: A large-scale replication study with 127 students across 18 datasets and 6 model families (11,536 runs) confirms power-law learning curves fit well, reveals approximate shared exponents within model families, and quantifies replicator-implementation variance independent of seed randomness.
AI.motivation: Prior learning-curve research was small-scale (single curves, small teams). The authors aim to rigorously test whether power-law learning curves generalize across datasets and model families at classroom scale, and to quantify reproducibility under independent re-implementations of the same protocol.
AI.method: 127 students each executed a fixed protocol on 3 assigned datasets from a pool of 18 tabular classification/regression tasks, using 6 model families (Boosting, Random Forest, SVM, Linear/Logistic, Ridge, Lasso). Each training run sampled increasing dataset sizes, fitting power laws of the form error(N) = a N^(-b) + c. In total: 11,536 training runs yielding 1,648 fitted power-law curves. Replicator variance was measured by comparing independent re-implementations with random_state=42 fixed.
AI.result: (1) Power laws achieved R² > 0.8 on 77.7% of cells; tree ensembles dominated at full data (Boosting best on 50% of datasets, Random Forest on 33%; linear models underperformed on classification). (2) Family-level shared exponents predicted cross-dataset curves nearly as well as per-dataset exponents (R² gap < 0.011), though AIC favored unconstrained fits and curve collapse was partial (32-58% within ±0.5 dex). Lasso failed as a negative control; Ridge was fragile under leave-one-dataset-out. (3) Replicator-implementation variance: mean CV(b) = 0.144 on fitted exponents, attributable to unconstrained protocol elements (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling), not seed variation.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates approximate predictive compressibility (not dataset-independent universality) of learning curves within model families, highlights significant replicator-implementation variance as a distinct source of irreproducibility, and provides a practical data-requirement table for practitioners.

title: When Is a Learned Command Adapter Worth It? Closed-Loop Identification and Counterfactual Auditing of Frozen Locomotion Policies
summary: Adding a learned adapter to a frozen, command-conditioned locomotion policy is worthwhile only if the interface exposes improvements that are both real and recoverable from deployment-time observations. We introduce an adapter necessity audit that separates global operating-point gain,same-state counterfactual headroom, deployment gain over a cross-fitted fixed action, and state-allocation gain over a frequency-matched randomized policy. Source-cluster learner refits map these quantities and constraint violations to a GO/NO-GO/ABSTAIN decision. Closed-loop command- response identification provides optional decision features. On Go2, an archived scale-prefix diagnostic finds 5.2% same-state headroom but only 0.55% recovered allocation gain. Our confirmatory audit evaluates direct, scale, heading, and yaw interventions on twenty independent clusters for each of three query distributions induced by direct control, VGCC, and MPC, using 200 full learner refits. At 1% deployment and allocation thresholds and a 5% violation tolerance, direct queries return NO-GO, while VGCC and MPC queries ABSTAIN. VGCC has the largest mean deployment gain (1.34%), but its allocation lower bound is 0.09% and its violation upper bound is 6.25%. A deployment-representative twenty-cluster H1 audit also returns NO-GO, whereas a learner-level synthetic control returns GO. The audit therefore tests whether observable signal justifies state-dependent adaptation rather than presuming that an adapter is valuable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an "adapter necessity audit" — a rigorous statistical framework for determining whether adding a learned adapter to a frozen locomotion policy is justified by recoverable, observation-based improvements, rather than presuming value. Applied to a Go2 robot, the audit reveals minimal recovered allocation gain (0.55%) despite measurable headroom, and returns NO-GO or ABSTAIN across most query distributions, cautioning against unwarranted adapter deployment.
AI.motivation: Adding learned adapters to frozen locomotion controllers is common practice, but the interface may expose improvements that are not recoverable from deployment-time observations. There is no principled framework to test whether observable signals genuinely justify state-dependent adaptation versus a fixed or randomized baseline, risking overconfident deployment of adapters that provide negligible real-world benefit.
AI.method: The authors introduce an adapter necessity audit that decomposes performance into four quantities: (1) global operating-point gain, (2) same-state counterfactual headroom, (3) deployment gain over a cross-fitted fixed action, and (4) state-allocation gain over a frequency-matched randomized policy. Source-cluster learner refits map these quantities plus constraint violations to a GO/NO-GO/ABSTAIN decision. Closed-loop command-response identification supplies optional decision features. The audit is applied to a Go2 quadruped across direct, VGCC, and MPC query distributions using 200 full learner refits on 20 independent clusters, plus an H1 humanoid audit with synthetic control.
AI.result: On Go2, a scale-prefix diagnostic finds 5.2% same-state headroom but only 0.55% recovered allocation gain. At 1% deployment and allocation thresholds with 5% violation tolerance, direct queries return NO-GO; VGCC and MPC queries ABSTAIN. VGCC shows the largest mean deployment gain (1.34%) but allocation lower bound of only 0.09% and violation upper bound of 6.25%. A deployment-representative H1 audit also returns NO-GO, while a learner-level synthetic control returns GO, underscoring the gap between idealized and realistic assessment.
AI.conclusion: The audit demonstrates that observable signal often does not justify state-dependent adaptation, even when headroom exists. Rather than presuming adapter value, practitioners should empirically test whether improvements are recoverable. The GO/NO-GO/ABSTAIN framework provides a disciplined decision rule for adapter deployment, and the findings urge caution in applying learned adapters without rigorous necessity testing.

title: Dynamic Capability Scoping for Enterprise AI Agents: A Synthetic Dataset and Three-Source Permission Architecture
comment: Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
summary:
Enterprise AI agents are typically granted static credential sets at configuration time, holding every tool the role might need for every task they perform. This persistent over-privilege expands the attack surface. We argue that capability scoping must follow a dynamic least-privilege principle and be treated as a prevention mechanism before a detection one. A credential that does not exist in an agent's context cannot be misused regardless of the agent's reasoning or evasion sophistication. We outline a three-source architecture instantiating this principle: role-based ceilings, a task-context classifier, and policy-derived combination prohibitions creating a layered proactive defense against LLM agent misalignment and misuse cases. The architecture supports both enforcing and observe-only deployment; the latter records agent permission requests inconsistent with task context, producing a behavioral signal usable in misalignment research.
  As a first step toward evaluating this architecture, we contribute a synthetic dataset of 600 enterprise task prompts grounded in a multi-department company policy, labeled with minimum required permissions across a 15-permission tool-based taxonomy that maps directly to deployable credentials or enforceable guardrails. The dataset is constructed via a two-pass pipeline that separates prompt generation from permission labeling to avoid circularity, and is validated against a 60-record/688 decisions human-reviewed sample (Cohen's $κ= 0.917$ pre-review and $κ= 0.967$ post-review). Iterating between dataset and policy reduced ceiling violations from 46 to 3, a 93% reduction. This shows that synthetic prompt generation can drive policy refinement when the two are developed together. The dataset, environment specification, and generation pipeline are released to support evaluation of dynamic scoping mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Enterprise AI agents suffer from static credential over-provisioning. The authors propose a dynamic least-privilege architecture using role ceilings, task classification, and policy-based combination prohibitions. They contribute a 600-prompt synthetic dataset labeled with minimal permissions across a 15-permission taxonomy, validated via human review (κ=0.967 post-review), demonstrating that co-developing policy and synthetic data reduces violations by 93%.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI agents are typically granted static, persistent credential sets encompassing all tools a role might ever need, creating a persistent over-privilege that expands the attack surface. The authors argue that capability scoping should follow a dynamic least-privilege principle as a proactive prevention mechanism: a credential absent from context cannot be misused, regardless of an agent's reasoning sophistication or evasion capability. Current approaches emphasize detection over prevention, leaving a gap for preemptive credential minimization.
AI.method: The paper proposes a three-source architecture: (1) role-based ceilings that cap maximum permissions per role, (2) a task-context classifier that dynamically determines permissions needed for a given task, and (3) policy-derived combination prohibitions that block risky permission pairings. The architecture supports both enforced and observe-only deployment modes. For evaluation, the authors construct a synthetic dataset of 600 enterprise task prompts grounded in a multi-department company policy, labeled with minimum required permissions across a 15-permission taxonomy. A two-pass pipeline separates prompt generation from permission labeling to prevent circularity. The dataset is validated against a 60-record, 688-decision human-reviewed sample using Cohen's κ.
AI.result: Human review validation achieved Cohen's κ=0.917 pre-review and κ=0.967 post-review, indicating strong inter-rater agreement. Iterating between dataset construction and policy refinement reduced ceiling violations from 46 to 3 — a 93% reduction — demonstrating that synthetic prompt generation can drive policy refinement when the two are co-developed.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic least-privilege credential scoping is a viable proactive defense against LLM agent misalignment and misuse. The three-source architecture, combined with co-development of synthetic task prompts and policy, yields measurable improvements in permission precision. The dataset, environment specification, and generation pipeline are publicly released to support further research on dynamic scoping mechanisms.

title: Variance-Reduced Q-Learning over Static and Time-Varying Networks
comment: Accepted at the 2026 American Control Conference (ACC 2026)
summary: We investigate a decentralized reinforcement learning problem involving multiple agents that interact with the same Markov Decision Process (MDP). The agents can exchange information over a network to collectively learn the optimal state-action value function. For this setting, we introduce a novel epoch-based distributed $Q$-learning algorithm called VRDQ, where within each epoch, agents locally estimate the Bellman optimality operator and diffuse information using a consensus-based protocol. For both static and time-varying networks, we establish high-probability finite-time convergence rates for VRDQ that enjoy linear speedups from collaboration. Crucially, we prove that such speedups in sample-complexity require only $\tilde{O}(1)$ communication, substantially improving upon the communication costs in prior work.

AI.tldr: VRDQ is a decentralized Q-learning algorithm that achieves linear speedups in sample complexity with only Õ(1) communication cost per agent, significantly improving over prior distributed RL methods.
AI.motivation: Decentralized multi-agent RL suffers from high communication overhead. The authors aim to design an algorithm that retains the linear speedup benefits of collaboration while drastically reducing communication costs compared to existing approaches.
AI.method: VRDQ is an epoch-based distributed Q-learning algorithm. Within each epoch, agents perform local estimates of the Bellman optimality operator and then diffuse information via a consensus-based protocol. The method handles both static and time-varying communication networks.
AI.result: High-probability finite-time convergence rates are established for both static and time-varying networks. The algorithm achieves linear speedups in sample complexity from multi-agent collaboration while requiring only Õ(1) communication.
AI.conclusion: VRDQ demonstrates that decentralized RL can achieve optimal collaboration speedups with near-constant communication overhead, representing a substantial improvement over prior work with higher communication costs.

title: Multi-Agent System-driven Digital Twins for predictive maintenance: architectures, technologies and open research challenges
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, paper submitted to Internet of Things Journal(Elsevier)
summary: Digital twins have emerged as a foundational technology within the context of Industry 4.0, offering a paradigm for the real-time virtual representation of physical systems. However, managing their growing complexity, particularly in distributed industrial environments, requires intelligent architectures capable of autonomous decision-making, dynamic adaptability, and inter-agent coordination. This systematic review explores the intersection between Multi-Agent Systems and Digital Twins, with a particular focus on predictive maintenance applications in resource-constrained contexts. Through a critical analysis of over 547 papers published in high-impact journals (IEEE Transactions, Nature, Elsevier, MDPI), we establish a taxonomy of existing hybrid architectures, identify persistent technological bottlenecks, and formulate three open research questions concerning: (i) the deployment of artificial intelligence on resource-constrained microcontrollers, (ii) distributed multi-node coordination via lightweight communication protocols, and (iii) the hierarchical orchestration of Digital Twins toward smart factory control integrating residual life estimation and explainable Artificial Intelligence. The results of this analysis reveal that, despite significant progress, no existing system offers an integrated embedded-distributed hierarchical solution that simultaneously meets the requirements of Industry 5.0.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 547+ papers examining hybrid Multi-Agent System–Digital Twin architectures for predictive maintenance, identifying that no existing integrated embedded-distributed hierarchical solution simultaneously meets Industry 5.0 requirements, and formulating three open research questions around resource-constrained AI, lightweight distributed coordination, and hierarchical orchestration with explainable AI.
AI.motivation: Digital Twins are foundational to Industry 4.0, but their growing complexity in distributed industrial environments demands intelligent architectures with autonomous decision-making, dynamic adaptability, and inter-agent coordination. The transition toward Industry 5.0 raises the bar further, and it is unclear whether any current solution integrates all necessary capabilities.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review, critically analyzing over 547 papers from high-impact venues (IEEE Transactions, Nature, Elsevier, MDPI). They established a taxonomy of existing MAS-DT hybrid architectures, identified technological bottlenecks, and synthesized findings into open research questions.
AI.result: The review reveals that despite significant progress, no existing system delivers an integrated embedded-distributed hierarchical solution satisfying all Industry 5.0 requirements. Three open research questions were formulated: (i) deploying AI on resource-constrained microcontrollers, (ii) distributed multi-node coordination via lightweight protocols, and (iii) hierarchical orchestration of DTs combining residual life estimation with explainable AI for smart factory control.
AI.conclusion: A critical gap exists in the literature: the absence of a unified embedded-distributed hierarchical MAS-DT architecture that simultaneously addresses resource constraints, lightweight coordination, and explainable AI-driven orchestration. Closing this gap is essential for realizing the transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 in predictive maintenance contexts.

title: Remedying Coarsening-Based GNN Training under Heterophily via Adaptive Complementary Enhancement
comment: Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, UAI 2026
summary: Coarsening-based training for graph neural networks (GNNs), i.e.\ training on coarsened graphs rather than the original large ones, has become a promising direction for scaling GNNs to massive graphs. However, prior work has been evaluated almost exclusively on \textit{homophilic} graphs, leaving the more challenging \textit{heterophilic} settings underexplored. We show, both empirically and theoretically, that existing coarsening-based training methods suffer significant performance degradation on heterophilic graphs due to inevitable loss of graph information during coarsening. To address this, we propose {\bf A}daptive {\bf C}omplementary {\bf E}nhancement, a plug-and-play, model-agnostic strategy that reintegrates the information discarded in coarsening: ACE learns a projector for re-constructing original node features and applies \textit{anisotropic structural regularization} to embed local heterophily. We further adopt \textit{homoscedastic uncertainty weighting} to adaptively balance the combined training objective of primary coarsened-graph training loss and full-graph auxiliary loss with augmented node features re-constructed by the heterophily-aware projector. Extensive experiments show that ACE drives consistent gains on heterophilic benchmarks while preserving competitive results on homophilic graphs with minimal computational overhead. Code is available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/vasile-paskardlgm/ACE.

AI.tldr: ACE is a plug-and-play strategy that addresses the performance degradation of coarsening-based GNN training on heterophilic graphs by adaptively reintegrating discarded structural and feature information through a heterophily-aware projector and homoscedastic uncertainty weighting.
AI.motivation: Existing coarsening-based GNN training methods are evaluated almost exclusively on homophilic graphs, but they suffer significant performance degradation on heterophilic graphs due to inevitable information loss during coarsening. This gap motivates a method that can handle both homophilic and heterophilic settings.
AI.method: The proposed ACE (Adaptive Complementary Enhancement) consists of three components: (1) a learnable projector that reconstructs original node features from coarsened representations, (2) anisotropic structural regularization to embed local heterophily patterns, and (3) homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to adaptively balance the primary coarsened-graph training loss with a full-graph auxiliary loss computed on the reconstructed features.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent accuracy gains on heterophilic benchmarks while maintaining competitive performance on homophilic graphs, all with minimal computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: ACE effectively bridges the gap between coarsening-based scalable GNN training and heterophilic graph learning, offering a model-agnostic, lightweight solution that preserves the efficiency benefits of coarsening while recovering critical structural information lost during the process.

title: TRW: TRACE-RealWorld---An Auditable Consistency Contract for World Models as Materialized Views
summary: TRACE-RealWorld addresses a core data-management problem: maintaining an actionable materialized view over a continuously changing physical world when reads of the base state are priced, delayed, heterogeneous, and fallible. Its data-management contributions are a commitment-level validity abstraction for materialized predictions; consequence-conditioned adaptive view maintenance; transaction-style, dependency-scoped compensation for commitments invalidated after authorization; and append-only provenance supporting exact replay. The work builds directly on materialized-view maintenance, adaptive stream synchronization, transaction recovery, sagas, data freshness, and provenance. The end-to-end Flood-SAR evaluation treats sensing as physical data acquisition and measures freshness, verification cost, stale reads, recovery scope, restoration failure, and replayability through six pre-registered questions with held-out seeds. The contribution is therefore not a new predictive model, but a consistency, recovery, and accountability contract for deploying learned world representations as operational data systems.

AI.tldr: TRACE-RealWorld introduces a data-management framework for maintaining actionable materialized views over dynamic physical environments where base-state reads are costly, delayed, heterogeneous, and fallible. It contributes a commitment-level validity abstraction, consequence-conditioned adaptive view maintenance, transaction-style dependency-scoped compensation for invalidated commitments, and append-only provenance for exact replay, evaluated via a Flood-SAR case study.
AI.motivation: Deploying learned world representations as operational data systems requires maintaining consistent, recoverable materialized views over continuously changing physical states. However, sensing (reading base state) is expensive, delayed, heterogeneous across sources, and prone to errors. Existing data-management techniques lack an integrated contract for consistency, recovery, and accountability under these real-world constraints.
AI.method: The paper proposes four core mechanisms: (1) a commitment-level validity abstraction for materialized predictions that bounds when a prediction can be acted upon; (2) consequence-conditioned adaptive view maintenance that adjusts refresh policies based on the downstream impact of staleness; (3) transaction-style, dependency-scoped compensation that repairs commitments invalidated after authorization using saga-like rollback semantics; and (4) append-only provenance enabling exact replay for auditability. These build on materialized-view maintenance, adaptive stream synchronization, transaction recovery, sagas, data freshness, and provenance literature.
AI.result: The Flood-SAR evaluation, treating sensing as physical data acquisition, demonstrates the framework's effectiveness across six pre-registered metrics with held-out seeds: freshness of views, verification cost, stale reads, recovery scope, restoration failure rates, and replayability. The system provides a measurable consistency, recovery, and accountability contract without introducing a new predictive model.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a novel predictive model but a principled data-management contract — encompassing consistency, recovery, and accountability — that enables learned world representations to function as reliable operational data systems in real-world, imperfect sensing environments.

title: MissHyper: Restoring Clinical Synchronicity in Missingness-Guided Hypergraph Forecasting
summary: Clinical irregular multivariate time series are shaped not only by physiological dynamics but also by the measurement process that determines when and what to observe. In event-centric models, however, co-timestamp structure can be flattened too early: measurements acquired at the same timestamp are embedded as isolated nodes, leaving local patient-state context unavailable until later message-passing layers. We study this pre-propagation representation bottleneck and address it by restoring co-timestamp context before message passing begins. We propose MissHyper, a missingness-guided hypergraph forecasting model with pre-propagation synchronicity restoration. MissHyper augments each event with a local support-density cue, aggregates co-timestamp records to recover patient-state context, and uses a missingness-guided gate to adaptively fuse node-specific evidence with the recovered context. Across PhysioNet 2012, MIMIC-III, and MIMIC-IV, MissHyper achieves consistent gains in multi-step forecasting and outperforms a strong hypergraph baseline. These results suggest that improving event initialization can benefit sparse clinical forecasting without requiring a redesigned downstream propagation architecture. Ablations indicate that snapshot restoration, adaptive fusion, and support-density encoding all contribute, pointing to event initialization as a critical design axis for sparse clinical forecasting.

AI.tldr: MissHyper is a missingness-guided hypergraph model that restores co-timestamp context before message passing, addressing a pre-propagation representation bottleneck in clinical irregular multivariate time series forecasting. It achieves consistent gains across three clinical datasets.
AI.motivation: In event-centric models for clinical irregular multivariate time series, measurements taken at the same timestamp are embedded as isolated nodes, flattening co-timestamp structure too early. This creates a "pre-propagation representation bottleneck" where local patient-state context is unavailable until later message-passing layers, degrading forecasting performance.
AI.method: MissHyper introduces three components: (1) a local support-density cue that augments each event with information about how many measurements co-occur, (2) aggregation of co-timestamp records to recover patient-state context before message passing, and (3) a missingness-guided gate that adaptively fuses node-specific evidence with the recovered contextual representation.
AI.result: MissHyper achieves consistent gains in multi-step forecasting across PhysioNet 2012, MIMIC-III, and MIMIC-IV, outperforming a strong hypergraph baseline. Ablations confirm that snapshot restoration, adaptive fusion, and support-density encoding all contribute positively.
AI.conclusion: Improving event initialization through synchronicity restoration is a critical and underexplored design axis for sparse clinical forecasting, and gains can be achieved without redesigning downstream propagation architectures.

title: Semiotic logical hexagon theory for LLM logical reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become powerful tools for language understanding and logical reasoning. However, they still make mistakes when a problem requires both understanding meaning and following logic. A key reason is that natural-language statements often carry implicit semantic relations before any formal reasoning begins. If these hidden meanings are not properly organized, the model may reach incorrect conclusions even when the subsequent reasoning process appears logically valid. Existing methods improve reasoning through decomposition, symbolic translation, external solvers, or self-verification, but pay comparatively less attention to the semantic structure on which reasoning depends. In this paper, we further investigate how semantic organization influences logical reasoning in LLMs. To this end, we propose HexLogicAgent, a framework that first organizes the meaning of natural-language statements and then guides logical reasoning through structured verification. In our investigation, we also make two observations. First, incomplete semantic representations, rather than deductive inference itself, are a major source of logical reasoning failures in LLMs. Second, explicitly modeling the complete structure of semantic opposition substantially delays the degradation of reasoning performance as logical complexity increases. Experiments on challenging logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that HexLogicAgent consistently improves reasoning reliability across multiple LLMs. The core idea is supported by a logical hexagon theory, which explains why a complete structure of opposing meanings is necessary for reliable reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HexLogicAgent, a framework that improves LLM logical reasoning by first organizing semantic structures (using logical hexagon theory) before performing deductive inference. It shows that incomplete semantic representation—not faulty deduction—is the primary cause of reasoning failures, and that explicitly modeling semantic opposition delays performance degradation as logical complexity increases.
AI.motivation: LLMs fail at tasks requiring both semantic understanding and logical reasoning because natural-language statements contain implicit semantic relations that, if unorganized, lead to incorrect conclusions even with valid deductive steps. Existing methods (decomposition, symbolic translation, external solvers, self-verification) focus on the reasoning mechanism rather than the underlying semantic structure.
AI.method: The authors propose HexLogicAgent, a framework grounded in logical hexagon theory. It operates in two stages: (1) organize the meaning of natural-language statements by explicitly constructing a complete structure of semantic oppositions, and (2) guide logical reasoning through structured verification based on this organized semantic representation.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) incomplete semantic representations, not deductive inference, are the major source of logical reasoning failures in LLMs; (2) explicitly modeling complete semantic opposition structures significantly delays reasoning performance degradation as logical complexity increases. HexLogicAgent consistently improves reasoning reliability across multiple LLMs on challenging logical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reliable logical reasoning in LLMs requires a complete structure of opposing meanings, as formalized by logical hexagon theory. The HexLogicAgent framework demonstrates that organizing semantic structure prior to reasoning is an effective and theoretically grounded approach to reducing reasoning errors.

title: RIS-Kernel: A Model-Agnostic Architecture for Long-Context LLM Inference via Sparse Attention
summary: Full self-attention in large language models scales as O(N^2), which limits long-context document analysis to 65,536 tokens and requires costly GPU clusters. The Reduced Interaction Sampling (RIS) inference engine addresses this constraint as a model-agnostic architecture. Without modifying weights, RIS reduces self-attention complexity to O(N log N) using sparse stochastic geometry that fits within commodity memory limits. We validate RIS on Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct across two regimes. In controlled evaluations at 32,768 tokens (where native dense attention serves as the upper bound), RIS-Stochastic at 1% density and 70 ensemble seeds achieves 75.00% accuracy, outperforming the native dense baseline (71.88%), while RIS-Stochastic at 5% density and 10 seeds matches it (71.88%). This demonstrates that sparse attention acts as a regularizer: low density (1%) over multiple seeds filters out sequence-level noise, whereas higher density (5%) reintroduces distractor noise. Under the tightest budget, RIS-Structural reaches 68.75% accuracy at 1% density with just 10 seeds, recovering 75% of the contextual gap relative to the zero-context floor (59.38%). At 65,536 tokens, where dense attention triggers out-of-memory faults, RIS yields retrieval gains of up to 14.06 percentage points over the zero-context floor (51.56%), which is confirmed as marginally significant under McNemar's paired test (p = 0.078 < 0.10). All evaluations run on commodity, unaccelerated CPU servers (16-128 GB of RAM), demonstrating that long-context LLM inference is feasible on standard academic hardware without GPU acceleration.

AI.tldr: RIS reduces self-attention complexity from O(N²) to O(N log N) via model-agnostic sparse stochastic geometry, enabling long-context LLM inference on commodity CPUs—matching or exceeding dense attention baselines at up to 65K tokens where dense attention OOMs.
AI.motivation: Full self-attention scales quadratically, limiting long-context document analysis to 65,536 tokens and requiring expensive GPU clusters. The authors seek to enable long-context inference on affordable, commodity CPU hardware without modifying model weights.
AI.method: The Reduced Interaction Sampling (RIS) inference engine employs sparse stochastic geometry to subsample the attention matrix. Two variants are tested: RIS-Stochastic (random sampling) and RIS-Structural (structure-informed sampling). Evaluations use Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct at 32,768 and 65,536 tokens, measuring accuracy against native dense attention and a zero-context floor, all on unaccelerated CPU servers with 16–128 GB RAM.
AI.result: At 32K tokens: RIS-Stochastic (1% density, 70 seeds) achieves 75.00% accuracy vs. dense baseline 71.88%; RIS-Stochastic (5% density, 10 seeds) matches at 71.88%; RIS-Structural (1% density, 10 seeds) reaches 68.75%, recovering 75% of the gap above the zero-context floor (59.38%). At 65K tokens, where dense attention OOMs, RIS yields gains up to 14.06 pp over the floor (51.56%), with marginal significance (McNemar's p = 0.078). Sparse attention acts as a regularizer: low density over many seeds filters noise; higher density reintroduces distractor noise.
AI.conclusion: RIS demonstrates that sparse stochastic attention can serve as an effective regularizer, matching or surpassing dense attention while eliminating OOM failures. Long-context LLM inference on commodity academic hardware without GPUs is viable, democratizing access to large-scale document analysis.

title: Learning as Reasoning Unfolds: Progressive Rollout Allocation for Efficient Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a highly effective framework for improving LLM reasoning, with methods such as GRPO among its most successful instantiations. However, GRPO relies on repeated generation of long chain-of-thought rollouts. Training time scales with the number of rollouts, a large fraction of which are uninformative. Thus, GRPO is computationally expensive and unstable. To mitigate this, existing approaches either generate a larger pool of rollouts and filter the most informative prompts, or leverage historical signals for filtering at later stages of training. These strategies offer modest performance gains, but slow down the overall process. To address this, we propose VarIance Guided Online Rollout allocation (VIGOR) which instead of allocating a fixed rollout budget per example, begins with a small number of rollouts for all examples in a batch and iteratively allocates additional rollouts to those with the highest group reward variance until a fixed total rollout budget is reached. Theoretically, we show that under RLVR, reward variance controls the gradient magnitude, and derive VIGOR's closed-form speedup ratio over GRPO, which grows with refinement rounds under Pareto-distributed reward variance. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks show that VIGOR reaches target accuracy with up to 2.3$\times$ fewer rollouts on math, reaches GRPO's final coding full pass rate with 1.49$\times$ fewer rollouts, and improves the coding average test pass rate by 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: VIGOR improves GRPO-style RLVR by dynamically allocating more rollout budget to examples with high reward variance, achieving up to 2.3× speedup in training while matching or exceeding baseline performance on math and coding tasks.
AI.motivation: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is computationally expensive because it wastes rollouts on uninformative examples with low reward variance. Existing filtering methods modestly improve efficiency but slow down the overall process. The authors aim to reduce wasted computation without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: VIGOR replaces fixed per-example rollout budgets with an iterative allocation scheme: it starts with a small number of rollouts for all examples in a batch, computes group reward variance for each, and iteratively assigns additional rollouts only to high-variance examples until a total budget is exhausted. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis showing reward variance controls gradient magnitude under RLVR, and derive a closed-form speedup ratio that grows with refinement rounds under Pareto-distributed reward variance.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning tasks, VIGOR reaches target accuracy with up to 2.3× fewer rollouts than GRPO. On coding tasks, it matches GRPO's final full pass rate with 1.49× fewer rollouts and improves the average test pass rate by 3.4 points.
AI.conclusion: VIGOR demonstrates that variance-guided online rollout allocation is an effective and theoretically grounded strategy for improving the sample efficiency and stability of RLVR methods like GRPO, enabling faster training without accuracy degradation.

title: Zero-Shot Mission-Level Evaluation for Aerial MLLM Agents
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are emerging as core reasoning modules for embodied agents, yet it remains unclear how well general-purpose models can solve long-horizon embodied tasks from a single high-level instruction. We introduce MissionBench, a benchmark for mission-level evaluation of MLLMs in aerial 3D environments. It comprises 120 missions across five simulated 3D environments and four task families. Agents must autonomously plan, navigate, and report outcomes using only egocentric observations and its action history, without aerial-specific fine-tuning. Across 22 open- and closed-source MLLMs, the strongest model succeeds on fewer than 35% of missions compared to 84.4% human performance, highlighting the difficulty of multi-step embodied tasks. Despite large variations between model families, we observe gains from scaling, indicating that larger general-purpose models possess stronger zero-shot embodied capabilities. Our analysis shows that mission-level competence requires coordinating multiple capabilities beyond spatial perception, including multi-step planning and adaptive reasoning. This motivates closed-loop evaluation and highlights both the promise and risk of scaling-driven improvements for embodied AI.

AI.tldr: MissionBench evaluates how well general-purpose Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) solve long-horizon embodied tasks in aerial 3D environments, revealing that even the strongest model succeeds on fewer than 35% of missions versus 84.4% human performance.
AI.motivation: MLLMs are increasingly used as reasoning modules for embodied agents, but their ability to handle long-horizon, mission-level tasks from a single high-level instruction — without domain-specific fine-tuning — remains poorly understood, especially in complex 3D environments like aerial navigation.
AI.method: The authors introduce MissionBench, a benchmark with 120 missions across five simulated 3D environments and four task families. Agents must autonomously plan, navigate, and report outcomes using only egocentric observations and action history. Twenty-two open- and closed-source MLLMs are evaluated in a zero-shot setting without aerial-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: The strongest MLLM achieves under 35% success rate compared to 84.4% for humans. However, scaling model size yields gains, suggesting larger general-purpose models possess stronger zero-shot embodied capabilities. Success requires coordinating multiple capabilities: spatial perception, multi-step planning, and adaptive reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Mission-level embodied competence demands more than spatial perception alone; it requires integrated multi-step planning and adaptive reasoning. The results motivate closed-loop evaluation paradigms and highlight both the promise and risk of scaling-driven improvements for embodied AI.

title: Multi-Agent Debate and Visual Information Extraction for SeePhys Pro: A 1st-Place Technical Report from ICML 2026 AI4Math Track 3 Challenge
summary: This technical report presents our approach to Challenge Track~3: SeePhys Pro at the 3rd AI for Math Workshop, where the task is to answer college-level physics questions whose statement and figure may be given partly or entirely as an image. Visual physics problems become substantially harder for large language models when the decisive information resides in a figure rather than in the text, and this modality gap widens as more of the problem migrates into the image. We address the task with a two-stage framework: a visual information extraction stage that re-expresses figure content as solver-readable text to close the modality gap, and a reasoning stage that orchestrates three heterogeneous solvers through multi-agent debate. Our analysis yields two findings: the gain from orchestration comes from reliable answer selection rather than from additional debate, and the value of a figure aid scales with how much of the problem is locked inside the image. The resulting pipeline improves overall accuracy over a single-agent baseline from 0.643 to 0.802 on the public split, and won 1st place on both the public and the private leaderboard (private overall 0.743).

AI.tldr: A two-stage framework combining visual information extraction with multi-agent orchestration achieves 1st place in a physics problem-solving competition, improving accuracy from 0.643 to 0.802 by bridging the text-image modality gap.
AI.motivation: Large language models struggle with visual physics problems where critical information is embedded in figures rather than text. As more problem content shifts to images, the modality gap grows, degrading model performance. The work aims to close this gap and improve reasoning on multimodal physics questions.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) Visual information extraction that converts figure content into solver-readable text to bridge the modality gap; (2) A reasoning stage employing three heterogeneous solvers orchestrated through multi-agent debate, where the gain derives primarily from reliable answer selection rather than debate itself.
AI.result: The pipeline improved overall accuracy from 0.643 (single-agent baseline) to 0.802 on the public split. The approach won 1st place on both public and private leaderboards, with a private overall accuracy of 0.743.
AI.conclusion: Closing the modality gap via figure-to-text extraction is critical for visual physics problems. Multi-agent orchestration aids performance mainly through improved answer selection. The benefit of figure extraction scales with the proportion of problem information contained in images.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Mode
summary: We present Nanbeige4.2-3B, a compact general agentic model with 3B non-embedding parameters. It delivers strong performance across code-agent, office-agent, and complex tool-use tasks while maintaining highly competitive reasoning capabilities in mathematics, coding, and science. Nanbeige4.2-3B is pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens with a Looped Transformer that reuses the layer stack to increase capacity without adding parameters. For SFT data and trajectory construction, we expand the diversity of executable environments, task assets, and agentic scaffolds through real-world deployment and large-scale synthesis. Our RL pipeline applies mixed-mode RLHF over Think and Non-Think responses to improve overall model quality and reduce failure cases, length-controlled reasoning RL to balance accuracy and reasoning efficiency, and agentic RL with outcome and process rewards to stabilize long-horizon training. Extensive evaluations show that Nanbeige4.2-3B outperforms larger models, including Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B, across diverse agentic benchmarks while remaining competitive on reasoning and alignment tasks. Performance with OpenClaw further supports its use as a compact local personal assistant.

AI.tldr: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a compact 3B-parameter agentic model that outperforms larger models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) on agentic benchmarks while maintaining strong reasoning, using a Looped Transformer architecture, diverse synthetic SFT data, and a multi-component RL pipeline.
AI.motivation: To develop a compact yet powerful general agentic model that can handle code-agent, office-agent, and complex tool-use tasks while remaining competitive on reasoning benchmarks, serving as an efficient local personal assistant without requiring large model sizes.
AI.method: (1) Looped Transformer architecture that reuses layer stacks to increase capacity without adding parameters, pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens. (2) SFT with diverse executable environments, task assets, and agentic scaffolds from real-world deployment and large-scale synthesis. (3) RL pipeline combining: mixed-mode RLHF over Think/Non-Think responses; length-controlled reasoning RL to balance accuracy and efficiency; and agentic RL with outcome and process rewards for stable long-horizon training.
AI.result: Nanbeige4.2-3B outperforms larger models including Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B on diverse agentic benchmarks while remaining competitive on reasoning and alignment tasks. Performance with OpenClaw supports its viability as a compact local personal assistant.
AI.conclusion: A compact 3B model, when equipped with parameter-efficient architecture (Looped Transformer), diverse agentic SFT data, and a carefully designed multi-component RL pipeline, can surpass much larger models on agentic tasks, enabling practical deployment as a local personal assistant.

title: MA-DAR: Manifold-Aligned Dynamic Adaptive Routing for Continual Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Continual temporal knowledge graph (TKG) reasoning aims to continuously incorporate newly emerging facts while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Replay-based continual learning has achieved promising performance by revisiting historical representations. However, existing methods primarily focus on what to replay, while largely overlooking how replayed representations should be integrated with current ones. Such direct integration often gives rise to two critical forms of representation conflict: \textit{norm domination} and \textit{semantic blurring}, ultimately degrading continual reasoning performance. To address these challenges, we propose MA-DAR (Manifold-Aligned Dynamic Adaptive Routing), a lightweight plug-and-play framework for replay representation fusion. MA-DAR first aligns replayed and current representations onto a shared manifold to alleviate distribution discrepancies. It then employs a dynamic gating mechanism to learn dimension-wise fusion weights, adaptively determining the contribution of replayed and current representations to the fused representation. Furthermore, a polarization regularizer encourages more decisive routing behaviors by discouraging ambiguous gating decisions, resulting in more stable and effective knowledge integration. Extensive experiments on four public continual TKG benchmarks demonstrate that MA-DAR consistently improves the performance of representative TKG encoders while remaining effective under different replay settings. Comprehensive ablation studies and visualization analyses further verify the effectiveness of manifold alignment and dynamic adaptive routing in mitigating representation conflicts and improving continual reasoning.

AI.tldr: MA-DAR is a lightweight plug-and-play framework for replay-based continual TKG reasoning that aligns replayed and current representations onto a shared manifold, then uses dynamic gating with polarization regularization to fuse them adaptively, mitigating representation conflicts (norm domination and semantic blurring).
AI.motivation: Existing replay-based continual TKG methods focus on what to replay but neglect how to integrate replayed representations with current ones, leading to two representation conflicts: norm domination (discrepancy in vector magnitudes) and semantic blurring (loss of distinct semantics). These conflicts degrade continual reasoning performance.
AI.method: MA-DAR proposes three components: (1) Manifold Alignment, which projects replayed and current representations onto a shared manifold to reduce distribution discrepancies; (2) Dynamic Adaptive Routing, a dimension-wise gating mechanism that learns fusion weights to adaptively combine representations; (3) Polarization Regularizer, which discourages ambiguous gating decisions to promote decisive routing behavior.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four public continual TKG benchmarks show MA-DAR consistently improves representative TKG encoders and remains effective across different replay settings. Ablation studies and visualizations confirm that manifold alignment and dynamic adaptive routing effectively mitigate representation conflicts.
AI.conclusion: MA-DAR effectively addresses representation conflicts in continual TKG reasoning through manifold alignment and dynamic adaptive routing with polarization regularization, serving as a lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement for existing replay-based methods.

title: Reasoning Denoiser: Denoising Reasoning Traces for Hallucination Detection in Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate long reasoning traces before producing final answers. While these traces may contain useful signals for hallucination detection, harnessing them is non-trivial because long trajectories often include noisy steps that obscure the cues relevant to truthfulness assessment. In this paper, we identify two prevalent forms of reasoning noises, i.e., irrelevant steps and repetitive steps, and show that both substantially degrade hallucination detection performance. Existing confidence-based scores and naive embedding-based filtering fail to reliably separate noisy from informative steps. To address this challenge, we propose REDE, a novel learning framework for denoising reasoning traces for hallucination detection. Specifically, REDE leverages final-answer attention as an automatic supervision signal to shape the step-level representation space, yielding refined embeddings in which noisy steps can be reliably identified and filtered. REDE can be readily plugged into diverse hallucination detectors by operating on the filtered reasoning trajectory after removing noisy steps. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning benchmarks show that REDE consistently improves detection performance over competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: REDE is a learning framework that denoises long reasoning traces from large reasoning models (LRMs) to improve hallucination detection. It uses final-answer attention as a supervision signal to refine step-level embeddings, enabling reliable identification and removal of two key noise types—irrelevant and repetitive steps—before feeding the cleaned trajectory into downstream detectors.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models produce extended reasoning traces that could aid hallucination detection, but these traces are contaminated by noisy steps (irrelevant and repetitive) that severely degrade detection performance. Existing confidence-based and naive embedding-based filtering methods fail to reliably separate noisy from informative steps.
AI.method: REDE (REasoning DEnoising) uses final-answer attention as an automatic supervision signal to learn a step-level representation space. In this space, noisy steps are pushed apart from informative ones, enabling reliable filtering. The denoised trajectory is then passed to any downstream hallucination detector.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that REDE consistently improves hallucination detection performance over competitive baselines when plugged into diverse detectors.
AI.conclusion: Denoising reasoning traces by removing irrelevant and repetitive steps is critical for effective hallucination detection in LRMs, and REDE provides an effective, plug-and-play solution that leverages final-answer attention as a self-supervision signal.

title: Teaching LLMs to Self-Evolve: Cultivating Core Meta-Skills with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Test-time scaling through iterative self-evolution with environment feedback, as demonstrated by AlphaEvolve, shows remarkable performance gains. We hypothesize that the success of such evolution frameworks hinges on meta-skills, such as self-reflection with environment feedback, that enable effective multi-round refinement, yet are largely neglected by traditional post-training. To bridge this gap, we present MetaEvolve, a framework designed to develop these meta-skills via a data synthesis pipeline, evolution-aware reinforcement learning (RL), and inference-time evolutionary search. Concretely, we ground MetaEvolve in coding, where program execution provides natural, continuous reward signals beyond binary correctness. Building on these signals, we synthesize evolution trajectories as training data, each containing a current program, its fitness score (combining correctness and efficiency), and a history of prior attempts, and train the model via RL with verifiable rewards derived from test case execution. By training on large-scale code data, we aim to inspire generalizable domain-agnostic meta-skills that can transfer broadly to open-ended problems where such rich training signals are scarce. Across seven coding benchmarks, MetaEvolve outperforms the strongest baseline by 10.01% absolute on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks. On open-ended algorithm optimization problems entirely outside the training domain, it further achieves a 46.9% relative improvement. These results demonstrate that explicitly cultivating self-evolution meta-skills offers a principled path toward more capable and autonomously self-evolving AI.

AI.tldr: MetaEvolve trains models to develop meta-skills for iterative self-evolution using environment feedback. By synthesizing evolution trajectories from code execution signals and applying evolution-aware RL, the model learns to self-reflect and improve across multiple rounds. It achieves substantial gains: +10.01% on in-distribution coding tasks, +24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks, and +46.9% relative improvement on open-ended algorithm optimization, demonstrating transferable self-evolution capabilities.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling via iterative self-evolution (e.g., AlphaEvolve) yields strong performance, but traditional post-training neglects the meta-skills (like self-reflection with environment feedback) that enable effective multi-round refinement. The authors aim to explicitly cultivate these meta-skills so models can autonomously improve in open-ended domains where rich training signals are scarce.
AI.method: MetaEvolve operates in three stages: (1) a data synthesis pipeline that generates evolution trajectories from code data, each containing a current program, a fitness score (correctness + efficiency), and prior attempt history; (2) evolution-aware reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards from test-case execution to train the model on these trajectories; and (3) inference-time evolutionary search. The framework is grounded in coding because program execution provides natural, continuous reward signals beyond binary correctness.
AI.result: On seven coding benchmarks, MetaEvolve outperforms the strongest baseline by 10.01% absolute on in-distribution tasks and 24.12% on out-of-distribution tasks. On open-ended algorithm optimization problems entirely outside the training domain, it achieves a 46.9% relative improvement.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly cultivating self-evolution meta-skills provides a principled path toward more capable, autonomously self-evolving AI. The strong transfer performance to out-of-distribution and open-ended problems suggests the learned meta-skills are domain-agnostic and broadly applicable beyond the training domain.

title: Industrial Tokenization for LLM-Based Health Intelligence: A Federated Architecture for Industrial Evidence Integration
summary: Industrial health management increasingly relies on heterogeneous information sources, including condition monitoring systems, supervisory control and data acquisition systems, maintenance records, inspection results, and prognostic models. Although large language models provide new opportunities for cross-source reasoning, industrial data and analytical outputs differ substantially in structure, temporal resolution, physical meaning, and reliability. Directly integrating such heterogeneous information into a monolithic model may reduce interpretability, traceability, and adaptability to equipment and data changes. This paper introduces Industrial Tokenization, a conceptual interface for transforming source-specific analytical outputs into structured and machine-interpretable units of industrial evidence, termed Industrial Tokens. Unlike numerical tokens used to encode raw time-series data, Industrial Tokens represent domain-grounded evidence together with source, temporal scope, operating context, analytical meaning, quality or confidence information, and provenance. Based on this concept, a federated industrial architecture is proposed, where heterogeneous analytical subsystems retain autonomy while exposing standardized Industrial Tokens to a central reasoning layer. As an initial implementation, this study presents an end-to-end DiagnosisToken pathway based on vibration-diagnostic outputs, rule-based event aggregation, structured textual token generation, and LLM-based interpretation. Other Industrial Tokens, including SCADA-based condition-monitoring tokens, maintenance tokens, and prognostic tokens, are reserved as future extensions. The proposed framework positions Industrial Tokenization as a semantic interface between domain-specific industrial intelligence and LLM- or agent-based reasoning, rather than another method for encoding raw industrial data.

AI.tldr: Proposes "Industrial Tokenization," a semantic interface that transforms heterogeneous industrial outputs (vibration diagnostics, SCADA, maintenance, prognostics) into structured, provenance-rich evidence units (Industrial Tokens) for LLM-based reasoning within a federated architecture, demonstrated via a vibration DiagnosisToken pathway.
AI.motivation: Industrial health management relies on heterogeneous information sources that differ in structure, temporal resolution, physical meaning, and reliability. Directly integrating such diverse data into monolithic LLMs reduces interpretability, traceability, and adaptability. A principled interface is needed to bridge domain-specific analytical outputs with LLM reasoning without sacrificing these qualities.
AI.method: Introduces the concept of "Industrial Tokens" — structured, machine-interpretable units encapsulating domain-grounded evidence along with source, temporal scope, operating context, analytical meaning, confidence/quality, and provenance metadata. Proposes a federated architecture where heterogeneous analytical subsystems retain autonomy and expose standardized Industrial Tokens to a central reasoning layer. An initial end-to-end DiagnosisToken pathway is implemented using vibration-diagnostic outputs, rule-based event aggregation, structured textual token generation, and LLM-based interpretation.
AI.result: An end-to-end DiagnosisToken pathway is presented as an initial implementation. Other token types (SCADA condition-monitoring, maintenance, prognostic tokens) are reserved for future work. The framework is positioned as a semantic interface rather than another raw-data encoding method.
AI.conclusion: Industrial Tokenization serves as a semantic bridge between domain-specific industrial intelligence and LLM/agent-based reasoning, preserving interpretability, traceability, and subsystem autonomy in federated industrial health management. The approach is conceptual with an initial demonstration, requiring further extension to additional token types.

title: On the Convergence of Stochastic Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) optimizes $J(B,A)=\mathcal L(W_\mathrm{base}+sBA)$ over two adapters $B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}$ that form a low-rank update to a frozen pretrained weight matrix $W_\mathrm{base} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$. The prior analysis shows LoRA-GD takes $\exp\{\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})\}$ oracle calls to find an $ε$-stationary point such that $\|\nabla J(B,A)\|\leq ε$ in the deterministic setting. We sharpen the analysis and show that $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ full-gradient evaluations suffice for the same first-order criterion. We further study stochastic LoRA under unbiased gradient estimates and finite variance. We propose LoRA-NSGDM, which finds an $ε$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-8})$ stochastic oracle complexity. Under the additional mean-square smoothness condition, we use variance reduction strategy and propose LoRA-STORM, which improves the stochastic oracle complexity to $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-6})$.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a sharper convergence analysis for deterministic LoRA gradient descent (from exponential to O(ε⁻⁴)), and proposes two stochastic LoRA algorithms—LoRA-NSGDM (O(ε⁻⁸)) and LoRA-STORM (O(ε⁻⁶) with variance reduction)—for finding ε-stationary points.
AI.motivation: Prior analysis of LoRA-GD required exponentially many oracle calls (exp{O(ε⁻²)}) to reach an ε-stationary point, which is impractical. The authors aim to derive tighter, polynomial-time convergence guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic LoRA optimization.
AI.method: For deterministic LoRA, the authors sharpen existing analysis to achieve O(ε⁻⁴) full-gradient complexity. For stochastic LoRA (unbiased gradients, finite variance), they propose LoRA-NSGDM (normalized stochastic gradient descent with momentum). Under an additional mean-square smoothness condition, they apply variance reduction (STORM-style) to design LoRA-STORM, improving complexity.
AI.result: Deterministic LoRA-GD: O(ε⁻⁴) oracle calls. Stochastic LoRA-NSGDM: O(ε⁻⁸) oracle complexity. LoRA-STORM with variance reduction: O(ε⁻⁶) oracle complexity. All bounds are for achieving ‖∇J(B,A)‖ ≤ ε.
AI.conclusion: The paper significantly improves the theoretical convergence guarantees for LoRA optimization, making polynomial-time convergence achievable in both deterministic and stochastic settings, and demonstrates that variance reduction further reduces stochastic oracle complexity.

title: Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents
summary: AI agents encounter learning opportunities in every episode they run, and discard nearly all of them: the underlying models are frozen at deployment, so an agent that resolves a difficult request today starts from zero when it recurs tomorrow. Yet ordinary operation already produces feedback, in the form of outcome verdicts and after-the-fact corrections. We show that this feedback is a sufficient signal for continual learning when the frozen model is paired with an external memory that distils each episode into retrievable natural-language rules. On the banking domain of $τ$-bench, against a static-RAG control retrieving over the complete policy corpus, learning from the one-bit outcome verdict lifts single-trial success to 1.6$\times$ the baseline, and learning from corrections to 2.6$\times$, converting 22 of the 84 tasks the baseline never solves. The result spans the deployment spectrum, measured on Mistral Large, an open-weights model that organisations with data sovereignty requirements can self-host, and replicated on a frontier model, Claude Sonnet 5. The accumulated memory also transfers: each model, reading the store built by the other, rises above its own no-memory baseline. The harness, protocol, and data are released.

AI.tldr: AI agents deployed with frozen models discard valuable learning signals from daily operation. The authors show that pairing a frozen LLM with an external memory that distills episode outcomes into retrievable natural-language rules enables continual learning, yielding up to 2.6× improvement over a static RAG baseline on the τ-bench banking domain, with rules transferring across models.
AI.motivation: Deployed AI agents fail to learn from experience because their underlying models are frozen at deployment. Every episode generates implicit feedback—outcome verdicts (success/failure) and corrections—but this signal is discarded. The authors aim to harness this already-available feedback for continual improvement without requiring model retraining.
AI.method: The approach pairs a frozen LLM with an external, persistent memory store. After each episode, the system distills the experience into natural-language rules based on the outcome verdict (1-bit success/failure signal) or explicit corrections. These rules are stored and retrieved at inference time for future episodes. This is benchmarked against a static RAG baseline that retrieves over the complete policy corpus, using the τ-bench banking domain. Experiments span Mistral Large (open-weights, self-hostable) and Claude Sonnet 5 (frontier model).
AI.result: Using only the 1-bit outcome verdict, single-trial success rate reached 1.6× the static-RAG baseline. With corrections, success rose to 2.6×, solving 22 of the 84 tasks that the baseline never solved. The accumulated memory transferred across models: each model, reading the memory store built by the other, outperformed its own no-memory baseline.
AI.conclusion: Episode-level feedback already produced during normal agent operation is sufficient for effective continual learning when distilled into retrievable natural-language rules stored in external memory. This lightweight, training-free approach works across both open-weights and frontier models, and the distilled knowledge transfers between models, suggesting a general mechanism for agents that improve with use.

title: From Perturbation Correction to Geometry-Aware Sampling: Sharpness-Guided Equilibrium Sampling for Balanced Flat Minima in Long-Tailed Learning
summary: Long-tailed learning couples two sources of poor generalization: head classes dominate training exposure, while under-represented classes often converge to sharper regions of the loss landscape. Conventional re-sampling addresses the former without considering geometry, whereas existing long-tailed sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) methods modify losses or perturbations only after biased mini-batches have been drawn. We introduce Sharpness-Guided Equilibrium Sampling (SGS), which treats the sampling distribution as an active control variable for optimization geometry. SGS dynamically adjusts subsequent mini-batches by increasing the sampling probability of less frequently sampled classes while suppressing classes with large SAM-induced loss changes, using only cumulative class counts and EMA sharpness estimates obtained from the standard SAM update, without class-wise perturbations or additional backward passes. We characterize this sampling process through a continuous-time stochastic differential equation and a sampling-dependent PAC-Bayes analysis, explaining how frequency-sharpness feedback can move training toward a more balanced flatness profile. On CIFAR-100 LT with an imbalance ratio of 100, SGS-SAM improves Focal-SAM by 10.85 points in tail accuracy and 3.56 points overall. On ImageNet-LT, it improves ImbSAM by 6.59 points on tail classes and 1.20 points overall. Its training time is only $1.02\times$ that of vanilla SAM. Beyond these gains, SGS establishes a sampling-side route to loss-landscape control, suggesting that future long-tailed methods can jointly regulate data exposure and optimization geometry rather than treating either as fixed.

AI.tldr: SGS dynamically adjusts mini-batch sampling using class frequency and SAM sharpness feedback to flatten the loss landscape for tail classes, achieving significant accuracy gains on long-tailed benchmarks with negligible overhead over vanilla SAM.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed learning suffers from both biased data exposure (head classes dominate) and poor optimization geometry (tail classes converge to sharper minima). Existing SAM-based methods only modify losses or perturbations post hoc on biased mini-batches, rather than actively controlling the sampling distribution to shape optimization geometry.
AI.method: Sharpness-Guided Equilibrium Sampling (SGS) treats the sampling distribution as a control variable.
