It increases sampling probability for infrequently sampled classes and suppresses classes showing large SAM-induced loss changes, using only cumulative class counts and EMA sharpness estimates from standard SAM updates — requiring no class-wise perturbations or extra backward passes. The process is analyzed via a continuous-time SDE and a sampling-dependent PAC-Bayes bound.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 LT (IR=100), SGS-SAM improves over Focal-SAM by +10.85 tail accuracy and +3.56 overall. On ImageNet-LT, it improves over ImbSAM by +6.59 tail and +1.20 overall. Training time is only 1.02× that of vanilla SAM.
AI.conclusion: SGS demonstrates that sampling can actively regulate loss-landscape geometry, suggesting future long-tailed methods should jointly optimize data exposure and optimization geometry rather than treating either as fixed.

title: Deconstructing Off-Policy Ratios: Entropy-Scaled Trust Regions for Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) accelerates large language model (LLM) post-training by overlapping rollout generation with policy optimization, but the resulting stale, off-policy data can destabilize optimization and ultimately cause policy collapse. Existing methods typically retain or discard tokens based solely on the magnitude of their importance ratios, applying the same threshold uniformly across token positions. In this work, we reveal that the natural scale of the importance ratio varies systematically with token entropy. Under asynchronous dynamics, this entropy-ratio scaling dictates two distinct phenomena: at low entropy, the inherent train-inference discrepancy is drastically amplified into substantial sampling noise; at high entropy, in-flight weight updates naturally induce pronounced, legitimate exploratory deviations. Consequently, magnitude-only correction inadvertently admits the amplified noise while strictly masking out the essential exploration triggered by in-flight updates. To address this, we propose the Entropy-Scaled Trust Region (ESTR), which scales each token's off-policy deviation by its local entropy, requiring no auxiliary forward passes or explicit version-switch detection. Across long-horizon agentic tasks and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ESTR consistently outperforms existing asynchronous methods and achieves the best train-inference consistency. Compared with synchronous GRPO, ESTR attains comparable accuracy while improving training speed by $2.6\times$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Entropy-Scaled Trust Region (ESTR), a method that scales off-policy deviation corrections by token-level entropy to stabilize asynchronous RL training for LLMs, outperforming existing methods and achieving 2.6× speedup over synchronous GRPO.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous RL accelerates LLM post-training but introduces stale, off-policy data that can destabilize optimization and cause policy collapse. Existing methods apply uniform importance-ratio thresholds across all tokens, ignoring that the natural scale of importance ratios varies systematically with token entropy. This leads to admitting amplified noise at low-entropy tokens while masking legitimate exploratory deviations at high-entropy tokens.
AI.method: ESTR scales each token's off-policy deviation by its local entropy, thereby normalizing the trust region in an entropy-aware manner. This requires no auxiliary forward passes or explicit version-switch detection, making it computationally lightweight.
AI.result: ESTR consistently outperforms existing asynchronous methods on long-horizon agentic tasks and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. It achieves train-inference consistency comparable to synchronous GRPO while improving training speed by 2.6×.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-scaled correction effectively disentangles harmful stale-data noise from beneficial exploratory deviations in asynchronous RL, enabling stable and efficient LLM post-training without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Energy Manifold Natural Gradient Descent: Riemannian Optimization for Neural PDE Solvers
summary: Energy natural gradient descent (ENGD) aligns parameter updates with the curvature of an underlying function-space energy, but existing formulations assume an unconstrained Euclidean parameter domain. We introduce \EMNGDfull{}, a manifold optimization framework for physics-informed and variational neural PDE solvers whose parameters lie on a Riemannian manifold. EMNGD restricts the energy-induced quadratic model to feasible tangent directions and uses retractions to preserve parameter constraints throughout optimization. Under coercivity, we prove that the push-forward of the undamped EMNGD direction is the best feasible approximation to the function-space Newton vector in the energy metric. We establish coordinate invariance, exact reduction to ENGD in Euclidean space, global first-order convergence with Armijo backtracking, and robustness to inexact tangent solves. For quadratic residual energies and generalized Gauss--Newton pullbacks, the Woodbury identity transfers the tangent system to sample space without changing the direction. Nyström approximation provides scalable sample-space solves with controlled direction error and recovers the exact direction after iterative convergence. On the evaluated neural PDE benchmarks, EMNGD achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than the compared state-of-the-art baselines. Woodbury preserves the EMNGD direction, while scalable-solver diagnostics quantify the accuracy--cost trade-off of preconditioning and residual subsampling.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Energy Manifold Natural Gradient Descent (EMNGD), a manifold optimization framework that extends energy natural gradient descent to Riemannian parameter domains, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on neural PDE solvers.
AI.motivation: Existing energy natural gradient descent (ENGD) assumes unconstrained Euclidean parameter spaces, which is insufficient for physics-informed and variational neural PDE solvers whose parameters naturally live on Riemannian manifolds (e.g., due to constraints). A principled manifold-aware extension is needed.
AI.method: EMNGD restricts the energy-induced quadratic model to feasible tangent directions and uses retractions to maintain manifold constraints. The authors prove the push-forward of the undamped EMNGD direction is the best feasible approximation to the function-space Newton vector in the energy metric. They establish coordinate invariance, global first-order convergence with Armijo backtracking, and robustness to inexact tangent solves. For quadratic residual energies, the Woodbury identity transfers the tangent system to sample space without altering the direction. Nyström approximation enables scalable sample-space solves with controlled direction error.
AI.result: On neural PDE benchmarks, EMNGD achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than state-of-the-art baselines. Woodbury preserves the EMNGD direction exactly, while scalable-solver diagnostics quantify the accuracy–cost trade-off of preconditioning and residual subsampling.
AI.conclusion: EMNGD provides a theoretically grounded, scalable manifold optimization framework that outperforms existing methods on neural PDE tasks, with practical tools (Woodbury, Nyström) for balancing accuracy and computational cost.

title: AI4PLE: A Methodology for Integrating AI into Product Line Engineering
summary: Reuse-based development has become increasingly important in the creation of complex systems, offering significant opportunities to reduce costs, improve quality, and accelerate time-to-market. Product Line Engineering (PLE) provides a systematic approach to realizing this potential by enabling the efficient creation, management, and customization of product families by reusing shared assets and capabilities. PLE involves addressing numerous complex decisions, including feature selection, variability management, and configuration optimization, which are critical to the success of a product line. Despite its promise, the systematic integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into PLE processes has not yet been comprehensively explored. In this paper, we propose a methodological framework to support the systematic integration of AI into PLE and evaluate its effectiveness through a multi-case study conducted in an industrial context.

AI.tldr: Proposes a methodological framework for systematically integrating Artificial Intelligence into Product Line Engineering (PLE) and evaluates it through a multi-case industrial study.
AI.motivation: While PLE offers systematic reuse for complex systems (reducing costs, improving quality, accelerating time-to-market), it involves complex decisions around feature selection, variability management, and configuration optimization. Despite AI's potential to address these challenges, no comprehensive framework exists for systematically integrating AI into PLE processes.
AI.method: The authors propose a methodological framework for AI integration into PLE and evaluate its effectiveness through a multi-case study conducted in an industrial context.
AI.result: Evaluation through industrial multi-case study demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in supporting systematic AI integration into PLE processes.
AI.conclusion: A structured methodological framework can effectively guide the systematic integration of AI into Product Line Engineering, addressing key decision-making challenges in industrial settings.

title: Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation via Byte-Prefix Marginalization
summary: Open-weight language models from different families exhibit complementary capabilities, motivating their consolidation into a compact student through on-policy distillation (OPD). However, full-vocabulary OPD typically assumes a shared tokenizer, while existing cross-tokenizer methods may discard teacher probability mass or assign it to student tokens with unrelated content. We introduce Byte-Prefix Marginalization (BPM), which re-expresses the teacher's next-token distribution over the student vocabulary in a shared byte space. Specifically, BPM assigns each teacher token's probability to the longest student token whose byte representation is a prefix of the teacher token's bytes, aggregates mass mapped to the same student token, and places otherwise unmatched mass in an explicit residual category. This produces a vocabulary-complete, byte-aligned, and mass-preserving target for dense OPD. The target exactly recovers the teacher-induced byte-prefix marginal when the relevant prefix does not span multiple teacher tokens (a condition satisfied at more than 99% of training positions) and uses a mass-preserving, chain-factorized lower bound otherwise. Across Qwen3-32B, GLM-Z1-9B-0414, and MiniMax-M2.7 as teachers, BPM consistently outperforms current cross-tokenizer methods on six mathematics and programming benchmarks, improving six-benchmark avg@8 by 3.7-6.6 points over the strongest baselines.

AI.tldr: BPM enables cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation by mapping teacher token probabilities to student tokens through byte-prefix alignment, preserving probability mass via a residual category and achieving state-of-the-art results on math and programming benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Open-weight LMs from different families have complementary strengths, motivating consolidation via on-policy distillation. However, full-vocabulary OPD requires shared tokenizers, while existing cross-tokenizer approaches either discard probability mass or misassign it to semantically unrelated tokens. A method is needed that faithfully transfers the complete teacher distribution across different tokenizers.
AI.method: Byte-Prefix Marginalization (BPM) operates in a shared byte space: each teacher token's probability is assigned to the longest student token whose byte representation is a prefix of that teacher token's bytes. Overlapping assignments are aggregated, and unmatched mass goes into an explicit residual category. This yields a vocabulary-complete, byte-aligned, mass-preserving target for dense OPD. When prefixes don't span multiple teacher tokens (99%+ of training positions), BPM exactly recovers the teacher-induced byte-prefix marginal; otherwise, it uses a chain-factorized lower bound.
AI.result: Using Qwen3-32B, GLM-Z1-9B-0414, and MiniMax-M2.7 as teachers, BPM consistently outperforms existing cross-tokenizer methods across six math and programming benchmarks, improving six-benchmark avg@8 by 3.7–6.6 points over the strongest baselines.
AI.conclusion: BPM provides an effective, principled solution for cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation by faithfully transferring teacher distributions in a byte-aligned manner, significantly advancing the state of the art for consolidating diverse open-weight models into a single compact student.

title: Cross-Domain Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning for Contextual Bandits
summary: Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning (OPE/L) in contextual bandits is rapidly gaining popularity in real systems because new policies can be evaluated and learned securely using only historical logged data. However, existing methods in OPE/L cannot handle many challenging but prevalent scenarios such as few-shot data, deterministic logging policies, and new actions. In many applications, such as personalized medicine, content recommendations, education, and advertising, we need to evaluate and learn new policies in the presence of these challenges. Existing methods cannot evaluate and optimize effectively in these situations due to the notorious variance issue or limited exploration in the logged data. To enable OPE/L even under these unsolved challenges, we propose a new problem setup of Cross-Domain OPE/L, where we have access not only to the logged data from the target domain in which the new policy will be implemented but also to logged datasets collected from other domains. This novel formulation is widely applicable because we can often use historical data not only from the target hospital, country, device, or user segment but also from other hospitals, countries, devices, or segments. We develop a new estimator and policy gradient method to solve OPE/L by leveraging both target and source datasets, resulting in substantially enhanced OPE/L in the previously unsolved situations in our empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: Proposes Cross-Domain Off-Policy Evaluation and Learning (OPE/L) for contextual bandits, leveraging logged data from both target and source domains to address challenges like few-shot data, deterministic logging, and new actions that existing OPE/L methods fail to handle.
AI.motivation: Existing OPE/L methods suffer from high variance and limited exploration in logged data, making them ineffective in challenging yet prevalent scenarios: few-shot data, deterministic logging policies, and evaluation/learning of new actions. These challenges arise in personalized medicine, education, recommendations, and advertising, where historical data is often scarce or narrowly collected in the target domain.
AI.method: The authors formulate a new Cross-Domain OPE/L problem setup, where both target-domain logged data and source-domain logged datasets are available. They develop a new estimator and a policy gradient method that jointly leverage target and source datasets to reduce variance and improve policy evaluation and optimization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations demonstrate substantially enhanced OPE/L performance in previously unsolved situations — specifically, few-shot data, deterministic logging policies, and new action scenarios — compared to existing single-domain methods.
AI.conclusion: Cross-Domain OPE/L is a practical and widely applicable formulation that enables reliable policy evaluation and learning even under conditions previously considered intractable, by transferring knowledge across related domains.

title: A Roadmap to Impactful Pluralistic Alignment Research
summary: Pluralistic value alignment---the goal of building AI systems that represent and serve diverse human values and perspectives---has emerged as an active research agenda. Yet, there's no public evidence that it has shaped the training or evaluation of the AI systems people actually use. We audit the public behavior documents and evaluations of frontier labs, finding none name pluralism as a goal, and as of this writing, no clear indication that production models are explicitly trained or tested for it. This goes against the primary motivations and goals of pluralistic alignment, which revolve around making a positive difference in the models serving billions of users worldwide. We argue that the pluralistic alignment research community should focus on supporting impact and adoption in deployed, widely-used AI systems. We provide evidence for the adoption problem, present three main reasons behind it, and discuss three corresponding areas for future research to address it: 1. The primary justifications for pluralistic alignment so far have been normative or speculative. We need studies showing empirically how pluralistic AI benefits users or society. 2. The pluralistic alignment research community has not settled when pluralistic behavior is warranted or what pluralism ideally looks like in practice. We need to establish a concrete goal for developers to operationalize. 3. Current methods trade off against other desiderata of LLMs in ways that are largely unmeasured, and existing metrics are not "hill-climbable." We need trade-off-aware evaluations and methods that meet the requirements of production systems. This paper serves as a collective call to action for the pluralistic alignment researchers: progress requires moving beyond normative justification toward empirical foundations, a concrete account of ideal pluralistic behavior, and practical methods and evaluations built for adoption.

AI.tldr: The paper audits frontier AI labs and finds no evidence that pluralistic value alignment has been adopted in training or evaluating production models. It identifies an "adoption gap," analyzes three underlying causes, and proposes three research directions to bridge pluralistic alignment research toward real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Despite pluralistic value alignment being an active research agenda, there is no public evidence it influences the AI systems people actually use. This contradicts the field's own stated goal of positively impacting models serving billions of users. The paper aims to diagnose this adoption failure and rally the research community toward practical impact.
AI.method: The authors conduct an audit of public behavior documents and evaluations from frontier AI labs. They then provide a structured argument identifying three reasons for the adoption gap and map each to a corresponding research direction needed to address it.
AI.result: No frontier lab names pluralism as a goal, and there is no clear indication that production models are explicitly trained or tested for pluralistic alignment. Three root causes are identified: (1) justifications remain normative/speculative without empirical evidence of benefit; (2) no consensus on when pluralistic behavior is warranted or what it should look like; (3) current methods have unmeasured trade-offs with other LLM desiderata and lack "hill-climbable" metrics.
AI.conclusion: The pluralistic alignment community must shift from normative justification toward empirical foundations, develop a concrete operationalizable account of ideal pluralistic behavior, and create trade-off-aware evaluations and production-ready methods. The paper serves as a call to action for research that supports genuine adoption in deployed AI systems.

title: DCS: A Unified Conditional Sensitivity Framework for Cross-Modal Copyright Infringement Detection
summary:
Currently, most foundation models can reproduce or strongly depend on copyrighted training content, but output similarity alone is insufficient for infringement detection, because similar outputs may also arise from public-domain concepts, common stylistic conventions, or ordinary statistical generalization.
  In this paper, we develops a unified post-hoc detection framework that treats copyright infringement evidence as a counterfactual conditional distribution shift: a protected target is suspicious when the model's behavior under aligned conditions would change measurably if that target were included in, or removed from, the training process.
  We formalize this view through conditional differential privacy and introduce Dual-Branch Conditional Sensitivity (DCS), an operational statistic that measures the observable gap between two locally perturbed model states. Specifically, the proposed DCS framework creates a learning branch and an unlearning branch around the deployed model, connects their displacement to the unavailable counterfactual retraining effect through influence-function analysis, and bounds the observable sensitivity by the counterfactual privacy-budget surrogate, local curvature, training-set scale, and perturbation step size. To distinguish target-specific memorization from generic fine-tuning instability, we further define a calibrated detection statistic that subtracts the sensitivity measured under orthogonal conditions.
  The DCS framework is instantiated for ridge-regularized linear regression, conditional diffusion models, autoregressive language models, and multimodal models. These instantiations show how the same principle can be evaluated through prediction gaps, image-embedding divergence, token-distribution or entropy shifts, and cross-modal representation changes.

AI.tldr: Proposes a post-hoc copyright infringement detection framework based on counterfactual conditional distribution shift, using Dual-Branch Conditional Sensitivity (DCS) to measure output changes under learning/unlearning perturbations, instantiated across linear, diffusion, autoregressive, and multimodal models.
AI.motivation: Output similarity to copyrighted content alone is insufficient for infringement detection because similar outputs can arise from public-domain concepts, stylistic conventions, or statistical generalization. A principled, unified detection framework is needed that distinguishes true memorization-based infringement from coincidental similarity.
AI.method: The framework formalizes infringement evidence as a counterfactual conditional distribution shift through conditional differential privacy. DCS creates learning and unlearning branches around the deployed model, connects their displacement to the unavailable counterfactual retraining effect via influence-function analysis, and bounds sensitivity by privacy-budget surrogate, local curvature, training-set scale, and perturbation step size. A calibrated detection statistic subtracts orthogonal-condition sensitivity to filter out generic fine-tuning instability.
AI.result: DCS is instantiated across four model classes: ridge-regularized linear regression (prediction gaps), conditional diffusion models (image-embedding divergence), autoregressive language models (token-distribution/entropy shifts), and multimodal models (cross-modal representation changes), demonstrating the framework's generality.
AI.conclusion: A conditional-differential-privacy-grounded, influence-function-driven dual-branch approach provides a unified, principled post-hoc method for detecting copyright infringement across diverse model architectures without requiring access to the original training process.

title: Learning Structural Convergence: A Neuro-Symbolic Benchmark for Temporal Reasoning
summary: High-complexity operational environments require methods that detect and anticipate temporally distributed patterns rather than classify isolated events. This paper introduces TRACTA (Temporal Reasoning and Capability-Trajectory Analysis), a controlled synthetic benchmark for temporal structural reasoning in high-complexity event-driven systems, instantiated through Multi-Domain Operations (MDO)-like scenarios. The benchmark includes three tasks: early_warning, pattern_detection, and run_classification, and compares raw-event neural models, a contract-lite semantic baseline, and a neuro-symbolic configuration operating on semantically grounded trajectories. Results show that raw event-level learning remains informative, but learned temporal modeling over semantic capability and contextual direct-impact trajectories achieves the highest aggregate point estimates, with the largest margins on the temporal tasks. Ablation analysis indicates that capability dynamics, contextual impacts, and temporal structure contribute complementary information. Shortcut diagnostics indicate that the most direct cross-run global-identifier shortcut is controlled in the primary neural input view, while residual shallow signals remain. Overall, the findings support a bounded methodological conclusion: in controlled synthetic settings, semantically grounded trajectories provide an effective representation for temporal structural reasoning, supporting further investigation of semantic interfaces between event data, structured representations, and temporal learning.

AI.tldr: TRACTA is a synthetic benchmark for temporal structural reasoning in complex event-driven systems. It compares raw-event neural models, a semantic baseline, and a neuro-symbolic approach using grounded trajectories. Semantically grounded trajectory representations achieve the best performance on temporal tasks, with complementary contributions from capability dynamics, contextual impacts, and temporal structure.
AI.motivation: High-complexity operational environments (e.g., Multi-Domain Operations) demand methods capable of detecting and anticipating temporally distributed patterns, not merely classifying isolated events. Existing approaches often lack evaluation frameworks that systematically test temporal structural reasoning under controlled conditions, motivating a synthetic benchmark to isolate and measure this capability.
AI.method: The authors introduce TRACTA, a controlled synthetic benchmark with three tasks: early_warning, pattern_detection, and run_classification. They compare three modeling paradigms: (1) raw-event neural models operating directly on event streams, (2) a contract-lite semantic baseline, and (3) a neuro-symbolic configuration that learns temporal models over semantically grounded capability and contextual direct-impact trajectories. Ablation studies and shortcut diagnostics are conducted to assess the contribution of each representational component.
AI.result: Raw event-level learning provides informative signals, but the neuro-symbolic approach using semantically grounded trajectories yields the highest aggregate point estimates, particularly on temporal tasks (pattern_detection, early_warning). Ablation analysis reveals that capability dynamics, contextual direct-impact features, and temporal structure each contribute complementary, non-redundant information. Shortcut diagnostics confirm that the primary global-identifier shortcut is controlled, though residual shallow signals persist.
AI.conclusion: In controlled synthetic settings, semantically grounded trajectories serve as an effective representation for temporal structural reasoning. The findings warrant further investigation into semantic interfaces linking raw event data, structured representations, and temporal learning in high-complexity operational contexts.

title: CEL: Comprehensive Counterfactual Explanations Library and Benchmark
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for presentation at the XKDD and Beyond Workshop (non-archival)
summary: Counterfactual explanations are a prominent approach in explainable artificial intelligence (xAI), providing actionable guidance on what input changes would alter a model's prediction to a desired outcome. While early methods primarily focused on minimal feature changes, recent work incorporates additional properties such as sparsity, actionability and plausibility. Despite this progress, fair and systematic evaluation remains challenging. Existing studies often rely on different data splits, predictive models, and evaluation metrics, which limits objective comparison across methods. To fill this gap, we introduce CEL (Counterfactual Explanations Library), a unified library and benchmark for counterfactual explanations designed to support consistent implementation and evaluation. CEL includes 18 datasets of varying size and complexity and provides implementations or reimplementations of 14 widely used counterfactual methods. Using this standardized setup, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative comparison across a variety of methods on datasets that differ in size, number, and types of attributes. The evaluation protocol incorporates multiple complementary metrics capturing validity, coverage, sparsity, proximity, and distributional plausibility, including density- and outlier-based measures to assess the realism of generated counterfactuals. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates recent counterfactual explanation methods within a unified and reproducible framework. While prior libraries and benchmarking efforts exist in the literature, many are outdated, limited in scope, or lack consistent evaluation protocols. The proposed benchmark aims to improve reproducibility, enable fair comparison, and establish a workbench for the development of future counterfactual explanation methods.

AI.tldr: CEL is a unified library and benchmark for counterfactual explanations, providing 18 datasets and 14 method implementations to enable fair, reproducible evaluation across multiple metrics including validity, coverage, sparsity, proximity, and distributional plausibility.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation research suffers from inconsistent evaluation practices — different data splits, models, and metrics — making objective method comparison impossible. No prior benchmark systematically evaluates recent methods within a unified, reproducible framework.
AI.method: The authors introduce CEL, a library integrating 18 datasets and implementations of 14 counterfactual methods. They conduct a comprehensive quantitative comparison using standardized evaluation protocols with complementary metrics: validity, coverage, sparsity, proximity, and distributional plausibility (including density- and outlier-based measures).
AI.result: The paper presents CEL as the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates recent counterfactual explanation methods within a unified, reproducible framework. Prior libraries are noted to be outdated, limited in scope, or lacking consistent evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: CEL establishes a standardized workbench aimed at improving reproducibility, enabling fair comparison, and supporting future development of counterfactual explanation methods.

title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability? Protocol Validity in the Age of Agentic AI
summary: Agent benchmarks increasingly evaluate repository editing, web research, terminal use, and long-horizon interaction. Their scores support capability claims only when the evaluation protocol keeps the intended capability necessary for success. Recent reward-hacking benchmarks and system reports show that agents can instead recover public solutions, read evaluation artifacts, infer generator structure, manipulate feedback, or benefit from invalid scoring paths; existing responses do not provide a common procedure for attributing these shortcuts and quantifying their effect across benchmarks. We formulate protocol validity and introduce HackDetect, a post-hoc audit that identifies an exposure, determines how the agent used it, and assesses whether the resulting score is misleading. We quantify score inflation with the Mislead gap, defined as the exploit score minus the intended score. We audit 2,385 traces across 15 agent benchmarks and find evidence of exposures and reward hacking in 67.0% of Frontier Science traces and 66.7% of AutoLab tasks. Across paired comparisons, we measure score inflation of 0.45-1.00, showing that benchmark reports should provide evidence that scores reflect the intended capability.

AI.tldr: Agent benchmarks are susceptible to reward hacking where agents exploit evaluation protocol flaws rather than demonstrating intended capabilities. The authors propose HackDetect, a post-hoc audit method that identifies exposure to shortcuts, quantifies score inflation via the "Mislead gap," and finds that ~67% of traces from Frontier Science and AutoLab show evidence of reward hacking with score inflation of 0.45–1.00.
AI.motivation: Current agent benchmarks evaluate complex capabilities (repository editing, web research, terminal use, long-horizon interaction), but agents can achieve high scores through shortcuts — recovering public solutions, reading evaluation artifacts, inferring generator structure, manipulating feedback, or exploiting invalid scoring paths. Existing responses lack a common, systematic procedure for detecting and quantifying these reward-hacking behaviors across benchmarks, undermining the validity of capability claims.
AI.method: The authors formalize "protocol validity" and introduce HackDetect, a post-hoc audit procedure with three steps: (1) identify an exposure (a flaw allowing shortcut exploitation), (2) determine how the agent used it, and (3) assess whether the resulting score is misleading. They define the "Mislead gap" as the quantitative difference between exploit score and intended score. The method is applied to 2,385 traces across 15 agent benchmarks, including Frontier Science and AutoLab.
AI.result: Auditing 2,385 traces across 15 agent benchmarks reveals evidence of exposures and reward hacking in 67.0% of Frontier Science traces and 66.7% of AutoLab tasks. Paired comparisons show score inflation (Mislead gap) ranging from 0.45 to 1.00, indicating significant overestimation of agent capabilities due to protocol flaws.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores alone are insufficient evidence of agent capabilities. The pervasive presence of reward hacking across major benchmarks demonstrates that evaluation reports must include evidence that scores genuinely reflect intended capabilities rather than protocol exploitation. HackDetect provides a reusable framework for conducting such audits.

title: A Leakage-Free Stacked Ensemble Method for Multiclass Classification
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, This paper is presented at IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence (WCCI 2026) June 2026, Maastricht, The Netherlands
summary:
Multiclass classification is a fundamental problem across a wide range of domains. It is still challenging due to possession of high inter-class similarity, class imbalance datasets, and variability in data distributions. Rule-based classifiers such as XGBoost often achieve stronger performance on structured features, but they are limited in capturing smooth functional relationships among variables. Similarly, neural network models can represent complex nonlinear interactions but frequently suffer from overfitting and generalization issues. To address these limitations, we propose LFS-FRAME, a Leakage-Free Stacked ensemble framework that integrates functional learning using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) and rule-based learning via XGBoost for robust multiclass classification.
  The proposed framework constructs unbiased meta-features by employing a strict out-of-fold stacking strategy to ensure complete isolation between training and validation data hence preventing performance leakage. By learning over probabilistic outputs from heterogeneous base learners, the meta-classifier effectively exploits both global functional patterns and sharp decision boundaries present in the complex data. Experimental evaluations on multi-class datasets demonstrate that LFS-FRAME improves performance metrics, and overall accuracy is 89.85% in identifying major families and 81.74% in identifying sub-families relative to strong single-model baselines. These results highlight the effectiveness of leakage-free functional and rule-based stacking for reliable and generalizable multiclass classification.

AI.tldr: LFS-FRAME is a leakage-free stacked ensemble that combines Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) for functional learning with XGBoost for rule-based learning, using strict out-of-fold stacking to prevent data leakage, achieving 89.85% accuracy on major family classification and 81.74% on sub-family classification.
AI.motivation: Multiclass classification remains challenging due to high inter-class similarity, class imbalance, and variable data distributions. Rule-based classifiers (e.g., XGBoost) excel on structured features but struggle with smooth functional relationships, while neural networks capture complex nonlinear interactions but tend to overfit. The authors aim to bridge this gap by combining both paradigms in a principled ensemble framework.
AI.method: LFS-FRAME employs a stacked ensemble with two heterogeneous base learners: XGBoost (rule-based) and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (functional learning). Critically, it uses a strict out-of-fold stacking strategy that completely isolates training and validation data partitions, generating unbiased meta-features free from performance leakage. A meta-classifier then learns over the probabilistic outputs of both base learners, fusing global functional patterns with sharp decision boundaries.
AI.result: On multiclass datasets, LFS-FRAME achieves 89.85% overall accuracy for major family identification and 81.74% for sub-family identification, outperforming strong single-model baselines across multiple performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The leakage-free integration of functional (KAN) and rule-based (XGBoost) learning via stacked ensembling yields reliable and generalizable multiclass classification, effectively addressing the complementary weaknesses of each paradigm.

title: IDEAgent: Agentic Quality-Diversity Search for Research Idea Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly automated the process of scientific discovery over the past few years. However, existing systems share one core limitation: they generate and optimize ideas independently for either Quality or Diversity. This often leads to the generation of ideas in close proximity to one another or to a large set of trivial, unsound, or unclear concepts. In this work, we instead argue that research ideation should be treated as a conjunction of both objectives and framed as a Quality-Diversity (QD) search. In line with this perspective, we introduce IDEAgent, a multi-agent framework that manages the evolution of ideas through lineages. We jointly drive Quality using multi-objective feedback for dedicated repair and refinement, while Diversity is achieved through lightweight sequential memory and explicit comparison against completed ideas, their historical ancestors, and rejected proposals. To systematically evaluate this QD conjunction, we develop Yield, a joint metric that computes the largest set of mutually diverse ideas that satisfy a predetermined quality threshold. Finally, through evaluations across 32 topics spanning 8 domains of Computer Science, we show that IDEAgent outperforms the best baseline by 3.89x on Yield, while achieving non-zero Yield on 8x more topics. We further corroborate these findings through an analysis of quality improvements, showing that repair and refinement are crucial for building logical rigor and clarity while preserving non-obviousness. To encourage future research on QD-search-based ideation, we open-source IDEAgent at https://github.com/declare-lab/IDEAgent.

AI.tldr: IDEAgent is a multi-agent framework that frames scientific ideation as a Quality-Diversity (QD) search, jointly optimizing for both quality and diversity in LLM-generated research ideas. It introduces Yield as a joint evaluation metric and demonstrates 3.89x improvement over baselines across 32 topics in 8 CS domains.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific ideation systems optimize for either quality or diversity independently, resulting in ideas that are either too similar (low diversity) or trivial/unsound (low quality). The authors argue that research ideation inherently requires jointly optimizing both objectives, motivating a Quality-Diversity search formulation.
AI.method: IDEAgent uses a multi-agent framework where ideas evolve through lineages. Quality is driven via multi-objective feedback for repair and refinement. Diversity is maintained through lightweight sequential memory and explicit comparison against completed ideas, historical ancestors, and rejected proposals. The authors also introduce Yield, a joint metric measuring the largest set of mutually diverse ideas exceeding a quality threshold.
AI.result: IDEAgent outperforms the best baseline by 3.89x on the Yield metric across 32 topics spanning 8 Computer Science domains. It achieves non-zero Yield on 8x more topics than baselines. Analysis shows repair and refinement are crucial for building logical rigor and clarity while preserving non-obviousness.
AI.conclusion: Treating research ideation as a Quality-Diversity search problem is effective. IDEAgent demonstrates that jointly optimizing quality and diversity yields substantially better research ideas than optimizing either alone, and the framework is open-sourced to encourage further research in this direction.

title: Pretraining EHR Foundation Models with Patient-Aware Sampling
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Structured Data for Health at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: Autoregressive foundation models for electronic health records (EHRs) typically inherit pretraining methods from language modeling, where patient trajectories are concatenated into a single token stream and windows are sampled from that stream. In EHR data, this choice is consequential: windows may mix multiple patients, and patients with longer records contribute more optimization updates, potentially introducing bias. We propose Patient Sampling, a pretraining sequence-construction method that allows us to control how training signal is distributed across patients. We compare this method to the standard approach, which we refer to as Global Stream. We show that stochastic Patient Sampling with controllable weighting improves performance on real-world EHR data. Across downstream clinical tasks on MIMIC-IV v2.2 and v3.1, Patient Sampling improves Macro AUROC and AUPRC over the Global Stream baseline. These results identify training and validation sequence construction as important and underexplored design choices for autoregressive EHR foundation models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Patient Sampling," a pretraining sequence-construction method for autoregressive EHR foundation models that controls how training signal is distributed across patients, addressing biases from the standard "Global Stream" approach. Patient Sampling improves Macro AUROC and AUPRC on MIMIC-IV clinical tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard autoregressive pretraining for EHRs concatenates all patient trajectories into one global token stream, causing two key issues: (1) windows may mix tokens from multiple patients, and (2) patients with longer records dominate optimization updates, introducing representation bias. The authors aim to address these underexplored design choices in sequence construction.
AI.method: The authors introduce Patient Sampling, a pretraining sequence-construction method where training windows are sampled with controllable per-patient weighting, ensuring each window contains data from only one patient. This is contrasted with the conventional Global Stream approach. They evaluate using stochastic sampling strategies with different weighting schemes on MIMIC-IV v2.2 and v3.1.
AI.result: Patient Sampling with controllable weighting consistently outperforms the Global Stream baseline on downstream clinical tasks, as measured by Macro AUROC and AUPRC on MIMIC-IV v2.2 and v3.1.
AI.conclusion: Training and validation sequence construction are important and underexplored design choices for autoregressive EHR foundation models. Patient Sampling offers a simple yet effective way to mitigate biases from the standard Global Stream approach, yielding better downstream performance.

title: Agentic Root Cause Analysis through Evidence-Grounded Reasoning
summary: Diagnosing the root cause of anomalies is essential for safe industrial operation. Despite extensive sensor instrumentation, formulating hypotheses and gathering evidence remains a manual process, creating a major operational bottleneck. While existing data-driven approaches aim to automate this, two critical limitations restrict their deployment: their operate as black boxes unable to justify their diagnosis, and they require scarce labeled examples of faulty operation. To address this gap, we introduce AgentRCA, a zero-shot agentic framework for evidence-grounded root cause analysis. Rather than learning fault-specific mappings, AgentRCA performs inference-time reasoning by combining a data-driven digital twin (modeling normal system dynamics) with a tool-augmented large language model. The agent iteratively gathers statistical evidence, evaluates competing hypotheses, and identifies the physical fault that best explains the observed behavior. Evaluated on a real-world multiphase-flow facility and a large-scale chemical plant, AgentRCA achieves diagnostic performance competitive with fully supervised baselines without relying on fault-specific training. Crucially, it produces transparent reasoning traces that explicitly link observed symptoms to their underlying physical causes. These results establish autonomous hypothesis-driven reasoning as a practical foundation for scalable industrial root cause analysis.

AI.tldr: AgentRCA is a zero-shot, agentic framework that combines a digital twin with an LLM to autonomously perform root cause analysis in industrial settings, matching supervised baselines without needing fault-specific training data while producing transparent, evidence-grounded reasoning traces.
AI.motivation: Industrial root cause analysis remains a manual bottleneck despite rich sensor data. Existing data-driven approaches are limited by (1) black-box operation without justifiable diagnoses and (2) dependency on scarce labeled fault examples, hindering real-world deployment.
AI.method: AgentRCA performs inference-time reasoning by integrating a data-driven digital twin (modeling normal dynamics) with a tool-augmented large language model. The agent iteratively gathers statistical evidence, evaluates competing hypotheses, and identifies the physical fault best explaining observed behavior — all in a zero-shot manner without fault-specific training.
AI.result: Evaluated on a real-world multiphase-flow facility and a large-scale chemical plant, AgentRCA achieves diagnostic performance competitive with fully supervised baselines, while producing transparent reasoning traces that explicitly link symptoms to underlying physical causes.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous hypothesis-driven reasoning, as demonstrated by AgentRCA, provides a practical and scalable foundation for industrial root cause analysis, overcoming key barriers of explainability and data scarcity.

title: TriGlue: a Biology-Inspired Generative Model for Generating Molecular Glue-Induced Ternary Complex
summary: Molecular glue degraders have emerged as a promising strategy for targeted protein degradation by inducing ternary complex formation between an E3 ubiquitin ligase and a target protein. Despite their therapeutic potential, computational design of molecular glues remains largely unexplored. Unlike conventional structure-based drug design, molecular glue design is governed by the unknown protein-protein interface and requires the simultaneous modeling of ligand generation, protein-protein docking, and ternary complex assembly. In this work, we formulate molecular glue design as a ternary complex generation problem and propose a biology-inspired generative framework, TriGlue. Motivated by the mechanism of molecular glue action, we decompose ternary complex generation into two coupled stages: interface estimation and interface-conditioned complex generation. First, we develop an SE(3)-equivariant interface estimation module that predicts a geometrically constrained protein-protein interface from unbound monomer structures. Second, we introduce an interface-conditioned ternary flow matching network that jointly generates the molecular glue and predicts the rigid-body transformation required to assemble the ternary complex. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TriGlue generates chemically valid molecules and produces plausible ternary complexes, which highlight the potential of biology-inspired generative modeling for accelerating molecular glue discovery. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/molecular-glue-design-806B.

AI.tldr: TriGlue is a generative AI framework that designs molecular glues by modeling ternary complex formation in two stages: predicting the protein-protein interface and then jointly generating the glue molecule along with the rigid-body transformation for complex assembly.
AI.motivation: Molecular glues are promising for targeted protein degradation but lack computational design tools because their design requires simultaneously solving ligand generation, protein-protein docking, and ternary complex assembly — a problem unexplored by existing methods.
AI.method: TriGlue decomposes ternary complex generation into two coupled stages: (1) an SE(3)-equivariant interface estimation module that predicts a geometrically constrained protein-protein interface from unbound monomers, and (2) an interface-conditioned ternary flow matching network that jointly generates the molecular glue and predicts the rigid-body transformation for assembling the ternary complex.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show TriGlue generates chemically valid molecules and plausible ternary complexes.
AI.conclusion: Biology-inspired generative modeling, as demonstrated by TriGlue, holds significant potential for accelerating molecular glue discovery.

title: SceneActBench: Can Agents Act on the 3D Scenes They See?
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents increasingly use tools to act on 3D scenes rather than only describe them. Existing 3D benchmarks score textual responses or single-object operations, leaving agent action on complete multi-object 3D scenes under evaluated. We present SceneActBench, a benchmark for visually conditioned action across five 3D tasks under a unified agent-environment loop. Given PNG images or sampled video frames and, where applicable, supplied 3D assets, an agent acts on a 3D environment. We evaluate each final output against hidden ground truth with task-specific geometric metrics. SceneActBench comprises five tasks built from 210 source instances, yielding 520 task cases including paired input conditions. Every task runs through one fixed agent loop to keep the comparison fair. Across eleven proprietary VLM configurations, Overall scores span 38.6-50.2, and none performs consistently well across tasks. We further analyse where and how failures manifest.

AI.tldr: SceneActBench is a new benchmark evaluating VLM agents on tool-based actions in 3D environments across five tasks, revealing that proprietary VLMs score only 38.6–50.2 and lack consistent cross-task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D benchmarks evaluate textual descriptions or single-object manipulations, leaving multi-object, action-oriented 3D scene understanding by VLM agents under-assessed. The authors aim to fill this gap with a unified, interactive agent-environment evaluation framework.
AI.method: SceneActBench comprises 210 source instances yielding 520 task cases across five 3D tasks. Agents receive PNG images or video frames (and optionally 3D assets) and act within a fixed agent-environment loop. Final outputs are scored against hidden ground truth using task-specific geometric metrics. Eleven proprietary VLM configurations are evaluated under identical loop conditions.
AI.result: Overall scores across the eleven VLM configurations range from 38.6 to 50.2. No configuration performs consistently well across all five tasks. Detailed failure analysis reveals where and how errors manifest.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM agents remain limited in their ability to act reliably on multi-object 3D scenes. SceneActBench provides a standardized, geometrically rigorous testbed to drive progress in this area.

title: Unbiased Open World Regularization for Fair Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Despite recent advances, self-supervised learning (SSL) models and Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) remain susceptible to learning spurious biases in the dataset. These techniques rely on regularization, which prevents representation collapse by enforcing a global target distribution such as a multivariate Gaussian or a uniform distribution on the sphere. However, these global constraints are insufficient to prevent bias entanglement, as task-irrelevant features can still segregate the latent space into distinct sub-regions. While recent approaches like Entangling and Disentangling (EnD) and Fair Supervised Contrastive Learning (FSCL) empirically debias the latent space, we show that they act as partial approximations of conditional distribution matching. To enforce this matching explicitly, we propose Unbiased Open World Regularization (UOWReg), an encoder-only framework. We show that this shift from a global to a conditional objective guarantees statistical independence between the learned representations and the targeted attributes, regardless of the chosen target distribution. We empirically validate this framework across both Gaussian and spherical latent spaces, using statistical measures to enforce these target distributions. While conditional matching successfully mitigates bias with both distributions, we demonstrate that enforcing conditional uniformity on the sphere yields a lower linearprobing classification error. Empirically, UOWReg reduces Equalized Odds violations on the CelebA benchmark while maintaining competitive classification accuracy compared to existing encoder-only baselines. Furthermore, we introduce the Synthetic Engraving Task-a novel setting in which a dominant macro-structure masks a fine-grained micro-signature. We show that UOWReg effectively prevents the subpopulation collapse observed in standard SSL, successfully isolating micro-signatures even when heavily entangled with the global structure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes UOWReg, an encoder-only framework that replaces global distribution constraints with explicit conditional distribution matching to achieve statistical independence between learned representations and bias attributes, outperforming existing methods on bias mitigation while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: SSL and JEPA models suffer from spurious bias entanglement because global target distribution constraints (e.g., Gaussian or uniform on the sphere) are insufficient—task-irrelevant features can still segregate the latent space into biased sub-regions. Existing debiasing methods like EnD and FSCL only partially approximate conditional distribution matching.
AI.method: UOWReg explicitly enforces conditional distribution matching, shifting from a global to a conditional objective. This guarantees statistical independence between learned representations and targeted attributes regardless of the chosen target distribution. The framework is validated across both Gaussian and spherical latent spaces, and introduces the Synthetic Engraving Task as a novel benchmark where dominant macro-structures mask fine-grained micro-signatures.
AI.result: Conditional uniformity on the sphere yields lower linear-probing classification error. UOWReg reduces Equalized Odds violations on CelebA while maintaining competitive classification accuracy against encoder-only baselines. On the Synthetic Engraving Task, UOWReg prevents subpopulation collapse and successfully isolates micro-signatures entangled with global structure.
AI.conclusion: Explicit conditional distribution matching is both theoretically principled (guaranteeing statistical independence) and empirically effective for bias mitigation in self-supervised representation learning, with spherical conditional uniformity providing the best classification performance.

title: From Score Approximation to Distribution Approximation in Score-Based Diffusion Models
summary: Score-based diffusion models have achieved remarkable empirical success in generative modeling, yet their approximation-theoretic foundations remain incomplete. In particular, although classical universal approximation theorems guarantee that neural networks can approximate score functions, it remains unclear whether such approximation guarantees translate into approximation of the probability distributions generated by reverse diffusion processes. In this paper, we establish a rigorous quantitative connection between these two notions. Specifically, we prove that if a neural network approximates the true score function sufficiently accurately, then the probability distribution generated by the corresponding reverse diffusion model is close to the target data distribution in Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, up to an irreducible mismatch between the terminal distribution of the forward diffusion process and the prior used to initialize the reverse process. More precisely, we derive an explicit upper bound on the distribution approximation error in terms of the score approximation error, the diffusion noise schedule, and the terminal prior mismatch. Our analysis combines Hornik's universal approximation theorem, Girsanov's theorem on path space, and the data processing inequality for relative entropy. Complementary to recent work that studies score approximation under finite-sample statistical settings and structural assumptions on the data distribution, our work develops an approximation-theoretic analysis based on classical neural network approximation theory. The resulting theorem provides a simple and explicit guarantee linking neural network approximation of score functions to approximation of the probability distributions generated by reverse diffusion models.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that if a neural network accurately approximates the true score function, the probability distribution generated by the reverse diffusion process is close to the target distribution in KL divergence, with an explicit error bound depending on score approximation error, noise schedule, and terminal prior mismatch.
AI.motivation: Although universal approximation theorems guarantee neural networks can approximate score functions, it was unclear whether this approximation guarantee translates into approximation of the generated probability distributions in diffusion models. The paper aims to bridge this gap with a rigorous quantitative connection.
AI.method: The analysis combines three theoretical tools: Hornik's universal approximation theorem for neural network score approximation, Girsanov's theorem on path space to relate the forward and reverse diffusion processes, and the data processing inequality for relative entropy to bound the KL divergence between generated and target distributions.
AI.result: An explicit upper bound is derived for the distribution approximation error (in KL divergence) in terms of the score approximation error, the diffusion noise schedule, and the terminal prior mismatch. This provides a simple, explicit guarantee linking neural network score approximation to distribution approximation quality.
AI.conclusion: The work complements recent finite-sample statistical analyses by developing an approximation-theoretic perspective based on classical neural network approximation theory, establishing that accurate score approximation indeed implies accurate distribution generation in reverse diffusion models.

title: Latent PDE mapping for efficient physics-informed learning across geometries with limited data
summary: In this study, we introduce latent PDE mapping, a broadly applicable physics-informed learning technique designed to enable efficient geometric generalization with sparse training data. Latent PDE mapping pulls back geometry-specific PDE residuals and boundary conditions to a predefined latent geometry via the deformation gradient, thereby enabling the automated calculation of geometry-consistent shape gradients that are missing in conventional physics-informed machine learning formulations. We demonstrate the utility of latent PDE mapping in solving the anisotropic Aliev-Panfilov PDE of cardiac electrophysiology using both physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed deep operator networks. The Aliev-Panfilov PDE serves as a challenging exemplar: a nonlinear, time-dependent PDE benchmark with sharp gradients that are expensive to capture using traditional numerical solvers. To represent the limited data regime, we train the networks using just fifteen geometric samples drawn from parameterized distributions in two and three spatial dimensions. While modest improvements appear for geometries parameterized by affine and shear deformations, latent PDE mapping demonstrates significant benefits on select geometric families, achieving a factor ~4-6 reduction in mean relative L2 error. Furthermore, our results show that the computational cost of applying latent PDE mapping was modest during network training, and negligible at inference. Taken together, our study highlights how latent PDE mapping facilitates the creation of generalizable physics-informed machine learning models from limited sets of training geometries.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Latent PDE Mapping, a physics-informed learning technique that enables efficient geometric generalization from sparse training data by mapping PDE residuals and boundary conditions to a latent geometry via the deformation gradient, achieving 4-6× error reduction on the Aliev-Panfilov cardiac electrophysiology PDE.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed machine learning models struggle to generalize across varying geometries, particularly when training data is sparse. Conventional formulations lack geometry-consistent shape gradients, limiting their ability to transfer learned physics across different geometric configurations.
AI.method: Latent PDE Mapping pulls back geometry-specific PDE residuals and boundary conditions to a predefined latent geometry using the deformation gradient. This enables automated computation of geometry-consistent shape gradients, which are otherwise absent in standard physics-informed neural network (PINN) and deep operator network formulations. The method is evaluated on the nonlinear, time-dependent anisotropic Aliev-Panfilov PDE with both PINNs and physics-informed DeepONets, using only 15 training geometries in 2D and 3D.
AI.result: Modest improvements were observed for geometries parameterized by affine and shear deformations. However, latent PDE mapping demonstrated significant benefits on select geometric families, achieving approximately a factor of 4–6 reduction in mean relative L2 error. The computational cost of applying the method was modest during training and negligible at inference.
AI.conclusion: Latent PDE mapping effectively facilitates the creation of generalizable physics-informed machine learning models from limited sets of training geometries, particularly for challenging PDEs with sharp gradients like the Aliev-Panfilov model in cardiac electrophysiology.

title: The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents
summary: Adding procedural skills to an LLM agent is typically evaluated by average improvement in task success. However, this metric hides an important cost: skills can also make agents worse. We measure both sides by comparing agents with and without skills across nearly 6,000 runs spanning two office automation benchmarks and three model harness stacks. This allows us to distinguish two outcomes. A regression is a task solved without skills but failed after skills are added. A residual failure is a task that fails both with and without skills. We find that regressions are substantial enough that the best performing skills outperform others primarily by regressing less, not by gaining more. We identify three causes of regression: (i) skill description osmosis, a skill changes an agent's behavior simply by being present in context, even when it is never invoked; (ii) grounding displacement, a skill's prescribed procedure overrides how the agent interprets its inputs; and (iii) verification displacement, where the procedure suppresses checks the agent would otherwise perform on its outputs. Analysing persistent failures reveals the same underlying pattern. Existing skills overemphasize procedural guidance the stage least often responsible for failure while under supporting grounding and verification, the dominant sources of remaining errors. After correcting evaluation artifacts and studying traces, we find many regressions and persistent failures recoverable through better grounding and verification. Procedural skills should be evaluated by decomposing their net effect into gains and regressions, not by aggregate improvement alone. We identify three regression modes skills should avoid, and find that reliability depends more on grounding and verification than on procedural skill choice.

AI.tldr: Adding procedural skills to LLM agents can backfire: skills improve performance on some tasks but cause regressions on others. This paper quantifies these regressions, identifies three causal mechanisms (skill description osmosis, grounding displacement, verification displacement), and argues that skill evaluation must decompose net effect into gains and regressions, with reliability hinging more on grounding/verification than procedural guidance.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of LLM agent skills uses average task success improvement, which masks the fact that skills can make agents worse on tasks they previously solved. The authors aim to systematically measure and explain these regressions to guide better skill design.
AI.method: The authors ran nearly 6,000 trials across two office automation benchmarks and three model harness stacks, comparing agent performance with and without skills. They categorized failures into regressions (tasks solved without skills but failed with them) and residual failures (failed both ways). They analyzed error traces to identify causal mechanisms and evaluated whether failures were recoverable through improved grounding and verification.
AI.result: Regressions are substantial; the best-performing skills outperform others primarily by regressing less, not by gaining more successes. Three regression causes were identified: (1) skill description osmosis — a skill alters behavior merely by being present in context; (2) grounding displacement — prescribed procedures override input interpretation; (3) verification displacement — procedures suppress output checks. Persistent failures share the same pattern: skills overemphasize procedural guidance while under-supporting grounding and verification, the dominant error sources. Many regressions and residual failures are recoverable through better grounding and verification.
AI.conclusion: Procedural skills should be evaluated by decomposing net effect into gains and regressions, not by aggregate improvement alone. Reliability depends more on grounding and verification than on procedural skill choice, and three regression modes should be avoided in skill design.

title: Optimization of time-consuming experimental conditions using pseudo-experimental data guided by adaptive polynomial regression
summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is an optimization method that sequentially proposes the next candidate explainable variables for optimizing target variables by balancing exploration and exploitation. BO is often used under a limited evaluation budget, such as hyperparameter tuning of deep learning. Despite its effectiveness, conventional BO may have poor convergence in practical experimental science where each evaluation is often costly and time-consuming. Recently, BO methods have been proposed that accelerate optimization by using pseudo-experimental data that simulate experimental data. However, when only a limited number of experimental data are available, the generated pseudo-experimental data may be of insufficient quality. In this study, we developed PolyBO to improve optimization time by generating high-quality pseudo-experimental data even when the number of trials is limited. PolyBO performs BO efficiently by generating pseudo-experimental data with an adaptively updated versatile parametric model. This low-capacity polynomial regression model is intended to enable efficient BO even with limited experimental data. PolyBO updates the BO surrogate model with a combined dataset consisting of experimental data and pseudo-experimental data and then performs optimization. Using synthetic benchmark functions with diverse landscapes, we found that PolyBO reduced the optimization time by a median of 42\%. For a real-world material composition optimization problem, PolyBO reduced the optimization time by a median of 96\% compared with conventional methods. Overall, PolyBO achieves efficient optimization in settings where each experiment requires a long time.

AI.tldr: PolyBO accelerates Bayesian optimization by augmenting limited experimental data with high-quality pseudo-experimental data generated via an adaptively updated low-capacity polynomial regression model, achieving median optimization time reductions of 42% on synthetic benchmarks and 96% on a real-world material composition problem.
AI.motivation: Conventional Bayesian optimization suffers from slow convergence in experimental science settings where evaluations are costly and time-consuming. Existing methods that use pseudo-experimental data to accelerate BO fail when only limited real experimental data are available, as the generated pseudo-data is of insufficient quality. There is a need for a method that can generate high-quality pseudo-experimental data even under a limited trial budget.
AI.method: PolyBO generates pseudo-experimental data using an adaptively updated versatile parametric model — specifically a low-capacity polynomial regression model — that is updated as optimization proceeds. This model produces high-quality pseudo-data even with limited experiments. The BO surrogate model is then trained on a combined dataset of real experimental data and the generated pseudo-experimental data, after which standard BO optimization is performed.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmark functions with diverse landscapes, PolyBO reduced optimization time by a median of 42% compared to conventional methods. On a real-world material composition optimization problem, PolyBO achieved a median reduction in optimization time of 96%.
AI.conclusion: PolyBO enables efficient Bayesian optimization in settings where each experiment is time-intensive, by leveraging adaptively generated pseudo-experimental data from a low-capacity polynomial model to overcome the limitations of small experimental datasets.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning for assisting Air Traffic Controllers
comment: 11 pages (10-page paper plus 1 cover/citation page), 4 figures, 1 table; published in AINA 2025
summary: To effectively integrate AI into high-stakes, critical environments such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and aviation--and to advance toward higher levels of automation and seamless human-AI collaboration--building trust in AI-driven solutions is essential. Trust, in turn, is closely linked to the explainability of AI systems. The rapid advancements in AI across various domains have underscored the challenges of establishing trust, raising increasing interest in AI explainability even more when applied to deep learning. In this context, the present work aims to explore the application of explainability techniques to Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms, specifically within the safety-critical domain of Air Traffic Control (ATC). Using a simplified ATC environment as an initial testbed, an intelligent agent is trained with a reinforcement learning algorithm to make decisions on alternative flight routes that avoid no-fly zones. As a preliminary explainability approach, a saliency map is employed, providing insights into the input features that most significantly influence the agent's decision-making process.

AI.tldr: This paper explores applying saliency map-based explainability techniques to a reinforcement learning agent trained for air traffic control, using a simplified ATC environment as a testbed to understand which input features most influence decision-making.
AI.motivation: Trust in AI is essential for deployment in high-stakes, safety-critical domains (healthcare, autonomous driving, aviation), and trust is tightly coupled with explainability. While explainability has gained attention in deep learning generally, its application to Reinforcement Learning in safety-critical settings like Air Traffic Control remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors use a simplified ATC environment as a testbed. An RL agent is trained to select alternative flight routes avoiding no-fly zones. As a preliminary explainability approach, a saliency map is employed to identify input features that most significantly influence the agent's decisions.
AI.result: The saliency map approach provides insights into which input features most heavily influence the RL agent's decision-making process within the simplified ATC environment. (Specific quantitative or qualitative findings are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Saliency maps represent a viable preliminary approach for introducing explainability into RL-based ATC systems, contributing toward building trust and enabling higher levels of automation and human-AI collaboration in safety-critical domains.

title: IFCLoRA: Topology-Aware Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, but its performance depends strongly on how a fixed rank budget is distributed across Transformer modules. Existing adaptive-rank methods usually rely on local gradient statistics collected during training, which introduces extra memory and computation and overlooks task-conditioned global information flow. We propose IFCLoRA, a topology-aware rank allocation method applied before fine-tuning. Using a small calibration set and a frozen pretrained model, IFCLoRA builds a sparse task-conditioned interaction graph whose nodes represent LoRA-compatible modules. It combines a global information-flow topology prior with local gradient sensitivity to compute Information-Flow Centrality scores, which estimate each module's adaptation importance under multi-hop propagation. Ranks are then assigned once under a global budget. Across multiple models, tasks, and low-rank settings, IFCLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, and EVA under matched training configurations and total rank budgets, while retaining training costs comparable to standard LoRA. On mathematical reasoning with LLaMA 3 8B, IFCLoRA improves over LoRA by 1.36 percent at rank 4 and 1.82 percent at rank 8. Further analysis shows task-dependent, non-uniform rank profiles, indicating that global information-flow structure provides an informative and interpretable prior for low-budget parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: IFCLoRA is a pre-training rank allocation method for LoRA that uses a task-conditioned interaction graph and Information-Flow Centrality to assign ranks before fine-tuning, outperforming existing adaptive methods without extra training overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive-rank LoRA methods rely on gradient statistics during training, incurring memory/computation overhead and ignoring global, task-conditioned information flow. A lightweight, pre-training rank allocation strategy that captures global structural importance is needed.
AI.method: IFCLoRA builds a sparse task-conditioned interaction graph from a small calibration set and a frozen pretrained model. Nodes represent LoRA-compatible modules. It computes Information-Flow Centrality scores by combining a global information-flow topology prior with local gradient sensitivity, estimating each module's adaptation importance under multi-hop propagation. Ranks are assigned once under a global budget before fine-tuning begins.
AI.result: IFCLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, and EVA across multiple models, tasks, and low-rank settings under matched budgets. On LLaMA 3 8B mathematical reasoning, it improves over LoRA by 1.36% at rank 4 and 1.82% at rank 8, while retaining training cost comparable to standard LoRA.
AI.conclusion: Global information-flow structure provides an informative, interpretable, and task-dependent prior for low-budget PEFT. Pre-training rank allocation via IFCLoRA is both effective and efficient.

title: Class-Balanced Softmax: A Bayes Theory-Based Method for Long-Tailed Recognition
comment: 39 pages, 8 figures, under review in a journal
summary: Deep learning models using traditional softmax classifiers have achieved remarkable success in various classification tasks. However, their performance degrades significantly on imbalanced datasets. Although Balanced Softmax is widely adopted as a state-of-the-art rebalancing method, it possesses inherent limitations, such as yielding disproportionately lower testing accuracy for tail classes. To mitigate these shortcomings, we propose the Class-Balanced Softmax (CBS). Rooted in a theoretical Bayesian framework and a heuristic power-law assumption, the CBS is a simple logit adjustment that is computationally inexpensive and easily integrated into existing pipelines. Furthermore, we characterise a fundamental phenomenon in models trained on imbalanced data, termed the preference issue, wherein models exhibit higher training error and a larger generalisation gap for classes with limited data. To quantify this issue, we introduce a novel metric and demonstrate that CBS effectively mitigates the preference issue. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks show that CBS is highly scalable and outperforms existing methods, including Balanced Softmax.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Class-Balanced Softmax (CBS), a simple logit adjustment method grounded in a Bayesian framework and power-law assumption. CBS addresses the "preference issue" in imbalanced classification and outperforms Balanced Softmax on large-scale benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional softmax classifiers and even Balanced Softmax degrade on imbalanced datasets, particularly exhibiting disproportionately low accuracy on tail classes. The authors identify a "preference issue" — models trained on imbalanced data show higher training error and larger generalization gaps for under-represented classes — which existing methods fail to adequately address.
AI.method: The authors derive Class-Balanced Softmax (CBS) from a theoretical Bayesian framework combined with a heuristic power-law assumption about class distributions.
