CBS is implemented as a simple logit adjustment (additive offset to logits before softmax) that requires minimal computation. The paper also introduces a novel metric to quantify the "preference issue" — the tendency of models to favor majority classes in terms of training error and generalization gap.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that CBS is highly scalable and outperforms existing rebalancing methods, including Balanced Softmax. CBS also effectively mitigates the preference issue as measured by the proposed metric.
AI.conclusion: CBS provides a computationally inexpensive, theoretically grounded, and easily integrable solution to the class imbalance problem, surpassing state-of-the-art methods like Balanced Softmax while addressing the fundamental preference issue in long-tailed recognition.

title: Autoregressive EHR Foundation Models with Multimodal Inputs
comment: 5 pages excluding references and supplements, 2 figures and 2 tables, Proceedings of the Workshop on Structured Data for Health at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Autoregressive foundation models trained on tokenized electronic health records (EHRs) can support zero-shot clinical prediction, yet most operate on structured event codes alone, and do not incorporate multiple modalities in a principled way. We present a framework for conditioning such models on auxiliary clinical modalities, including ECG waveforms, chest X-ray images, and clinical notes, using modality-specific latent compression and gated cross-attention with temporal alignment. We investigate two key design choices: (1) how to compress long per-modality sequences (e.g., ECG time series) before they enter the multi-modal cross-attention. This feature may be essential to reduce compute overheads and may be beneficial for generalization; (2) how the choice of pretrained encoder for each modality impacts downstream performance. Through controlled ablations on MIMIC-IV, we show that the best latent-compression configurations outperforms both uncompressed cross-attention and mean pooling. Encoder choice has a clear within-modality effect, with stronger pretrained encoders consistently outperforming weaker alternatives. We further show that merely adding auxiliary modalities does not guarantee improvement on ICU mortality prediction over an EHR-only baseline. This implies that careful design of the fusion architecture and an appropriate evaluation in the clinical context are required.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for integrating auxiliary modalities (ECG, CXR, notes) into autoregressive EHR foundation models via latent compression and gated cross-attention, finding that compression design and encoder quality significantly affect performance, and that naive modality addition does not guarantee improvement over EHR-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing autoregressive EHR foundation models operate on structured event codes alone and lack a principled mechanism for incorporating multiple clinical modalities such as ECG waveforms, chest X-rays, and clinical notes, limiting their predictive capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that conditions autoregressive EHR models on auxiliary modalities using modality-specific latent compression followed by gated cross-attention with temporal alignment. They systematically ablate two design axes: (1) compression strategies for long per-modality sequences (e.g., uncompressed, mean pooling, and various latent compression configurations) and (2) the choice of pretrained encoder for each modality. Experiments are conducted on MIMIC-IV for ICU mortality prediction.
AI.result: The best latent-compression configuration outperforms both uncompressed cross-attention and mean pooling. Stronger pretrained encoders consistently yield better downstream performance within each modality. Simply adding auxiliary modalities does not reliably improve ICU mortality prediction over the EHR-only baseline, highlighting the need for careful fusion architecture design.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-modal conditioning of autoregressive EHR models requires deliberate architectural choices—particularly around compression and encoder selection—and does not automatically benefit from additional modalities. Proper evaluation in the clinical context is essential.

title: An Insight on Evaluation Metrics Under the Imbalanced Case of Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection is inherently characterised by severe class imbalance, making the interpretation of evaluation metrics challenging. Although metrics such as AUROC, AUPR, F1-score, and MCC are widely used, their values convey different meanings depending on the anomaly ratio. In this work, we analyse the behaviour of those four common anomaly detection metrics under varying levels of imbalance. We focus on the study of metric landscapes, visualisations that relate metric values to true positive and true negative rates, providing an intuitive view of metric preferences and stability. Our analysis offers practical guidance for interpreting and comparing anomaly detection results across datasets with different imbalance ratios.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how four common anomaly detection metrics (AUROC, AUPR, F1-score, MCC) behave under varying class imbalance ratios, using metric landscapes to visualize metric preferences and stability, and provides practical guidance for interpreting results across datasets with different anomaly ratios.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection suffers from severe class imbalance, which makes interpreting evaluation metrics challenging — the same metric value can convey different meanings depending on the anomaly ratio. Existing practice lacks systematic understanding of how metrics behave under varying imbalance, hindering fair comparison across datasets.
AI.method: The authors employ the concept of metric landscapes — visualizations that map metric values as functions of true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR). They systematically analyze the behavior of AUROC, AUPR, F1-score, and MCC across varying anomaly ratios, examining how these landscapes shift in shape, peak locations, and stability as imbalance changes.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that different metrics exhibit distinct preference patterns (e.g., favoring TPR vs. TNR trade-offs) and varying stability under changing imbalance. Metric landscapes provide an intuitive visual tool for understanding these differences, showing how each metric's optimal operating point and value distribution respond to the anomaly ratio.
AI.conclusion: There is no universally best metric; the choice should align with application-specific priorities. The metric landscape framework offers practitioners an intuitive tool for interpreting and comparing anomaly detection results across datasets with different imbalance ratios, enabling more informed metric selection and result interpretation.

title: Efficient Recommendations via Graph Coarsening and Label Propagation
summary:
Graph-based recommendations are widely adopted in real-world industrial applications. However, graphs in these systems often reach a massive scale, posing notable scalability and efficiency challenges. This requires techniques that can effectively balance predictive quality with computational cost. One promising approach is graph coarsening, an adaptive graph reduction technique that offers a way to systematically construct smaller, yet structurally representative, versions of the original large-scale graphs.
  In this work, we propose a flexible two-stage diffusion framework that combines graph coarsening with multi-step label propagation in the telecommunications domain. Domain-specific heuristics are applied to first aggregate nodes into meaningful communities, reducing graph size while preserving essential business-relevant relationships. An initial diffusion process done by a Label Propagation Algorithm (LPA) or a Graph Neural Network (GNN) propagates labels across the coarsened graph to produce coarse-grained predictions. Finally, a second LPA within subgraphs generates the final recommendations for individual users.
  On a real-world telecommunications dataset, when using LPA in both stages, our method achieves up to +24% NDCG@5 over the full-graph LPA baseline. Incorporating a lightweight GNN in the first stage further boosts NDCG@5 by more than 50%, but requires substantial training and inference time. Through extensive experiments and a detailed ablation, we quantify these trade-offs and demonstrate that our coarsening-driven approach delivers an optimal balance between scalability, latency, and recommendation quality.

AI.tldr: A two-stage diffusion framework using graph coarsening and multi-step label propagation improves telecom recommendations, achieving up to +24% NDCG@5 with LPA alone and +50% with a lightweight GNN, while balancing scalability, latency, and quality.
AI.motivation: Large-scale graphs in industrial recommendation systems pose scalability and efficiency challenges. Existing methods struggle to balance predictive quality with computational cost, motivating a need for graph reduction techniques that preserve structural fidelity while enabling faster inference.
AI.method: A two-stage diffusion framework: (1) domain-specific heuristics aggregate nodes into communities to coarsen the graph; (2) an initial diffusion stage (LPA or lightweight GNN) propagates labels on the coarsened graph for coarse predictions; (3) a second LPA stage within subgraphs produces final per-user recommendations.
AI.result: On a real-world telecom dataset, the LPA+LPA variant achieves +24% NDCG@5 over a full-graph LPA baseline. Adding a lightweight GNN in the first stage boosts NDCG@5 by over 50% but incurs higher training/inference costs.
AI.conclusion: The coarsening-driven two-stage diffusion approach delivers an optimal trade-off between scalability, latency, and recommendation quality, with flexible configurations (LPA vs. GNN) to suit different operational constraints.

title: Synthetic Speech, Real Signal: Paralinguistic Preservation and Cross-Lingual Augmentation via Voice Cloning
summary: Synthetic data augmentation in speech is common practice for linguistic tasks like ASR, but has seen far less work for paralinguistic ones, especially clinical tasks where labelled data is expensive and some patient groups are underrepresented. Voice cloning is one such augmentation approach, but is typically evaluated on speech intelligibility (WER) or speaker similarity (SS) rather than on downstream performance, and it remains unclear whether these preserve the paralinguistic signal such tasks depend on. We benchmark eight voice cloning models on five paralinguistic tasks across public and clinical datasets, showing most preserve signal with modest degradation. We then clone English clinical speech into Japanese and find that training on cloned data outperforms raw cross-lingual transfer for depression and anxiety detection on real Japanese speech, suggesting voice cloning is a promising direction for augmenting clinical speech data in low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks eight voice cloning models across five paralinguistic tasks, finding that most preserve the paralinguistic signal with only modest degradation. It further demonstrates that cloning English clinical speech into Japanese improves depression and anxiety detection on real Japanese speech, outperforming raw cross-lingual transfer.
AI.motivation: Synthetic data augmentation via voice cloning is underexplored for paralinguistic tasks, particularly in clinical settings where labeled data is scarce and patient groups are underrepresented. Existing voice cloning evaluations focus on speech intelligibility (WER) or speaker similarity (SS), leaving it unclear whether cloned speech retains the paralinguistic features essential for downstream clinical tasks.
AI.method: The authors benchmark eight voice cloning models on five paralinguistic tasks using both public and clinical datasets to assess preservation of paralinguistic signal. They further conduct a cross-lingual experiment by cloning English clinical speech into Japanese, then training on the cloned data and evaluating on real Japanese speech for depression and anxiety detection, comparing against raw cross-lingual transfer baselines.
AI.result: Most voice cloning models preserve the paralinguistic signal with only modest degradation across the five tasks. Training on Japanese-cloned English clinical speech outperforms raw cross-lingual transfer for detecting depression and anxiety on real Japanese speech.
AI.conclusion: Voice cloning is a promising direction for augmenting clinical speech data, especially for low-resource languages where labeled paralinguistic data is limited. The approach can enable effective cross-lingual transfer of clinical speech resources.

title: Evolution-Aware MSA Reasoning for Subsampling via Factor Graphs
summary: Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) provide protein language models with explicit evolutionary context, but their large depth makes subsampling unavoidable under limited token budgets. Existing strategies, including random selection, identity-based filtering, and diversity-driven sampling, are effective heuristics, yet provide limited control over the evolutionary signals retained in the subset. In this work, we recast MSA subsampling as an explicit optimization problem, where key evolutionary measures, including query identity and diversity, are treated as controllable objectives. Building on this view, we introduce AP-REASONER, an Affinity-Propagation-based factor-graph approach. With evolution-aware unary factors, exemplar-consistency factors, and two control knobs, AP-REASONER performs factor-graph reasoning through message passing to infer a fixed-budget MSA subset. Experiments on long-range contact prediction and conformational ensemble prediction show that AP-REASONER outperforms baseline subsamplers on structure-sensitive downstream tasks and enables controllable recovery of alternative protein conformations. These results highlight the value of modeling MSA subsampling as a controllable optimization problem, where factor-graph reasoning offers an effective alternative to heuristic selection.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts MSA subsampling as a controllable optimization problem and proposes AP-REASONER, an Affinity-Propagation-based factor-graph approach with evolution-aware factors and tunable knobs, outperforming heuristic baselines on structure-sensitive tasks.
AI.motivation: MSAs are critical for protein language models but are too deep for fixed token budgets, forcing subsampling. Existing heuristics (random, identity-filtering, diversity-driven) lack explicit control over which evolutionary signals — particularly query identity and diversity — are preserved in the subset, limiting downstream structural task performance.
AI.method: AP-REASONER frames MSA subsampling as an explicit optimization over controllable objectives. It uses an Affinity-Propagation factor-graph with: (1) evolution-aware unary factors encoding per-sequence relevance, (2) exemplar-consistency factors promoting representative sequence selection, and (3) two control knobs that modulate the trade-off between query identity and diversity. Message-passing inference selects a fixed-budget subset.
AI.result: AP-REASONER outperforms baseline subsamplers on long-range contact prediction and conformational ensemble prediction. It also enables controllable recovery of alternative protein conformations, demonstrating that explicit optimization yields better structure-sensitive downstream performance than heuristic selection.
AI.conclusion: Modeling MSA subsampling as a controllable optimization problem, solved via factor-graph reasoning with Affinity Propagation, provides an effective and principled alternative to heuristic subsampling, with practical benefits for protein structure-related tasks and conformational diversity recovery.

title: Beyond Binary Rooftop Mapping: A Four-Class Deep Learning Framework for Green Roof Potential Assessment from Open Swiss Geospatial Data
summary: The development of effective urban climate adaptation strategies requires comprehensive spatial information on rooftops and buildings, since such information underpins the assessment of ecosystem services provided by green infrastructure, particularly for urban heat island (UHI) mitigation. Although green roofs are widely acknowledged as a promising measure for improving urban thermal comfort, most existing research maps either current green rooftops or rooftops with greening potential, but not both. This study presents a modified deep convolutional neural network rooftop classification framework based on Roofpedia, developed by the Urban Analytics Lab at the National University of Singapore. The proposed model combines high resolution aerial imagery with rooftop slope information derived from a digital surface model and relies entirely on publicly available Swisstopo datasets: SWISSIMAGE orthophotos, swissSURFACE3D elevation data, and swissTLM3D building footprints. Applied to Bern, Switzerland, the model labels rooftops into four categories: existing green roofs, rooftops suitable for green roof installation, rooftops with solar panels, and flat rooftops unsuitable for greening. The framework identifies realistic opportunities for green roof expansion and supplies urban planners with evidence-based information for green infrastructure deployment in Bern and other Swiss cities. Because it is fully open source, the framework is transferable to cities worldwide.

AI.tldr: A modified deep CNN framework based on Roofpedia classifies rooftops in Bern, Switzerland into four categories (existing green roofs, greening-suitable, solar panels, unsuitable flat roofs) using publicly available aerial imagery, elevation data, and building footprints. The open-source model aids urban planners in identifying green roof expansion opportunities for UHI mitigation.
AI.motivation: Urban climate adaptation strategies require detailed rooftop spatial information to assess ecosystem services from green infrastructure, especially for urban heat island (UHI) mitigation. Existing studies typically map either current green roofs or potential green roofs, but not both simultaneously.
AI.method: A modified deep convolutional neural network classification framework, building on Roofpedia (NUS Urban Analytics Lab), integrates high-resolution SWISSIMAGE orthophotos, swissSURFACE3D-derived rooftop slope, and swissTLM3D building footprints — all publicly available Swisstopo datasets — to classify rooftops into four categories in Bern, Switzerland.
AI.result: The model successfully labels rooftops into: (1) existing green roofs, (2) rooftops suitable for green roof installation, (3) rooftops with solar panels, and (4) flat rooftops unsuitable for greening. It identifies realistic opportunities for green roof expansion in Bern.
AI.conclusion: The fully open-source framework provides urban planners with evidence-based, spatially explicit information for deploying green infrastructure in Bern and other Swiss cities, and is transferable to cities worldwide due to its reliance on commonly available data types.

title: IQ-JEPA: A Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with a Hermitian Vision Transformer for Sound Speed and Attenuation Estimation from Ultrasound IQ Data
summary: The speed of sound in tissue is a prerequisite for well-focused imaging and has diagnostic value, but recovering it from raw pulse-echo channel data is fundamentally a nonlinear inverse problem. Learned solvers are fast yet label hungry. Simulated sound-speed labels are expensive, while abundant real channel data is unlabeled. We propose IQ-JEPA to exploit both data types. An encoder is pretrained without labels to predict the latent representation of masked in-phase and quadrature (IQ) regions from visible context, then fine-tuned on simulated maps. Sound speed appears in the IQ signal as a phase difference, invariant to the constant phase offset. The encoder is a Hermitian vision transformer that operates on the complex signal directly. Its attention is equivariant to that phase and its conjugate-product feed-forward is invariant to it, so the encoder reads a quantity analogous to the one classical coherence methods use. On 79,293 Fullwave 2.5 simulations at 2.5 MHz, pretraining on the 63,435 unlabeled acquisitions reaches 15.60 m/s at 10,000 labels. This is a roughly threefold gain in label efficiency over supervised training, growing to over fourfold at 1,000 labels. It is about 2.2x below an InversionNet baseline, and 8.71 m/s at full labels. The gain still grows with more unlabeled pretraining data. Our comparisons point to self-supervision as the dominant factor. The same encoder transfers. Its frozen features expose sound speed and attenuation, and cross-distribution pretraining between layered and abdominal phantoms costs little accuracy. We see this as a first step toward a foundation model for quantitative ultrasound.

AI.tldr: IQ-JEPA is a self-supervised pretraining framework for ultrasound sound-speed estimation that trains a Hermitian vision transformer on unlabeled IQ data via a masked prediction objective, then fine-tunes on simulated labels, achieving ~3× label efficiency gains over supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Recovering sound speed from raw pulse-echo ultrasound channel data is a nonlinear inverse problem. Learned solvers are fast but require expensive simulated labels, while abundant real channel data remains unlabeled. The authors seek to exploit both data types to improve label efficiency.
AI.method: IQ-JEPA pretrains a Hermitian vision transformer encoder without labels using a self-supervised objective: predict latent representations of masked IQ regions from visible context. The architecture exploits the physics that sound speed manifests as a phase difference in IQ signals, invariant to constant phase offset. Attention is designed to be equivariant to this phase, and the conjugate-product feed-forward is invariant to it — mimicking classical coherence-based estimators. After pretraining on unlabeled acquisitions, the encoder is fine-tuned on simulated sound-speed maps.
AI.result: On 79,293 Fullwave 2.5 simulations at 2.5 MHz, pretraining on 63,435 unlabeled acquisitions achieves 15.60 m/s RMSE at 10,000 labels — roughly 3× label efficiency gain over supervised training (growing to >4× at 1,000 labels). At full labels, it reaches 8.71 m/s, about 2.2× below an InversionNet baseline. Gains continue growing with more unlabeled data. Frozen encoder features expose both sound speed and attenuation. Cross-distribution pretraining between layered and abdominal phantoms incurs little accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervision is the dominant factor driving label efficiency gains. The approach represents a first step toward a foundation model for quantitative ultrasound, with the encoder transferring across distributions and its features revealing physically meaningful tissue properties.

title: Integrated Order Dispatching and Routing for Last-Mile Pickup via Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: In recent years, the growing complexity of last-mile pickup operations has increased the need for fast and accurate decision-making on logistics platforms. This challenge is fundamentally driven by two key and tightly coupled decision-making processes: order dispatching and routing. Solving them separately overlooks their interdependence, while fully end-to-end learning can be unstable and costly on large, variable-scale instances due to sparse rewards. To solve this problem, we propose an integrated optimization framework which couples a learned routing oracle with real-time dispatching heuristics. For the routing subproblem, we develop a Dynamic-Residual Graph Attention Network encoder with a Look-Ahead Courier-Personalized decoder. For the dispatching subproblem, we develop a routing-oracle-guided dispatching heuristic with local search, where the oracle provides near-optimal solutions to select candidate couriers while retaining real-time scalability. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets from Cainiao Logistics are used to test the performance of our approach, including an offline evaluation and an online rolling-horizon simulation. The experimental results show that our approach outperforms other benchmarks regarding solution quality and solving time, indicating it can effectively support logistics companies in solving real-time and large-scale last-mile pickup problems.

AI.tldr: Proposes an integrated optimization framework combining a learned routing oracle (Dynamic-Residual GAT encoder + Look-Ahead Courier-Personalized decoder) with oracle-guided dispatching heuristics for real-time last-mile pickup operations, outperforming benchmarks on Cainiao logistics data.
AI.motivation: Last-mile pickup operations involve tightly coupled order dispatching and routing decisions. Solving them separately ignores interdependence, while end-to-end learning suffers from instability and high cost due to sparse rewards on large, variable-scale instances.
AI.method: An integrated two-stage framework: (1) For routing, a Dynamic-Residual Graph Attention Network (GAT) encoder with a Look-Ahead Courier-Personalized decoder learns a near-optimal routing oracle. (2) For dispatching, a heuristic guided by the routing oracle with local search selects candidate couriers in real time while preserving scalability.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world Cainiao Logistics datasets in both offline evaluation and online rolling-horizon simulation show the approach outperforms benchmarks in solution quality and solving time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively supports logistics companies in solving real-time, large-scale last-mile pickup problems by integrating learned routing with dispatching heuristics.

title: Indexing: the Beginning and the End
summary:
We study information bottlenecks in modern deep-learning architectures -- RNNs, softmax transformers, linear-attention transformers and state-space models -- through the lens of the indexing primitive. In this primitive, the input consists of $n$ bits and one integer $i$ from $1$ to $n$ called the index, and the output equals the value of the $i$-th bit.
  We introduce causal complexity for masked architectures. We show that architectures with low causal complexity cannot solve the indexing primitive in any constant number of layers when the index appears at the end of the input. In particular, this limitation applies to low-parameter RNNs, SSMs and masked linear-attention transformers. In contrast, small softmax transformers can solve it in one layer, while non-masked linear-attention transformers can solve it in 2, which separates them from their masked counterparts. In turn, when the index appears at the beginning, we show that small RNNs are capable of solving this task in 1 layer, while all the other architectures require 2.
  All our impossibility results are unconditional and apply even to models that employ infinite-precision real arithmetic. Moreover, experiments for up to $n=64$ qualitatively align with our theory: configurations with low-parameter theoretical solutions learn the indexing task easily, while configurations that do not admit such theoretical solutions struggle to learn as the sequence length grows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "causal complexity" to analyze information bottlenecks in masked architectures (RNNs, SSMs, masked linear-attention transformers) by studying the indexing primitive. It proves unconditional impossibility results showing low-causal-complexity architectures cannot solve indexing when the index appears at the end, while softmax and non-masked linear-attention transformers can. Experiments up to n=64 corroborate the theory.
AI.motivation: To formally characterize and separate the representational capabilities of modern deep-learning architectures (RNNs, softmax transformers, linear-attention transformers, SSMs) by identifying fundamental information bottlenecks, particularly in masked/autoregressive settings relevant to language modeling.
AI.method: The authors introduce the indexing primitive (n bits + index i, output the i-th bit) as a probe task. They define "causal complexity" — a formal measure of information flow in masked architectures — and prove unconditional lower bounds: architectures with low causal complexity cannot solve indexing in constant layers when the index is at the end. The analysis holds even with infinite-precision real arithmetic. They also provide constructive upper bounds showing small softmax transformers (1 layer) and non-masked linear-attention transformers (2 layers) can solve it.
AI.result: Key separations: (1) Low-parameter RNNs, SSMs, and masked linear-attention transformers cannot solve indexing with end-positioned index in any constant layers. (2) Small softmax transformers solve it in 1 layer; non-masked linear-attention transformers in 2 layers. (3) With index at the beginning, small RNNs solve in 1 layer, while all others require 2. Experiments on n≤64 confirm that configurations with theoretical solutions learn easily, while those without struggle as sequence length grows.
AI.conclusion: The indexing primitive and causal complexity framework reveal fundamental separations between modern architectures. Softmax attention and non-masked linear attention possess greater representational capacity for certain sequential reasoning tasks than their masked counterparts and low-parameter recurrent/state-space models, with implications for architecture design in language modeling.

title: Interior interpretability with attention rollout: contraction and propagation profiles in Transformers
summary: Feature-attribution methods assign scores relating input variables to a model's output, but do not by themselves characterize how explicitly defined interaction operators compose across its intermediate layers. We introduce \emph{interior interpretability}, a propagation-based perspective on internal model organization, and instantiate it for tabular Transformers using attention rollout. We interpret rollout as a row-stochastic operator encoding attention-mediated propagation between feature tokens. By applying classical Doeblin--Dobrushin contraction theory, we show that a rollout operator with a small Dobrushin coefficient is quantitatively close to a rank-one stochastic matrix whose common row is determined by its normalized column sums. This result gives a structural interpretation to the corresponding rollout propagation profile. In Transformers trained for metabolomic age prediction, the measured rollout contraction strengthens with depth. Trained and randomly initialized models also exhibit different propagation profiles, although the present experiments do not establish the predictive relevance of individual rollout-ranked variables. Exploratory comparisons with PCA and GradientExplainer approximations to SHAP reveal localized agreement among highly ranked variables but weak agreement across complete rankings. Attention rollout is therefore used here as a diagnostic of attention-mediated propagation, not as a causal explanation or faithful attribution of the complete Transformer.

AI.tldr: Introduces "interior interpretability" — analyzing how attention-mediated propagation operates across internal layers of tabular Transformers via rollout. Applies Doeblin–Dobrushin contraction theory to show low-Dobrushin-coefficient rollout operators are near rank-one, structurally interpretable matrices. Demonstrates in metabolomic age prediction that rollout contraction strengthens with depth and differs between trained vs. random models, while noting rollout is a diagnostic, not a causal explanation.
AI.motivation: Feature-attribution methods (e.g., SHAP) assign input–output importance scores but fail to characterize how explicitly defined interaction operators compose across a model's intermediate layers. The authors seek to understand internal propagation structure in Transformers, particularly for tabular data, going beyond single-step attribution to multi-layer information flow.
AI.method: The authors propose "interior interpretability," instantiating it via attention rollout — a row-stochastic operator encoding attention-mediated propagation between feature tokens across Transformer layers. They apply classical Doeblin–Dobrushin contraction theory to prove that when the rollout operator has a small Dobrushin coefficient, it approximates a rank-one stochastic matrix whose rows equal normalized column sums, providing a structural interpretation. Empirically, they train Transformers for metabolomic age prediction, measure rollout contraction dynamics across depth, compare trained vs. randomly initialized models, and contrast rollout rankings with PCA and GradientExplainer-SHAP approximations.
AI.result: Rollout contraction (Dobrushin coefficient) strengthens monotonically with depth in trained Transformers. Trained and random models exhibit distinct propagation profiles. Localized agreement exists between rollout, PCA, and SHAP-based rankings for highly ranked variables, but global ranking agreement is weak. The authors explicitly caution that rollout rankings are not established as predictively relevant, and that attention rollout serves as a diagnostic of propagation, not a causal or faithful attribution method.
AI.conclusion: Attention rollout with contraction-theoretic analysis offers a mathematically grounded diagnostic for understanding how information propagates internally across Transformer layers. The rank-one approximation property under low Dobrushin coefficients gives structural interpretability. However, rollout remains descriptive rather than causally explanatory, and agreement with attribution methods is limited to top-ranked variables. The framework opens avenues for interior analysis complementary to input-level feature attribution.

title: Local-Global Geometric Insights for Graph Neural Networks via Entropic Curvature
summary: Curvature notions on graphs, particularly Ollivier-Ricci and Forman, have emerged as powerful tools for addressing fundamental issues in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) such as oversmoothing and oversquashing, but rely almost exclusively on local edge-level comparisons and therefore fail to certify how information actually propagates over long distances. We introduce Entropic Curvature, a global, transport-based curvature obtained by extending the Lott-Sturm-Villani framework to graphs through the displacement convexity of entropy along Wasserstein geodesics. We define a tractable Weak Entropic Curvature proxy that lower-bounds the global entropic curvature, and from it derive (i) a Poincare-type inequality controlling oversmoothing, (ii) a transport-entropy generalization bound, and (iii) an expansion paradox proving that sparsity, strong spectral expansion, and positive entropic curvature cannot coexist in large graphs, unifying oversmoothing and oversquashing as opposite ends of a single curvature spectrum. We translate the theory into three practical mechanisms, the E-Gate aggregator, the ENT structural encoding, and Midpoint-Completion Rewiring (MCR), and benchmark them against SDRF, FoSR, BORF, LCP, and Graph Ricci Flow on six node-classification benchmarks, and graph-classification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Entropic Curvature, a global transport-based graph curvature extending the Lott-Sturm-Villani framework to graphs. It provides theoretical results unifying oversmoothing and oversquashing as ends of a curvature spectrum, and translates theory into three practical mechanisms: E-Gate aggregator, ENT structural encoding, and Midpoint-Completion Rewiring (MCR).
AI.motivation: Existing graph curvature notions (Ollivier-Ricci, Forman) rely on local edge-level comparisons and cannot certify how information propagates over long distances in GNNs, limiting their ability to address oversmoothing and oversquashing in a unified manner.
AI.method: Extends the Lott-Sturm-Villani framework to graphs via displacement convexity of entropy along Wasserstein geodesics, defining Entropic Curvature. Derives a tractable Weak Entropic Curvature proxy that lower-bounds the global curvature. From this, proves a Poincaré-type inequality, a transport-entropy generalization bound, and an expansion paradox. Translates theory into E-Gate aggregator, ENT structural encoding, and Midpoint-Completion Rewiring.
AI.result: The expansion paradox proves sparsity, strong spectral expansion, and positive entropic curvature cannot coexist in large graphs. The three practical mechanisms are benchmarked against SDRF, FoSR, BORF, LCP, and Graph Ricci Flow on six node-classification and graph-classification benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Entropic Curvature provides a unified theoretical framework for oversmoothing and oversquashing in GNNs, positioned as opposite ends of a single curvature spectrum, with practical architectural and rewiring interventions that are empirically validated.

title: LunarFM: A Shared Multimodal Representation of the Moon's Surface
summary: The renewed global focus on lunar exploration, driven by the prospect of in-situ resource utilization and a sustained human presence on the Moon, has created growing demand for accurate, large-scale characterization of the lunar surface. Although vast quantities of orbital remote-sensing data have been collected, scientific analysis and resource mapping remain fragmented by heterogeneous multiinstrument observations, sparse labels, and bespoke task-specific modelling workflows. Here we introduce LunarFM, a multimodal foundation model that learns a general representation of the lunar surface from diverse orbital measurements. LunarFM assimilates observations from six instruments across three lunar missions, mapping 18 input channels to a shared embedding space. We demonstrate that this embedding space supports a diverse range of downstream applications, including similarity search, few-shot resource mapping, mineral abundance regression, and geological unit classification, enabling efficient scientific investigation and resource-oriented analysis. We provide a machine-learning-ready dataset of co-registered multimodal observations spanning latitudes from 70°S to 70°N, a pretrained multimodal masked autoencoder, and a companion embedding dataset providing a joint 768-dimensional representation of lunar surface properties. All code and data are available at https://lunarfm.trillium.tech/

AI.tldr: LunarFM is a multimodal foundation model that fuses observations from six instruments across three lunar missions into a shared 768-dimensional embedding space, enabling diverse downstream tasks such as similarity search, few-shot resource mapping, mineral abundance regression, and geological classification.
AI.motivation: Lunar exploration and in-situ resource utilization demand large-scale, accurate characterization of the lunar surface, but current approaches are fragmented by heterogeneous multi-instrument data, sparse labels, and task-specific workflows that hinder unified analysis.
AI.method: LunarFM employs a multimodal masked autoencoder architecture that assimilates 18 input channels from six instruments across three lunar missions. It maps co-registered observations into a joint 768-dimensional embedding space via self-supervised pretraining, producing a general-purpose representation of lunar surface properties spanning 70°S to 70°N.
AI.result: The learned embedding space supports diverse downstream applications: similarity search across the lunar surface, few-shot resource mapping with limited labels, mineral abundance regression, and geological unit classification. The authors also release a machine-learning-ready co-registered multimodal dataset and a companion embedding dataset.
AI.conclusion: LunarFM demonstrates that foundation model pretraining on heterogeneous orbital remote-sensing data can produce a unified, versatile representation of planetary surfaces, streamlining both scientific investigation and resource-oriented analysis. All code, data, and model weights are publicly released.

title: On the Identifiability of Controlled World Models
summary: Learning world models that infer environment dynamics from high-dimensional observations and predict outcomes under candidate actions is central to planning and control. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide a compelling framework for learning such models in representation space. Recent action-conditioned extensions perform promisingly in visual control and latent-space planning, but leave a fundamental question unresolved: when does controlled latent prediction identify both the underlying state and the controlled dynamics? This is challenging under nonlinear observations and behavior policies with limited conditional action variation, where state-dependent evolution and action effects can be statistically confounded. We establish a joint identifiability theory for controlled world models with Gaussian latent states under state-dependent Gaussian behavior policies. We identify two policy-dependent conditions: spectral separation of the predictable signal governs representation identifiability, while non-degenerate conditional action variation governs transition identifiability. We prove that when both conditions hold, every global minimizer of the JEPA objective identifies the latent state and controlled transition up to an orthogonal transformation. We further derive quantitative bounds on representation and transition identifiability under approximate optimization. Finally, we construct predictor perturbations along weakly excited action directions whose counterfactual-to-on-policy error ratio is the inverse transition-identifiability margin, revealing the cost of limited action coverage. Experiments across nonlinear observation maps and behavior policies corroborate the theory and demonstrate implications for transition identifiability, counterfactual prediction, and goal-conditioned latent planning.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a joint identifiability theory for action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) with Gaussian latent states under state-dependent Gaussian policies. It identifies two policy-dependent conditions — spectral separation of predictable signal (for representation recovery) and non-degenerate conditional action variation (for transition recovery) — proving that global minimizers identify latent states and transitions up to an orthogonal transformation. The theory also quantifies counterfactual prediction error when action coverage is limited.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned JEPAs show empirical promise for visual control and latent-space planning, but it remains fundamentally unclear *when* controlled latent prediction actually identifies the true underlying state and transition dynamics. The core challenge is statistical confounding: under nonlinear observations and behavior policies with limited action variation, state-dependent evolution and action effects become entangled, threatening identifiability. No prior theory addresses this joint identifiability question.
AI.method: The authors formulate a Gaussian linear-quadratic controlled world model with nonlinear observations. They analyze the JEPA objective's global minimizers under state-dependent Gaussian behavior policies. Two key conditions are derived: (1) spectral separation — the predictable signal's covariance spectrum must be well-separated to identify the representation; (2) non-degenerate conditional action variation — the action-conditioned covariance must have full rank to identify transition parameters. They prove that when both hold, minimizers recover the latent state and controlled transition up to an orthogonal transformation, and provide quantitative bounds under approximate optimization. They further construct predictor perturbations along weakly-excited action directions to characterize the counterfactual-to-on-policy error ratio.
AI.result: The main theoretical result is a joint identifiability theorem: under spectral separation and non-degenerate action variation, every global minimizer of the JEPA objective identifies the latent state and controlled transition uniquely up to an orthogonal transformation. Quantitative bounds are derived for approximate optimization regimes. The counterfactual error analysis reveals that the error ratio along weakly-excited action directions equals the inverse transition-identifiability margin, explicitly characterizing the cost of limited action coverage. Experiments across nonlinear observation maps and behavior policies corroborate the theory and demonstrate practical implications for transition identifiability, counterfactual prediction, and goal-conditioned latent planning.
AI.conclusion: Controlled world model identifiability hinges critically on policy-dependent conditions: spectral separation for representation learning and sufficient conditional action variation for transition learning. When action coverage is limited, counterfactual prediction error can be precisely quantified. These results provide theoretical grounding for JEPA-based world models and offer practical guidance for behavior policy design in visual control and latent planning tasks.

title: Hyperball May Not Be a Free Lunch
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Code: https://github.com/mangocrazz/hyperball-may-not-be-a-free-lunch. Equal contribution: Yihao Xiao and Jialong Sun. Corresponding author: Bryan Dai
summary: For scale-invariant deep networks, Hyperball-style optimizers have shown strong performance in large-scale training by fixing the norms of matrix-valued parameters and normalizing updates. However, the source of their advantage remains unclear. Starting from the angular displacement between consecutive parameter states, we derive an angular effective learning rate that accounts for the parameter-update angle, parameter norm, and update norm. We also show that the conventional norm-based measure is a special case under parameter-update orthogonality. We then decompose optimizer updates into radial and tangential components and analyze how radial updates affect one-step angular displacement. Under the training configurations considered, numerical results show that the radial component has only a limited direct effect on the angular effective learning rate. It therefore cannot explain why MuonH converges more slowly than MuonWD early in training but overtakes it later. To further isolate the underlying mechanism, we devise a heuristic experiment that modifies only the learning-rate schedule so that the dynamics of each optimizer reproduce those of the other. The results suggest that their main difference stems from the evolution of the effective step size rather than an intrinsically superior update direction induced by Hyperball. Our pretraining experiments further show that more aggressive learning-rate decay can accelerate MuonH early in training but may impair its later performance. Thus, maintaining a constant angular velocity does not eliminate the learning-rate-scheduling problem; careful scheduling remains essential to realizing the potential of Hyperball-style optimizers. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mangocrazz/hyperball-may-not-be-a-free-lunch.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why Hyperball-style optimizers (MuonH, MuonWD) differ in training dynamics. Through angular effective learning rate analysis and radial/tangential decomposition, the authors find that performance differences stem from effective step-size evolution rather than intrinsically superior update directions. They demonstrate that aggressive LR decay can accelerate early MuonH training but may impair later performance, showing that Hyperball does not eliminate the need for careful learning-rate scheduling.
AI.motivation: Hyperball-style optimizers (which fix parameter norms and normalize updates) perform well in large-scale training, but the source of their advantage remains unclear. Beyond aggregate performance, understanding why MuonH and MuonWD exhibit different convergence trajectories — MuonWD converges faster early on but is later overtaken by MuonH — motivates a deeper mechanistic analysis.
AI.method: The authors derive an angular effective learning rate from the angular displacement between consecutive parameter states, accounting for the parameter-update angle, parameter norm, and update norm. They decompose optimizer updates into radial and tangential components and analyze how radial updates affect one-step angular displacement. They also devise a heuristic experiment that modifies the learning-rate schedule so that each optimizer reproduces the other's dynamics, isolating the role of effective step size versus update direction.
AI.result: Numerical results show the radial component has limited direct effect on the angular effective learning rate, so it cannot explain the MuonH vs. MuonWD convergence crossover. The heuristic swap experiment reveals that the main difference stems from effective step-size evolution, not a superior update direction. Pretraining experiments show aggressive LR decay accelerates early MuonH training but may impair later performance.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a constant angular velocity (as in Hyperball) does not eliminate the learning-rate scheduling problem. Careful scheduling remains essential to fully realize the potential of Hyperball-style optimizers. The advantage is more about effective step-size dynamics than intrinsically better update geometry.

title: Phylogenetic signal in marine mammal and bird vocalizations captured by audio foundation models: the limited benefit of domain-specific pretraining
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 2 supplementary tables. Code, embeddings and derived matrices: https://github.com/rinvictor/bioacoustic-phylogeny-embeddings
summary:
Do learned audio embeddings encode structure that nobody told them to encode? We probe four large pretrained audio models (AST, CLAP, BEATs-bio and BirdNET) with a downstream task none of them saw during training: recovering phylogenetic distance from species vocalizations. If the geometry of the embedding space tracks the tree of life, the representation is picking up something deeper than the labels the model was optimized for.
  We run Mantel tests across two independent radiations. In 32 marine mammal species (1,754 recordings from the Watkins Marine Mammal Sound Database) the foundation models recover strong phylogenetic signal within the 26 cetaceans (CLAP r=0.82, BEATs-bio r=0.82, AST r=0.74; all p<0.001), among the highest acoustic-phylogenetic correlations reported for any taxon. Hand-crafted MFCC features (105d) find nothing (r=0.040, p=0.338). The gap survives after PCA-projecting every embedding down to 105 dimensions, so it is not an artefact of representation size. It also survives a partial Mantel test controlling for dominant frequency (partial Mantel r=0.404, keeping 97% of the variance explained), so it is not just pitch in disguise.
  We repeat the analysis on 20 bird species using the Jetz et al. (2012) phylogeny, and this time add BirdNET, a classifier trained end-to-end on around 6,000 bird species. The general-purpose foundation models recover the signal again (AST r=0.55, CLAP r=0.52). The unexpected result is that neither BirdNET nor the bioacoustic BEATs-bio beat them (r around 0.32 to 0.36). Matching the training domain to the target taxon does not, by itself, help. Pretrained audio embeddings carry evolutionary information across two independent radiations, and domain-specific pretraining is not required for it to emerge.

AI.tldr: Pretrained audio foundation models (AST, CLAP, BEATs-bio) encode phylogenetic structure in embedding spaces — recovering evolutionary distance from species vocalizations — despite never being trained on such a task. This signal is absent in hand-crafted MFCC features and persists after controlling for pitch and dimensionality. Surprisingly, domain-specific models (BirdNET, BEATs-bio) do not outperform general-purpose models.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether large pretrained audio models spontaneously learn representations that reflect deep biological structure (phylogenetic relationships) from animal vocalizations, even when optimized only for tasks like classification or contrastive learning.
AI.method: Probed four pretrained audio models (AST, CLAP, BEATs-bio, BirdNET) on a downstream task of recovering phylogenetic distance from vocalization embeddings. Ran Mantel tests on two independent datasets: (1) 32 marine mammal species (1,754 recordings from Watkins Marine Mammal Sound Database) and (2) 20 bird species using the Jetz et al. (2012) phylogeny. Compared against MFCC baselines. Applied PCA dimensionality reduction controls and partial Mantel tests controlling for dominant frequency.
AI.result: Foundation models showed strong phylogenetic signal in cetaceans (CLAP r=0.82, BEATs-bio r=0.82, AST r=0.74; all p<0.001). MFCC features showed none (r=0.040, p=0.338). Signal survived PCA reduction to 105 dimensions and partial Mantel controlling for dominant frequency (r=0.404, 97% variance retained). In birds, general-purpose models (AST r=0.55, CLAP r=0.52) outperformed domain-specific BirdNET and BEATs-bio (r≈0.32–0.36). Domain-specific pretraining did not enhance phylogenetic recovery.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained audio embeddings carry evolutionary information across independent taxonomic radiations. This emergent phylogenetic structure does not require domain-specific pretraining, suggesting that large-scale audio pretraining captures fundamental acoustic properties that align with evolutionary relationships.

title: Complexity Bounds and Approaches to Learning Projected Gradient Descent Solver Iterates
summary: Data scarcity poses a fundamental challenge in training generative models to produce initial guesses for parametric optimization problems that are otherwise numerically expensive to solve. We therefore study a $k$-neighborhood data collection strategy that augments datasets of converged solutions with intermediate solver iterates, increasing the amount of training data without additional solver runs. To understand the benefits of this approach, we derive a generalization bound based on Rademacher complexity that reveals the role of the $k$-neighborhoods and related parameters. To achieve this result, we focus on one-sided box-constrained quadratic programs solved by projected gradient descent. We illustrate the behavior of this solver on two examples. The approach proposed in this paper enables a more capable DDDAS paradigm by improving the efficiency of the data-model-optimization loop. We finish by discussing two views of learning solver-iterate data and connect our analysis with GLENS, a new data-efficient global search method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a k-neighborhood data collection strategy that augments training datasets with intermediate solver iterates to mitigate data scarcity in learning-based parametric optimization. A Rademacher complexity generalization bound is derived for box-constrained quadratic programs solved via projected gradient descent, revealing how k-neighborhood parameters affect learning. The approach improves the DDDAS paradigm and connects to the GLENS global search method.
AI.motivation: Training generative models to produce initial guesses for expensive parametric optimization problems suffers from data scarcity, since obtaining converged solutions requires costly numerical solver runs. The authors aim to increase training data volume without additional solver runs by exploiting intermediate solver iterates.
AI.method: The paper proposes a k-neighborhood data collection strategy that samples intermediate iterates from solver trajectories and augments the dataset of converged solutions. The analysis focuses on one-sided box-constrained quadratic programs solved by projected gradient descent. A generalization bound based on Rademacher complexity is derived to characterize how k-neighborhood parameters influence learning guarantees. The method is illustrated on two examples and connected to the GLENS global search framework.
AI.result: The derived Rademacher complexity bound formally quantifies the trade-offs of the k-neighborhood data augmentation strategy, revealing the role of neighborhood size and related parameters. The approach enhances the efficiency of the data-model-optimization loop within the DDDAS (Dynamic Data-Driven Application Systems) paradigm. The connection to GLENS demonstrates data-efficient global search capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The k-neighborhood data collection strategy effectively addresses data scarcity in learning-to-optimize settings by leveraging intermediate solver iterates. The theoretical generalization bound provides principled guidance for parameter selection. The approach strengthens the DDDAS framework and integrates with data-efficient global search methods like GLENS.

title: Beyond Negative-Ridge Endpoints: Mixed-Sign Spectral Regularization via Negative-Shifted Gradient Descent
summary: In overparameterized linear regression, many weak spectral directions act like a ridge penalty on the signal-bearing spectrum; negative ridge is the natural correction, pushing filters above one. The stable negative-ridge endpoint, however, is structurally limited: its pole must stay below the smallest nonzero empirical eigenvalue, and it anti-shrinks smaller eigenvalues more than larger ones. Early-stopped negative-shifted gradient descent escapes this constraint. Its filter is smooth at the would-be pole and mixed-sign-capable: above-ridgeless directions form a leading prefix, with lower directions shrunk or exposure-controlled while stopping sets the crossover. In a Gaussian spike-plus-flat model we discover a Marchenko-Pastur barrier: the shift that cancels the implicit penalty lies a bulk width above the smallest empirical eigenvalue, and the stopped path improves on every admissible endpoint by a polynomial factor in risk under explicit conditions. Our main theorem permits a general high-effective-rank tail: its trace sets the implicit floor, its squared spectrum controls exposure, and the floor-critical path recovers all head scales at once, beyond positive shrinkage and, once scales separate, every uniform rescaling of ridgeless. Handling the noncontractive shifted dynamics is the central technical challenge; localized Duhamel integrals control them. A finite-grid hold-out inequality transfers the separations to the validation-selected algorithm.

AI.tldr: In overparameterized linear regression, early-stopped negative-shifted gradient descent outperforms both standard ridge and the structural negative-ridge endpoint by creating a smooth, mixed-sign filter that escapes Marchenko-Pastur constraints, achieving polynomial-factor risk improvements under explicit conditions.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized linear regression exhibits an implicit ridge penalty from weak spectral directions. While negative ridge emerges as a natural correction, its endpoint is structurally limited: the pole must stay below the smallest nonzero empirical eigenvalue, and it anti-shrinks smaller eigenvalues more than larger ones. The authors seek a method that escapes these constraints to achieve better risk performance.
AI.method: The authors analyze early-stopped gradient descent with a negative shift (negative-shifted GD). They model the problem using a Gaussian spike-plus-flat spectrum and characterize the filter behavior along the optimization path. Key technical tools include: (1) identifying a Marchenko-Pastur barrier that places the optimal shift a bulk width above the smallest empirical eigenvalue; (2) localized Duhamel integrals to control noncontractive shifted dynamics; (3) a finite-grid hold-out inequality to transfer spectral separations to a validation-selected algorithm. The main theorem accommodates a general high-effective-rank tail, where the tail's trace sets the implicit floor and its squared spectrum controls exposure.
AI.result: A Marchenko-Pastur barrier is discovered: the shift that cancels the implicit penalty sits one bulk width above the smallest empirical eigenvalue. The early-stopped negative-shifted GD path improves on every admissible negative-ridge endpoint by a polynomial factor in risk under explicit conditions. The floor-critical path recovers all head scales simultaneously, surpassing positive shrinkage and, once scales separate, every uniform rescaling of ridgeless regression.
AI.conclusion: Early-stopped negative-shifted gradient descent provides a practical and theoretically grounded way to exceed the limitations of negative-ridge endpoints in overparameterized linear regression. By leveraging the optimization path rather than a fixed endpoint, the method achieves superior risk performance across diverse spectral configurations.

title: \k{appa}-LoRA: Condition Numbers Reveal Which LoRA Matrices Worth Updating
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely adopted technique for efficient neural network fine-tuning, decomposing model updates into low-rank matrices. However, LoRA remains computationally costly because it updates all matrices uniformly, regardless of their actual contribution to adaptation. This cost is especially prohibitive for large-scale models with billions of parameters and for resource-constrained settings such as edge deployment and on-device fine-tuning. We show for the first time that not all LoRA matrices are equally worth tuning: matrices with smaller condition numbers (the ratio of largest to smallest singular value) are already well-balanced across directions and contribute only marginally to adaptation, whereas matrices with larger condition numbers contain underdeveloped directions that span richer subspaces and drive most of the performance gains. This observation itself is a key contribution of our work, and it motivates a more selective approach to fine-tuning. Building on this insight, we propose \k{appa}-LoRA, a method that optimizes LoRA by focusing updates on the matrices with the largest condition numbers, which capture the most informative directions of change. By restricting LoRA updates to the top 50% of weight matrices ranked by condition number, \k{appa}-LoRA halves the trainable parameter count and correspondingly reduces compute and memory cost. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that this design cuts fine-tuning time by 16.2% on average while matching the accuracy of standard LoRA and reducing memory cost by 4.5%. Further analysis reveals that the condition numbers of the selected matrices consistently decrease over training, suggesting that \k{appa}-LoRA's effectiveness stems from targeted spectral rebalancing rather than parameter selection alone.

AI.tldr: κ-LoRA selectively applies low-rank adaptation only to weight matrices with the largest condition numbers (top 50%), halving trainable parameters while matching standard LoRA accuracy. This cuts fine-tuning time by 16.2% and memory by 4.5%, driven by the insight that high-condition-number matrices contribute most to adaptation gains.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA applies low-rank updates uniformly across all weight matrices, incurring unnecessary computational and memory costs. This is prohibitive for billion-parameter models and resource-constrained settings like edge deployment. The authors observed that not all LoRA matrices contribute equally — motivating a selective approach that focuses tuning only where it matters most.
AI.method: The authors first establish that weight matrices with larger condition numbers (ratio of largest to smallest singular value) contain underdeveloped spectral directions that drive most performance gains, while low-condition-number matrices are already well-balanced and contribute marginally. Building on this, κ-LoRA ranks all LoRA-eligible matrices by condition number and restricts low-rank updates to only the top 50%, thereby halving the number of trainable parameters. The method requires no additional hyperparameters beyond the selection threshold.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, κ-LoRA reduces fine-tuning time by 16.2% on average and memory cost by 4.5% while matching standard LoRA accuracy. Additionally, the condition numbers of selected matrices consistently decrease over training, indicating that κ-LoRA achieves targeted spectral rebalancing rather than merely benefiting from parameter subset selection.
AI.conclusion: κ-LoRA demonstrates that condition number is an effective, principled criterion for identifying which weight matrices benefit most from low-rank adaptation. By focusing updates on spectrally imbalanced matrices, the method achieves notable efficiency gains without sacrificing accuracy, offering a practical solution for large-scale and resource-constrained fine-tuning scenarios.

title: Susceptible Reservoir Architectures for Regime-Conditional Volatility Forecasting
summary: Volatility forecasting is dominated by persistence and measurement noise, leaving limited residual structure for nonlinear models to exploit. We introduce Susceptible Architectures (SUSA), a reservoir-design principle for volatility forecasting, and its two concrete implementations, based on complex-valued open-chain and periodic reservoirs and regime-conditioned experts to interpret reservoir features across calm, onset, recovery, and persistent-stress states. We also implement open-system $q$-qubit counterparts in Qiskit while retaining a common AR-Ridge anchor and a bounded residual correction trained under QLIKE. We evaluate models on 16 U.S. equity and exchange-traded-fund series using three disjoint chronological training, validation, and test folds, a 12-observation input window, and a five-observation forecast horizon. The proposed models perform competitively with GARCH, achieving statistically significant QLIKE improvements for specific assets (IWM, XLP). Also models' forecasts complement HARQ-style predictions: a stacked ensemble improves mean QLIKE by 0.0116 over its strongest constituent and wins in 75% of test scenarios.

AI.tldr: Proposes SUSA, a reservoir-computing design principle for volatility forecasting with complex-valued and periodic reservoir implementations plus regime-conditioned experts, demonstrating competitive QLIKE performance against GARCH and complementary gains when stacked with HARQ-style models.
AI.motivation: Volatility series are dominated by persistence and measurement noise, leaving minimal residual structure for nonlinear models to exploit. The authors seek to design reservoir architectures that can nevertheless capture subtle nonlinear patterns useful for volatility forecasting.
AI.method: Introduces Susceptible Architectures (SUSA) with two implementations: (1) complex-valued open-chain and periodic reservoirs, and (2) regime-conditioned experts that interpret reservoir features across calm, onset, recovery, and persistent-stress states. Also implements open-system q-qubit counterparts in Qiskit. All models share a common AR-Ridge anchor and bounded residual correction trained under QLIKE loss. Evaluated on 16 U.S. equity and ETF series using three disjoint chronological folds, 12-observation input windows, and 5-step forecast horizons.
AI.result: Proposed models perform competitively with GARCH, achieving statistically significant QLIKE improvements for specific assets (IWM, XLP). A stacked ensemble combining the models' forecasts with HARQ-style predictions improves mean QLIKE by 0.0116 over its strongest constituent and wins in 75% of test scenarios.
AI.conclusion: SUSA-based reservoir architectures provide a viable nonlinear complement to traditional volatility models, particularly valuable in ensemble settings where they capture residual structure that persistence-dominated benchmarks miss.

title: Interpretable EEG biomarkers with bag-of-waves: Spatial and temporal waveform dictionaries for low-data regimes
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to diagnose neurological conditions, but its analysis usually relies on either predefined spectral features or deep neural networks. Predefined features carry a strong bias, since they fix in advance what counts as informative, while deep neural networks and foundation models are hard to interpret and need large amounts of data and compute. We present bag-of-waves, an interpretable framework that learns a small dictionary of recurring EEG waveform templates, called atoms, using shift-invariant k-means without labels. The continuous EEG is then turned into a sequence of atom tokens, whose counts feed a simple downstream classifier or clustering step. We extend this representation in two ways: we add atom-to-atom transitions, which we call n- grams, to capture temporal structure, and we move from single-channel atoms to regional and cross-channel spatial atoms for the multichannel case. We test the method on three complementary datasets, each probing a different aspect: single-channel mouse genotype clustering with only sixteen animals (the low-data and temporal case), resting-state dementia classification (the spatial case), and the TUEV benchmark, a six-way classification of clinical EEG events (a high-data comparison against strong deep and foundation baselines). Across all three datasets, bag-of-waves achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art deep and foundation models. Yet, it operates with a fraction of the parameter count and provides full interpretability: because every atom corresponds to an inspectable waveform, the method explicitly recovers known clinical morphologies that a neurophysiologist can directly validate. Its main advantage is that it works in the low-data regime where heavier models are a poor fit.

AI.tldr: Bag-of-waves is an interpretable EEG analysis framework that learns a dictionary of waveform templates via unsupervised shift-invariant k-means, converts EEG into atom token sequences, and uses token counts (plus optional n-gram transitions and spatial atoms) for classification/clustering. It achieves competitive performance with deep learning models while using far fewer parameters and providing full neurophysiological interpretability, particularly excelling in low-data regimes.
AI.motivation: Traditional EEG analysis relies on predefined spectral features (strong bias) or deep neural networks/foundation models (poor interpretability, data-hungry, computationally expensive). There is a need for a method that is both interpretable and effective in low-data settings, where heavy models fail.
AI.method: The method, bag-of-waves, uses shift-invariant k-means (unsupervised) to learn a compact dictionary of recurring EEG waveform templates called "atoms." Continuous EEG is discretized into sequences of atom tokens. Token counts feed a lightweight downstream classifier/clusterer. Two extensions are introduced: (1) n-grams capturing atom-to-atom transition structure, and (2) regional and cross-channel spatial atoms for multichannel data.
AI.result: Across three datasets — single-channel mouse genotype clustering (16 animals, low-data), resting-state dementia classification (spatial), and TUEV six-way clinical EEG event classification (high-data benchmark) — bag-of-waves matched or approached state-of-the-art deep and foundation model performance with a fraction of the parameters and full interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Bag-of-waves offers a compelling middle ground: competitive with deep models, interpretable (atoms map to clinically validatable morphologies), and particularly well-suited to low-data regimes where large models are inappropriate.

title: Dysphagia Risk Stratification in Head and Neck Cancer via Two-Stage PRO-Clinical Stacking
summary:
Dysphagia is a debilitating late effect of head and neck cancer (HNC) treatment, yet timely identification of at-risk patients remains challenging in survivorship care. Definitive assessment relies on videofluoroscopic imaging, as captured by the Dynamic Imaging Grade of Swallowing Toxicity (CTCAE-DIGEST), which, while validated, requires specialized equipment, trained personnel, and significant patient burden, limiting its routine use in surveillance. Patient-reported outcomes (PROs), by contrast, are low-cost, scalable, and easily collected at any clinical encounter, making them an attractive alternative signal for identifying patients who may warrant further evaluation. However, a clear clinical framework for translating PRO responses into actionable interventions is still evolving. In particular, uncertainty remains regarding when a patient's self-reported symptom burden should prompt escalation of care.
  This study addresses this gap by formulating a single-visit PRO-clinical prediction framework and introducing a clinically interpretable two-stage stacking model to predict swallowing impairment risk using PRO responses and structured clinical variables, without requiring videofluoroscopic imaging. The proposed framework quantifies the independent contributions of patient-reported symptoms and clinical factors within a unified and interpretable risk assessment model. Our findings demonstrate that individual MDADI responses contain predictive information beyond that captured by composite or global summary scores, while interpretability analyses reveal symptom patterns and clinical risk factors associated with swallowing impairment. Together, these results support the use of structured PRO-clinical integration as a practical, imaging-free approach for dysphagia risk stratification in HNC survivorship.

AI.tldr: A two-stage stacking model using patient-reported outcomes (MDADI responses) and clinical variables predicts swallowing impairment risk in head and neck cancer survivors without requiring videofluoroscopic imaging, offering a practical, imaging-free dysphagia risk stratification tool.
AI.motivation: Dysphagia is a debilitating late effect of HNC treatment, but routine surveillance via videofluoroscopic imaging (DIGEST) is resource-intensive and burdensome. PROs are scalable and low-cost, yet no clear clinical framework exists for translating PRO responses into actionable care escalation decisions. The study addresses the gap between easily collected PRO data and interpretable clinical risk assessment.
AI.method: A single-visit PRO-clinical prediction framework using a clinically interpretable two-stage stacking model. Stage 1 extracts predictive signals from individual MDADI item responses (beyond composite/summary scores); Stage 2 integrates these with structured clinical variables into a unified risk model. Interpretability analyses identify symptom patterns and clinical risk factors associated with swallowing impairment.
AI.result: Individual MDADI responses contain predictive information beyond what composite or global summary scores capture. The stacking model successfully quantifies independent contributions of patient-reported symptoms and clinical factors. Interpretability analyses reveal specific symptom patterns and clinical risk factors linked to swallowing impairment.
AI.conclusion: Structured PRO-clinical integration enables practical, imaging-free dysphagia risk stratification in HNC survivorship, supporting routine surveillance and timely identification of at-risk patients without requiring specialized videofluoroscopic assessment.
